Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference

Vishesh Karwa    Edoardo Airoldi

We develop a design-based minimax theory for linear causal estimands under interference. We study the minimax risks of three problems: optimizing an estimator under a fixed design, optimizing an estimator and a design from a restricted class, or optimizing both over all possible designs. In each problem, we study the minimax risk over the class of all estimators and design-unbiased estimators separately. We allow any correctly specified exposure mapping, including the identity. Our minimax theory represents causal inference under interference as a constrained sampling design on an expanded finite-population. For a given exposure mapping, the expanded finite population consists of ∑idi\sum_{i}d_{i} potential outcomes, where did_{i} is the number of exposure levels attainable by unit ii. We describe the constrained sampling design by a weighted sampling hypergraph: its vertices are ∑idi\sum_{i}d_{i} potential outcomes, and its hyperedges are the maximal sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly sampled under feasible treatment assignments. The hyperedge weights correspond to the sampling design induced by the randomization design. We show that the minimax risks of the fixed-design, restricted-design, and all-design problems depend, respectively, on the weighted hypergraph induced by the randomization design, the collection of weighted hypergraphs attainable within the restricted class of designs, and the unweighted sampling hypergraph. Our Bayes lower bounds compare potential outcome tables that differ on jointly missing sets of potential outcomes. We show that joint-missingness probabilities govern the lower bounds over all estimators, whereas the corresponding odds govern the lower bounds over unbiased estimators. We illustrate the theory across a wide range of interference structures and estimands, including average treatment effects without interference, total, direct, and contagion effects under neighborhood interference, and bipartite dose-response contrasts. The upper and lower bounds match in several settings.

1 Introduction

In finite-population design-based causal inference, we define an estimation strategy as a pair consisting of a randomized design and an estimator. This terminology follows the finite-population sampling literature (Godambe, 1955; Cassel et al., 1977; Nedyalkova and Tillé, 2008, see, e.g.,). Two estimation strategies can be compared through their design-based risks, defined as the expected mean squared error induced by a design–estimator pair. The expectation is taken over the randomization and the potential outcomes are held fixed.

Most existing works under interference evaluate a specified estimation strategy rather than determining the smallest risk attainable across strategies. For a given exposure mapping and estimand, one typically pairs a design with a Horvitz–Thompson or Hájek-type estimator, and bounds the design-based risk of the resulting estimation strategy, see for example, Hudgens and Halloran (2008); Aronow and Samii (2017); Ugander and Yin (2023). In some cases, the design is also optimally chosen from a prescribed family to improve the precision of a fixed estimator (Baird et al., 2018; Jagadeesan et al., 2020; Leung, 2022; Viviano et al., 2023; Candogan et al., 2024). Such an analysis establishes how the proposed strategy performs. It cannot determine whether the design-based risk can be reduced further by choosing a different estimator under the same design, by jointly choosing a different design–estimator pair within some constraints on the design, or by choosing a design–estimator pair without any constraints. A general minimax theory covering these three problems across interference structures, exposure mappings and estimands is lacking. In this paper, we develop a design-based minimax analysis of these three problems for finite linear causal estimands under interference for an arbitrary, but correctly specified exposure mapping, including the identity. We consider the worst-case risk over uniformly bounded potential outcome tables. In each problem, the minimax risk is defined as the smallest such worst-case design-based risk over the choices available to the statistician see Section 3 for formal definitions.

The three problems correspond to situations that arise at the design and analysis stages of an experiment. At the analysis stage, the design is given, so the risk is minimized only over the choice of estimators. This gives the fixed-design minimax problem. At the design stage, the risk can be minimized jointly over the design and estimator, but the design may be restricted to a prescribed family, for example, because of a treatment budget or because the interference graph may be unknown at the design stage. This gives the restricted-design minimax problem. When the risk is minimized jointly over all designs and estimators, we obtain the all-design minimax problem. Comparing the three problems shows whether a large risk is due to the given design, a design restriction, or a limit of the experiment.

For each problem, we study the minimax risk over two classes of estimators: the class of all estimators and the smaller class of design unbiased estimators. We define the price of unbiasedness as the ratio of the minimax risk over unbiased estimators to the minimax risk over all estimators. This ratio measures the multiplicative cost of requiring unbiasedness. The theory applies under no interference, partial interference, neighborhood interference, and bipartite interference, and permits an arbitrary, but correctly specified exposure mapping. This includes the identity exposure mapping, which retains the full treatment configuration relevant to a unit, as well as coarser mappings based on treatment counts or thresholds. The estimands are finite linear functionals of the resulting potential outcomes, including one-arm means, two-arm contrasts, and policy means and policy contrasts. Our examples include the average treatment effect without interference; the total and direct treatment effects under partial and neighborhood interference; a complex-contagion contrast under neighborhood interference; and dose-response contrasts under bipartite interference. The all-design problem was recently studied under neighborhood interference and identity exposure mapping for the all estimator class by Kandiros et al. (2026a); Section 2 gives a detailed comparison.

Overview of the results

At the center of our minimax theory is a constrained sampling design on an expanded finite population consisting of potential outcomes. This sampling design is induced by a randomization design, interference graph and an exposure mapping. In particular, the interference graph, exposure mapping, and assignment restrictions constrain which potential outcomes can be jointly observed, while the randomization design assigns probabilities to the feasible samples. We represent these constraints by a sampling hypergraph and, for a given randomization design, the sampling probabilities by weights on its hyperedges, which we call the induced sampling design. The nodes of the hypergraph correspond to potential outcomes. Each hyperedge records a maximal feasible sample, and its weight gives the probability of observing the corresponding sample under the randomization design. We describe these objects next.

Consider a finite population of nn units, indexed by i∈[n]i\in[n] with a binary treatment assignment vector z=(z1,…,zn)∈{0,1}nz=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}. The unrestricted potential outcome table has nn rows and 2n2^{n} columns corresponding to the fixed but unknown potential outcomes Yi​(z)Y_{i}(z). A correctly specified exposure mapping reduces this table to a ragged table. Row ii of this ragged table contains did_{i} cells, each corresponding to a reduced potential outcome Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e), one for each exposure level e∈𝒟ie\in\mathcal{D}_{i}, where 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} is the set of exposure levels attainable by unit ii. Let di=|𝒟i|≥2d_{i}=|\mathcal{D}_{i}|\geq 2 be the number of exposure levels attainable by unit ii. Hence, the ragged table contains |K|=∑i=1ndi|K|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i} potential outcome cells, each cell is indexed by the attainable unit–exposure pairs (i,e)(i,e). The expanded finite population is the set K={(i,e):i∈[n],e∈𝒟i}K=\{(i,e):i\in[n],\ e\in\mathcal{D}_{i}\}. Each element (i,e)∈K(i,e)\in K carries the fixed potential-outcome value Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e). A single treatment assignment selects a sample of nn potential outcomes from the expanded finite population KK and thereby produces a missingness pattern on the ragged table of potential outcomes. Within each row of the table, exactly one cell is observed and all remaining cells are missing. This is the usual within-unit counterfactual missingness, and corresponds to a sampling constraint that only one potential outcome per row can be observed. The missingness pattern also has an across-row component. In particular, the interference graph, exposure mapping, and restrictions, if any, on the set of treatment assignments together constrain which cells from different rows can be sampled together.

For each feasible assignment zz, let M⁡(z)⊆KM(z)\subseteq K denote the set of potential outcome cells of the ragged table that are jointly missing under zz, and let O⁡(z)O(z) denote its complement, the set of feasible potential outcome cells jointly observed under zz. The collection of sets O⁡(z)O(z) of potential outcomes, as zz ranges over all feasible treatment assignments, forms the hyperedge set of the sampling hypergraph. Its nodes are the elements of the expanded finite population KK, representing the unit–exposure pairs (i,e)(i,e). Each hyperedge represents one feasible sample by recording the maximal set of potential outcome cells that can be jointly observed under a feasible assignment. Note that the hypergraph includes every feasible sample, including those assigned probability zero by a particular randomization design. A randomized design assigns each hyperedge a probability of jointly observing the potential outcomes in the set O⁡(z)O(z). For a given design, we call the sampling hypergraph equipped with these design-induced probabilities a weighted sampling hypergraph, see Section 4 for formal definitions. Figure 1 illustrates the construction of a sampling hypergraph for an exposure mapping that records a unit’s treatment along with the number of treated neighbors.

The minimax risks of the three problems depend on the induced sampling design and the corresponding (weighted) sampling hypergraph as follows. In the fixed-design problem, the randomization design is given and only the estimator can be optimized. The minimax risk depends on this randomization design only through its induced sampling design, represented by the weighted sampling hypergraph. In the restricted-design problem, we optimize over randomization designs in a prescribed class of designs and over estimators. The minimax risk therefore depends on the collection of induced sampling designs attainable within that class. In the all-design problem, every randomization design on the feasible assignment set is allowed. We can then optimize over all probability distributions on feasible samples and over estimators. Hence, when the estimand and potential outcome class is fixed, the minimax risk of the all-design problem depends only on the unweighted sampling hypergraph (Proposition 4.2.1).

The general lower-bound theory is developed in Section 4. All of our lower bounds are obtained by constructing prior distributions over potential outcome tables. The key idea is a design-based indistinguishability principle: two potential-outcome tables with different estimand values cannot be distinguished using the observed data, whenever all potential outcomes on which the tables differ are missing under the randomization design. Specifically, consider two potential outcome tables that differ only on a set BB of estimand-relevant potential outcomes. For a random assignment ZZ, consider the event B⊆M⁡(Z)B\subseteq M(Z), meaning that every potential outcome in the set BB is missing under the treatment assignment ZZ; equivalently, B∩O⁡(Z)=∅B\cap O(Z)=\varnothing. On this event, the two tables produce the same observed data even though the corresponding estimand values differ. We place an equal-weight prior on these two tables. The resulting Bayes risk provides a lower bound on the worst-case design-based risk.

We extend this two-table construction to a family of tables by varying potential outcomes within disjoint sets of estimand-relevant cells. We call this collection of disjoint sets a potential outcome packing defined on the vertices of the sampling hypergraph. Formally, let B1,…,BmB_{1},\ldots,B_{m} be disjoint sets of estimand-relevant potential outcomes. Let cbc_{b} be the contribution to the estimand from a signed perturbation of the potential outcomes in BbB_{b}, and let ρP​(Bb)\rho_{P}(B_{b}) be the probability under the randomization design PP that every cell in BbB_{b} is missing. Then the fixed-design minimax risks Rall​(P)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P) and Runb​(P)R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P) over all estimators and over unbiased estimators respectively satisfy

Rall​(P)≥∑b=1mcb2​ρP​(Bb),Runb​(P)≥∑b=1mcb2​ρP​(Bb)1−ρP​(Bb).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P)\geq\sum_{b=1}^{m}c_{b}^{2}\,\rho_{P}(B_{b}),\qquad R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P)\geq\sum_{b=1}^{m}c_{b}^{2}\,\frac{\rho_{P}(B_{b})}{1-\rho_{P}(B_{b})}. (1)

(Theorem 4.1.2). For all estimators, the lower bound depends on the probability that the relevant potential outcomes are jointly missing; for unbiased estimators, the lower bound depends on the odds of the same event instead of its probability. For the restricted-design problem, we may choose a different potential outcome packing for each feasible design within the restricted class to strengthen its lower bound, then take the infimum of the resulting bounds over those designs. When all randomization designs are allowed, we obtain lower bounds for general linear estimands that depend only on the sampling hypergraph and the estimand coefficients (Theorem B.6.1). We present two simpler bounds for estimands that contrasts two exposure levels, called arms. The first uses the sampling rank of one estimand arm, defined as the largest number of its potential outcomes that a single assignment can reveal. This rank plays the role of an effective sample size within the arm. For some two-arm contrasts, the one arm rank based lower bound can be weaker. In such a case, we derive a second lower bound that accounts for which potential outcomes in the two arms can be observed together (Theorems 4.3.1 and 4.3.2).

For a fixed design problem, we show that the minimax risk depends on the entire induced sampling design and not just the first-order inclusion probabilities and sampling hypergraph (Theorem B.4.1). We give sufficient conditions under which exposure Horvitz–Thompson (H-T) is minimax rate optimal for a fixed design problem (Theorem 5.2.1). We also illustrate a randomized-saturation counterexample where the exposure H-T is not minimax rate optimal (Proposition 5.3.1). For the restricted- and all-design problems, our upper bounds pair exposure HT, conditional HT, or a biased shrinkage estimator with designs adapted to the estimand. We provide two new constructions: an ordered-proposal design, which thins focal units into an independent set, and a budget-constrained lit-ball design, which treats unions of selected neighborhoods.

We apply the general bounds to several causal estimands under four interference structures.

  1. (i)

    No interference (Section 6). For the average treatment effect, we derive all-design minimax risks of 4/n4/n over unbiased estimators and (4+o⁡(1))/n(4+o(1))/n over all estimators (Theorem 6.1.1). We also show that if at most mm units can be treated, both risks are of order 1/m1/m (Theorem 6.2.1).

  2. (ii)

    Partial interference (Section 7). We show that when the cluster memberships are known, the total and direct effects have minimax rate 1/ξ1/\xi over both estimator classes, where ξ\xi is the number of clusters. If the design must be chosen without knowing the memberships at the design stage, we show that the minimax risk of the total effect increases by a factor that can be exponential in the cluster size (Theorem 7.2.3).

  3. (iii)

    Neighborhood interference (Section 8). For the direct treatment effect, we construct core–periphery graphs on which unbiasedness multiplies the minimax risk by a factor of up to order n\sqrt{n}, because a biased strategy can omit a small, hard-to-observe part of the population (Theorem 8.1.2), thereby reducing the minimax risk. For the total treatment effect on graphs with restricted growth, we show that graph cluster randomization with the exposure Horvitz–Thompson estimator attains the minimax rate (d¯+1)/n(\bar{d}+1)/n (Theorem 8.2.1). Under a sufficiently large budget of mm treated units, the rate is (d+1)/m(d+1)/m on restricted-growth dd-regular graphs (Theorem 8.2.2).

    We also study the minimax risk of a complex-contagion contrast that compares treated units above and below a threshold number of treated neighbors, motivated by threshold models of contagion (Granovetter, 1978; Centola and Macy, 2007). We show that lower bounds based only on which pairs of potential outcomes can be observed together (for example, through a conflict graph) understate the minimax risk by a growing factor (Theorem 8.3.1 and Corollary 8.3.2).

  4. (iv)

    Bipartite interference (Section 9). We study the minimax risk of dose–response contrasts between nearby doses when each outcome unit is linked to dd treatment units drawn uniformly at random from a common pool, and the exposure of an outcome unit is its number of treated neighbors. We show that lower bounds based only on which pairs of potential outcomes can be observed together again understate the minimax risk, by a factor that grows as the dose moves away from the endpoints (Theorem 9.1 and Corollary 9.2).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses related work; Sections 3–5 develop the framework, lower bounds, and fixed-design comparison; and Sections 6–9 give the applications. Section 10 concludes, and the appendices contain proofs and additional results.

2 Related work

Design-based inference under interference was developed for partial interference by Sobel (2006) and Hudgens and Halloran (2008). Exposure mappings under general interference were formalized by Manski (2013) and Aronow and Samii (2017). Zigler and Papadogeorgou (2021) developed the framework for bipartite interference. Most literature on causal inference under interference develops designs or estimators for particular exposure mappings and estimands: two-stage designs under partial interference (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008; Basse and Feller, 2018), graph-cluster randomization for the total effect (Ugander et al., 2013; Ugander and Yin, 2023), independent-set and sequential designs for direct or peer effects (Karwa and Airoldi, 2018; Toulis and Kao, 2013), conflict-graph designs (Kandiros et al., 2026b), and estimators based on low-order outcome models (Yu et al., 2022; Cortez-Rodriguez et al., 2023). Their risk bounds are upper bounds on the corresponding minimax risks, but most of this work does not study lower bounds.

A line of work fixes the estimator and chooses a design to minimize its risk under a model for the potential outcomes. For example, under partial interference, Baird et al. (2018); Cai et al. (2022) choose treatment saturations under random-effects and linear interference models, respectively. Other designs aim to reduce bias for the direct effect (Jagadeesan et al., 2020) or compare the bias of total-effect estimators under two clusterings (Pouget-Abadie et al., 2018). Some works study the fixed-design problem in limited settings. Sussman and Airoldi (2017) derive minimum integrated-variance estimators within the class of linear unbiased estimators, Karwa and Airoldi (2023) study the admissibility of the Horvitz–Thompson estimator within the class of linear estimators, and Cortez-Rodriguez et al. (2023) bound the risk of every estimator under Bernoulli assignment and bounded-order interactions.

Closer to our restricted-design problem is work that fixes the estimator and chooses a design within a prescribed family to minimize a worst-case risk. Without interference, Kallus (2018); Kallus (2021) optimize the design for difference in means over a class of potential outcome models. Under interference, related work optimizes the clustering for difference in means (Viviano et al., 2023) or the dependence in treatment assignment for Horvitz–Thompson estimation (Candogan et al., 2024; Thiyageswaran et al., 2026). Under spatially decaying interference, Leung (2022); Leung (2026) choose the number of clusters for estimators that vary within a small family. These works target the global average treatment effect under interference. Our restricted-design problem optimizes over both the designs in a class and all estimators, for general exposure mappings and linear estimands. This formulation draws on finite-population sampling, where an estimation strategy pairs a sampling design with an estimator (Godambe, 1955; Fienberg and Tanur, 1987).

Minimax analyses that optimize jointly over all designs and estimators are recent, both with and without interference. Without interference, in a superpopulation model with covariates, Bai (2023) shows that complete randomization with the difference-in-means estimator is minimax optimal over all designs and linear estimators, when the class of outcome distributions is permutation-invariant. For the average treatment effect with bounded outcomes, Hull (2026) shows that independent assignment, rather than complete randomization, is minimax optimal over all designs and estimators, because the random number of treated units carries information when outcomes are bounded. Sudijono et al. (2026) study binary outcomes and characterize the minimax risk up to its second-order term. It is attained by Bernoulli randomization with a nonlinear shrinkage estimator, whereas complete randomization with the difference-in-means estimator is optimal only to first order. Under interference, Faridani and Niehaus (2026) derive the minimax rate for the global average treatment effect over all designs and linear estimators under spatially decaying interference. Borusyak et al. (2026) jointly choose a design and a regression estimator under a linear exposure mapping.

Comparison with Kandiros, Harshaw and Sävje

The work closest to ours is Kandiros et al. (2026a), who study the all-design minimax problem under neighborhood interference and the identity exposure mapping, without any restrictions on the set of treatment assignments. They show that the minimax rate for this setting is governed by a conflict graph that records which pairs of estimand-relevant potential outcomes cannot be observed together under any treatment assignment. Their general results cover equal-weight two-arm contrasts, with applications to the direct and total treatment effects. They consider potential outcome classes defined by moment restrictions of order q≥2q\geq 2. Our uniformly bounded class corresponds to their setting q=∞q=\infty.

The two formulations use different combinatorial objects. The conflict graph of Kandiros et al. (2026a) records pairwise conflicts: an edge in the conflict graph joins two potential outcomes that cannot be observed together. Our sampling hypergraph instead records the sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly observed, and therefore retains higher-order information. Apart from the higher order information, another distinction between the two objects is that the sampling hypergraph describes feasibility by listing maximal feasible samples, whereas the conflict graph describes infeasibility through pairs that cannot be observed together. Under neighborhood interference with the identity exposure mapping and unrestricted assignments, Kandiros et al. (2026a, Proposition 2.2) show that the labelled conflict graph determines the all-design minimax risk. In this setting, we show that the conflict graph and sampling hypergraph determine one another (Theorem B.7.1 in Appendix B.7.2). In particular, if every pair in a collection of potential outcomes can be jointly observed, possibly under different assignments, then the entire collection can be observed under one assignment. Our sampling-rank lower bound (Theorem 4.3.1) reduces to the independence-number lower bound of Kandiros et al. (2026a, Theorem 3.2) when q=∞q=\infty.

However, when the exposure mapping is coarsened, or there are constraints on the set of possible treatment assignments, the conflict graph, in general, is no longer sufficient to determine the all-design minimax risk. In such cases, the sampling hypergraph retains the joint sampling constraints needed for the characterization of the all-design minimax risk. For example, under a count or threshold mapping, a pairwise-observable collection of potential outcomes need not be jointly observable. In our complex-contagion and bipartite examples, this higher-order constraint causes a conflict-graph lower bound to understate the minimax risk by a growing factor. Even under neighborhood interference, the conflict graph can be insufficient when there are constraints on the set of feasible treatment assignments. For example, under a budget on the number of treated units, the minimax rates for the direct and total treatment effects under neighborhood interference are governed by higher-order sampling constraints that the conflict graph does not record; see Appendix F.6 and Section 8.2.1.

Beyond this overlap in the all-design minimax problem, we also consider the fixed- and restricted-design minimax problems. For these problems, neither the unweighted sampling hypergraph nor the conflict graph is sufficient. Instead, the lower bounds also depend on the probabilities assigned to jointly observable sets, not just on which sets are feasible. Our framework also covers arbitrary linear estimands, including one-arm means, weighted two-arm and multi-arm contrasts, and policy contrasts, for the three minimax problems. For each minimax problem, we also compare the minimax risks over all estimators and over unbiased estimators. Kandiros et al. (2026a) discuss a bias–variance trade-off, dropping some conflict-graph vertices to improve their upper bound, and illustrate the improvement under a second-moment restriction. Their lower bounds apply to all estimators and hence also to unbiased estimators, but need not be sufficient to determine the minimax rate over the unbiased class and do not establish a cost of unbiasedness. We derive lower bounds that exploit the unbiasedness restriction and show that this cost can be a factor of order n\sqrt{n} (Theorem 8.1.2). In turn, Kandiros et al. (2026a) cover outcome classes with finite qq and give a general spectral upper bound, neither of which we study. Remarks 8.1, 8.2, and 8.3 compare the direct- and total-effect results with theirs, and Appendix B.7.2 gives a more detailed comparison.

3 Potential outcomes, constrained sampling design, and the three minimax problems

In this section, we define the potential outcome table under interference, its missing-data representation using a constrained sampling problem induced by a given randomization design, and the three minimax problems.

3.1 Potential outcomes under interference

Let [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\} index a finite population under binary treatment. The feasible assignments form a set 𝒵0⊆{0,1}n\mathcal{Z}_{0}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}, and a randomization design is a law P∈𝒫⁡(𝒵0)P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}) generating Z∼PZ\sim P. Thus PP is a probability distribution on treatment assignments. We use the term “design” to mean randomization design unless explicitly referring to the induced sampling design. Each unit has a fixed but unknown potential outcome Yi​(z)Y_{i}(z) for every z∈{0,1}nz\in\{0,1\}^{n}; all randomness comes from the design. Without further structure the table 𝕋={Yi(z):i∈[n],z∈{0,1}n}\mathbb{T}=\{Y_{i}(z):i\in[n],z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\} has n​2nn2^{n} entries. We reduce this table using an interference graph and an exposure mapping.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an undirected graph with vertices given by the units in the finite population [n][n]. The lack of an edge {i,j}\{i,j\} in GG encodes the assumption that the potential outcome of unit ii is not affected by the treatment assigned to unit jj, and vice versa. Formally, let NiN_{i} denote the neighbors of unit ii in GG and Ni+={i}∪NiN_{i}^{+}=\{i\}\cup N_{i} denote the closed neighborhood of ii. More generally, Br​(i)={j:distG⁡(i,j)≤r}B_{r}(i)=\{j:\operatorname{dist}_{G}(i,j)\leq r\} denotes the units within distance rr of ii, so that B1​(i)=Ni+B_{1}(i)=N_{i}^{+}. We assume

zNi+=zNi+′⟹Yi​(z)=Yi​(z′)for each ​i.z_{N_{i}^{+}}=z^{\prime}_{N_{i}^{+}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_{i}(z)=Y_{i}(z^{\prime})\qquad\text{for each }i. (2)

Different assumptions on interference can be specified as restrictions on GG. For example, an empty GG encodes the no interference assumption, disjoint cliques give partial interference, and arbitrary GG gives neighborhood interference (extendable to rr-hop structure by enlarging NiN_{i} to Br​(i)B_{r}(i)). A complete GG encodes global interference.

For each unit ii, let hi​(⋅,θi):{0,1}Ni+⟶𝒟ih_{i}(\cdot;\theta_{i}):\{0,1\}^{N_{i}^{+}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{D}_{i} be a function of the treatment assignments in ii’s closed neighborhood. The corresponding effective treatment function or exposure mapping (Manski, 2013; Aronow and Samii, 2017) is defined on the full assignment vector zz by

fi:{0,1}n⟶𝒟i,fi​(z,θi)=hi​(zNi+,θi).f_{i}:\{0,1\}^{n}\longrightarrow\mathcal{D}_{i},\qquad f_{i}(z;\theta_{i})=h_{i}(z_{N_{i}^{+}};\theta_{i}).

Thus GG specifies which treatment assignments may enter the exposure, and hih_{i} specifies how they are summarized. We call e=fi​(z,θi)e=f_{i}(z;\theta_{i}) the effective treatment level or exposure level of unit ii. It is correctly specified when, for every unit ii and assignments z,z′z,z^{\prime},

fi​(z,θi)=fi​(z′,θi)⟹Yi​(z)=Yi​(z′).f_{i}(z;\theta_{i})=f_{i}(z^{\prime};\theta_{i})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_{i}(z)=Y_{i}(z^{\prime}). (3)

We suppress θi\theta_{i} when it is clear and write f={fi}f=\{f_{i}\}. The identity mapping fi​(z)=zNi+f_{i}(z)=z_{N_{i}^{+}} retains the full neighborhood assignment. Two coarser mappings used later are the anonymous count fi​(z)=(zi,∑j∈Nizj)f_{i}(z)=(z_{i},\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j}) and, for θ≥1\theta\geq 1, the threshold fi(z;θ)=(zi,𝟏{∑j∈Nizj≥θ})f_{i}(z;\theta)=(z_{i},\mathbf{1}\{\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j}\geq\theta\}). In general, we take 𝒟i=fi​({0,1}n)\mathcal{D}_{i}=f_{i}(\{0,1\}^{n}) to contain exactly the exposure levels attainable by unit ii. These levels depend on its neighborhood and exposure mapping. For example, a unit with no neighbors cannot attain an exposure level requiring at least one treated neighbor.

We assume that the exposure mapping is correctly specified. Hence, all assignments giving unit ii the same exposure ee have the same potential outcome. With a slight abuse of notation, we denote this common value by Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e), the reduced potential outcome under exposure mapping ff. We collect these values in the table of reduced potential outcomes {Yi(e):i∈[n],e∈𝒟i}\{Y_{i}(e):i\in[n],\ e\in\mathcal{D}_{i}\}. Since the attainable exposure levels can differ across units, the table of reduced potential outcomes is ragged.

Definition 3.1 (Potential outcome indices).

Let K={(i,e):i∈[n],e∈𝒟i}K=\{(i,e):i\in[n],\ e\in\mathcal{D}_{i}\} be the index set of the reduced potential outcome table. Each k=(i,e)∈Kk=(i,e)\in K is called a potential outcome index; the corresponding potential outcome is Yk=Yi​(e)Y_{k}=Y_{i}(e).

Thus (Yk)k∈K(Y_{k})_{k\in K} is a vector of length |K|=∑i|𝒟i||K|=\sum_{i}|\mathcal{D}_{i}|. We use (i,e)(i,e) when the row and exposure matter and k∈Kk\in K for the vector representation, and hereafter usually omit the word “reduced.” When referring to collections of potential outcomes, we identify each potential outcome with its unit–exposure index, Yi​(e)↔(i,e)Y_{i}(e)\leftrightarrow(i,e). We assume that the (reduced) potential outcomes are uniformly bounded, and, without loss of generality, we normalize the bound to one: for a given exposure mapping ff, the outcome class is 𝒴⁡(f)={Y=(Yk)k∈K:|Yk|≤1​ for every ​k∈K}\mathcal{Y}(f)=\{Y=(Y_{k})_{k\in K}:|Y_{k}|\leq 1\text{ for every }k\in K\}. We call a potential-outcome table YY admissible if Y∈𝒴⁡(f)Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f).

3.2 Estimands

The estimands of interest are known linear functionals of the reduced potential outcomes Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e). A generic estimand is

τa​(Y)=∑(i,e)∈Ka(i,e)​Yi​(e),\tau_{a}(Y)=\sum_{(i,e)\in K}a_{(i,e)}Y_{i}(e), (4)

with Ka={(i,e)∈K:a(i,e)≠0}K_{a}=\{(i,e)\in K:a_{(i,e)}\neq 0\} the set of estimand relevant potential outcome indices. This formulation includes finite-population means and contrasts. A finite-population mean at a fixed exposure level ee attainable by every unit, e∈⋂i𝒟ie\in\bigcap_{i}\mathcal{D}_{i}, is

μe​(Y)=1n​∑i=1nYi​(e).\mu_{e}(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_{i}(e).

Linear combinations of fixed-exposure means are obtained by choosing a(i,e)=αena_{(i,e)}=\frac{\alpha_{e}}{n} for each such level ee, which gives

τα​(Y)=∑eαe​μe​(Y)=∑eαe​{1n​∑i=1nYi​(e)}.\tau_{\alpha}(Y)=\sum_{e}\alpha_{e}\mu_{e}(Y)=\sum_{e}\alpha_{e}\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_{i}(e)\right\}. (5)

where both sums over ee range over the exposure levels attainable by every unit. An average causal effect is a contrast τα​(Y)\tau_{\alpha}(Y) with ∑eαe=0\sum_{e}\alpha_{e}=0. A policy Γ\Gamma is a specified probability distribution on treatment assignments. Policy means, with coefficients ωi,Γ(e)=PrΓ{fi(Z)=e}\omega_{i,\Gamma}(e)=\Pr_{\Gamma}\{f_{i}(Z)=e\}, follow similarly:

μΓ​(Y)=1n​∑i=1n∑e∈𝒟iωi,Γ​(e)​Yi​(e).\mu_{\Gamma}(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\omega_{i,\Gamma}(e)Y_{i}(e). (6)

A policy effect is a contrast of policy means.

3.3 The sampling design on an expanded finite population

We now formulate the patterns of missing and observed potential outcomes as a constrained sampling problem from an expanded finite population. This population consists of the potential-outcome indices K={(i,e):i∈[n],e∈𝒟i}K=\{(i,e):i\in[n],e\in\mathcal{D}_{i}\}, with fixed values (Yk)k∈K(Y_{k})_{k\in K} assigned to each element of KK. Note that the finite population changes with the exposure mapping. In general |K|=∑idi|K|=\sum_{i}d_{i}. For example, in the simplest case of no-interference, where fi​(z)=zif_{i}(z)=z_{i}, and di=2d_{i}=2, the expanded finite population consists of 2​n2n elements. A random treatment assignment Z∼PZ\sim P selects a sample of size nn from this population. For k=(i,e)∈Kk=(i,e)\in K, define the sampling or the observation indicator Ik(Z)=𝟏{fi(Z)=e}I_{k}(Z)=\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=e\}, which records whether the potential outcome Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e) is sampled (or equivalently, observed). The observed and missing index sets of potential outcomes are defined as

Of​(Z)={k∈K:Ik​(Z)=1},Mf​(Z)=K∖Of​(Z).O_{f}(Z)=\{k\in K:I_{k}(Z)=1\},\qquad M_{f}(Z)=K\setminus O_{f}(Z). (7)

Equivalently, for a fixed treatment assignment zz, Of​(z)={(i,e)∈K:fi​(z)=e}O_{f}(z)=\{(i,e)\in K:f_{i}(z)=e\}. Thus, Of​(Z)⊂KO_{f}(Z)\subset K indexes the set of potential outcomes of the ragged table that are jointly observed under a treatment assignment ZZ. The observed outcomes are YOf​(Z)={Yk:k∈Of​(Z)}Y_{O_{f}(Z)}=\{Y_{k}:k\in O_{f}(Z)\}. The observed data is defined as the vector of the treatment assignment ZZ and the observed outcomes (Z,YOf​(Z))(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}). For any feasible treatment assignment z∈𝒵0z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}, we call Of​(z)O_{f}(z) a feasible sample. The design PP induces a law on the feasible samples.

Definition 3.2 (Induced sampling design).

The randomization design PP, together with the exposure mapping ff, induces a sampling design on KK, defined as

QP,f(A)=P{Of(Z)=A}=∑z∈𝒵0:Of​(z)=AP(Z=z),A⊆K.Q_{P,f}(A)=P\{O_{f}(Z)=A\}=\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}:\,O_{f}(z)=A}P(Z=z),\qquad A\subseteq K.

The randomization design PP assigns probabilities to treatment assignments; the induced sampling design QP,fQ_{P,f} assigns probabilities to observed samples of potential-outcome indices.

For fixed PP and ff, this sampling design does not depend on the potential-outcome values. Changing the table YY changes the values observed, but leaves the probability of selecting each sample unchanged. Equivalently, QP,fQ_{P,f} is the joint distribution of the sample inclusion indicators (Ik​(Z))k∈K(I_{k}(Z))_{k\in K}. In missing-data terms, the fixed potential-outcome table is incompletely observed: Ik​(Z)=1I_{k}(Z)=1 indicates that YkY_{k} is observed, and Ik​(Z)=0I_{k}(Z)=0 indicates that it is missing. The induced sampling design QP,fQ_{P,f} therefore specifies the distribution of the missingness pattern. For fixed PP and ff, this distribution is known and is the same for every potential-outcome table. See Rubin (1978) for the missing-data formulation of causal inference and Ding and Li (2018) for a review.

Two types of sampling constraints are imposed on which sets of potential outcomes can be sampled together in Of​(Z)O_{f}(Z). The first is within-unit counterfactual missingness. Each treatment assignment selects exactly one cell from each row of the ragged table; all remaining potential outcomes are missing. Thus ∑e∈𝒟iI(i,e)​(Z)=1\sum_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}I_{(i,e)}(Z)=1 for every i∈[n]i\in[n], and the sample Of​(Z)O_{f}(Z) has size nn. The second sampling constraint is across rows: here, the interference graph, exposure mapping, and restrictions on treatment assignments additionally constrain which potential outcomes from different units can be observed together. The sampling hypergraph described in Section 4.2 records these constraints implicitly by recording all feasible samples, and the hyperedge weights give the sample probabilities QP,f​(A)Q_{P,f}(A).

The first-order inclusion probability that a relevant potential outcome is observed is

πP,k=P{k∈Of(Z)}.\pi_{P,k}=P\{k\in O_{f}(Z)\}. (8)

These are one-dimensional margins of the induced sampling design QP,fQ_{P,f}. For k=(i,e)k=(i,e), this is πP,k=P{fi(Z)=e}\pi_{P,k}=P\{f_{i}(Z)=e\}, also called the exposure probability of unit ii at exposure ee. For an exposure level ee, define the observed exposure count ne(Z)=∑i:e∈𝒟i𝟏{fi(Z)=e}n_{e}(Z)=\sum_{i:e\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=e\}. This is the number of units revealing Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e) under assignment ZZ; its expectation under randomization design PP is 𝔼Pne(Z)=∑i:e∈𝒟iπP,(i,e)\mathbb{E}_{P}n_{e}(Z)=\sum_{i:e\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\pi_{P,(i,e)}.

3.4 The three minimax problems and the estimator classes

Given PP, let TPT_{P} denote any estimator and 𝒯⁡(P,f)\mathcal{T}(P,f) be the set of all estimators measurable with respect to (Z,YOf​(Z))(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}).

Definition 3.3 (Estimation strategy).

For estimating τa\tau_{a} under exposure mapping ff, an estimation strategy is a pair (P,TP)(P,T_{P}) consisting of a randomization design P∈𝒫⁡(𝒵)P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}) and an estimator TP∈𝒯⁡(P,f)T_{P}\in\mathcal{T}(P,f).

The fixed-design minimax risk over all estimators is

Rall​(P,f,a)=infTP∈𝒯⁡(P,f)supY∈𝒴⁡(f)𝔼P​[{TP−τa​(Y)}2∣Y].R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)=\inf_{T_{P}\in\mathcal{T}(P,f)}\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\{T_{P}-\tau_{a}(Y)\}^{2}\mid Y\right]. (9)

An estimator is design-unbiased when 𝔼P​(TP∣Y)=τa​(Y)\mathbb{E}_{P}(T_{P}\mid Y)=\tau_{a}(Y) for every Y∈𝒴⁡(f)Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f). A design PP is positive for τa\tau_{a} when every relevant potential outcome can be observed with positive probability:

𝒫+​(f,a)={P∈𝒫⁡(𝒵0):πP,k>0​ for every ​k∈Ka}.\mathcal{P}_{+}(f,a)=\{P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}):\pi_{P,k}>0\text{ for every }k\in K_{a}\}. (10)

Positivity is required for unbiasedness, but not for unrestricted estimation, since a biased estimator remains well defined even when a relevant entry is always missing.

The corresponding fixed-design minimax risk is

Runb​(P,f,a)=infTP∈𝒯⁡(P,f)TP​exactly​unbiasedsupY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡(TP∣Y),R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}T_{P}\in\mathcal{T}(P,f)\\ T_{P}\ \mathrm{exactly\ unbiased}\end{subarray}}\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(T_{P}\mid Y), (11)

with value +∞+\infty when the unbiased class is empty. We always have Rall​(P,f,a)≤Runb​(P,f,a)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\leq R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a). When ff and aa are fixed, we write Rall​(P)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P) and Runb​(P)R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P). For a design class 𝒞⊆𝒫⁡(𝒵)\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}), let 𝒞+=𝒞∩𝒫+​(f,a)\mathcal{C}_{+}=\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{P}_{+}(f,a) be the class of positive designs within 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Define

Rall∗​(𝒞,f,a)=infP∈𝒞Rall​(P,f,a),Runb∗​(𝒞,f,a)=infP∈𝒞+Runb​(P,f,a).R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C};f,a)=\inf_{P\in\mathcal{C}}R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a),\qquad R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C};f,a)=\inf_{P\in\mathcal{C}_{+}}R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a). (12)

We suppress ff and aa when they are clear. This gives three minimax problems:

Problem 1:Rall​(P),Runb​(P),the design is fixed;Problem 2:Rall∗​(𝒞),Runb∗​(𝒞),the design class is restricted;Problem 3:Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵)),Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵)),all designs are allowed.\begin{array}[]{lll}\text{Problem 1:}&R_{\mathrm{all}}(P),\ R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P),&\text{the design is fixed};\\ \text{Problem 2:}&R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C}),\ R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C}),&\text{the design class is restricted};\\ \text{Problem 3:}&R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z})),\ R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z})),&\text{all designs are allowed}.\end{array}

The estimand coefficients, exposure mapping, and outcome class are fixed in all three problems; what changes is whether the design is fixed, optimized within a restricted class, or optimized over all distributions on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}. In the next section, we show that the minimax risks of these three problems are governed by three different objects: the law of Of​(Z)O_{f}(Z) under a fixed design, the set of such laws that a design class can generate, and the collection of observation patterns possible over all feasible assignments. The notation 𝒫⁡(𝒵0)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}) denotes all probability laws supported on an assignment set 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}, for example an exact-count set 𝒵m\mathcal{Z}_{m} or a budget set 𝒵≤m\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}. We reserve 𝒞\mathcal{C} for design restrictions that are not only support restrictions, such as product Bernoulli designs or the label-invariant class in Section 7.

Some upper bound constructions use auxiliary randomization UU, such as a randomly selected set of units on which treatment is randomized. An estimator that uses UU in addition to the observed data need not belong to 𝒯⁡(P,f)\mathcal{T}(P,f). The following lemma (proof in Appendix A) gives a Rao–Blackwellized estimator in 𝒯⁡(P,f)\mathcal{T}(P,f) with no greater mean squared error for every admissible table.

Lemma 3.4.1 (Rao–Blackwellized estimator).

Suppose UU takes values in a finite or countable set 𝒰\mathcal{U}, and the joint law of UU and assignment ZZ is known and does not depend on YY. Let D=(Z,YOf​(Z))D=(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}) and let T⁡(U,D)T(U,D) have finite second moment for every admissible table. Then T~​(D)=𝔼​[T​(U,D)∣D]\widetilde{T}(D)=\mathbb{E}[T(U,D)\mid D] depends only on the observed data DD and satisfies

𝔼⁡[(T~−τa​(Y))2∣Y]≤𝔼⁡[(T−τa​(Y))2∣Y]for every ​Y∈𝒴⁡(f).\mathbb{E}[(\widetilde{T}-\tau_{a}(Y))^{2}\mid Y]\leq\mathbb{E}[(T-\tau_{a}(Y))^{2}\mid Y]\qquad\text{for every }Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f). (13)

If TT is unbiased, so is T~\widetilde{T}, and its variance is no larger.

4 Minimax lower bounds from jointly missing potential outcomes

The lower bounds in this section are based on the following principle. Let τa\tau_{a} be a linear estimand, with estimand coefficient vector aa on the relevant potential outcomes. Consider two potential outcome tables Y,Y′∈𝒴⁡(f)Y,Y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}(f) that agree outside a set B⊆KaB\subseteq K_{a} and differ in the potential outcome at every index in BB. We choose the potential outcome values at BB so that τa​(Y)≠τa​(Y′)\tau_{a}(Y)\neq\tau_{a}(Y^{\prime}). When all potential outcomes in BB are missing, the two tables produce identical observed data. Hence, under this event, the design cannot distinguish the corresponding estimand values. Therefore, an adversarial perturbation on BB gives a lower bound on the design-based mean squared error determined by the difference in estimand values and the probability that the potential outcomes in BB are jointly missing. Using this principle, Section 4.1 derives lower bounds under a fixed design, for two tables that differ on a single set BB and a disjoint collection of sets. Section 4.2 shows that the fixed-design minimax risk depends on the design only through its induced sampling design, the restricted-design risks only through the set of attainable induced sampling designs, and the all-design risks only through the sampling hypergraph; the fixed-design bounds therefore extend to the other two problems. Section 4.3 gives two lower-bound constructions for the all-design problem.

4.1 Lower bounds under a fixed design

Fix an exposure mapping ff, estimand coefficients aa, and a design PP on an allowed assignment set 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}. Recall that KaK_{a} is the set of relevant potential outcomes with nonzero estimand coefficients.

Definition 4.1 (Perturbation set).

A perturbation set is a nonempty subset B⊆KaB\subseteq K_{a} of potential outcomes. Two admissible potential outcome tables Y,Y′∈𝒴⁡(f)Y,Y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}(f) are said to differ exactly on BB if {k∈K:Yk≠Yk′}=B.\{k\in K:Y_{k}\neq Y^{\prime}_{k}\}=B.

Consider two tables Y,Y′∈𝒴⁡(f)Y,Y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}(f) that differ exactly on a set BB and have different estimands τa​(Y)≠τa​(Y′)\tau_{a}(Y)\neq\tau_{a}(Y^{\prime}). The set and the tables may depend on the design PP, but are chosen before the assignment Z∼PZ\sim P is realized. Let M={Of(Z)∩B=∅}M=\{O_{f}(Z)\cap B=\varnothing\} be the event that all potential outcomes in BB are jointly missing. Under MM, the tables YY and Y′Y^{\prime} produce the same observed data (Z,YOf​(Z))(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}), so their estimands cannot be distinguished. We place an equal-weight two-point prior on the two tables, independently of ZZ. This is the two-point construction underlying Le Cam’s method (Le Cam, 1973), and its Bayes risk gives a lower bound on the worst-case design mean squared error.

Definition 4.2 (Joint missingness probability).

For a nonempty set B⊆KaB\subseteq K_{a} of potential outcomes, its joint missingness probability under design PP is ρP(B)=P{Of(Z)∩B=∅}.\rho_{P}(B)=P\{O_{f}(Z)\cap B=\varnothing\}.

The joint missingness probability can be read from the induced sampling design QP,fQ_{P,f} defined in Section 3.3 as ρP(B)=∑A:A∩B=∅QP,f(A)\rho_{P}(B)=\sum_{A:A\cap B=\varnothing}Q_{P,f}(A).

Lemma 4.1.1 (Two-table lower bound).

Let Y,Y′∈𝒴⁡(f)Y,Y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}(f) differ exactly on a nonempty set B⊆KaB\subseteq K_{a}, and let Δ=|τa​(Y)−τa​(Y′)|>0\Delta=|\tau_{a}(Y)-\tau_{a}(Y^{\prime})|>0. For every design PP,

Rall​(P,f,a)≥Δ24​ρP​(B),andRunb​(P,f,a)≥Δ24​ρP​(B)1−ρP​(B).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}\rho_{P}(B),\mathrm{and}\qquad R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\geq\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}\frac{\rho_{P}(B)}{1-\rho_{P}(B)}.

If ρP​(B)=1\rho_{P}(B)=1, no unbiased estimator exists and the second bound is +∞+\infty.

The proof is in Appendix B.2. Under the two-point prior, the posterior variance of the estimand is Δ2/4\Delta^{2}/4 on the event that all potential outcomes in BB are missing and zero otherwise, which gives the first bound. Unbiasedness gives the stronger second bound, in which the joint missingness probability ρP​(B)\rho_{P}(B) is replaced by its odds ρP​(B)/{1−ρP​(B)}\rho_{P}(B)/\{1-\rho_{P}(B)\}. The choice of BB involves a tradeoff: a larger perturbation set BB can increase the separation Δ\Delta between the estimands, but it decreases the probability ρP​(B)\rho_{P}(B) that all the potential outcomes in BB are jointly missing. For bounded outcomes, we use perturbations based on signs. Fix perturbation signs sk∈{−1,1}s_{k}\in\{-1,1\} and set Yk=skY_{k}=s_{k} and Yk′=−skY^{\prime}_{k}=-s_{k} for k∈Bk\in B, with both tables zero elsewhere. Then τa​(Y)=cB\tau_{a}(Y)=c_{B} and τa​(Y′)=−cB\tau_{a}(Y^{\prime})=-c_{B}, where cB=∑k∈Bak​skc_{B}=\sum_{k\in B}a_{k}s_{k}, so Δ=2​|cB|\Delta=2|c_{B}| and Lemma 4.1.1 gives the lower bounds cB2​ρP​(B)c_{B}^{2}\rho_{P}(B) and cB2​ρP​(B)/{1−ρP​(B)}c_{B}^{2}\rho_{P}(B)/\{1-\rho_{P}(B)\}. Choosing sks_{k} to have the sign of aka_{k} makes cB=∑k∈B|ak|c_{B}=\sum_{k\in B}|a_{k}| positive.

Several disjoint perturbation sets

We now extend the two-table construction from a single perturbation set to independent perturbations of several disjoint sets, with one independent random sign for each set.

Definition 4.3 (Perturbation packing).

A perturbation packing is a finite collection ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\} of pairwise disjoint perturbation sets. The sets need not cover all estimand-relevant potential outcomes in KaK_{a}.

Fix the perturbation signs sb,k∈{−1,1}s_{b,k}\in\{-1,1\} for k∈Bbk\in B_{b}. Consider an mm-dimensional sign vector θ=(θ1,…,θm)∈{−1,1}m\theta=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{m})\in\{-1,1\}^{m}, and for each θ\theta define a potential outcome table Yθ=(Ykθ)k∈KY^{\theta}=(Y_{k}^{\theta})_{k\in K} by

Ykθ={sb,k​θb,k∈Bb,0,k∉⋃b=1mBb.Y_{k}^{\theta}=\begin{cases}s_{b,k}\theta_{b},&k\in B_{b},\\ 0,&k\notin\bigcup_{b=1}^{m}B_{b}.\end{cases}

Each sign vector θ\theta gives one potential outcome table, so the 2m2^{m} sign vectors give 2m2^{m} distinct tables YθY^{\theta}. We place a uniform hypercube prior on these tables: the components θ1,…,θm\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{m} are independent Rademacher signs, taking the values ±1\pm 1 with probability 1/21/2 each, drawn independently of Z∼PZ\sim P. The corresponding estimand values are

τa​(Yθ)=∑b=1mcb​θb,\tau_{a}(Y^{\theta})=\sum_{b=1}^{m}c_{b}\theta_{b},

where cb=∑k∈Bbak​sb,k.c_{b}=\sum_{k\in B_{b}}a_{k}s_{b,k}. Observing any potential outcome in BbB_{b} reveals θb\theta_{b}, because the perturbation signs sb,ks_{b,k} are fixed. If every potential outcome in BbB_{b} is missing, θb\theta_{b} remains equally likely to be +1+1 or −1-1 given the observed data. The unresolved signs remain independent, so their contributions to the posterior variance add. This is the hypercube construction used in Assouad’s method (Assouad, 1983): changing one sign changes the table only on the corresponding set BbB_{b}. It gives the following lower bound.

Theorem 4.1.2 (Lower bounds from disjoint perturbations).

Fix a design PP, a perturbation packing ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\}, and signs defining cbc_{b}.

  1. (i)

    Over all estimators,

    Rall​(P,f,a)≥∑b=1mcb2​ρP​(Bb).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq\sum_{b=1}^{m}c_{b}^{2}\rho_{P}(B_{b}). (14)
  2. (ii)

    Over unbiased estimators,

    Runb(P;f,a)≥∑b:cb≠0cb2ρP​(Bb)1−ρP​(Bb).R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\geq\sum_{b:c_{b}\neq 0}c_{b}^{2}\frac{\rho_{P}(B_{b})}{1-\rho_{P}(B_{b})}. (15)

    If cb≠0c_{b}\neq 0 and ρP​(Bb)=1\rho_{P}(B_{b})=1 for some set, no unbiased estimator exists and the bound is +∞+\infty.

The proof is in Appendix B.2. The bound holds even though the observation events of different perturbation sets BbB_{b} are dependent, since they are determined by the common assignment. When m=1m=1, the theorem recovers the two-table lower bound of Lemma 4.1.1 above. Taking the singleton packing ℬ={{k}:k∈Ka}\mathcal{B}=\{\{k\}:k\in K_{a}\} gives a lower bound in terms of the inclusion probabilities πP,k=P{k∈Of(Z)}\pi_{P,k}=P\{k\in O_{f}(Z)\}.

Corollary 4.1.3 (Singleton lower bound).

For every design PP,

Rall​(P,f,a)≥∑k∈Kaak2​(1−πP,k).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq\sum_{k\in K_{a}}a_{k}^{2}(1-\pi_{P,k}). (16)

If πP,k>0\pi_{P,k}>0 for every k∈Kak\in K_{a}, then

Runb​(P,f,a)≥∑k∈Kaak2​(πP,k−1−1).R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\geq\sum_{k\in K_{a}}a_{k}^{2}\bigl(\pi_{P,k}^{-1}-1\bigr). (17)

If πP,k=0\pi_{P,k}=0 for some k∈Kak\in K_{a}, no unbiased estimator exists.

The proof is in Appendix B.2. Rarely observed potential outcomes constrain unbiased estimation: an estimator that allows bias can ignore such a potential outcome and accept the bias, whereas an unbiased estimator must compensate for its small inclusion probability. The unbiased lower bound matches the diagonal variance term of the corresponding Horvitz–Thompson estimator, which uses inverse inclusion probabilities as weights.

4.2 The sampling hypergraph and the three minimax problems

We now characterize the objects that govern the minimax risks of the three problems introduced in Section 3.4. The central objects are the sampling hypergraph and its weighted version, defined below. Recall that Of​(Z)O_{f}(Z) indexes the potential outcomes observed under assignment ZZ. The sampling hypergraph records the maximal collections of potential outcomes that can be jointly observed.

Definition 4.4 (Sampling hypergraph).

For an assignment set 𝒵0⊆𝒵\mathcal{Z}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{Z}, the sampling hypergraph is defined as ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)=(K,ℰ),\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0})=\bigl(K,\mathcal{E}\bigr), where KK is the vertex set and ℰ\mathcal{E} is the set of hyperedges. Each vertex k=(i,e)∈Kk=(i,e)\in K represents the reduced potential outcome Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e), and the hyperedge set is ℰ={Of​(z):z∈𝒵0}\mathcal{E}=\{O_{f}(z):z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}\}.

For a treatment assignment z∈𝒵0z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}, the corresponding hyperedge E=Of​(z)E=O_{f}(z) records exactly one potential outcome per unit and therefore has size nn. Thus every hyperedge is maximal. The hyperedge set includes every feasible sample, including samples assigned probability zero by a particular randomization design. When 𝒵0=𝒵\mathcal{Z}_{0}=\mathcal{Z}, we write ℋobs​(f)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f). When ff and 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} are fixed, we often abbreviate the hypergraph by ℋ\mathcal{H}.

We next define a weighted sampling hypergraph. The induced sampling design QP,fQ_{P,f}, defined in Section 3.3, supplies its hyperedge weights.

Definition 4.5 (Weighted sampling hypergraph).

For a randomization design PP on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}, the weighted sampling hypergraph is (ℋobs​(f,𝒵0),wP)(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0}),w_{P}), with weights wP​(A)=QP,f​(A)w_{P}(A)=Q_{P,f}(A) for every A∈ℰA\in\mathcal{E}.

When the design varies within a class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, its induced sampling design varies within the following set of laws, corresponding to the weighted hypergraphs attainable within the class.

Definition 4.6 (Attainable induced sampling designs).

For a design class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the set of attainable induced sampling designs is 𝒬f​(𝒞)={QP,f:P∈𝒞}\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C})=\{Q_{P,f}:P\in\mathcal{C}\}.

Finally, suppose that every design on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} is allowed. We can then optimize over all probability distributions on {Of​(z):z∈𝒵0}\{O_{f}(z):z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}\}. The minimax risk then depends only on the unweighted sampling hypergraph. The next proposition shows that these objects determine the minimax risks of the fixed design, constrained design and all designs problem.

Proposition 4.2.1 (Sampling-design reduction of the three minimax problems).

Fix ff, aa, and 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f).

  1. (i)

    For a fixed design PP, both Rall​(P)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P) and Runb​(P)R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P) depend on PP only through QP,fQ_{P,f}.

  2. (ii)

    For a restricted design class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the joint minimax risk Rall∗​(𝒞)R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C}) depends on the class only through 𝒬f​(𝒞)\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}). The corresponding risk Runb∗​(𝒞)R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C}) depends only on 𝒬f​(𝒞+)\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}_{+}), where 𝒞+=𝒞∩𝒫+​(f,a)\mathcal{C}_{+}=\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{P}_{+}(f,a).

  3. (iii)

    When all designs on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} are allowed, both Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})) and Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})) depend on the assignment and exposure model only through ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0}).

The proof is in Appendix B.3. Proposition 4.2.1 lets us work with induced sampling designs QP,fQ_{P,f} in place of assignment laws PP. To obtain a lower bound at a given induced sampling design, we compute the joint missingness probabilities of a perturbation packing and substitute them into the lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2). Taking the supremum over packings gives a lower bound for that law; taking the infimum over the laws attainable by a design class gives a lower bound for its joint minimax risk. Corollary B.5.1 in Appendix B.2 states these bounds for both estimator classes.

Remark 4.1.

The minimax risk of the fixed design problem (part (i)) depends on the full induced sampling design QP,fQ_{P,f} and cannot be reduced to just the supported hyperedges or the first-order inclusion probabilities. Theorem B.4.1 in Appendix B.4 gives two designs for the no-interference ATE with the same sampling hypergraph and the same first-order inclusion probabilities, but the unbiased fixed-design risks of these two designs are of order 1/n1/n and one, respectively.

Comparison with the conflict graph

The sampling hypergraph records which collections of potential outcomes can be observed together. To relate the sampling hypergraph to the conflict graph used by Kandiros et al. (2026a), we distinguish between observing pairs of potential outcomes and observing entire collections of potential outcomes. Formally, for an exposure mapping ff and a nonempty feasible assignment set 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}, we say two distinct potential outcomes Yk,YℓY_{k},Y_{\ell} have a pairwise conflict if Ik​(z)​Iℓ​(z)=0I_{k}(z)I_{\ell}(z)=0 for every z∈𝒵0z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}: at least one potential outcome in the pair must remain missing under every feasible assignment. For each k∈Kk\in K, define the revelation set 𝒵k={z∈𝒵0:Ik​(z)=1}\mathcal{Z}_{k}=\{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}:I_{k}(z)=1\} as the set of treatment assignments that reveal the potential outcome YkY_{k}. Thus YkY_{k} and YℓY_{\ell} have a pairwise conflict if and only if 𝒵k∩𝒵ℓ=∅\mathcal{Z}_{k}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}=\varnothing. The conflict-graph of Kandiros et al. (2026a), is defined as HconfH_{\rm conf}, with vertex set KK, with an edge joining each conflicting pair of potential outcomes.

For a collection S⊆KS\subseteq K of potential outcomes attainable under 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}, we call SS pairwise observable if, for every pair of distinct k,ℓ∈Sk,\ell\in S, there exists an assignment z∈𝒵0z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0} with Ik​(z)​Iℓ​(z)=1I_{k}(z)I_{\ell}(z)=1. The assignment may differ across pairs. Equivalently, 𝒵k∩𝒵ℓ≠∅\mathcal{Z}_{k}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\neq\varnothing for every distinct k,ℓ∈Sk,\ell\in S. Thus SS is pairwise observable if and only if it is an independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf}. On the other hand, we call the set SS jointly observable if there exists one assignment z∈𝒵0z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0} such that Ik​(z)=1I_{k}(z)=1 for every k∈Sk\in S. Equivalently, ⋂k∈S𝒵k≠∅\bigcap_{k\in S}\mathcal{Z}_{k}\neq\varnothing, or S⊆Of​(z)S\subseteq O_{f}(z) for some z∈𝒵0z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}. In the sampling hypergraph, this means that SS is contained in a hyperedge.

Every jointly observable collection of potential outcomes is pairwise observable, but the converse need not hold. Thus the conflict graph implicitly records which pairs can be observed together by recording pairwise conflicts, whereas the sampling hypergraph records which entire collections of potential outcomes can be observed together. Appendix B.7 gives a formal comparison of the conflict graph and the sampling hypergraph, establishes sufficient conditions under which pairwise observability implies joint observability, and provides examples where pairwise observability does not imply joint observability.

4.3 Lower bounds valid for every design

Proposition 4.2.1 shows that the joint minimax risks over 𝒫⁡(𝒵0)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}) depend only on the sampling hypergraph. We give two lower-bound constructions based on this hypergraph, for estimands that contrast two arms, and use them in the no-interference, neighborhood, and bipartite examples in Sections 6, 8, and 9. In some examples, perturbations within one arm give a matching lower bound; in others, we need perturbations in both arms. The one-arm result also applies to one arm of a contrast with more than two arms. Lower bounds for general linear estimands are given in the general hypergraph lower bound (Theorem B.6.1) in Appendix B.6. The next theorem uses the largest number of potential outcomes from one estimand arm that a single feasible assignment can observe. We call this number the sampling rank of that arm.

Theorem 4.3.1 (Reciprocal sampling-rank lower bound).

Let V⊆KaV\subseteq K_{a} contain NV=|V|N_{V}=|V| relevant potential outcomes from one estimand arm, each with estimand coefficient satisfying |ak|=A/NV|a_{k}|=A/N_{V}. Write ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)=(K,ℰ)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0})=(K,\mathcal{E}). The sampling rank r⁡(V)=maxE∈ℰ⁡|E∩V|r(V)=\max_{E\in\mathcal{E}}|E\cap V| is the largest number of outcomes in VV observable under a single feasible assignment. If r⁡(V)≥1r(V)\geq 1, then

Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥A2​{1r⁡(V)−1NV}.R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\geq A^{2}\left\{\frac{1}{r(V)}-\frac{1}{N_{V}}\right\}. (18)

For all estimators, if 1≤r⁡(V)≤(1−ϵ)​NV1\leq r(V)\leq(1-\epsilon)N_{V} for some 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, then

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥A2​cϵr⁡(V)R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\geq\frac{A^{2}c_{\epsilon}}{r(V)} (19)

for a constant cϵ>0c_{\epsilon}>0 depending only on ϵ\epsilon.

The rank r⁡(V)r(V) is the largest exposure count in the chosen arm over all feasible assignments. For an arm corresponding to exposure dd across all eligible units, this is r⁡(V)=maxz∈𝒵0⁡nd​(z)r(V)=\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}}n_{d}(z). The theorem is informative when the sampling rank r⁡(V)r(V) is smaller than the arm size NVN_{V}. If r⁡(V)=0r(V)=0, the entire arm is unobservable: the all-estimator risk is at least A2A^{2}, and no unbiased estimator exists. If 1≤r⁡(V)≤(1−ϵ)​NV1\leq r(V)\leq(1-\epsilon)N_{V}, both lower bounds have order A2/r⁡(V)A^{2}/r(V). At the other extreme, when r⁡(V)=NVr(V)=N_{V}, the one-arm bounds are uninformative. This can happen for each arm separately even when no assignment observes both arms in full. We therefore need a lower bound that accounts for which parts of the two arms can be observed together. Specifically, for two arm contrasts, we count pairs of perturbation sets rather than individual potential outcomes. Choose mm pairs of perturbation sets (Bb+,Bb−)(B_{b}^{+},B_{b}^{-}), where Bb+B_{b}^{+} contains potential outcomes from the first arm and Bb−B_{b}^{-} from the second, and all 2​m2m sets are nonempty and pairwise disjoint. For this choice of pairs, define

ℳ=maxE∈ℋobs⁡#⁡{b:E∩Bb+≠∅​and​E∩Bb−≠∅}.\mathcal{M}=\max_{E\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}}\#\{b:E\cap B_{b}^{+}\neq\varnothing\ \text{and}\ E\cap B_{b}^{-}\neq\varnothing\}.

Thus ℳ\mathcal{M} is the largest number of pairs of perturbation sets for which a single assignment observes at least one potential outcome on both sides. Like the sampling rank r⁡(V)r(V) in the sampling-rank lower bound (Theorem 4.3.1), it is determined by the hypergraph once the perturbation sets are chosen.

Theorem 4.3.2 (Lower bound from paired perturbation sets).

For the pairs above, suppose that each of the 2​m2m sets carries the same estimand weight,

∑k∈Bb+|ak|=∑k∈Bb−|ak|=Am,b=1,…,m.\sum_{k\in B_{b}^{+}}|a_{k}|=\sum_{k\in B_{b}^{-}}|a_{k}|=\frac{A}{m},\qquad b=1,\ldots,m.

Then

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥A2​m−ℳm2.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\geq A^{2}\frac{m-\mathcal{M}}{m^{2}}.

The same bound holds for Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr).

Both theorems use the hypercube prior of the lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2). To prove the sampling-rank lower bound (Theorem 4.3.1), we choose a perturbation packing ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\} and bound how many of its sets an allowed assignment can intersect. Observing one potential outcome in BbB_{b} reveals its shared Rademacher sign θb\theta_{b}; the other potential outcomes in BbB_{b} need not be observed. If every set has coefficient magnitude |cb|=c|c_{b}|=c and every hyperedge intersects at most r<mr<m sets, then every assignment leaves at least m−rm-r sets of potential outcomes entirely missing. These missing sets contribute at least (m−r)​c2(m-r)c^{2} to the posterior variance. Averaging over any design gives the same lower bound on the Bayes risk and hence on the joint minimax risk. For the unbiased bound in Theorem 4.3.1, the singleton packing instead uses ∑k∈VπP,k≤r⁡(V)\sum_{k\in V}\pi_{P,k}\leq r(V). The full proof is in Appendix B.6.

For Theorem 4.3.2’s proof, there is one independent Rademacher sign for each of the 2​m2m sets. A pair contributes (A/m)2(A/m)^{2} to the posterior variance unless the assignment observes a potential outcome on both sides, and at most ℳ\mathcal{M} pairs can be resolved. The bound for unbiased estimators follows because they form a smaller class. The full proof is in Appendix B.6.4. For a two-arm contrast with coefficients ±1/n\pm 1/n, the equal-weight condition in Theorem 4.3.2 requires all 2​m2m sets to have the same cardinality. Theorem B.6.4 in Appendix B.6.4 allows the weights to vary across pairs and gives the corresponding weighted lower bound.

5 Minimax estimation under a fixed design

In this section, we consider the fixed-design problem and give matching upper and lower bounds for a class of designs with bounded positive same-exposure dependence, under which the exposure Horvitz–Thompson estimator is minimax-rate optimal (Horvitz and Thompson, 1952; Aronow and Samii, 2017). We then consider designs with stronger positive dependence, where the H-T estimator remains minimax optimal but a larger joint-missingness lower bound is needed to match its variance. We conclude with an example in which the exposure HT estimator is not minimax-rate optimal.

5.1 Bounded positive dependence

Fix an exposure mapping ff, an estimand coefficient vector aa, and a design PP such that πP,k>0\pi_{P,k}>0 for every k∈Kak\in K_{a}. Write Ii,e=𝟏{fi(Z)=e}I_{i,e}=\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=e\} and πP,i(e)=P{Ii,e=1}\pi_{P,i}(e)=P\{I_{i,e}=1\}. For distinct units ii and jj, let

ϕP,i​j​(e,e)=P⁡{Ii,e=1,Ij,e=1}πP,i​(e)​πP,j​(e)−1.\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)=\frac{P\{I_{i,e}=1,I_{j,e}=1\}}{\pi_{P,i}(e)\pi_{P,j}(e)}-1.

Thus ϕP,i​j​(e,e)\phi_{P,ij}(e,e) is the normalized covariance between the indicators for observing Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e) and Yj​(e)Y_{j}(e). Define

Da​(P)\displaystyle D_{a}(P) =∑(i,e)∈Kaai,e2​{πP,i​(e)−1−1},\displaystyle=\sum_{(i,e)\in K_{a}}a_{i,e}^{2}\{\pi_{P,i}(e)^{-1}-1\}, (20)
ODa+​(P)\displaystyle\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P) =∑e∑i≠j(i,e),(j,e)∈Ka|ai,e​aj,e|​{ϕP,i​j​(e,e)}+.\displaystyle=\sum_{e}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j\\ (i,e),(j,e)\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}|a_{i,e}a_{j,e}|\{\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)\}^{+}. (21)

Da​(P)D_{a}(P) is the diagonal term in the variance of the exposure HT estimator. O​Da+​(P)OD_{a}^{+}(P) is the positive off-diagonal contribution from pairs of units at the same exposure. Let La=|{e:(i,e)∈Ka​ for some ​i}|L_{a}=|\{e:(i,e)\in K_{a}\text{ for some }i\}| be the number of exposure levels represented in the estimand.

Definition 5.1 (Bounded positive same-exposure dependence).

For an exposure mapping ff and estimand aa, a design PP has bounded positive same-exposure dependence, or bounded positive dependence for short, if ODa+​(P)≤C0​Da​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\leq C_{0}D_{a}(P) for a fixed constant C0C_{0}.

The condition restricts only positive dependence between observation indicators for the same exposure. It also holds for designs when same-exposure indicators are pairwise independent or nonpositively correlated. Positive dependence is also allowed, provided that ODa+​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P) is of the same order as Da​(P)D_{a}(P). No separate condition on negative covariance terms is needed: Lemma C.2.1 bounds their total magnitude by Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)D_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P).

Theorem 5.1.1 (Bounded positive dependence).

Suppose that PP has bounded positive same-exposure dependence with ODa+​(P)≤C0​Da​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\leq C_{0}D_{a}(P), and that La≤L0L_{a}\leq L_{0}. Then

Da​(P)≤Runb​(P,f,a)≤2​L0​(1+C0)​Da​(P).D_{a}(P)\leq R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\leq 2L_{0}(1+C_{0})D_{a}(P). (22)

If, in addition, πP,k≥c>0\pi_{P,k}\geq c>0 for every k∈Kak\in K_{a}, with cc independent of the population size, then

c​Da​(P)≤Rall​(P,f,a)≤Runb​(P,f,a)≤2​L0​(1+C0)​Da​(P).cD_{a}(P)\leq R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\leq R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\leq 2L_{0}(1+C_{0})D_{a}(P). (23)

Thus Runb​(P,f,a)≍Da​(P)R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\asymp D_{a}(P), and when the inclusion probabilities are bounded away from zero, Rall​(P,f,a)≍Runb​(P,f,a)≍Da​(P)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\asymp R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\asymp D_{a}(P), with constants depending only on C0C_{0}, L0L_{0} and cc. The upper bounds are attained by the exposure Horvitz–Thompson estimator

τ^HT,P=∑(i,e)∈Kaai,e​Ii,e​Yi​(e)πP,i​(e),\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}=\sum_{(i,e)\in K_{a}}a_{i,e}\frac{I_{i,e}Y_{i}(e)}{\pi_{P,i}(e)},

which is unbiased. Write VHT​(P)=supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡{τ^HT,P∣Y}V_{\mathrm{HT}}(P)=\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}\{\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y\} for its worst-case variance. Proposition C.2.2 gives

VHT​(P)≤2​La​{Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)}.V_{\mathrm{HT}}(P)\leq 2L_{a}\{D_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\}. (24)

The first inequality in equation (22) is the unbiased singleton lower bound of Corollary 4.1.3.

We now show that commonly used designs, estimands, and exposure mappings satisfy bounded positive dependence. For these examples, exposure HT is minimax-rate optimal over both all estimators and unbiased estimators. Detailed calculations are in Appendix C.4.

Example 1 (No-interference ATE). Consider the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) (1/n)​∑iYi​(1)−Yi​(0)(1/n)\sum_{i}Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0) with exposure mapping fi​(Z)=Zif_{i}(Z)=Z_{i}. For each e∈{0,1}e\in\{0,1\} and distinct units i≠ji\neq j, the observation indicators Ii,eI_{i,e} and Ij,eI_{j,e} are independent under Bernoulli assignment. Under complete randomization, their covariance is nonpositive. Thus ODa+​(P)=0\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)=0, and both designs have bounded positive dependence for the ATE. For Bernoulli assignment, Da​(P)=n−1​{p−1+(1−p)−1−2}D_{a}(P)=n^{-1}\{p^{-1}+(1-p)^{-1}-2\}, and the same formula holds with pp replaced by n1/nn_{1}/n under complete randomization of n1n_{1} units. If pp, or n1/nn_{1}/n, is bounded away from zero and one, Theorem  5.1.1 gives Rall​(P,f,a)≍Runb​(P,f,a)≍n−1R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\asymp R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\asymp n^{-1}.

Example 2 (Bounded-degree neighborhood interference). Consider Bernoulli assignment with treatment probability bounded away from zero and one, and let the maximum degree of the interference graph be bounded. Under the identity exposure mapping, the direct treatment effect compares (1,0Ni)(1,0_{N_{i}}) with (0,0Ni)(0,0_{N_{i}}), and the total treatment effect compares (1,1Ni)(1,1_{N_{i}}) with (0,0Ni)(0,0_{N_{i}}). Each closed neighborhood Ni+N_{i}^{+} overlaps only a bounded number of other closed neighborhoods. Consequently,

Da​(P)≍n−1,ODa+​(P)=O⁡(n−1).D_{a}(P)\asymp n^{-1},\qquad\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)=O(n^{-1}).

The relevant exposure probabilities are bounded away from zero, so Theorem  5.1.1 again gives Rall​(P,f,a)≍Runb​(P,f,a)≍n−1R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\asymp R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\asymp n^{-1}.

The next example shows that uniformly positive exposure probabilities are sufficient, but not necessary, for fixed design minimax optimality of HT.

Example 3 (A rare exposure on a regular graph). For the DTE on a dd-regular graph, let the Bernoulli treatment probability be p=1/(d+2)p=1/(d+2). Bounded degree is sufficient but not necessary for bounded positive dependence: even when dd grows, this design, exposure mapping, and estimand have bounded positive dependence because Da​(P)≍(d+1)/nD_{a}(P)\asymp(d+1)/n and ODa+​(P)=O⁡{(d+1)/n}\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)=O\{(d+1)/n\}. However, The treated-exposure probability is of order 1/(d+1)1/(d+1), and is not bounded away from zero. Direct calculation gives Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)≍(d+1)/nD_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\asymp(d+1)/n, and Proposition C.4.2 gives a matching all-estimator lower bound when n≥6​(d+2)3n\geq 6(d+2)^{3}. Hence Rall​(P,f,a)≍Runb​(P,f,a)≍(d+1)/nR_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\asymp R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\asymp(d+1)/n.

5.2 When the singleton lower bound is not enough

We now consider designs for which positive same-exposure dependence is not bounded by Da​(P)D_{a}(P). We give a sufficient condition under which exposure HT remains minimax-rate optimal. However, the singleton lower bound of the previous subsection does not match the HT upper bound for these designs, so we use a joint-missingness packing-based lower bound. For a perturbation packing ℬ\mathcal{B}, with signs chosen to agree with the signs of the estimand coefficients, write

Lℬ​(P)=∑B∈ℬ(∑k∈B|ak|)2​ρP​(B).L_{\mathcal{B}}(P)=\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\left(\sum_{k\in B}|a_{k}|\right)^{2}\rho_{P}(B).

The lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2(i)) gives Rall​(P,f,a)≥Lℬ​(P)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq L_{\mathcal{B}}(P). We say that positive dependence is packing-matched when ODa+​(P)=O⁡{Lℬ​(P)}\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)=O\{L_{\mathcal{B}}(P)\} for such a packing.

Theorem 5.2.1 (HT optimality under packing-matched dependence).

Suppose that La≤L0L_{a}\leq L_{0}, πP,k≥c\pi_{P,k}\geq c for every k∈Kak\in K_{a}, and

ODa+​(P)≤C0​Lℬ​(P),\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\leq C_{0}L_{\mathcal{B}}(P), (25)

where L0L_{0}, c>0c>0, and C0C_{0} are independent of the population size. Then

max⁡{c​Da​(P),Lℬ​(P)}\displaystyle\max\{cD_{a}(P),L_{\mathcal{B}}(P)\} ≤Rall​(P,f,a)≤Runb​(P,f,a)\displaystyle\leq R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\leq R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a) (26)
≤VHT​(P)≤2​L0​{c−1+C0}​Rall​(P,f,a).\displaystyle\leq V_{\mathrm{HT}}(P)\leq 2L_{0}\{c^{-1}+C_{0}\}R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a).

Thus exposure HT remains rate optimal when joint missingness matches positive dependence.

The theorem replaces the diagonal lower bound by Lℬ​(P)L_{\mathcal{B}}(P). Therefore, even when ODa+​(P)/Da​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)/D_{a}(P) grows, HT remains rate optimal if a packing of jointly missing potential outcomes has the same order as ODa+​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P). The next two examples have this property and do not satisfy bounded positive dependence when the cluster size grows.

Example 4 (Cluster randomization). Partition the population into ξ\xi administrative clusters of size mm, and assign each cluster entirely to treatment with probability pp, independently across clusters. Assume that pp is bounded away from zero and one. The interference graph is empty and the exposure is fi​(Z)=Zif_{i}(Z)=Z_{i}; the clusters only determine which units are assigned together. For the ATE, outcomes in the same cluster and treatment arm are observed together. Hence ODa+​(P)/Da​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)/D_{a}(P) grows with mm. A packing with one set for each cluster and arm satisfies Lℬ​(P)≍ODa+​(P)L_{\mathcal{B}}(P)\asymp\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P), which gives Rall​(P,f,a)≍Runb​(P,f,a)≍1/ξR_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\asymp R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\asymp 1/\xi.

Example 5 (Randomized saturation). For the policy effect μΓq​(Y)−μΓq′​(Y)\mu_{\Gamma_{q}}(Y)-\mu_{\Gamma_{q^{\prime}}}(Y), clusters independently draw a saturation Qg∈{q,q′}Q_{g}\in\{q,q^{\prime}\} and treat m​QgmQ_{g} units uniformly. The exposure fi​(Z)=(Zi,Qg⁡(i))f_{i}(Z)=(Z_{i},Q_{g(i)}) records a unit’s treatment and saturation. A cluster at saturation q′q^{\prime} reveals no outcomes at qq. A packing by cluster and saturation therefore matches the positive-dependence term and gives both risks of order 1/ξ1/\xi under the conditions in Appendix C.

5.3 When exposure Horvitz–Thompson is not rate optimal

The preceding results match the HT variance either with the singleton lower bound or with a lower bound from jointly missing blocks. In this subsection, we give a two-stage design for which exposure HT is suboptimal but a conditional HT estimator is minimax-rate optimal. Consider a finite population of n=ξ​mn=\xi m units partitioned into ξ\xi administrative clusters of common even size mm. Each administrative cluster contains m/2m/2 two-person households. Interference is confined to households, so the interference graph GG is the matching formed by the household pairs. Let h⁡(i)h(i) denote the other member of unit ii’s household. We use the identity exposure mapping on this two-person neighborhood, fi​(Z)=(Zi,Zh⁡(i))∈{0,1}2f_{i}(Z)=(Z_{i},Z_{h(i)})\in\{0,1\}^{2}. The estimand compares the two target exposures (1,1)(1,1), in which both household members are treated, and (0,0)(0,0), in which both are untreated:

τ⁡(Y)=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(1,1)−Yi​(0,0)}.\tau(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(1,1)-Y_{i}(0,0)\}.

The treatment is assigned in two stages. First, each administrative cluster independently draws a saturation Qg∈{qL,qH}Q_{g}\in\{q_{L},q_{H}\}, where P⁡(Qg=qH)=rP(Q_{g}=q_{H})=r and P⁡(Qg=qL)=1−rP(Q_{g}=q_{L})=1-r. Second, exactly m​QgmQ_{g} units are treated uniformly within the cluster. Write πi​(e∣q)=P⁡{fi​(Z)=e∣Qg⁡(i)=q}\pi_{i}(e\mid q)=P\{f_{i}(Z)=e\mid Q_{g(i)}=q\} for the conditional exposure probability and πi(e)=P{fi(Z)=e}\pi_{i}(e)=P\{f_{i}(Z)=e\} for its marginal counterpart. The cluster’s realized saturation is observed from ZZ. The conditional HT estimator τ^cond\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cond}} uses πi​(e∣Qg⁡(i))\pi_{i}(e\mid Q_{g(i)}) in place of the marginal probabilities in the HT denominators. Appendix C.5 gives the estimator and the two sets of probabilities.

Proposition 5.3.1 (Conditioning on randomized saturation).

Under the design above, assume that r,qL,qHr,q_{L},q_{H} are bounded away from zero and one, that qL<qHq_{L}<q_{H} with qH−qLq_{H}-q_{L} bounded away from zero, and that m​qmq is an integer satisfying 2≤m​q≤m−22\leq mq\leq m-2 for each q∈{qL,qH}q\in\{q_{L},q_{H}\}, with all bounds uniform in the population size. Then

Rall​(P,f,a)≍Runb​(P,f,a)≍1n,VHT​(P)≍1ξ.R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\asymp R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\asymp\frac{1}{n},\qquad V_{\mathrm{HT}}(P)\asymp\frac{1}{\xi}.

The estimator τ^cond\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cond}} is unbiased and has worst-case variance of order 1/n1/n, so it attains the rates in Proposition 5.3.1. By contrast, exposure HT uses the marginal exposure probabilities and retains the cluster-level variation induced by the shared QgQ_{g}. Consequently, when the cluster size m=n/ξm=n/\xi grows, exposure HT is not minimax-rate optimal. The proof is in Appendix C.5, and Appendix C.5.1 gives the same separation under no interference. τ^cond\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cond}} uses observed design information in the sense of Pashley et al. (2021)

6 Experiments without interference

In this section, we illustrate the lower and upper bounds for the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) under no interference. We consider two problems: the unrestricted problem, where all designs on {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} are allowed, and a constrained problem, where the number of treated units is fixed or bounded above by mm.
