The unrestricted minimax rate is 1/n1/n and with exactly mm treated units, the rate is 1/m+1/(n−m)1/m+1/(n-m).

6.1 No-interference ATE benchmark

Let 𝒵={0,1}n\mathcal{Z}=\{0,1\}^{n}, fi​(z)=zif_{i}(z)=z_{i}, and

τATE​(Y)=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)}.\tau_{\rm ATE}(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\}. (27)
Theorem 6.1.1 (Joint minimax risk of ATE without interference).

Let 𝒵={0,1}n\mathcal{Z}=\{0,1\}^{n}. For τATE\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}, over all designs, Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵))=(4+o⁡(1))/nR^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}))=(4+o(1))/n over all estimators and Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵))=4/nR^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}))=4/n over unbiased estimators.

Thus Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵))/Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵))=1+o⁡(1)R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}))/R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}))=1+o(1): unbiasedness does not change the minimax rate, or even the first-order constant, for the no-interference ATE. The unbiased minimax risk in Theorem 6.1.1 is attained by the estimation strategy (P1/2,τ^HT)(P_{1/2},\widehat{\tau}_{\rm HT}) where P1/2P_{1/2} is the independent Bernoulli assignment with probability 1/21/2 and τ^HT=2​n−1​∑i{Zi​Yiobs−(1−Zi)​Yiobs}\widehat{\tau}_{\rm HT}=2n^{-1}\sum_{i}\{Z_{i}Y_{i}^{\rm obs}-(1-Z_{i})Y_{i}^{\rm obs}\} is the usual HT estimator. The all-estimator upper bound in Theorem 6.1.1 comes from the strategy (P1/2,τ^αn)(P_{1/2},\widehat{\tau}_{\alpha_{n}}) with the shrunken estimator

τ^αn=αnn​∑i=1n{Zi​Yi​(1)−(1−Zi)​Yi​(0)},αn=2​nn+1.\widehat{\tau}_{\alpha_{n}}=\frac{\alpha_{n}}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Z_{i}Y_{i}(1)-(1-Z_{i})Y_{i}(0)\},\qquad\alpha_{n}=\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{n}+1}.

Its worst-case risk is at most 4/(n+1)24/(\sqrt{n}+1)^{2}, a finite-sample improvement over HT with the same first-order constant 44.

For the all-design minimax risk over all estimators, Sudijono et al. (2026) give an exact characterization of the joint minimax risk and identify its second-order term. On our bounded potential outcome class with scale [−1,1][-1,1], their expansion is 4/n−4CAn−4/3+o(n−4/3)4/n-4C_{A}n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}), where CA>0C_{A}>0 is their Airy-function constant. They show that independent Bernoulli assignment with treatment probability 1/21/2, paired with an optimal estimator, attains the joint minimax risk at each finite nn. Our proof in Appendix D uses the weighted sampling hypergraph to obtain the sharp first-order lower bound and treats the exact unbiased estimator class separately.

6.2 No-interference ATE under a constraint on the number of treated units

We restrict the number of treated units, either exactly or through a budget. For m∈{1,…,n−1}m\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}, let

𝒵m={z∈{0,1}n:∑izi=m},𝒵≤m={z∈{0,1}n:∑izi≤m}\mathcal{Z}_{m}=\left\{z\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\sum_{i}z_{i}=m\right\},\qquad\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}=\left\{z\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\sum_{i}z_{i}\leq m\right\}

be the exact-count and budget assignment spaces.

Theorem 6.2.1 (Minimax risk of ATE under constraints on the number of treated units).

For the ATE in equation (27) and every m∈{1,…,n−1}m\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}, the following statements hold.

  1. (i)

    The joint minimax risk over all designs with exactly mm treated units is

    Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵m))≍Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵m))≍1m+1n−m.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{m}))\asymp R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{m}))\asymp\frac{1}{m}+\frac{1}{n-m}. (28)
  2. (ii)

    Let km=min⁡{m,⌊n/2⌋}k_{m}=\min\{m,\lfloor n/2\rfloor\}. The joint minimax risk over all designs with at most mm treated units is

    Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m))≍Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m))≍1km+1n−km≍1m.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}))\asymp R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}))\asymp\frac{1}{k_{m}}+\frac{1}{n-k_{m}}\asymp\frac{1}{m}. (29)

The implied constants are universal and do not depend on mm or nn.

Thus, uniformly over mm, unbiasedness does not change the minimax rate under either constraint on the number of treated units.

The proof is in Appendix D.3. Let PkP_{k} be uniform on 𝒵k\mathcal{Z}_{k} and SS the treated set. Write τ^DIM(k)=Y¯S​(1)−Y¯Sc​(0)\widehat{\tau}^{(k)}_{\rm DIM}=\bar{Y}_{S}(1)-\bar{Y}_{S^{c}}(0) for the difference between the treated and control sample means. The unbiased strategies (Pm,τ^DIM(m))(P_{m},\widehat{\tau}^{(m)}_{\rm DIM}) and (Pkm,τ^DIM(km))(P_{k_{m}},\widehat{\tau}^{(k_{m})}_{\rm DIM}) attain the exact-count and budget rates, respectively, and are also rate optimal over all estimators. Both rates have the form 1/k+1/(n−k)1/k+1/(n-k): the exact constraint fixes k=mk=m, whereas the budget permits the balanced choice km=min⁡{m,⌊n/2⌋}k_{m}=\min\{m,\lfloor n/2\rfloor\}.

For the lower bound, an exact-count assignment reveals mm treated and n−mn-m control potential outcomes, so the sampling ranks of the two arms (Theorem 4.3.1) give the scale 1/min⁡{m,n−m}1/\min\{m,n-m\}. Pairing the two potential outcomes of each unit, which are never observed together (Proposition B.2.3), sharpens this to 1/m+1/(n−m)1/m+1/(n-m) (Remark D.1). Under the unrestricted assignment space each arm has sampling rank nn, but no assignment observes both potential outcomes of a unit; the same pairing then gives the 1/n1/n scale.

Remark 6.1 (The conflict graph under a constraint on the number of treated units).

For 2≤m≤n−22\leq m\leq n-2, the pairwise conflict graph of both 𝒵m\mathcal{Z}_{m} and 𝒵≤m\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m} is the same as for the unrestricted ATE: the only pairwise conflicts are between Yi​(1)Y_{i}(1) and Yi​(0)Y_{i}(0) of the same unit. A lower bound that uses only this graph therefore gives only the no-interference scale 1/n1/n. The sampling hypergraph also records the condition that every assignment in 𝒵m\mathcal{Z}_{m} must reveal exactly mm treated and n−mn-m control potential outcomes, and this restriction on hyperedge composition produces the rate 1/m+1/(n−m)1/m+1/(n-m). The rate differs from 1/n1/n when m=o⁡(n)m=o(n) (Appendix D.3).

7 Graph-aware and graph-unaware designs under partial interference

In this section, we consider partial interference, where the population is partitioned into disjoint clusters. We compare the minimax risk over two design classes. In the graph-aware class, every design is allowed, including designs that use the cluster memberships to assign treatments. In the graph-unaware class, the design cannot use the memberships. We show that it suffices to consider permutation-invariant designs for the graph-unware risk. The graph-unaware problem arises when the interference structure is unavailable at the design stage but is collected for the analysis, as can happen when social contacts are measured during follow-up (Alexandria et al., 2023). It can also represent an situation where individual-level randomization may be more practical even when the memberships are known. In both cases, we assume that the memberships are available to the estimator. Comparing the two minimax risks quantifies the price of not using the cluster memberships at the design stage.

7.1 Partial interference, exposure mapping and estimands

The population is partitioned into ξ\xi clusters of common size mm, so that n=ξ​mn=\xi m. For a unit ii, let g⁡(i)g(i) denote its cluster and let Ni={j:g(j)=g(i),j≠i}N_{i}=\{j:g(j)=g(i),\ j\neq i\} be its m−1m-1 cluster peers. Thus the interference graph GG is a disjoint union of cliques of size mm. We assume anonymous within-cluster interference: Yi​(z)Y_{i}(z) depends on zNiz_{N_{i}} only through the number of treated peers Ci​(z)=∑j∈NizjC_{i}(z)=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j}. The exposure mapping is therefore

fi​(z)=(zi,Ci​(z))∈𝒟={0,1}×{0,…,m−1}.f_{i}(z)=\bigl(z_{i},C_{i}(z)\bigr)\in\mathcal{D}=\{0,1\}\times\{0,\ldots,m-1\}. (30)

Write an exposure level as e=(t,a)e=(t,a), where tt is own treatment and aa is the number of treated peers. Define the exposure mean as μt,a=n−1​∑i=1nYi​(t,a)\mu_{t,a}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_{i}(t,a). The two estimands studied in this section are

τTTE=μ1,m−1−μ0,0,τDTE​(c)=μ1,c−μ0,c,0≤c≤m−1.\tau_{\mathrm{TTE}}=\mu_{1,m-1}-\mu_{0,0},\qquad\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}(c)=\mu_{1,c}-\mu_{0,c},\qquad 0\leq c\leq m-1. (31)

The total treatment effect compares a treated unit whose m−1m-1 peers are all treated with an untreated unit whose peers are all untreated. The direct treatment effect with cc treated peers holds the number of treated peers fixed at cc and changes only the unit’s own treatment. In particular, τDTE​(0)\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}(0) is the usual direct treatment effect with no treated peers. For an assignment zz, let kg​(z)k_{g}(z) be the number of treated units in cluster gg, and let Kg=kg​(Z)K_{g}=k_{g}(Z) be the random number of treated units in cluster gg. We index exposures by the number of treated peers rather than by the number of treated units in the cluster, kg⁡(i)​(z)=Ci​(z)+zik_{g(i)}(z)=C_{i}(z)+z_{i}: a contrast at a fixed number of treated units in the cluster changes both the unit’s own treatment and its number of treated peers, so it is not a direct effect (Remark E.1 in Appendix E).

7.2 Graph-unaware and permutation-invariant designs

We now introduce the graph-unaware design class. A graph-unaware design is a law on {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} that does not use the interference graph. Such a law need not be permutation invariant: for example, it could use unit labels or baseline covariates. We study the narrower permutation-invariant class because Proposition 7.2.1 below shows that it suffices to consider this class when the design must be chosen without the cluster memberships.

Definition 7.1 (Permutation-invariant design).

A design PP is permutation invariant, or equivalently exchangeable, if P⁡(σ​z)=P⁡(z)P(\sigma z)=P(z) for every permutation σ\sigma of [n][n] and every z∈{0,1}nz\in\{0,1\}^{n}. We write 𝒞inv\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}} for the class of permutation-invariant designs.

Let Π\Pi be the set of all partitions of [n][n] into ξ\xi clusters of size mm. The true partition π∈Π\pi\in\Pi determines the exposure mapping fπf^{\pi}, the outcome class 𝒴⁡(fπ)\mathcal{Y}(f^{\pi}) and the estimand coefficients aπa^{\pi}. In the graph-unaware problem, the experimenter first chooses a single assignment law PP without knowing π\pi. The same law must be used for every π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, although the estimator may use the partition after it is revealed at the analysis stage.

Proposition 7.2.1 (Permutation invariance is sufficient when memberships are unknown).

For every fixed reference partition π0∈Π\pi_{0}\in\Pi,

infP∈𝒫⁡(𝒵)supπ∈ΠRall​(P,fπ,aπ)=infP∈𝒞invRall​(P,fπ0,aπ0),\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z})}\ \sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\ R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f^{\pi},a^{\pi})\;=\;\inf_{P\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}}}R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f^{\pi_{0}},a^{\pi_{0}}), (32)

and the same identity holds with RunbR_{\mathrm{unb}} in place of RallR_{\mathrm{all}}.

Proposition 7.2.1 says that permutation-invariant designs are sufficient for the graph-unaware problem. The left side of equation (32) also includes graph-unaware laws that are not permutation invariant, such as heterogeneous Bernoulli assignment, but these cannot improve the worst-partition minimax risk.

The problem is symmetric in the unit labels: renaming the units and their cluster memberships together changes neither the outcome class nor the estimand. The proof therefore symmetrizes any fixed design by averaging it over unit relabellings. Because the true partition may be any element of Π\Pi, the worst-partition risk dominates the average over relabelled partitions. The random relabelling is auxiliary randomization, so Lemma 3.4.1 shows that the symmetrized design has no larger risk. The partition is unknown only when the design is chosen and remains available to the estimator, while the cluster size mm may be used at both stages. Appendix E.1 gives the proof. We next characterize permutation-invariant designs.

Lemma 7.2.2 (Permutation-invariant designs randomize only the number of treated units).

A design is permutation invariant if and only if it draws the number MM of treated units from a law on {0,1,…,n}\{0,1,\ldots,n\} and then treats a uniformly chosen set of MM units.

Bernoulli assignment at a common rate and complete randomization of the population are permutation invariant, as is any mixture of them. Conditional on MM, the number KgK_{g} of treated units in each cluster is hypergeometric.

Theorem 7.2.3 (The price of graph-unaware assignment under partial interference).

Let ξ≥2\xi\geq 2.

  1. (i)

    Graph-aware designs. The total treatment effect and every direct treatment effect τDTE​(c)\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}(c), 0≤c≤m−10\leq c\leq m-1, satisfy

    1ξ≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵))≤4ξ,2ξ≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵))≤4ξ.\frac{1}{\xi}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}))\leq\frac{4}{\xi},\qquad\frac{2}{\xi}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}))\leq\frac{4}{\xi}. (33)
  2. (ii)

    Graph-unaware designs: total treatment effect. Over permutation-invariant designs, the minimax risks satisfy

    18​min⁡{1,2mξ}≤Rall∗​(𝒞inv)≤Runb∗​(𝒞inv)≤min⁡{4,2m+1ξ}.\frac{1}{8}\min\Bigl\{1,\frac{2^{m}}{\xi}\Bigr\}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}})\leq\min\Bigl\{4,\frac{2^{m+1}}{\xi}\Bigr\}. (34)
  3. (iii)

    Graph-unaware designs: direct treatment effect away from the extremes. Fix δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2). If δ​m≤c≤(1−δ)​m−1\delta m\leq c\leq(1-\delta)m-1 and m≥m0​(δ)m\geq m_{0}(\delta), then the minimax risks satisfy

    Runb∗(𝒞inv)≍δmξ,Rall∗(𝒞inv)≍δmin{1,mξ}.R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}})\asymp_{\delta}\frac{\sqrt{m}}{\xi},\qquad R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}})\asymp_{\delta}\min\Bigl\{1,\frac{\sqrt{m}}{\xi}\Bigr\}. (35)
  4. (iv)

    Graph-unaware designs: direct treatment effect at the two extremes. For c=0c=0 and c=m−1c=m-1, the minimax risks satisfy

    Rall∗​(𝒞inv)≍Runb∗​(𝒞inv)≍1ξ,c∈{0,m−1}.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}})\asymp R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}})\asymp\frac{1}{\xi},\qquad c\in\{0,m-1\}. (36)

The theorem is driven by two properties of the hypergeometric distribution; see Lemma E.2.1. For any fixed δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and δ​m≤ℓ≤(1−δ)​m\delta m\leq\ell\leq(1-\delta)m, every permutation-invariant design satisfies P(Kg=ℓ)≤Cδm−1/2P(K_{g}=\ell)\leq C_{\delta}m^{-1/2}. Also, conditional on MM, at least one of Kg=0K_{g}=0 and Kg=mK_{g}=m has probability at most 2−m2^{-m}. The first fact gives the m\sqrt{m} cost in part (iii), and the second gives the 2m2^{m} cost in part (ii). The cluster counts required by the estimands explain these two costs. The total effect needs clusters with Kg=0K_{g}=0 and Kg=mK_{g}=m. The direct effect with cc treated peers needs Kg=cK_{g}=c for its untreated units and Kg=c+1K_{g}=c+1 for its treated units. At c=0c=0 or c=m−1c=m-1, a sparse or dense Bernoulli design makes both required counts common, so there is no rate cost. Consequently, for the total effect no permutation-invariant design is consistent once mm is larger than a constant multiple of log⁡ξ\log\xi, whereas a membership-aware design retains rate 1/ξ1/\xi. For a direct effect satisfying δ​m≤c≤(1−δ)​m−1\delta m\leq c\leq(1-\delta)m-1, the cost is m\sqrt{m} for unbiased estimators and min⁡{ξ,m}\min\{\xi,\sqrt{m}\} for all estimators.

The upper bounds use the exposure HT estimator from Section 5. When memberships are available, independently give each cluster one of the two required treated counts with probability one half and then sample uniformly within the cluster; this attains 1/ξ1/\xi. Without memberships, Bernoulli rates 1/21/2, (c+1/2)/m(c+1/2)/m, and 1/(m+1)1/(m+1) attain the displayed total-effect bound, the direct-effect bound for δ​m≤c≤(1−δ)​m−1\delta m\leq c\leq(1-\delta)m-1, and the bound for c=0c=0, respectively. A fair coin that treats the whole population or none of it gives the constant upper bound for the total effect. Appendix E.1 gives the proof, including lower bounds that apply uniformly to every permutation-invariant design.

Remark 7.1 (The price of unbiasedness in the graph-unaware class).

Unbiasedness has no rate cost for the total effect or for the direct effects at the two extremes c=0c=0 and c=m−1c=m-1, with or without the memberships. For δ​m≤c≤(1−δ)​m−1\delta m\leq c\leq(1-\delta)m-1, it has a cost under permutation-invariant designs only when ξ≲m\xi\lesssim\sqrt{m}: the minimax risk is then of constant order over all estimators but of order m/ξ\sqrt{m}/\xi over unbiased estimators. When ξ≳m\xi\gtrsim\sqrt{m}, both are of order m/ξ\sqrt{m}/\xi.

8 Neighborhood interference

In this section, we study minimax risks under neighborhood interference for three different estimands. We consider the direct and total treatment effects with the identity exposure mapping fi​(z)=(zi,zNi)f_{i}(z)=(z_{i},z_{N_{i}}) and a spillover effect under the threshold exposure mapping fi(z)=(zi,𝟏{∑j∈Nizj≥θ}),f_{i}(z)=\bigl(z_{i},\mathbf{1}\{\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j}\geq\theta\}\bigr), for an integer θ≥1\theta\geq 1. The lower bounds for these three estimands come from different constraints on which sets of potential outcomes can be jointly observed, and the third estimand illustrates that pairwise observability alone can miss such a constraint.

8.1 The direct treatment effect

The direct treatment effect is the effect of treating a unit vs not, when all its neighbors are untreated:

τDTE​(Y)=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(1,0Ni)−Yi​(0,0Ni)}.\tau_{\rm DTE}(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}})-Y_{i}(0,0_{N_{i}})\}. (37)

The treatment-arm potential outcome Yi​(1,0Ni)Y_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}}) is observed only when unit ii is treated and all its neighbors are untreated. Hence, units whose treatment-arm potential outcomes are jointly observed form an independent set of GG. Conversely, treating an independent set while leaving all other units untreated reveals the treatment-arm potential outcome of every unit in the independent set. Therefore, the treatment arm’s sampling rank is α⁡(G)\alpha(G), the independence number of GG. The control arm potential outcome Yi​(0,0Ni)Y_{i}(0,0_{N_{i}}) has sampling rank nn, since the z=0z=0 reveals all nn control arm potential outcomes. We have the following result:

Theorem 8.1.1 (Minimax rates for the neighborhood DTE).

There are universal constants c,C>0c,C>0 such that the following hold.

  1. (i)

    For every graph GG,

    cα⁡(G)≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE).\frac{c}{\alpha(G)}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE}).
  2. (ii)

    If GG is dd-regular, then

    cα⁡(G)≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤C​d+1n.\frac{c}{\alpha(G)}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq C\,\frac{d+1}{n}. (38)
  3. (iii)

    If GG is a uniformly random simple dd-regular graph, there are universal constants d0,c0>0d_{0},c_{0}>0 such that, whenever d0≤d<n−c0​n/log⁡nd_{0}\leq d<n-c_{0}n/\log n and n​dnd is even, with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1) as n→∞n\to\infty,

    dn​log⁡d≲Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≲dn.\frac{d}{n\log d}\lesssim R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\lesssim\frac{d}{n}. (39)

The following argument establishes the lower bound c/α⁡(G)c/\alpha(G). If α⁡(G)≤n/2\alpha(G)\leq n/2, applying the sampling-rank lower bound (Theorem 4.3.1) to the treatment arm gives the stated lower bound. If α⁡(G)>n/2\alpha(G)>n/2, it is enough to obtain a lower bound of order 1/n1/n. The two target potential outcomes of each unit cannot be observed together, so their inclusion probabilities sum to at most one. Hence, summing the singleton lower bound (Corollary 4.1.3) over units gives the required 1/n1/n bound. Part (iii) combines the upper bound in part (ii) with the estimate α⁡(G)≲n​log⁡d/d\alpha(G)\lesssim n\log d/d for a uniformly random regular graph (Frieze and Łuczak, 1992; Cooper et al., 2002; Krivelevich et al., 2001). The complete proof is given in Appendix F.2.

The upper bounds in parts (ii) and (iii) are attained by a design that selects a random independent set ℐ\mathcal{I}, assigns its units to treatment or control by fair coins, and assigns all other units to control. Since every neighbor of a unit in ℐ\mathcal{I} is untreated, a unit in ℐ\mathcal{I} reveals the target potential outcomes Yi​(1,0Ni)Y_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}}) or Yi​(0,0Ni)Y_{i}(0,0_{N_{i}}). The design is a variant of the independent-set design of Karwa and Airoldi (2018). Their design builds a maximal independent set by repeatedly selecting a random remaining unit and removing its neighbors, and its inclusion probabilities generally have to be approximated by Monte Carlo. We instead use the following construction, whose inclusion probabilities have a closed form.

Definition 8.1 (Ordered proposal design).

Fix an order ≺\prec on [n][n] and proposal probabilities pi∈(0,1]p_{i}\in(0,1], i∈[n]i\in[n]. Each unit proposes independently with probability pip_{i}. A proposing unit ii is included in ℐ\mathcal{I} when no neighbor j≺ij\prec i proposes. Units in ℐ\mathcal{I} are independently assigned to treatment or control with equal probability, and every other unit is left untreated. We write P≺,pP_{\prec,p} for the resulting assignment law, where p={pi}p=\{p_{i}\} is the collection of proposal probabilities.

The set ℐ\mathcal{I} is an independent set because, whenever two neighboring units propose, only the earlier one can be included. Inclusion depends on earlier proposals rather than earlier inclusions, so, unlike the greedy construction, ℐ\mathcal{I} need not be maximal. For a fixed order ≺\prec, unit ii is included in ℐ\mathcal{I} with probability

qi=pi∏j∈Ni:j≺i(1−pj),q_{i}=p_{i}\prod_{j\in N_{i}:j\prec i}(1-p_{j}),

and then reveals each of its two target potential outcomes with probability qi/2q_{i}/2. If the order ≺\prec is uniformly random and every unit proposes, then qi=1/(di+1)q_{i}=1/(d_{i}+1), and unit ii is included in ℐ\mathcal{I} exactly when it precedes all of its neighbors in the ordering ≺\prec. The inverse-probability estimator of τDTE\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}} based on ℐ\mathcal{I} is

τ^ℐ=2n​∑i=1nYiobsqi​[𝟏​{i∈ℐ,fi​(Z)=(1,0Ni)}−𝟏​{i∈ℐ,fi​(Z)=(0,0Ni)}].\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Y_{i}^{\rm obs}}{q_{i}}\left[\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I},\ f_{i}(Z)=(1,0_{N_{i}})\}-\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I},\ f_{i}(Z)=(0,0_{N_{i}})\}\right].

For either target exposure b∈{(1,0Ni),(0,0Ni)}b\in\{(1,0_{N_{i}}),(0,0_{N_{i}})\}, consistency gives

𝟏​{i∈ℐ,fi​(Z)=b}​Yiobs=𝟏​{i∈ℐ,fi​(Z)=b}​Yi​(b).\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I},\ f_{i}(Z)=b\}Y_{i}^{\rm obs}=\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I},\ f_{i}(Z)=b\}Y_{i}(b).

Because 𝔼⁡[𝟏​{i∈ℐ,fi​(Z)=b}​Yiobs]=qi2​Yi​(b),\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I},\ f_{i}(Z)=b\}Y_{i}^{\rm obs}\bigr]=\frac{q_{i}}{2}Y_{i}(b), τ^ℐ\hat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}} is unbiased. However, τℐ\tau_{\mathcal{I}} uses the auxiliary randomization ℐ\mathcal{I}, it does not belong to the estimator class 𝒯⁡(P,f)\mathcal{T}(P,f). Therefore, we use its Rao–Blackwellized version τ^RB=𝔼[τ^ℐ∣Z,YOf​(Z)]\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}]. Lemma 3.4.1 shows that τ^RB\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB} remains unbiased and has no larger variance. Proposition F.2.2 in Appendix F.2 upper bounds the worst-case variance of τ^RB\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB} for every order and choice of proposal probabilities. Appendix F.2 also gives choices of order and proposal probabilities for bounded-degree graphs, disjoint stars, and disjoint cliques of equal size.

Remark 8.1 (Comparison with Kandiros, Harshaw and Sävje).

At q=∞q=\infty, Kandiros et al. (2026a) obtain the same independence-number lower bound. Under the identity exposure mapping and unrestricted assignments, the induced conflict graph on the estimand-relevant potential outcomes characterizes their joint observability, so their conflict-graph bound agrees with our sampling-rank bound. For the upper bound, their conflict-graph design and our ordered proposal design are related but distinct constructions: The conflict graph design operates on the exposure vertices of the conflict graph, whereas the ordered proposal design operates directly on the units of GG. Both attain order (d+1)/n(d+1)/n on regular graphs and hence give the same logarithmic bracket for random regular graphs.

A rate price of unbiasedness

In the graph families considered above, unbiased and all estimator classes have the same minimax rate. This need not hold on every graph. Consider a core-periphery family with a core of SS units that forms a clique, 1≤S<n1\leq S<n, and let the remaining n−Sn-S units form the periphery. Every periphery unit is adjacent to every core unit, and the subgraph induced by the periphery has maximum degree at most a fixed constant rr.

Theorem 8.1.2 (Unbiasedness can cost a rate).

For a core–periphery graph,

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≍1n+S2n2,Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≍Sn,R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\asymp\frac{1}{n}+\frac{S^{2}}{n^{2}},\qquad R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\asymp\frac{S}{n},

so that the ratio of the two minimax risks is of order min⁡{S,n/S}\min\{S,n/S\}, with constants depending only on rr. The price is largest, of order n\sqrt{n}, when S≍nS\asymp\sqrt{n}.

The gap follows from a bias–variance trade-off. No assignment can simultaneously reveal the treatment-arm potential outcomes of the core and the periphery. A biased estimator can ignore the core, incurring bias of order S/nS/n to reduce the variance to order 1/n1/n. On the other hand, an unbiased estimator must estimate the core’s contribution, which costs variance of order S/nS/n. The proof is given in Appendix F.3.

Remark 8.2 (Comparison with the Kandiros–Harshaw–Sävje bias–variance trade-off).

Kandiros et al. (2026a) also use a bias–variance trade-off in their upper bounds by dropping a set of conflict-graph vertices Under their second-moment restriction (q=2q=2), when the conflict graph is a star, their upper bound for the unbiased conflict-graph design is of order 1/n1/\sqrt{n}, while dropping the center gives an upper bound of order 1/n1/n. Their lower bound shows that 1/n1/n is the all-estimator minimax rate, but it does not lower-bound the risk over unbiased estimators. By contrast, Theorem 8.1.2 lower-bounds every unbiased stratergy and shows that unbiasedness can cost a factor of order n\sqrt{n}.

8.2 The total treatment effect

We now study the minimax risk of the Total Treatment Effect (TTE) with and without a treatment budget. The TTE compares the potential outcome when treating the entire closed neighborhood of unit ii with leaving it untreated:

τTTE​(Y)=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(1Ni+)−Yi​(0Ni+)}.\tau_{\rm TTE}(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(1_{N_{i}^{+}})-Y_{i}(0_{N_{i}^{+}})\}. (40)

The TTE creates two distinct constraints on jointly observed potential outcomes. Hence, its minimax lower bound depends on two graph quantities. The first quantity identifies closed neighborhoods that are far enough to serve as disjoint perturbation sets (Definition 4.1). Define

𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1(G)=maxC⊆V:distG⁡(c,c′)≥3∑c∈C|B1(c)|2,\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)=\max_{C\subseteq V:\operatorname{dist}_{G}(c,c^{\prime})\geq 3}\sum_{c\in C}|B_{1}(c)|^{2},

where the distance condition applies to distinct units in CC, which serve as neighborhood centers. The quantity 𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G) is a weighted packing of disjoint closed neighborhoods. On a dd-regular graph, it equals (d+1)2(d+1)^{2} times the maximum number of centers at pairwise distance at least three. The second quantity measures how many potential outcomes from the two arms can be revealed simultaneously by a single assignment. For an assignment zz, let T={i:zi=1}T=\{i:z_{i}=1\} be the set of treated units and define

AT={i:B1​(i)⊆T},BT={i:B1​(i)⊆V∖T}.A_{T}=\{i:B_{1}(i)\subseteq T\},\qquad B_{T}=\{i:B_{1}(i)\subseteq V\setminus T\}.

Thus ATA_{T} and BTB_{T} index the observed treatment- and control-arm outcomes. The quantity M⁡(G)=maxT⊆V⁡min⁡{|AT|,|BT|}M(G)=\max_{T\subseteq V}\min\{|A_{T}|,|B_{T}|\} is the largest number rr for which one assignment reveals at least rr outcomes from each arm. For the upper bound, we consider graphs with restricted growth from radius one. With Br​(i)B_{r}(i) the rr-hop closed neighborhood, this means |Br+1​(i)|≤κ​|Br​(i)||B_{r+1}(i)|\leq\kappa|B_{r}(i)| for every unit ii and r≥1r\geq 1, where κ\kappa is the restricted-growth coefficient. Let di=|B1​(i)|−1d_{i}=|B_{1}(i)|-1 and d¯=n−1​∑idi\bar{d}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}d_{i}.

Theorem 8.2.1 (Minimax rates for the neighborhood TTE).

The following hold.

  1. (i)

    For every graph GG with M⁡(G)≥1M(G)\geq 1,

    max⁡{𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)n2,116​M​(G)}≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE).\max\left\{\frac{\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)}{n^{2}},\frac{1}{16M(G)}\right\}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE}).

    If M⁡(G)=0M(G)=0, then Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≥1R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\geq 1.

  2. (ii)

    If GG has restricted-growth coefficient κ\kappa, then

    d¯+1κ​n≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≤C⁡(κ)​d¯+1n,\frac{\bar{d}+1}{\kappa n}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq C(\kappa)\frac{\bar{d}+1}{n},

    where C⁡(κ)C(\kappa) depends only on κ\kappa.

The detailed proof is in Appendix F.4. The proof uses Lemma F.4.4 which constructs a packing by repeatedly choosing a largest remaining closed neighborhood centered at a unit and excluding other centers within distance two. The restricted growth condition then bounds the sum of neighborhood sizes over the excluded centers by κ\kappa times the squared size of the chosen neighborhood, so 𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)≥n⁡(d¯+1)/κ\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)\geq n(\bar{d}+1)/\kappa, giving the lower bound in part (ii).

Graph-cluster randomization (Ugander et al., 2013) attains the upper bound in part (ii). Choose a maximal set CC of units at pairwise distance at least three. These units serve as cluster centers. Assign every unit to its nearest center, and independently treat each cluster with probability 1/21/2. Restricted growth ensures that each closed neighborhood intersects only a bounded number of clusters. Both TTE exposures therefore have probabilities bounded away from zero, and the exposure Horvitz–Thompson estimator has worst-case variance at most C​(κ)​(d¯+1)/nC(\kappa)(\bar{d}+1)/n. Proposition F.4.5 gives the details. Part (ii) holds for every restricted-growth graph, including graphs with unequal degrees. For a restricted-growth regular graph, the rate is (d+1)/n(d+1)/n, and dd may grow with nn.

For graphs without restricted growth, Appendix F.4.2 gives an upper bound using a distance-two independent-set design with small proposal probabilities. It applies the ordered proposal construction to G2G^{2}, so the selected units have disjoint closed neighborhoods, and assigns each selected neighborhood entirely to treatment or control. It gives an unbiased upper bound on every graph. On dd-regular spectral expanders, it gives the bracket

dn≲Rall∗≤Runb∗≲min⁡{1,d2+1n}.\frac{d}{n}\lesssim R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\lesssim\min\left\{1,\frac{d^{2}+1}{n}\right\}.
Remark 8.3 (Comparison with conflict-graph bounds).

For the TTE on a restricted-growth dd-regular graph, the bounds of Kandiros et al. (2026a) give

max{1n,d+1n3/2}≲Rall∗≤Runb∗≲κd+1n.\max\left\{\frac{1}{n},\frac{d+1}{n^{3/2}}\right\}\ \lesssim\ R^{*}_{\rm all}\ \leq\ R^{*}_{\rm unb}\ \lesssim_{\kappa}\ \frac{d+1}{n}.

Their stated lower and upper bounds can therefore differ by a factor of order min⁡{d+1,n}\min\{d+1,\sqrt{n}\}. Our packing lower bound is of order (d+1)/n(d+1)/n and closes this gap (see Appendix F.4.1).

8.2.1 The total effect under a treatment budget

Consider a budget constraint of at most mm treated units. With a treatment budget, the choice of which units to treat matters. To reveal a treatment-arm potential outcome Yi​(1Ni+)Y_{i}(1_{N_{i}^{+}}), the design must treat a unit along with all its neighbors, so the budget should cover as many complete neighborhoods as possible. Fix a treatment budget mm and restrict the assignment set to 𝒵≤m={z∈{0,1}n:|T⁡(z)|≤m},\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}=\{z\in\{0,1\}^{n}:|T(z)|\leq m\}, where T⁡(z)T(z) is the set of treated units. The corresponding design class is 𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}). Under a given assignment, let SS be the set of units whose treatment-arm potential outcomes are observed. The design must then treat every unit in the set

N⁡[S]=⋃i∈SB1​(i),N[S]=\bigcup_{i\in S}B_{1}(i),

so any such set must satisfy |N⁡[S]|≤m|N[S]|\leq m. The number of treatment-arm potential outcomes that can be observed together therefore depends on how the neighborhoods overlap. When they overlap heavily, the same treated units may reveal several outcomes; when they overlap less, the budget is used up more quickly.

Theorem 8.2.2 (Budgeted TTE under restricted growth).

Let GG be dd-regular with restricted-growth coefficient κ\kappa. There is a constant crg​(κ)∈(0,1]c_{\rm rg}(\kappa)\in(0,1] such that, if 1≤m≤n/21\leq m\leq n/2 and (d+1)/m≤crg​(κ)(d+1)/m\leq c_{\rm rg}(\kappa), then

c⁡(κ)​d+1m≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m),f,aTTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m),f,aTTE)≤C⁡(κ)​d+1m.c(\kappa)\frac{d+1}{m}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq C(\kappa)\frac{d+1}{m}.

The condition (d+1)/m≤crg​(κ)(d+1)/m\leq c_{\rm rg}(\kappa) ensures that the budget is sufficiently large for positivity to hold in the upper bound construction below. For fixed κ\kappa, both minimax risks vanish at rate (d+1)/m(d+1)/m when d+1=o⁡(m)d+1=o(m). Without the budget, Theorem 8.2.1 gives rate (d+1)/n(d+1)/n on the same graph class. When the budget is large enough relative to the neighborhood size, it therefore replaces nn by mm in the minimax rate. The lit-ball design attains the upper bound.

Definition 8.2 (Lit-ball design).

Fix 1≤ℓ≤⌊m/(d+1)⌋1\leq\ell\leq\lfloor m/(d+1)\rfloor. Draw ClitC_{\rm lit} uniformly from all ℓ\ell-element subsets of [n][n]. Assign every unit in ⋃i∈ClitB1​(i)\bigcup_{i\in C_{\rm lit}}B_{1}(i) to treatment and the rest to control.

Choosing ℓ≤m/(d+1)\ell\leq m/(d+1) respects the budget. For the theorem, take ℓ≍κm/(d+1)\ell\asymp_{\kappa}m/(d+1), where the comparison constants depend only on κ\kappa. Units in ClitC_{\rm lit} reveal the treatment arm. A unit reveals the control arm when no selected unit lies within two hops. Restricted growth and the condition (d+1)/m≤crg​(κ)(d+1)/m\leq c_{\rm rg}(\kappa) keep these control-exposure probabilities bounded away from zero. Inverse-probability weighting over the sampled units gives an unbiased estimator. Its Rao–Blackwellized version depends only on the observed assignment and outcomes and has variance of order (d+1)/m(d+1)/m.

The lower bound uses a perturbation packing construction, which we describe next. Choose a maximal set CC of units at pairwise distance at least five. The two-hop neighborhoods B2​(c)B_{2}(c), c∈Cc\in C, are then pairwise disjoint. If Yi​(1Ni+)Y_{i}(1_{N_{i}^{+}}) for a unit i∈B1​(c)i\in B_{1}(c) is observed, at least d+1d+1 units inside B2​(c)B_{2}(c) must be treated. An assignment with at most mm treated units can therefore reveal treatment-arm outcomes in at most J=⌊m/(d+1)⌋J=\lfloor m/(d+1)\rfloor of the closed neighborhoods B1​(c)B_{1}(c), c∈Cc\in C. When |C|≥2​J|C|\geq 2J, partition CC into 2​J2J groups C1,…,C2​JC_{1},\ldots,C_{2J} of nearly equal size. For each group, define the perturbation set

ℬb={(i,1):i∈⋃c∈CbB1(c)},b=1,…,2J.\mathcal{B}_{b}=\left\{(i,1):i\in\bigcup_{c\in C_{b}}B_{1}(c)\right\},\qquad b=1,\ldots,2J.

Thus ℬb\mathcal{B}_{b} contains the treatment-arm potential outcomes of all units in the closed neighborhoods centered at units in CbC_{b}. These perturbation sets are disjoint because the neighborhoods B1​(c)B_{1}(c), c∈Cc\in C, are pairwise disjoint. Since the budget can reach at most JJ neighborhoods, at least JJ perturbation sets remain unobserved under every assignment. Restricted growth ensures that each set carries estimand weight at least a constant multiple of 1/J1/J. The joint-missingness bound therefore gives risk of order J​(1/J)2=1/J≍(d+1)/m.J(1/J)^{2}=1/J\asymp(d+1)/m. Appendix F.5 gives the explicit grouping construction and handles the case |C|<2​J|C|<2J; it also gives the estimator and an extension to budget-expanding graphs.

Remark 8.4 (Why pairwise observability is not enough).

The budget creates a higher-order constraint that is not recorded by the conflict graph. If m≥2​(d+1)m\geq 2(d+1), any two treatment-arm potential outcomes can be observed together by treating the union of their closed neighborhoods. The induced conflict graph on the treatment arm therefore has no edges. A collection of rr disjoint closed neighborhoods, however, requires r⁡(d+1)r(d+1) treated units and cannot be observed jointly when r⁡(d+1)>mr(d+1)>m. The sampling hypergraph records this restriction and gives the lower bound of order (d+1)/m(d+1)/m.

Appendix F.6 gives an analogous result for the minimax risk of the DTE under a treatment budget. The budget and the independence number jointly limit how many treatment-arm outcomes can be observed. The treated-arm rank min⁡{m,α⁡(G)}\min\{m,\alpha(G)\} gives the lower bound.

8.3 A local complex-contagion contrast

Consider the threshold exposure mapping fi(z)=(zi,𝟏{Ci(z)≥θ})f_{i}(z)=(z_{i},\mathbf{1}\{C_{i}(z)\geq\theta\}), where Ci​(z)=∑j∈NizjC_{i}(z)=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j} is the number of treated neighbors of unit ii. It records whether unit ii is treated and whether at least θ\theta of its neighbors are treated. We study the minimax risk of a contrast that compares treated units with at least θ\theta treated neighbors to treated units with fewer that θ\theta treated neighobors. Writing bhi=(1,1)b_{\rm hi}=(1,1) and blo=(1,0)b_{\rm lo}=(1,0), the estimand is

τθ​(Y)=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(bhi)−Yi​(blo)}.\tau_{\theta}(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(b_{\rm hi})-Y_{i}(b_{\rm lo})\}. (41)

All assignments are allowed. In the graph families considered below, both target exposures are attainable, and the relevant potential outcomes are bounded by one. At θ=1\theta=1, the contrast compares treated units with at least one treated neighbor to treated units with none. For θ≥2\theta\geq 2, it measures the effect of crossing a threshold that requires several treated neighbors, as in models of complex contagion (Granovetter, 1978; Watts, 2002; Centola and Macy, 2007). In the terminology of Ugander et al. (2013), bhib_{\rm hi} is absolute θ\theta-neighborhood exposure to treatment.

Observation constraint and regular-graph bounds

Let SS be the set of units that reveal their low-exposure potential outcomes Yi​(blo)Y_{i}(b_{\rm lo}). Every unit in SS is treated and has fewer than θ\theta treated neighbors, so it has at most θ−1\theta-1 neighbors within SS. Conversely, if every unit in a set SS has at most θ−1\theta-1 neighbors within SS, then treating all units in SS and leaving all units in ScS^{c} untreated reveals the low-exposure potential outcome of every unit in SS. The largest number of low-exposure potential outcomes that one assignment can reveal is therefore the (θ−1)(\theta-1)-dissociation number

dissθ−1(G)=max{|S|:S⊆V,Δ(G[S])≤θ−1}.\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq V,\ \Delta(G[S])\leq\theta-1\}.

This is the sampling rank of the low-exposure arm; at θ=1\theta=1, it reduces to α⁡(G)\alpha(G).

Theorem 8.3.1 (Threshold-contrast bounds on regular graphs).

Fix θ≥1\theta\geq 1. Let GG be dd-regular on nn units, with d≥16​θd\geq 16\theta and n≥4​dn\geq 4\sqrt{d}. Then

cθ​max⁡{1dissθ−1⁡(G),dn}≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aθ)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aθ)≤Cθ​dn.c_{\theta}\max\left\{\frac{1}{\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G)},\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n}\right\}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\leq C_{\theta}\frac{d}{n}.

The constants depend only on θ\theta. The Bernoulli design with p=θ/dp=\theta/d and the exposure Horvitz–Thompson estimator attain the upper bound.

For the lower bounds, the reciprocal dissociation term follows from the sampling-rank lower bound. The d/n\sqrt{d}/n term comes from balancing two packing-based lower bounds. Let πv\pi_{v} be the probability that the low-exposure outcome of unit vv is observed. For a threshold π\pi, if πv≤π\pi_{v}\leq\pi for many units, a packing of singleton low-exposure potential outcomes gives a lower bound of order 1/(π​n)1/(\pi n). If πv>π\pi_{v}>\pi for many units, observing the low exposure at vv leaves all but at most θ−1\theta-1 of its dd neighbors untreated. Packing blocks of these neighbors gives a lower bound of order d​π/nd\pi/n. The two bounds balance at π≍d−1/2\pi\asymp d^{-1/2}, giving d/n\sqrt{d}/n.

For the upper bound, under a Bernoulli design with p=θ/dp=\theta/d, both target exposures have probabilities of order 1/d1/d. Exposure indicators are independent for units at distance greater than two; bounding the remaining covariance terms gives the d/nd/n upper bound. Appendix F.7 gives the lower-bound proofs and the upper-bound variance calculation.

On the random regular graphs considered in Theorem 8.1.1(iii), α⁡(G)≲n​log⁡d/d\alpha(G)\lesssim n\log d/d with high probability. Since dissθ−1⁡(G)≤θ​α​(G)\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G)\leq\theta\alpha(G), the lower bound strengthens to order d/(n​log⁡d)d/(n\log d), while the Bernoulli upper bound remains of order d/nd/n leaving a logarithmic gap.

The d/nd/n upper bound is sharp on some regular graph families for every fixed 1≤θ≤d−11\leq\theta\leq d-1. For example, consider disjoint cliques of size d+1d+1. Independently in each clique, treat either θ\theta or θ+1\theta+1 units. The first choice gives the selected units the low exposure, and the second gives them the high exposure. Both minimax risks are then of order d/nd/n. The same rate holds on disjoint copies of the complete bipartite graph Kd,dK_{d,d} (Appendix F.7). Whether a regular graph family has minimax risk of order d/n\sqrt{d}/n remains open.

What pairwise observability misses

For θ≥2\theta\geq 2, any two low-exposure potential outcomes are jointly observable, but a unit and θ\theta of its neighbors cannot simultaneously receive the low exposure. The sampling hypergraph retains this higher-order restriction, whereas its pairwise projection discards it.

Corollary 8.3.2 (Lower-bound certificate gap on graphs of girth at least five).

Fix θ≥2\theta\geq 2 and let GG be dd-regular with d≥16​θd\geq 16\theta and girth at least five. The pairwise conflict graph gives a lower bound of order 1/n1/n, whereas the sampling hypergraph yields

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aθ)≥cθ​dn.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\geq c_{\theta}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n}.

Lemma F.7.9 shows that the only pairwise conflicts are between the two exposures of the same unit. The hypergraph lower bound is therefore stronger by a factor of order d\sqrt{d}, reflecting higher-order observation constraints that pairwise observability does not record. At θ=1\theta=1, the low-exposure conflict graph is instead exactly GG (Remark F.4).

9 Bipartite interference

In a bipartite experiment, treatment is assigned to one population and outcomes are measured on another. Examples include interventions at pollution sources with outcomes measured in nearby populations (Zigler and Papadogeorgou, 2021), and marketplace experiments in which sellers are randomized and buyer outcomes are measured (Harshaw et al., 2023).

Let UU be the treatment population, with |U|=M|U|=M, and let VV be the outcome population, with |V|=n|V|=n. The interference graph GG is bipartite, with edges only between UU and VV. Each outcome unit vv has a nonempty neighborhood Av⊆UA_{v}\subseteq U of treatment units that can affect its outcome. Write dv=|Av|d_{v}=|A_{v}| for its outcome-unit degree, the number of treatment units connected to outcome unit vv. For an assignment z∈{0,1}Uz\in\{0,1\}^{U}, the exposure of outcome unit vv is the number of treated units in its neighborhood, fv​(z)=∑u∈Avzuf_{v}(z)=\sum_{u\in A_{v}}z_{u}. For two doses 0≤k′<k≤minv⁡dv0\leq k^{\prime}<k\leq\min_{v}d_{v}, we study the corresponding dose-response contrast:

τk,k′​(Y)=1n​∑v∈V{Yv​(k)−Yv​(k′)}.\tau_{k,k^{\prime}}(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v\in V}\{Y_{v}(k)-Y_{v}(k^{\prime})\}. (42)

Write ak,k′a_{k,k^{\prime}} for the estimand coefficient vector of τk,k′\tau_{k,k^{\prime}}. The potential outcomes are bounded by one, and the design class contains all distributions on {0,1}U\{0,1\}^{U}. We call the doses 00 and dvd_{v} the extreme doses of outcome unit vv. Doses strictly between 00 and dvd_{v} are interior doses.

We study the minimax risk of a contrast between two interior doses when many outcome units randomly draw their neighborhoods from a common pool of MM treatment units. For example, each buyer may depend on several sellers randomly drawn from a common seller population.

Definition 9.1 (Uniform dd-out bipartite interference graph).

Fix a pool UU of treatment units with |U|=M|U|=M, and let d≤Md\leq M be the number of treatment neighbors of each outcome unit. Each of the nn outcome units draws its neighborhood independently of the others, uniformly at random among the (Md)\binom{M}{d} subsets of UU of size dd. Thus dv=dd_{v}=d for every outcome unit vv, and its realized dose ranges from 00 to dd.

For two interior doses k′<kk^{\prime}<k, define s=min⁡{k,d−k}+1s=\sqrt{\min\{k,d-k\}+1}. Note that s2−1=min⁡{k,d−k}s^{2}-1=\min\{k,d-k\} is the distance from kk to the closest extreme dose. We consider a treatment pool of size M≍n/sM\asymp n/s.

Theorem 9.1 (Nearby interior doses on a shared pool).

Assume a uniform dd-out bipartite interference graph (Definition 9.1), with n≥3n\geq 3, M≥16M\geq 16, and 3≤d≤M3\leq d\leq\sqrt{M}. Let 0<k′<k<d0<k^{\prime}<k<d with k−k′≤c0​sk-k^{\prime}\leq c_{0}s for a fixed c0c_{0}, and suppose M≍n/sM\asymp n/s. Then, with probability at least 1−2/n21-2/n^{2} over the graph draw,

c​sn≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡({0,1}U),f,ak,k′)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡({0,1}U),f,ak,k′)≤C​s​log⁡nn.c\frac{s}{n}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\{0,1\}^{U});f,a_{k,k^{\prime}})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\{0,1\}^{U});f,a_{k,k^{\prime}})\leq C\frac{s\log n}{n}.

The constants depend only on c0c_{0} and the constants implicit in M≍n/sM\asymp n/s.

Lower bound

Let JkJ_{k} be the maximum number of outcome units whose potential outcomes Yv​(k)Y_{v}(k) are jointly observed under one assignment. With high probability over the graph draw, Jk≤C⁡(n/s+M+log⁡n)J_{k}\leq C(n/s+M+\log n), giving Jk≲n/sJ_{k}\lesssim n/s when M≍n/sM\asymp n/s. Thus, every assignment leaves most dose-kk potential outcomes unobserved when ss is large. A paired-arm perturbation packing uses this limit on joint observation to give the lower bound of order s/ns/n. The construction of the packing groups outcome units and pairs their sets of dose-kk and dose-k′k^{\prime} potential outcomes, so that every assignment leaves at least one set completely missing in sufficiently many pairs. The lower bound of Theorem B.6.4 converts the resulting packing into the risk bound. The details are in Appendix G.1.

Upper bound

The upper bound is attained by a completely randomized design on the treatment population paired with the exposure Horvitz–Thompson estimator. Let tt be the nearest integer to M⁡(k+k′)/(2​d)M(k+k^{\prime})/(2d), and treat a uniformly chosen tt-subset of UU. Conditional on the realized interference graph, every outcome unit has exposure probabilities

πj=(tj)​(M−td−j)(Md),j∈{k,k′},\pi_{j}=\frac{\binom{t}{j}\binom{M-t}{d-j}}{\binom{M}{d}},\qquad j\in\{k,k^{\prime}\},

The condition k−k′≤c0​sk-k^{\prime}\leq c_{0}s ensures that this design gives both target doses exposure probabilities of order 1/s1/s, so πk,πk′≍1/s\pi_{k},\pi_{k^{\prime}}\asymp 1/s. The estimator

τ^fix=1n​∑v∈V{𝟏{fv(Z)=k}πk−𝟏{fv(Z)=k′}πk′}​Yvobs\widehat{\tau}_{\rm fix}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v\in V}\left\{\frac{\mathbf{1}\{f_{v}(Z)=k\}}{\pi_{k}}-\frac{\mathbf{1}\{f_{v}(Z)=k^{\prime}\}}{\pi_{k^{\prime}}}\right\}Y_{v}^{\rm obs}

is unbiased for every realized interference graph. The diagonal contribution to its variance is of order s/ns/n. For the off diagonal contribution, note that under a Bernoulli assignment, the number of treated units in the pool would fluctuate and shift the doses of all outcome units together. Fixing the number of treated units removes this common fluctuation, and Appendix G.1 controls the remaining covariance from overlapping neighborhoods, giving an upper bound rate of s​log⁡n/ns\log n/n. The upper and lower bounds differ by a factor of log⁡n\log n. The proofs are in Appendix G.1.

The adjacent-dose contrasts τk,k−1\tau_{k,k-1} are the increments of the dose–response curve k↦n−1​∑vYv​(k)k\mapsto n^{-1}\sum_{v}Y_{v}(k). By Theorem 9.1, the difficulty of estimating these increments depends on the dose kk. For adjacent doses near either extreme, with min⁡{k,d−k}\min\{k,d-k\} bounded, the lower and upper bounds are of order 1/n1/n and log⁡n/n\log n/n, respectively. For adjacent doses near the middle dose d/2d/2, they are of order d/n\sqrt{d}/n and d​log⁡n/n\sqrt{d}\log n/n. In each case, the comparison assumes a treatment pool of size M≍n/sM\asymp n/s.

For interior-dose contrasts, the conflict graph can lose information needed for the lower bound. An interior dose specifies how many treatment units in a neighborhood are treated, so the corresponding potential outcomes may be pairwise observable even though the entire collection is not jointly observable. For the extreme doses 00 and dvd_{v}, the induced conflict graph on the two extreme-dose arms determines which collections are jointly observable: each extreme exposure fixes all treatment assignments in its neighborhood, so a pairwise-observable collection of extreme-dose potential outcomes is jointly observable, by the same argument as in the proof of Theorem B.7.1.

Corollary 9.2 (A two-arm lower-bound certificate gap).

Under the uniform dd-out bipartite interference graph model, take adjacent interior doses k′=k−1k^{\prime}=k-1, with 0<k′<k<d0<k^{\prime}<k<d, 3≤d≤M3\leq d\leq\sqrt{M}, and M≍n/sM\asymp n/s. If (Md)/n2→∞\binom{M}{d}/n^{2}\to\infty, then with probability tending to one the pairwise conflict graph gives a lower bound of order 1/n1/n, whereas the minimax risks satisfy

c​sn≤Rall∗≤Runb∗≤C​s​log⁡nn.c\frac{s}{n}\leq R^{*}_{\rm all}\leq R^{*}_{\rm unb}\leq C\frac{s\log n}{n}.

The hypergraph lower bound is stronger by a factor of order ss, which grows when both kk and d−kd-k grow and is of order d\sqrt{d} for central doses. For adjacent doses, target exposures of distinct outcome units conflict only when their neighborhoods are identical. The probability of any duplicate neighborhood is at most n⁡(n−1)/{2​(Md)}n(n-1)/\{2\binom{M}{d}\}, which vanishes under the stated condition. Thus the induced conflict graph on the two target-dose arms consists only of the nn same-unit exposure pairs and misses the higher-order restrictions on joint observation. The proof is in Appendix G.1.

10 Discussion

We study the design based minimax risk of estimating causal effects under interference for three problems: When a design is fixed, under a restricted class of designs, and when the design is unrestricted. In all three cases, we consider the minimax risk over the class of all and unbiased estimators. These problems correspond to practical situations faced by an experimenter: analyzing an experiment whose design is fixed, choosing a design subject to constraints, and assessing what is achievable without those constraints. In all three problems, the minimax risk depends on which estimand-relevant potential outcomes can be observed together and how often they are observed. The minimax risks are determined jointly by the interference structure, exposure mapping, and estimand. An optimal design must therefore be tailored to the estimand and to the constraints of the experiment. For example, the direct and total treatment effects impose different joint observation requirements on the same graph and lead to different design constructions. This raises a broader question: when can one estimation strategy be simultaneously minimax-rate optimal for several estimands?

The framework also shows which part of the estimation strategy limits the rate: the estimator, the design, or the requirement of unbiasedness. For example, under randomized saturation, changing the estimator under the same design improves the rate from 1/ξ1/\xi to 1/n1/n (Proposition 5.3.1). By contrast, constraints on the number of treated units, budgets, and lack of knowledge of cluster memberships at design stage can make the design the bottleneck. For instance, estimating the total treatment effect when cluster memberships are unknown leads to an exponential dependence on cluster size. (Theorem 7.2.3). Unbiasedness usually has no rate cost in most of our examples, and no first-order cost for the no-interference average treatment effect. But it is the bottleneck in the core–periphery family. There, a biased strategy can omit a small, difficult-to-observe part of the population, whereas an unbiased strategy cannot, and the ratio of the two minimax risks can be of order up to n\sqrt{n} (Theorem 8.1.2). Several questions remain. Characterizing when unbiasedness has no minimax-rate cost remains open. We have identified settings where pairwise observability implies joint observability, but a broader characterization is open. The lower and upper bounds also leave gaps for complex contagion and bipartite dose contrasts. Closing these gaps requires better designs and estimators or stronger lower bounds. Another question is how estimation changes when the exposure mapping is misspecified or the interference structure is only partly known.

A.1 Proof of Rao–Blackwellization of the estimator

In this section, we prove Lemma 3.4.1, which removes auxiliary randomization UU in an estimator T⁡(U,D)T(U,D) by using Rao–Blackwellization and conditioning on DD. Here, D=(Z,YOf​(Z))D=(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}) is the observed data.

Lemma 3.4.1 (Rao–Blackwellized estimator).

Suppose UU takes values in a finite or countable set 𝒰\mathcal{U}, and the joint law of UU and assignment ZZ is known and does not depend on YY. Let D=(Z,YOf​(Z))D=(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}) and let T⁡(U,D)T(U,D) have finite second moment for every admissible table. Then T~​(D)=𝔼​[T​(U,D)∣D]\widetilde{T}(D)=\mathbb{E}[T(U,D)\mid D] depends only on the observed data DD and satisfies

𝔼⁡[(T~−τa​(Y))2∣Y]≤𝔼⁡[(T−τa​(Y))2∣Y]for every ​Y∈𝒴⁡(f).\mathbb{E}[(\widetilde{T}-\tau_{a}(Y))^{2}\mid Y]\leq\mathbb{E}[(T-\tau_{a}(Y))^{2}\mid Y]\qquad\text{for every }Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f).

If TT is unbiased, so is T~\widetilde{T}, and its variance is no larger.

Recall that UU is the auxiliary randomization and D=(Z,YOf​(Z))D=(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}) consists of the treatment assignment and the observed outcomes. An estimator T⁡(U,D)T(U,D) uses both the auxiliary randomization and the observed data. We apply Rao–Blackwellization to T⁡(U,D)T(U,D) by taking its conditional expectation given DD, obtaining 𝔼⁡[T⁡(U,D)∣D]\mathbb{E}[T(U,D)\mid D]. We show that this conditional expectation can be computed from the observed data without knowing the unobserved potential outcomes.

Fix an admissible table y∈𝒴⁡(f)y\in\mathcal{Y}(f) and write D=(Z,yOf​(Z))D=(Z,y_{O_{f}(Z)}). All probabilities and expectations below are over the known joint randomization law of (U,Z)(U,Z), with the potential outcome table yy held fixed. For this fixed table, DD is a deterministic function of ZZ and contains ZZ. Hence σ⁡(D)=σ⁡(Z)\sigma(D)=\sigma(Z), where σ⁡(X)\sigma(X) denotes the sigma-algebra generated by a random vector XX (since DD is a function of ZZ, σ⁡(D)⊆σ⁡(Z)\sigma(D)\subseteq\sigma(Z), and since ZZ is the first component of DD, σ⁡(Z)⊆σ⁡(D)\sigma(Z)\subseteq\sigma(D)). Thus conditioning on DD gives the same information as conditioning on ZZ, and the conditional law of UU given DD is its known conditional law given ZZ. Hence

T~​(D)=𝔼⁡[T⁡(U,D)∣D]=∑u∈𝒰T⁡(u,D)​Pr⁡(U=u∣Z).\widetilde{T}(D)=\mathbb{E}[T(U,D)\mid D]=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}T(u,D)\Pr(U=u\mid Z).

The formula for T~\widetilde{T} uses only the observed data and the known randomization probabilities, so it defines the same observed-data rule for every admissible table. Assignments of probability zero may be assigned any value of T~\widetilde{T}. Conditional Jensen’s inequality and iterated expectation now give

𝔼⁡[(T~​(D)−τa​(y))2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\widetilde{T}(D)-\tau_{a}(y))^{2}] =𝔼⁡[(𝔼⁡[T⁡(U,D)−τa​(y)∣D])2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(\mathbb{E}[T(U,D)-\tau_{a}(y)\mid D]\bigr)^{2}\right]
≤𝔼⁡[(T⁡(U,D)−τa​(y))2],\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[(T(U,D)-\tau_{a}(y))^{2}],

which proves equation (13). Moreover, if TT is design-unbiased, then iterated expectation gives

𝔼⁡[T~​(D)]=𝔼⁡{𝔼⁡[T⁡(U,D)∣D]}=𝔼⁡[T⁡(U,D)]=τa​(y).\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{T}(D)]=\mathbb{E}\{\mathbb{E}[T(U,D)\mid D]\}=\mathbb{E}[T(U,D)]=\tau_{a}(y).

Thus design-unbiasedness is preserved. For unbiased estimators, mean squared error equals design variance, giving the variance inequality. ∎

B Supporting results for Section 4

In this section, we provide proofs for the lower-bound results in Section 4 and give additional lower-bound analyses. We first establish preliminary lemmas and prove the two-table packing lower bound in Lemma 4.1.1, the lower bounds from packing disjoint perturbations in Theorem 4.1.2, and the singleton packing lower bound in Corollary 4.1.3. We next prove Proposition 4.2.1, which represents the fixed-design, restricted-design, and all-design minimax risks in terms of the weighted sampling hypergraphs. The example in Section B.4 then shows that two designs with the same sampling hypergraph and first-order inclusion probabilities can have fixed-design unbiased minimax risks differing by a factor of order nn. Corollary B.5.1 provides lower bounds over a design class. For all design minimax problem, we derive the hypergraph based lower bounds in Theorem B.6.1 and use them to prove the sampling-rank lower bound in Theorem 4.3.1 and the paired-set lower bound in Theorem 4.3.2. The final subsection compares the sampling hypergraph with the conflict graph of Kandiros et al. (2026a).

B.1 Preliminary lemmas

In this section, we collect some standard technical lemmas used throughout the proofs. Lemma B.1.1 shows that the fixed-design minimax risk is bounded below by the expected posterior variance of the estimand under any finite-support prior ν\nu on the potential outcomes. We then establish a second-moment bound in Lemma B.1.2, conditional moments under a hypercube prior in Lemma B.1.3, and a weighted probability bound in Lemma B.1.4.

Lemma B.1.1 (Conditional bias–variance decomposition).

Fix a design PP and a finite-support prior ν\nu on 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f). Draw 𝖸∼ν\mathsf{Y}\sim\nu and Z∼PZ\sim P independently, and let D=(Z,𝖸Of​(Z))D=(Z,\mathsf{Y}_{O_{f}(Z)}). Write 𝔼ν,P\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P} for expectation under this joint law and m⁡(D)=𝔼ν,P​[τa​(𝖸)∣D]m(D)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}[\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y})\mid D]. For any estimator TP​(D)T_{P}(D) with finite second moment under this law,

𝔼ν,P​[(TP​(D)−τa​(𝖸))2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}[(T_{P}(D)-\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y}))^{2}] =𝔼ν,P​[(TP​(D)−m⁡(D))2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}[(T_{P}(D)-m(D))^{2}]
+𝔼ν,P​[Varν,P⁡(τa​(𝖸)∣D)].\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}[\operatorname{Var}_{\nu,P}(\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y})\mid D)].

Consequently, the fixed-design minimax risk satisfies

Rall​(P,f,a)=infTP∈𝒯⁡(P,f)supy∈𝒴⁡(f)𝔼P​[(TP−τa​(y))2∣y]≥𝔼ν,P​[Varν,P⁡(τa​(𝖸)∣D)].R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)=\inf_{T_{P}\in\mathcal{T}(P,f)}\sup_{y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\mathbb{E}_{P}[(T_{P}-\tau_{a}(y))^{2}\mid y]\geq\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}[\operatorname{Var}_{\nu,P}(\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y})\mid D)]. (43)

Conditional on DD, the bias–variance decomposition gives

𝔼ν,P​[(TP​(D)−τa​(𝖸))2∣D]=(TP​(D)−m⁡(D))2+Varν,P⁡(τa​(𝖸)∣D).\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}[(T_{P}(D)-\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y}))^{2}\mid D]=(T_{P}(D)-m(D))^{2}+\operatorname{Var}_{\nu,P}(\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y})\mid D).

Taking expectations proves the identity. The inequality follows because worst-case risk is at least prior-averaged risk and the squared term is nonnegative. Taking the infimum over estimators gives the minimax lower bound, since the right-hand side does not depend on the estimator. ∎

Lemma B.1.2 (A second-moment bound).

Let T,V1,…,VrT,V_{1},\ldots,V_{r} be square-integrable random variables on the same probability space, with 𝔼⁡(Vb​Vd)=0\mathbb{E}(V_{b}V_{d})=0 for b≠db\neq d and vb=𝔼​Vb2>0v_{b}=\mathbb{E}V_{b}^{2}>0. Then

𝔼​T2≥∑b=1r{𝔼⁡(T​Vb)}2vb.\mathbb{E}T^{2}\geq\sum_{b=1}^{r}\frac{\{\mathbb{E}(TV_{b})\}^{2}}{v_{b}}.

Write αb=𝔼⁡(T​Vb)/vb\alpha_{b}=\mathbb{E}(TV_{b})/v_{b}. Expanding a nonnegative square and using the zero cross moments gives

0\displaystyle 0 ≤𝔼​(T−∑b=1rαb​Vb)2\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left(T-\sum_{b=1}^{r}\alpha_{b}V_{b}\right)^{2}
=𝔼​T2−2​∑b=1rαb​𝔼​(T​Vb)+∑b=1rαb2​vb\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}T^{2}-2\sum_{b=1}^{r}\alpha_{b}\mathbb{E}(TV_{b})+\sum_{b=1}^{r}\alpha_{b}^{2}v_{b}
=𝔼​T2−∑b=1r{𝔼⁡(T​Vb)}2vb.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}T^{2}-\sum_{b=1}^{r}\frac{\{\mathbb{E}(TV_{b})\}^{2}}{v_{b}}.

Rearranging proves the inequality. ∎

Lemma B.1.3 (Conditional moments under a hypercube prior).

Fix a design PP, pairwise disjoint nonempty perturbation sets B1,…,Bm⊆KaB_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\subseteq K_{a}, and fixed signs sb,k∈{−1,1}s_{b,k}\in\{-1,1\} for k∈Bbk\in B_{b}. Let θ=(θ1,…,θm)∈{−1,1}m\theta=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{m})\in\{-1,1\}^{m}, with independent components, each taking values −1-1 and 11 with probability 1/21/2, independently of Z∼PZ\sim P. Define the random potential outcome table

Ykθ={sb,k​θb,k∈Bb,0,k∉⋃b=1mBb.Y_{k}^{\theta}=\begin{cases}s_{b,k}\theta_{b},&k\in B_{b},\\ 0,&k\notin\bigcup_{b=1}^{m}B_{b}.\end{cases}

This construction gives a hypercube prior on 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f): each of the 2m2^{m} sign vectors has probability 2−m2^{-m}. Let D=(Z,YOf​(Z)θ)D=(Z,Y^{\theta}_{O_{f}(Z)}) and Jb=𝟏{Of(Z)∩Bb≠∅}J_{b}=\mathbf{1}\{O_{f}(Z)\cap B_{b}\neq\varnothing\}. Under the joint law of this prior and design,

𝔼⁡(θb∣D)={θb,Jb=1,0,Jb=0,Var⁡(θb∣D)=1−Jb,Cov⁡(θb,θd∣D)=0(b≠d).\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\mid D)=\begin{cases}\theta_{b},&J_{b}=1,\\ 0,&J_{b}=0,\end{cases}\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\theta_{b}\mid D)=1-J_{b},\\ \operatorname{Cov}(\theta_{b},\theta_{d}\mid D)=0\quad(b\neq d).\end{gathered} (44)

In the first case, observing the potential outcome at an index k∈Bbk\in B_{b} gives θb=sb,k​Ykθ\theta_{b}=s_{b,k}Y_{k}^{\theta}, so θb\theta_{b} is determined by DD.

Since the perturbation sets BbB_{b} are pairwise disjoint and all entries lie in [−1,1][-1,1], each table YθY^{\theta} belongs to 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f). Fix data D=(z,yOf​(z))D=(z,y_{O_{f}(z)}) having positive probability. If Jb=1J_{b}=1, an observed potential outcome in BbB_{b} determines θb\theta_{b}, so 𝔼⁡(θb∣D)=θb\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\mid D)=\theta_{b}. If Jb=0J_{b}=0, changing only θb\theta_{b} to −θb-\theta_{b} leaves (z,yOf​(z))(z,y_{O_{f}(z)}) unchanged. Flipping θb\theta_{b} pairs each sign vector consistent with (z,yOf​(z))(z,y_{O_{f}(z)}) with another consistent vector of the same prior probability 2−m2^{-m} and opposite value of θb\theta_{b}. The assignment probability P⁡(z)P(z) is also unchanged. The paired terms cancel in the conditional expectation, giving 𝔼⁡(θb∣D)=0\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\mid D)=0. Thus

𝔼⁡(θb∣D)={θb,Jb=1,0,Jb=0.\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\mid D)=\begin{cases}\theta_{b},&J_{b}=1,\\ 0,&J_{b}=0.\end{cases}

Since θb2=1\theta_{b}^{2}=1, the two cases give

Var⁡(θb∣D)=𝔼⁡(θb2∣D)−{𝔼⁡(θb∣D)}2=1−Jb.\operatorname{Var}(\theta_{b}\mid D)=\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}^{2}\mid D)-\{\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\mid D)\}^{2}=1-J_{b}.

For b≠db\neq d, if either Jb=0J_{b}=0 or Jd=0J_{d}=0, flipping an unobserved sign pairs equal-probability terms with opposite values of θb​θd\theta_{b}\theta_{d}. Hence 𝔼⁡(θb​θd∣D)=0\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\theta_{d}\mid D)=0. If both indicators equal one, both signs are determined by the data, so 𝔼⁡(θb​θd∣D)=θb​θd\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\theta_{d}\mid D)=\theta_{b}\theta_{d}. Combining the two cases gives

Cov⁡(θb,θd∣D)=𝔼⁡(θb​θd∣D)−𝔼⁡(θb∣D)​𝔼​(θd∣D)=Jb​Jd​θb​θd−Jb​Jd​θb​θd=0.\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_{b},\theta_{d}\mid D)=\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\theta_{d}\mid D)-\mathbb{E}(\theta_{b}\mid D)\mathbb{E}(\theta_{d}\mid D)=J_{b}J_{d}\theta_{b}\theta_{d}-J_{b}J_{d}\theta_{b}\theta_{d}=0.

∎

Remark B.1 (Role of the random signs).

The perturbation sets BbB_{b} specify which potential outcomes vary together. The independent uniform signs θb\theta_{b} in Lemma B.1.3, also called Rademacher signs, turn this packing into a finite prior on 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f). All potential outcomes in BbB_{b} share the same random sign, so observing any one of them reveals θb\theta_{b}. If none is observed, the conditional variance of θb\theta_{b} remains one. The lower-bound proofs use the conditional moments in equation (44) to compute the uncertainty in the estimand left by an assignment.

Lemma B.1.4 (A weighted reciprocal-probability bound).

Let p1,…,pr>0p_{1},\ldots,p_{r}>0 and w1,…,wr∈ℝw_{1},\ldots,w_{r}\in\mathbb{R}. Then

∑k=1rwk2pk≥(∑k=1r|wk|)2∑k=1rpk.\sum_{k=1}^{r}\frac{w_{k}^{2}}{p_{k}}\geq\frac{\left(\sum_{k=1}^{r}|w_{k}|\right)^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{r}p_{k}}. (45)

In particular, if ∑kpk≤C\sum_{k}p_{k}\leq C for some C>0C>0, the left-hand side is at least (∑k|wk|)2/C(\sum_{k}|w_{k}|)^{2}/C.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives

(∑k=1r|wk|)2=(∑k=1r|wk|pk​pk)2≤(∑k=1rwk2pk)​(∑k=1rpk).\left(\sum_{k=1}^{r}|w_{k}|\right)^{2}=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{r}\frac{|w_{k}|}{\sqrt{p_{k}}}\sqrt{p_{k}}\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{r}\frac{w_{k}^{2}}{p_{k}}\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^{r}p_{k}\right).

Divide by ∑kpk>0\sum_{k}p_{k}>0. The final assertion follows by replacing this sum in the denominator by its upper bound CC. ∎

B.2 Fixed-design lower bounds and refinements

We first prove the two-table lower bound for unbiased and all estimator classes stated in Lemma 4.1.1 using the two-point prior, followed by the lower bounds from disjoint perturbations in Theorem 4.1.2 which uses the hypercube prior. We then derive its single-set consequence in Lemma B.2.1 and prove the singleton lower bound in Corollary 4.1.3. We finish with the mutually exclusive-set refinement in Proposition B.2.3. Throughout this subsection the design is fixed. Section B.5 treats optimization over a design class.

B.2.1 The two-table lower bound

We restate the lemma.

Lemma 4.1.1 (Two-table lower bound).

Let Y,Y′∈𝒴⁡(f)Y,Y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}(f) differ exactly on a nonempty set B⊆KaB\subseteq K_{a}, and let Δ=|τa​(Y)−τa​(Y′)|>0\Delta=|\tau_{a}(Y)-\tau_{a}(Y^{\prime})|>0. For every design PP,

Rall​(P,f,a)≥Δ24​ρP​(B),andRunb​(P,f,a)≥Δ24​ρP​(B)1−ρP​(B).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}\rho_{P}(B),\mathrm{and}\qquad R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\geq\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}\frac{\rho_{P}(B)}{1-\rho_{P}(B)}.

The second bound is interpreted as +∞+\infty when ρP​(B)=1\rho_{P}(B)=1; in that case no unbiased estimator exists.

We first prove the lower bound over all estimators. This argument has two parts: in part (i), we bound the worst-case design mean squared error of any estimator from below by the expected posterior variance of the estimand under a two-point prior; in part (ii), we compute this posterior variance.

Part (i): Bounding risk by the expected posterior variance. Write Y(0)=YY^{(0)}=Y, Y(1)=Y′Y^{(1)}=Y^{\prime}, tj=τa​(Y(j))t_{j}=\tau_{a}(Y^{(j)}) for j∈{0,1}j\in\{0,1\}, and t¯=(t0+t1)/2\bar{t}=(t_{0}+t_{1})/2. Let ν\nu be a prior on 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f) that assigns probability 1/21/2 to each of Y(0)Y^{(0)} and Y(1)Y^{(1)}, and zero probability to all other tables. For a random table 𝖸∼ν\mathsf{Y}\sim\nu, this means

Prν{𝖸=Y(0)}=Prν{𝖸=Y(1)}=12.\Pr_{\nu}\{\mathsf{Y}=Y^{(0)}\}=\Pr_{\nu}\{\mathsf{Y}=Y^{(1)}\}=\frac{1}{2}.

Draw Z∼PZ\sim P independently of 𝖸\mathsf{Y}. The prior ν\nu and the design PP therefore induce the product joint law ν⊗P\nu\otimes P on (𝖸,Z)(\mathsf{Y},Z). Write 𝔼ν,P\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P} for expectation under this law. The observed data are D=(Z,𝖸Of​(Z))D=(Z,\mathsf{Y}_{O_{f}(Z)}). Conditional on 𝖸=y\mathsf{Y}=y, only the assignment is random, with law PP.

Let

M={Of(Z)∩B=∅}M=\{O_{f}(Z)\cap B=\varnothing\}

be the event that all potential outcomes in a perturbation set BB are missing. Write ρ=P⁡(M)=ρP​(B)\rho=P(M)=\rho_{P}(B) and q=P⁡(Mc)=1−ρq=P(M^{c})=1-\rho.

Let TP∈𝒯⁡(P,f)T_{P}\in\mathcal{T}(P,f) be an estimator with finite worst-case risk; otherwise the lower bound is immediate. Applying Lemma B.1.1 to this two-point prior gives

supy∈𝒴⁡(f)𝔼P​[(TP−τa​(y))2∣y]\displaystyle\sup_{y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\mathbb{E}_{P}[(T_{P}-\tau_{a}(y))^{2}\mid y] ≥12​∑j=01𝔼P​[(TP−tj)2∣Y(j)]\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=0}^{1}\mathbb{E}_{P}[(T_{P}-t_{j})^{2}\mid Y^{(j)}]
=𝔼ν,P​[(TP​(D)−τa​(𝖸))2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}[(T_{P}(D)-\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y}))^{2}]
≥𝔼ν,P​[Varν,P⁡(τa​(𝖸)∣D)].\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}[\operatorname{Var}_{\nu,P}(\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y})\mid D)].

Part (ii): Computing the posterior variance. We now compute the posterior variance of τa​(𝖸)\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y}) under the two-point prior. On MM, no potential outcome in BB is observed. Since the two tables agree outside BB, they give identical observed data at each assignment zz for which MM occurs. The prior assigns equal probability to the tables, and the assignment probability P⁡(z)P(z) is the same under both. Hence, on MM,

Prν,P{𝖸=Y(j)∣D}=12,j=0,1.\Pr_{\nu,P}\{\mathsf{Y}=Y^{(j)}\mid D\}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad j=0,1.

On McM^{c}, an observed potential outcome in BB identifies the table, since the tables differ in the potential outcome at every index in BB. The posterior variance is therefore zero on McM^{c}, whereas on MM the two estimand values retain equal posterior probabilities. Consequently, almost surely,

Varν,P⁡(τa​(𝖸)∣D)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}_{\nu,P}(\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y})\mid D) ={12​(t0−t¯)2+12​(t1−t¯)2}​𝟏M\displaystyle=\left\{\frac{1}{2}(t_{0}-\bar{t})^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(t_{1}-\bar{t})^{2}\right\}\mathbf{1}_{M}
=Δ24​𝟏M.\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}\mathbf{1}_{M}.

supy∈𝒴⁡(f)𝔼P​[(TP−τa​(y))2∣y]\displaystyle\sup_{y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\mathbb{E}_{P}[(T_{P}-\tau_{a}(y))^{2}\mid y] ≥𝔼ν,P​[Varν,P⁡(τa​(𝖸)∣D)]\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}_{\nu,P}\!\left[\operatorname{Var}_{\nu,P}(\tau_{a}(\mathsf{Y})\mid D)\right]
=Δ24​Prν,P⁡(M)=Δ24​ρP​(B).\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}\Pr_{\nu,P}(M)=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}\rho_{P}(B).

Taking the infimum over all estimators proves the first bound.

We next prove the lower bound over unbiased estimators. Suppose that TPT_{P} is unbiased at every potential outcome table in 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f). First suppose 0<ρP​(B)<10<\rho_{P}(B)<1. ≥ρP​(B)1−ρP​(B)​(t0−u)2+(t1−u)22\displaystyle\geq\frac{\rho_{P}(B)}{1-\rho_{P}(B)}\,\frac{(t_{0}-u)^{2}+(t_{1}-u)^{2}}{2}

Taking the infimum over unbiased estimators proves the second bound for 0<ρP​(B)<10<\rho_{P}(B)<1. When ρP​(B)=0\rho_{P}(B)=0, the bound is zero and holds by nonnegativity of squared error. When ρP​(B)=1\rho_{P}(B)=1, the observed-data laws under the two tables coincide, so every integrable estimator has the same expectation under both. Since t0≠t1t_{0}\neq t_{1}, no estimator can be unbiased at both tables, and Runb​(P,f,a)=+∞R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)=+\infty. ∎

Remark B.2 (Detection probability and total variation).

Recall that ρP​(B)\rho_{P}(B) is the probability that every potential outcome in BB is missing, whereas qP​(B)=1−ρP​(B)q_{P}(B)=1-\rho_{P}(B) is the probability of observing at least one such potential outcome. The latter event distinguishes the two tables in Lemma 4.1.1.

For the tables Y,Y′Y,Y^{\prime} in Lemma 4.1.1, let ℒY\mathcal{L}_{Y} and ℒY′\mathcal{L}_{Y^{\prime}} denote the laws of (Z,YOf​(Z))(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}) and (Z,YOf​(Z)′)(Z,Y^{\prime}_{O_{f}(Z)}), respectively, under the same design PP. The detection probability equals the total-variation distance:

‖ℒY−ℒY′‖TV=1−ρP​(B)=qP​(B).\|\mathcal{L}_{Y}-\mathcal{L}_{Y^{\prime}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=1-\rho_{P}(B)=q_{P}(B). (46)

Indeed, the laws agree on assignments observing no potential outcome in BB. On the complementary event, their observed outcomes differ. Because the assignment itself is observed and has the same law under both tables, the total-variation distance equals the probability of observing at least one potential outcome in BB. Thus the all-estimator bound in Lemma 4.1.1 can be written as

Rall​(P,f,a)≥Δ24​(1−‖ℒY−ℒY′‖TV).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4}\bigl(1-\|\mathcal{L}_{Y}-\mathcal{L}_{Y^{\prime}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigr).

This is the same bound expressed through the overlap of the two data laws, as in classical two-point lower-bound arguments. In this experiment, the assignment is observed and outcomes are deterministic given the assignment and table, so the overlap is exactly the joint missingness probability. The total-variation formulation therefore does not give a stronger bound here.

B.2.2 Lower bounds from disjoint perturbation sets

We restate and prove the lower bound from disjoint perturbations. Recall that a perturbation packing ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\} consists of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of KaK_{a}. For fixed signs sb,k∈{−1,1}s_{b,k}\in\{-1,1\}, its estimand relevant coefficients are cb=∑k∈Bbak​sb,kc_{b}=\sum_{k\in B_{b}}a_{k}s_{b,k}.

Theorem 4.1.2 (Lower bounds from disjoint perturbations).

Fix a design PP, a perturbation packing ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\}, and signs defining cbc_{b}.

    Over all estimators,

    Over unbiased estimators,

    Runb(P;f,a)≥∑b:cb≠0cb2ρP​(Bb)1−ρP​(Bb).R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\geq\sum_{b:c_{b}\neq 0}c_{b}^{2}\frac{\rho_{P}(B_{b})}{1-\rho_{P}(B_{b})}.

    If cb≠0c_{b}\neq 0 and ρP​(Bb)=1\rho_{P}(B_{b})=1 for some set, no unbiased estimator exists and the bound is +∞+\infty.

Fix the design PP and the potential-outcome packing ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\}, with the signs sb,ks_{b,k} specified in the theorem. We first construct a hypercube prior on 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f). For part (i) of the theorem, to prove the all-estimator lower bound, we compute the expected posterior variance of the estimand under this prior. For part (ii), to prove the unbiased-estimator lower bound, we establish a second-moment bound for an unbiased estimator, then subtract the prior second moment of the estimand to obtain a lower bound on the design variance.

Construction of the hypercube prior. Use the prior of Lemma B.1.3 with the perturbation sets B1,…,BmB_{1},\ldots,B_{m} and fixed signs sb,ks_{b,k} from the theorem. Thus θ=(θ1,…,θm)\theta=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{m}) has one independent uniform sign for each perturbation set BbB_{b}, and Ykθ=sb,k​θbY_{k}^{\theta}=s_{b,k}\theta_{b} for k∈Bbk\in B_{b}, with zero entries outside ⋃b=1mBb\bigcup_{b=1}^{m}B_{b}. B.2.3 Lower bounds from a single perturbation set and singleton packings

The next lemma records the single-perturbation-set case of the lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2).

Lemma B.2.1 (Lower bounds from joint missingness).

For every fixed design PP, every nonempty B⊆KaB\subseteq K_{a}, and every choice of signs defining cBc_{B},

Rall​(P,f,a)≥cB2​ρP​(B).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq c_{B}^{2}\rho_{P}(B).

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡(TP∣Y)≥cB2​ρP​(B)1−ρP​(B).\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(T_{P}\mid Y)\geq c_{B}^{2}\frac{\rho_{P}(B)}{1-\rho_{P}(B)}.

If cB≠0c_{B}\neq 0 and ρP​(B)=1\rho_{P}(B)=1, no unbiased estimator exists.

Take the packing ℬ={B}\mathcal{B}=\{B\}, consisting of one perturbation set, with the signs defining cBc_{B}. Its coefficient is cBc_{B}, and its detection probability is qP​(B)=1−ρP​(B)q_{P}(B)=1-\rho_{P}(B). Part (i) of the lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2) gives

Rall​(P,f,a)≥cB2​{1−qP​(B)}=cB2​ρP​(B).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq c_{B}^{2}\{1-q_{P}(B)\}=c_{B}^{2}\rho_{P}(B).

If ρP​(B)<1\rho_{P}(B)<1, then qP​(B)>0q_{P}(B)>0. Part (ii) of the same theorem gives, for every unbiased estimator,

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡(TP∣Y)≥cB2​{1qP​(B)−1}=cB2​ρP​(B)1−ρP​(B).\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(T_{P}\mid Y)\geq c_{B}^{2}\left\{\frac{1}{q_{P}(B)}-1\right\}=c_{B}^{2}\frac{\rho_{P}(B)}{1-\rho_{P}(B)}.

When cB=0c_{B}=0, this inequality holds by nonnegativity of variance. Finally, if cB≠0c_{B}\neq 0 and ρP​(B)=1\rho_{P}(B)=1, then qP​(B)=0q_{P}(B)=0, so the impossibility statement in part (ii) of the theorem applies. ∎

Apply the lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2) to the singleton packing Bk={k}B_{k}=\{k\}, k∈Kak\in K_{a}, with sk=sign⁡(ak)s_{k}=\operatorname{sign}(a_{k}). Then ρP​(Bk)=1−πP,k\rho_{P}(B_{k})=1-\pi_{P,k} and ck=|ak|c_{k}=|a_{k}|, so part (i) gives equation (16), part (ii) gives equation (17), and part (ii) also shows that no unbiased estimator exists when πP,k=0\pi_{P,k}=0 for some k∈Kak\in K_{a}. ∎

The missingness lower bounds are attained when one unknown scalar is either observed exactly or missing, as the following proposition shows.

Proposition B.2.2 (Exact price of unbiasedness for one missing component).

Suppose we observe θ∈[−C,C]\theta\in[-C,C] exactly with probability q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1). Conditional on θ\theta being missing, the law of the data does not depend on θ\theta. Then

infTsup|θ|≤C𝔼θ​(T−θ)2\displaystyle\inf_{T}\sup_{|\theta|\leq C}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}(T-\theta)^{2} =C2​(1−q),\displaystyle=C^{2}(1-q), (49)

Let JJ indicate that the scalar is observed, so Pr⁡(J=1)=q\Pr(J=1)=q. For unrestricted estimation, use T0=J​θT_{0}=J\theta, interpreted as zero when J=0J=0. Its risk is

𝔼θ​[(T0−θ)2]=(1−q)​θ2≤(1−q)​C2.\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[(T_{0}-\theta)^{2}]=(1-q)\theta^{2}\leq(1-q)C^{2}.

For unbiasedness, the same two values give the lower bound C2​(1−q)/qC^{2}(1-q)/q from the unbiased part of the two-table lemma. Use T1=J​θ/qT_{1}=J\theta/q. Since 𝔼θ​T1=θ\mathbb{E}_{\theta}T_{1}=\theta and 𝔼θ​T12=θ2/q\mathbb{E}_{\theta}T_{1}^{2}=\theta^{2}/q, its variance is

Varθ⁡(T1)=θ2/q−θ2=θ2​(1−q)/q≤C2​(1−q)/q.\operatorname{Var}_{\theta}(T_{1})=\theta^{2}/q-\theta^{2}=\theta^{2}(1-q)/q\leq C^{2}(1-q)/q.

This attains the second lower bound. If q=1q=1, both estimators recover θ\theta exactly and both risks are zero. ∎

B.2.4 Lower bounds from mutually exclusive perturbation sets

The lower bound from disjoint perturbations in Theorem 4.1.2(ii) can be strengthened when two perturbation sets cannot be observed together. Proposition B.2.3 gives the refinement for one pair of perturbations; Equation (53) gives the extension to disjoint pairs of perturbations. Write

λP​(B)=ρP​(B)1−ρP​(B)=1−qP​(B)qP​(B),\lambda_{P}(B)=\frac{\rho_{P}(B)}{1-\rho_{P}(B)}=\frac{1-q_{P}(B)}{q_{P}(B)}, (51)

with value +∞+\infty when ρP​(B)=1\rho_{P}(B)=1.

The refinement adds a positive cross term for opposite-signed coefficient sums. It is used in the no-interference benchmarks in Appendix D. For the no-interference ATE under independent balanced assignment, it improves the unbiased lower bound from 2/n2/n to the exact value 4/n4/n (Theorem 6.1.1).

Proposition B.2.3 (Mutually exclusive, opposite-signed sets).

Let B1,B2⊆KaB_{1},B_{2}\subseteq K_{a} be disjoint packed sets. For r=1,2r=1,2, let

cr=∑k∈Brsr,kak,Jr(Z)=𝟏{Of(Z)∩Br≠∅},qP,r=P{Jr(Z)=1},c_{r}=\sum_{k\in B_{r}}s_{r,k}a_{k},\qquad J_{r}(Z)=\mathbf{1}\{O_{f}(Z)\cap B_{r}\neq\varnothing\},\qquad q_{P,r}=P\{J_{r}(Z)=1\},
