If cr≠0c_{r}\neq 0 but qP,r=0q_{P,r}=0, the unbiased class is empty. Products cr2​λP​(Br)c_{r}^{2}\lambda_{P}(B_{r}) with cr=0c_{r}=0 are interpreted as zero, including when qP,r=0q_{P,r}=0.

The last term strengthens the lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2(ii)) when c1​c2<0c_{1}c_{2}<0, as it does for opposite-signed components of a causal contrast.

More generally, suppose all 2​J2J sets in the pairs {(Bj​1,Bj​2):j=1,…,J}\{(B_{j1},B_{j2}):j=1,\ldots,J\} are pairwise disjoint and the two observation indicators within each pair are mutually exclusive. Then

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡(TP∣Y)≥∑j=1J{cj​12​λP​(Bj​1)+cj​22​λP​(Bj​2)−2​cj​1​cj​2}.\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(T_{P}\mid Y)\geq\sum_{j=1}^{J}\left\{c_{j1}^{2}\lambda_{P}(B_{j1})+c_{j2}^{2}\lambda_{P}(B_{j2})-2c_{j1}c_{j2}\right\}. (53)

B.3 Sampling-design reduction of the three minimax problems

In this subsection, we prove Proposition 4.2.1 using two lemmas. Lemma B.3.1 shows that the fixed-design minimax risks are unchanged when estimators T⁡(Z,YOf​(Z))T(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}) are restricted to functions of (Of​(Z),YOf​(Z))(O_{f}(Z),Y_{O_{f}(Z)}). The proof constructs such an estimator by averaging over assignments that reveal the same indices; this averaging cannot increase risk and preserves unbiasedness. This reduces the fixed-design problem to the induced sampling design, or equivalently the weighted sampling hypergraph, and the restricted-design problem to the collection of attainable induced sampling designs. Lemma B.3.2 shows that, when all designs on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} are allowed, every probability distribution on the feasible hyperedges is attainable. Optimizing over these probabilities then leaves only the unweighted sampling hypergraph.

Lemma B.3.1 (Sufficiency of the induced sampling design).

Fix a design PP. For squared-error loss, both the minimax risk over all estimators, Rall​(P,f,a)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a), and the minimax risk over unbiased estimators, Runb​(P,f,a)R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a), are unchanged if estimators are restricted to measurable functions of Of​(Z)O_{f}(Z) and YOf​(Z)Y_{O_{f}(Z)}.

Fix PP and an admissible table YY. Let T⁡(D)T(D) be an estimator based on the full observed data D=(Z,YOf​(Z))D=(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}). Put A=Of​(Z)A=O_{f}(Z) and let D0=(A,YA)D_{0}=(A,Y_{A}) be the data retained after discarding the assignment. For an observed data pattern AA with QP,f​(A)>0Q_{P,f}(A)>0, the conditional probability of assignment zz given this pattern is

P⁡(Z=z∣Of​(Z)=A)=P(z)𝟏{Of(z)=A}QP,f​(A).P(Z=z\mid O_{f}(Z)=A)=\frac{P(z)\mathbf{1}\{O_{f}(z)=A\}}{Q_{P,f}(A)}.

For the fixed table YY, the event {D0=(A,YA)}\{D_{0}=(A,Y_{A})\} is precisely the event {Of(Z)=A}\{O_{f}(Z)=A\}. Thus the same conditional probabilities apply when we condition on D0D_{0}. Define

T¯(A,yA)=∑z:Of​(z)=AP⁡(z)QP,f​(A)T(z,yA).\overline{T}(A,y_{A})=\sum_{z:O_{f}(z)=A}\frac{P(z)}{Q_{P,f}(A)}T(z,y_{A}).

The probabilities in this sum are known and independent of the table, so the formula defines a single estimator using only (A,yA)(A,y_{A}). For each fixed YY, T¯(D0)=𝔼P[T(D)∣D0,Y]\overline{T}(D_{0})=\mathbb{E}_{P}[T(D)\mid D_{0},Y]. This is Rao–Blackwellization of the design-based estimator with respect to the retained data. Conditional Jensen and iterated expectation give

𝔼P​[(T¯​(D0)−τa​(Y))2∣Y]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{P}[(\overline{T}(D_{0})-\tau_{a}(Y))^{2}\mid Y] ≤𝔼P{𝔼P[(T(D)−τa(Y))2∣D0,Y]∣Y}\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{P}\{\mathbb{E}_{P}[(T(D)-\tau_{a}(Y))^{2}\mid D_{0},Y]\mid Y\}
=𝔼P​[(T⁡(D)−τa​(Y))2∣Y],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{P}[(T(D)-\tau_{a}(Y))^{2}\mid Y],
𝔼P​[T¯​(D0)∣Y]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{P}[\overline{T}(D_{0})\mid Y] =𝔼P​[T​(D)∣Y].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{P}[T(D)\mid Y].

Thus averaging cannot increase risk and preserves unbiasedness. Conversely, every function of D0D_{0} is also a function of the full data DD, so it is allowed in the original estimator class. The infima over full-data estimators and retained-data estimators therefore agree, both for all estimators and for unbiased estimators. Patterns of probability zero may be assigned any value. ∎

Lemma B.3.2 (Every hypergraph law is implementable).

Every probability distribution on the hyperedges of ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0}) is induced by some design in 𝒫⁡(𝒵0)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}).

Write ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)=(K,ℰ)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0})=(K,\mathcal{E}). For each hyperedge A∈ℰA\in\mathcal{E}, choose one witness assignment zA∈𝒵0z_{A}\in\mathcal{Z}_{0} such that Of​(zA)=AO_{f}(z_{A})=A. Given a probability law QQ on the hyperedges, define P⁡(zA)=Q⁡(A)P(z_{A})=Q(A) and assign probability zero to all other assignments. Witnesses for distinct hyperedges are distinct, since one assignment has only one observation pattern. Consequently PP is a probability law on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} and, for every hyperedge AA,

QP,f(A)=∑z:Of​(z)=AP(z)=P(zA)=Q(A).Q_{P,f}(A)=\sum_{z:O_{f}(z)=A}P(z)=P(z_{A})=Q(A).

∎

Proposition 4.2.1 (Sampling-design reduction of the three minimax problems).

Fix ff, aa, and 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f).

  1. (i)

    For a fixed design PP, both Rall​(P)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P) and Runb​(P)R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P) depend on PP only through QP,fQ_{P,f}.

  2. (ii)

    For a restricted design class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the joint minimax risk Rall∗​(𝒞)R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C}) depends on the class only through 𝒬f​(𝒞)\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}). The corresponding risk Runb∗​(𝒞)R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C}) depends only on 𝒬f​(𝒞+)\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}_{+}), where 𝒞+=𝒞∩𝒫+​(f,a)\mathcal{C}_{+}=\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{P}_{+}(f,a).

  3. (iii)

    When all designs on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} are allowed, both Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})) and Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})) depend on the assignment and exposure model only through ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0}).

By Lemma B.3.1, the fixed-design risks can be computed using estimators of (A,YA)(A,Y_{A}), where A∼QP,fA\sim Q_{P,f}. For every fixed table, the distribution of (A,YA)(A,Y_{A}) is specified by QP,fQ_{P,f}. Recall from Definition 4.5 that, writing ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)=(K,ℰ)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0})=(K,\mathcal{E}), the weighted sampling hypergraph is (ℋobs​(f,𝒵0),wP)(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0}),w_{P}), where wP​(A)=QP,f​(A)w_{P}(A)=Q_{P,f}(A) for A∈ℰA\in\mathcal{E}. In particular,

supp⁡(QP,f)={A∈ℰ:wP​(A)>0}.\operatorname{supp}(Q_{P,f})=\{A\in\mathcal{E}:w_{P}(A)>0\}.

Conversely, the weighted hypergraph determines the induced sampling design by QP,f​(A)=wP​(A)Q_{P,f}(A)=w_{P}(A) for A∈ℰA\in\mathcal{E} and QP,f​(A)=0Q_{P,f}(A)=0 otherwise. Thus two designs inducing the same weighted sampling hypergraph induce the same distribution of (A,YA)(A,Y_{A}) for every fixed table and hence have the same minimax risks, proving part (i).

For part (ii), recall that

Rall∗​(𝒞)=infP∈𝒞Rall​(P),Runb∗​(𝒞)=infP∈𝒞+Runb​(P).R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C})=\inf_{P\in\mathcal{C}}R_{\mathrm{all}}(P),\qquad R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C})=\inf_{P\in\mathcal{C}_{+}}R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P).

By part (i), designs with the same induced sampling design contribute the same value of Rall​(P)R_{\mathrm{all}}(P) to the first infimum and the same value of Runb​(P)R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P) to the second. Thus Rall∗​(𝒞)R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C}) is determined by the set 𝒬f​(𝒞)={QP,f:P∈𝒞}\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C})=\{Q_{P,f}:P\in\mathcal{C}\}, and Runb∗​(𝒞)R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C}) by 𝒬f​(𝒞+)={QP,f:P∈𝒞+}\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}_{+})=\{Q_{P,f}:P\in\mathcal{C}_{+}\}. These are precisely the collections of weighted sampling hypergraphs attainable in the two classes. This proves part (ii).

For part (iii), write ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)=(K,ℰ)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0})=(K,\mathcal{E}) and let Δ⁡(ℰ)\Delta(\mathcal{E}) denote all probability laws on ℰ\mathcal{E}. Every design P∈𝒫⁡(𝒵0)P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}) induces a sampling design QP,f∈Δ⁡(ℰ)Q_{P,f}\in\Delta(\mathcal{E}), or equivalently a weighted sampling hypergraph. Conversely, Lemma B.3.2 constructs a design inducing any chosen Q∈Δ⁡(ℰ)Q\in\Delta(\mathcal{E}). Consequently,

𝒬f​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))=Δ⁡(ℰ).\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}))=\Delta(\mathcal{E}).

Thus optimization over all designs is equivalent to optimization over all probability laws on the feasible hyperedges. In the unbiased problem, positivity requires ∑A∈ℰ:k∈AQ(A)>0\sum_{A\in\mathcal{E}:k\in A}Q(A)>0 for each k∈Kak\in K_{a}, which is a condition on QQ alone. Hence the attainable induced sampling designs for this problem are precisely the laws in Δ⁡(ℰ)\Delta(\mathcal{E}) satisfying these inequalities. In both cases, the hyperedge probabilities are optimized over, and both risks therefore depend only on the unweighted sampling hypergraph, with ff, aa, and 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f) held fixed. This proves part (iii). ∎

B.4 An example with same hypergraph, but different fixed design minimax rates

Proposition 4.2.1(i) shows that the the fixed-design minimax risks depend on the full induced sampling design QP,fQ_{P,f}, or equivalently, the weighted sampling hypergraph. In this subsection, we construct an example with two different designs and same unweighted sampling hypergraph and first-order inclusion probabilities, but different unbiased minimax rates. These examples show that the fixed design minimax risks depend on the weighted sampling hypergraph and not just the unweighted hypergraph, or the marginal probabilities. We use the no-interference setup of Section 6.1, with 𝒵={0,1}n\mathcal{Z}=\{0,1\}^{n}, fi​(z)=zif_{i}(z)=z_{i}, potential outcomes in [−1,1][-1,1], and ATE coefficients ai,1=1/na_{i,1}=1/n and ai,0=−1/na_{i,0}=-1/n.

The first design is the independent Bernoulli law P1/2P_{1/2} with P⁡(Zi=1)=1/2P(Z_{i}=1)=1/2, for which

Runb​(P1/2,f,a)=4nR_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{1/2};f,a)=\frac{4}{n} (54)

by Theorem 6.1.1. The second is a clustered design built from a common shock and independent noise. Let C∼Bernoulli⁡(1/2)C\sim{\rm Bernoulli}(1/2) and let ε1,…,εn\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{n} be independent Bernoulli⁡(η){\rm Bernoulli}(\eta) variables, independent of CC, where η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1). Set

Zi=C⊕εi,i=1,…,n.Z_{i}=C\mathbin{\oplus}\varepsilon_{i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n. (55)

where ⊕\oplus denotes addition modulo two. Write PcwP_{\rm cw} for this design. Both designs are laws on 𝒵={0,1}n\mathcal{Z}=\{0,1\}^{n} that give positive probability to every assignment, so they have the same sampling hypergraph ℋobs​(f)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f), the family of all one-index-per-unit transversals. Moreover PrPcw⁡(Zi=1)=1/2\Pr_{P_{\rm cw}}(Z_{i}=1)=1/2 for every ii, so every first-order inclusion probability matches P1/2P_{1/2}. The designs differ only in their joint dependence. For η=c/n\eta=c/n, the probabilities that all units are untreated and that all units are treated are equal:

Pcw​(Z=0n)=Pcw​(Z=1n)=12​{(1−c/n)n+(c/n)n}⟶e−c2.P_{\rm cw}(Z=0^{n})=P_{\rm cw}(Z=1^{n})=\frac{1}{2}\{(1-c/n)^{n}+(c/n)^{n}\}\longrightarrow\frac{e^{-c}}{2}.
Theorem B.4.1 (Cluster randomization with vanishing noise).

Let η=c/n\eta=c/n for a fixed c>0c>0 and n>cn>c, and let PcwP_{\rm cw} denote the design defined by equation (55). Then PcwP_{\rm cw} and P1/2P_{1/2} have the same sampling hypergraph and the same first-order inclusion probabilities, and as n→∞n\to\infty,

Runb​(Pcw,f,a)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{\rm cw};f,a) ≥2​e−c2−e−c​{1−o⁡(1)},\displaystyle\geq\frac{2e^{-c}}{2-e^{-c}}\,\{1-o(1)\}, (56)
Runb​(Pcw,f,a)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{\rm cw};f,a) ≤4​{1n+(1−1n)​(1−2​η)2}≤4+o⁡(1).\displaystyle\leq 4\left\{\frac{1}{n}+\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)(1-2\eta)^{2}\right\}\leq 4+o(1). (57)

Hence Runb​(Pcw,f,a)=Θ⁡(1)R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{\rm cw};f,a)=\Theta(1), whereas Runb​(P1/2,f,a)=4/nR_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{1/2};f,a)=4/n.

For the lower bound, we use the lower bound from disjoint perturbations with the two sets

B1={(i,1):i=1,…,n},B0={(i,0):i=1,…,n}.B_{1}=\{(i,1):i=1,\ldots,n\},\qquad B_{0}=\{(i,0):i=1,\ldots,n\}.

These sets partition the potential-outcome table into its treatment and control arms. To see the associated perturbations explicitly, let θ1,θ0\theta_{1},\theta_{0} be independent uniform signs and set Yi​(1)=θ1Y_{i}(1)=\theta_{1} and Yi​(0)=θ0Y_{i}(0)=\theta_{0} for every unit ii. This gives four admissible tables, and their ATE is τa​(Yθ)=θ1−θ0\tau_{a}(Y^{\theta})=\theta_{1}-\theta_{0}. Thus the perturbation coefficients are c1=1c_{1}=1 and c0=−1c_{0}=-1.

The treatment-arm set B1B_{1} is entirely missing exactly when every unit receives control. Under the common-shock construction, this occurs either when C=0C=0 and all εi=0\varepsilon_{i}=0, or when C=1C=1 and all εi=1\varepsilon_{i}=1. Its probability is therefore

ρn=12​{(1−η)n+ηn}=e−c2​{1−o⁡(1)}\rho_{n}=\frac{1}{2}\{(1-\eta)^{n}+\eta^{n}\}=\frac{e^{-c}}{2}\{1-o(1)\}

along the sequence η=c/n\eta=c/n. By symmetry, the control-arm set B0B_{0} is entirely missing with the same probability, on the event Z=1nZ=1^{n}. Although every unit has treatment probability 1/21/2, each entire arm therefore remains unobserved with probability bounded away from zero. Applying Theorem 4.1.2(ii) to the packing {B1,B0}\{B_{1},B_{0}\} gives

Runb​(Pcw,f,a)≥c12​ρn1−ρn+c02​ρn1−ρn=2​ρn1−ρn=2​e−c2−e−c​{1−o⁡(1)},R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{\rm cw};f,a)\geq c_{1}^{2}\frac{\rho_{n}}{1-\rho_{n}}+c_{0}^{2}\frac{\rho_{n}}{1-\rho_{n}}=2\frac{\rho_{n}}{1-\rho_{n}}=\frac{2e^{-c}}{2-e^{-c}}\,\{1-o(1)\},

which proves equation (56).

For the upper bound, use the HT estimator with the marginal treatment probabilities 1/21/2. Write Si=2​Zi−1S_{i}=2Z_{i}-1 and bi=Yi​(1)+Yi​(0)b_{i}=Y_{i}(1)+Y_{i}(0). Direct expansion gives

τ^HT=2n​∑i{Zi​Yi​(1)−(1−Zi)​Yi​(0)}=τa​(Y)+1n​∑ibi​Si.\widehat{\tau}_{\rm HT}=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i}\{Z_{i}Y_{i}(1)-(1-Z_{i})Y_{i}(0)\}=\tau_{a}(Y)+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}b_{i}S_{i}.

Since 𝔼​Si=0\mathbb{E}S_{i}=0, this estimator is unbiased for every admissible table. Moreover, Si=(2​C−1)​(1−2​εi)S_{i}=(2C-1)(1-2\varepsilon_{i}), so Var⁡(Si)=1\operatorname{Var}(S_{i})=1 and, for i≠ji\neq j, Cov⁡(Si,Sj)=𝔼⁡(Si​Sj)=(1−2​η)2\operatorname{Cov}(S_{i},S_{j})=\mathbb{E}(S_{i}S_{j})=(1-2\eta)^{2}. Consequently,

VarPcw⁡(τ^HT)=1n2​{∑ibi2+(1−2​η)2​∑i≠jbi​bj}≤4​{1n+(1−1n)​(1−2​η)2},\operatorname{Var}_{P_{\rm cw}}(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm HT})=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i}b_{i}^{2}+(1-2\eta)^{2}\sum_{i\neq j}b_{i}b_{j}\right\}\leq 4\left\{\frac{1}{n}+\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)(1-2\eta)^{2}\right\},

where the inequality uses |bi|≤2|b_{i}|\leq 2. This bound holds uniformly over the potential-outcome tables and proves equation (57).

∎

For fixed η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), each arm block is detected with probability tending to one, so the resulting missingness lower bound tends to zero. The scaling η=c/n\eta=c/n keeps the joint missingness probabilities bounded away from zero and gives the constant-order lower bound above. The example shows that the unweighted sampling hypergraph and first-order inclusion probabilities do not suffice to determine the unbiased fixed-design minimax rate.

B.5 From fixed-design lower bounds to lower bounds on restricted designs

In this subsection, we derive lower bounds for the joint minimax risks over a design class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The lower bounds from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2) bound the risk under a specified design and perturbation packing. To obtain a lower bound that optimizes over the design, we first take the supremum of the fixed design lower bounds over perturbation packings ℬ\mathcal{B} and the fixed perturbation signs sb,k∈{−1,1}s_{b,k}\in\{-1,1\}, and then take the infimum over designs in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The packing and signs giving the strongest lower bound may therefore differ across designs. We express the resulting bounds in terms of the attainable induced sampling designs 𝒬f​(𝒞)\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}), using Proposition 4.2.1. Corollary B.5.1 states these bounds for both estimator classes.

For an induced sampling design QQ, define

qQ(B)=∑A:A∩B≠∅Q(A)q_{Q}(B)=\sum_{A:A\cap B\neq\varnothing}Q(A)

to be the probability that at least one potential outcome in BB is observed. For a perturbation packing ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\}, define the detection vector qQ=(qQ​(B1),…,qQ​(Bm))q_{Q}=(q_{Q}(B_{1}),\ldots,q_{Q}(B_{m})). Its bbth entry is the probability that at least one potential outcome in BbB_{b} is observed under QQ. Fix perturbation signs s=(sb,k)s=(s_{b,k}), giving coefficients cb=∑k∈Bbak​sb,kc_{b}=\sum_{k\in B_{b}}a_{k}s_{b,k}. The all-estimator and unbiased-estimator lower bounds in Theorem 4.1.2 depend on QQ only through qQq_{Q}. Write their respective lower-bound expressions as

Φall(q;ℬ,s)=∑bcb2(1−qb),Φunb(q;ℬ,s)=∑b:cb≠0cb2(1qb−1).\Phi_{\rm all}(q;\mathcal{B},s)=\sum_{b}c_{b}^{2}(1-q_{b}),\qquad\Phi_{\rm unb}(q;\mathcal{B},s)=\sum_{b:c_{b}\neq 0}c_{b}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{q_{b}}-1\right). (58)

A term in Φunb\Phi_{\rm unb} is +∞+\infty if qb=0q_{b}=0 and cb≠0c_{b}\neq 0.

Corollary B.5.1 (Lower bounds under design restrictions).

For a design class 𝒞\mathcal{C},

Rall∗​(𝒞)≥infQ∈𝒬f​(𝒞)sup(ℬ,s)Φall​(qQ,ℬ,s),R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{C})\geq\inf_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C})}\sup_{(\mathcal{B},s)}\Phi_{\rm all}(q_{Q};\mathcal{B},s), (59)

and for unbiased estimation,

Runb∗​(𝒞)≥infQ∈𝒬f​(𝒞+)sup(ℬ,s)Φunb​(qQ,ℬ,s),R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{C})\geq\inf_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}_{+})}\sup_{(\mathcal{B},s)}\Phi_{\rm unb}(q_{Q};\mathcal{B},s), (60)

where in both displays the supremum is over perturbation packings and choices of signs.

For a fixed design PP, let Q=QP,fQ=Q_{P,f} be its induced sampling design. The lower bounds from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2) hold for every perturbation packing ℬ\mathcal{B} and choice of perturbation signs ss. Taking the supremum over these choices gives

Rall​(P)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{all}}(P) ≥sup(ℬ,s)Φall​(qQ,ℬ,s),\displaystyle\geq\sup_{(\mathcal{B},s)}\Phi_{\rm all}(q_{Q};\mathcal{B},s),
Runb​(P)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P) ≥sup(ℬ,s)Φunb​(qQ,ℬ,s).\displaystyle\geq\sup_{(\mathcal{B},s)}\Phi_{\rm unb}(q_{Q};\mathcal{B},s).

Taking the infimum over designs P∈𝒞P\in\mathcal{C} in the first inequality gives

infP∈𝒞Rall​(P)≥infP∈𝒞sup(ℬ,s)Φall​(qQP,f,ℬ,s)=infQ∈𝒬f​(𝒞)sup(ℬ,s)Φall​(qQ,ℬ,s).\inf_{P\in\mathcal{C}}R_{\mathrm{all}}(P)\geq\inf_{P\in\mathcal{C}}\sup_{(\mathcal{B},s)}\Phi_{\rm all}(q_{Q_{P,f}};\mathcal{B},s)=\inf_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C})}\sup_{(\mathcal{B},s)}\Phi_{\rm all}(q_{Q};\mathcal{B},s).

The last equality follows from the definition of 𝒬f​(𝒞)\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}): it is exactly the set of laws QP,fQ_{P,f} induced by designs in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The same calculation with Φunb\Phi_{\rm unb} and 𝒞+\mathcal{C}_{+} proves the unbiased statement. Designs outside 𝒞+\mathcal{C}_{+} have an unobservable relevant potential outcome and admit no unbiased estimator. ∎

When all designs on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} are allowed, take 𝒞=𝒫⁡(𝒵0)\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}) in the same bounds. The infimum then ranges over all probability laws on the hyperedges of ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0}). For the unbiased bound, restrict to laws that give every relevant potential outcome positive probability of observation.

For a restricted class, the feasible observed sets are not sufficient to specify the attainable probabilities. Section B.4 gives two designs with the same support and first-order inclusion probabilities whose minimax risks differ by a factor of nn.

Remark B.3 (Order of optimization).

Corollary B.5.1 places the supremum over perturbation packings and signs inside the infimum over induced sampling designs. The inequality infQsup(ℬ,s)Φ≥sup(ℬ,s)infQΦ\inf_{Q}\sup_{(\mathcal{B},s)}\Phi\geq\sup_{(\mathcal{B},s)}\inf_{Q}\Phi holds for either lower-bound expression Φ\Phi, but the two orders have different meanings. In the stated order, the perturbation packing and signs may be chosen separately for each allowed induced sampling design QQ, to give the strongest lower bound for that law. Thus the worst-case potential-outcome perturbations may differ across designs in the class. In the swapped order, a single packing and choice of signs must give a lower bound uniformly over all allowed induced sampling designs; the resulting lower bound can be zero even when the stated order gives a positive lower bound. Any fixed packing ℬ\mathcal{B} and signs ss nevertheless give the valid, and in general weaker, lower bound infQ∈𝒬f​(𝒞)Φ⁡(qQ,ℬ,s)\inf_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C})}\Phi(q_{Q};\mathcal{B},s). For the unbiased problem, the same comparison uses Q∈𝒬f​(𝒞+)Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{f}(\mathcal{C}_{+}).

B.6 Lower bounds for the all-design minimax risk from the sampling hypergraph

The preceding subsection optimized the fixed-design packing lower bounds over attainable induced sampling designs. When all designs on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} are allowed, every probability law on the feasible hyperedges is attainable (Lemma B.3.2). In this subsection, we derive explicit lower-bound functionals of the unweighted sampling hypergraph for the joint minimax problems, optimizing over all designs and either all estimators or unbiased estimators. We obtain these lower bounds by controlling which perturbation sets of potential outcomes a feasible assignment can reveal and which must remain unobserved. The functionals use the hypergraph restricted to the estimand-relevant indices and the estimand coefficients.

We begin by proving Theorem B.6.1, which is the general result underlying all the lower bound results in this subsection. It applies to arbitrary linear estimands and gives lower bounds for both estimator classes. We then develop three specializations of this theorem, used throughout the applications to exploit different constraints on which relevant potential outcomes can be observed together. First, in Section B.6.2, Theorem 4.3.1 gives a reciprocal sampling-rank lower bound. This lower bound uses only one arm of an estimand and bounds minimax risks of both estimator classes in terms of the largest number of that arm’s potential outcomes observable under a single assignment. Second, in Section B.6.3, Corollary B.6.2 gives lower bounds based on exposure counts by using two arms together, and Corollary B.6.3 extends the result to finitely many arms. These bounds apply to unbiased estimators and depend on the expected exposure counts jointly attainable across the arms. Third, the specialization in Section B.6.4 groups potential-outcomes within two arms and pairs the groups across arms. Theorem B.6.4 allows unequal weights across pairs and gives a lower bound valid for all estimators. When all pairs have equal weight, it yields Theorem 4.3.2.

Before developing these bounds, we define the restrictions of the sampling hypergraph to the estimand-relevant potential outcomes and to individual arms.

Definition B.1 (Estimand and arm traces).

For an estimand aa, let Ka={k∈K:ak≠0}K_{a}=\{k\in K:a_{k}\neq 0\} be its relevant set of potential outcomes. The estimand trace of the sampling hypergraph is

ℋobsa​(f,𝒵0)=(Ka,{Of​(z)∩Ka:z∈𝒵0}).\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}^{a}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0})=\bigl(K_{a},\{O_{f}(z)\cap K_{a}:z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}\}\bigr). (61)

If A⊆KaA\subseteq K_{a} is a set of potential outcomes, the trace on AA is

ℋobsA​(f,𝒵0)=(A,{Of​(z)∩A:z∈𝒵0}).\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}^{A}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0})=\bigl(A,\{O_{f}(z)\cap A:z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}\}\bigr).

When the sampling hypergraph is abbreviated by ℋ\mathcal{H}, we write these traces as ℋa\mathcal{H}^{a} and ℋA\mathcal{H}^{A}. Thus ℋa\mathcal{H}^{a} is the sampling hypergraph restricted to the estimand-relevant potential outcomes. The trace ℋA\mathcal{H}^{A} retains only the vertices in AA and intersects each original hyperedge with AA. When AA consists of the potential outcomes in one exposure arm of a two-arm contrast, we call it an arm trace. The estimand trace retains constraints on observing different arms together, even when each arm can be observed in full under a separate assignment. To derive a lower bound using only a subset A⊆KaA\subseteq K_{a}, we restrict attention to admissible tables whose potential outcomes outside AA are fixed at zero. A lower bound over this smaller class is also a lower bound for the original problem. We use this restriction below to obtain one-arm lower bounds.

B.6.1 General lower bounds for linear estimands from the sampling hypergraph

In this subsection, we derive general lower bounds for the joint minimax risks of an arbitrary linear estimand τa\tau_{a}, optimizing over all designs on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} and either all estimators or unbiased estimators. The lower bounds are expressed as functionals of the estimand trace ℋobsa\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}^{a} and the coefficients of the estimand.

Fix a perturbation packing ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\} and perturbation signs sb,k∈{−1,1}s_{b,k}\in\{-1,1\}, defining cb=∑k∈Bbak​sb,kc_{b}=\sum_{k\in B_{b}}a_{k}s_{b,k}. Each BbB_{b} indexes a set of potential outcomes that vary with one unknown sign θb\theta_{b} under the hypercube prior. Observing any outcome in BbB_{b} reveals θb\theta_{b}; observing no outcome in BbB_{b} leaves θb\theta_{b} unknown. Thus, an assignment zz detects the perturbation on BbB_{b} exactly when the corresponding hyperedge Of​(z)O_{f}(z) intersects BbB_{b}. For the all-estimator lower bound, each undetected set BbB_{b} contributes cb2c_{b}^{2} to the posterior variance of the estimand. The expected posterior variance lower bounds the minimax risk. We therefore bound the posterior variance of the estimand remaining under every feasible assignment.

Write ℋobsa=(Ka,ℰa)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}^{a}=(K_{a},\mathcal{E}_{a}), where ℰa={Of​(z)∩Ka:z∈𝒵0}\mathcal{E}_{a}=\{O_{f}(z)\cap K_{a}:z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}\} is its set of hyperedges. To quantify how much a feasible assignment detects or misses a perturbation, assign a nonnegative weight ubu_{b} to each perturbation set BbB_{b}, and write u=(ub)u=(u_{b}). The maximum observed weight is the largest total weight of perturbation sets detected by a feasible hyperedge,

νu(ℋobsa,ℬ)=maxE∈ℰa∑b:E∩Bb≠∅ub,\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})=\max_{E\in\mathcal{E}_{a}}\sum_{b:E\cap B_{b}\neq\varnothing}u_{b}, (62)

and the minimum missing weight is the smallest total weight of perturbation sets missed by a feasible hyperedge,

μu(ℋobsa,ℬ)=minE∈ℰa∑b:E∩Bb=∅ub=∑bub−νu(ℋobsa,ℬ).\mu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})=\min_{E\in\mathcal{E}_{a}}\sum_{b:E\cap B_{b}=\varnothing}u_{b}=\sum_{b}u_{b}-\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B}). (63)

For fixed packing and weights, both quantities depend only on the feasible hyperedges. For the all-estimator bound, we take ub=cb2u_{b}=c_{b}^{2}. The minimum missing weight, written μc2\mu_{c^{2}}, then bounds the posterior variance remaining under every assignment. For the unbiased bound, the weights can be chosen freely. In this case, the maximum observed weight bounds ∑bub​qb\sum_{b}u_{b}q_{b}, where qbq_{b} is the probability of detecting BbB_{b}. The proof uses this bound with Cauchy–Schwarz to control the reciprocal detection probabilities.

Theorem B.6.1 (General lower bounds from the sampling hypergraph).

For every perturbation packing and every choice of signs,

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0),f,a)≥μc2​(ℋobsa,ℬ).R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0});f,a\bigr)\geq\mu_{c^{2}}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B}). (64)

For every such packing and signs, and every u≥0u\geq 0 with νu​(ℋobsa,ℬ)>0\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})>0,

Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0),f,a)≥(∑b|cb|​ub)2νu​(ℋobsa,ℬ)−∑bcb2.R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0});f,a\bigr)\geq\frac{\bigl(\sum_{b}|c_{b}|\sqrt{u_{b}}\bigr)^{2}}{\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})}-\sum_{b}c_{b}^{2}. (65)

Both right-hand sides may be maximized over packings and signs.

When every perturbation set has weight u0u_{0}, the minimum missing weight is u0u_{0} times the smallest number of sets missed by a feasible hyperedge:

μu​(ℋobsa,ℬ)=u0​{|ℬ|−maxE∈ℰa⁡#⁡{b:E∩Bb≠∅}},\mu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})=u_{0}\Bigl\{|\mathcal{B}|-\max_{E\in\mathcal{E}_{a}}\#\{b:E\cap B_{b}\neq\varnothing\}\Bigr\}, (66)

Fix a perturbation packing, its signs, and a design PP. We first apply the fixed-design lower bounds from disjoint perturbations. For each estimator class, we then obtain a lower bound independent of PP, which also bounds the infimum over all designs. Write Q=QP,fQ=Q_{P,f}, qb=qQ​(Bb)=qP​(Bb)q_{b}=q_{Q}(B_{b})=q_{P}(B_{b}), and E=Of​(Z)E=O_{f}(Z) for the observed hyperedge. Since each Bb⊆KaB_{b}\subseteq K_{a}, replacing EE by its trace E∩KaE\cap K_{a} does not change whether it intersects BbB_{b}.

For all estimators, the fixed-design lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2(i)) gives

Rall​(P)≥∑bcb2​(1−qb).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P)\geq\sum_{b}c_{b}^{2}(1-q_{b}).

For each feasible observed hyperedge EE, the definition of the maximum observed weight gives

∑b:E∩Bb≠∅cb2≤νc2(ℋobsa,ℬ).\sum_{b:E\cap B_{b}\neq\varnothing}c_{b}^{2}\leq\nu_{c^{2}}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B}).

Therefore,

∑bcb2qb=𝔼Q[∑b:E∩Bb≠∅cb2]≤νc2(ℋobsa,ℬ).\sum_{b}c_{b}^{2}q_{b}=\mathbb{E}_{Q}\left[\sum_{b:E\cap B_{b}\neq\varnothing}c_{b}^{2}\right]\leq\nu_{c^{2}}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B}).

Substituting into the fixed-design lower bound yields

Rall​(P)≥∑bcb2−νc2​(ℋobsa,ℬ)=μc2​(ℋobsa,ℬ).R_{\mathrm{all}}(P)\geq\sum_{b}c_{b}^{2}-\nu_{c^{2}}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})=\mu_{c^{2}}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B}).

The right-hand side is the same for every PP. Taking the infimum over all designs proves equation (64).

For unbiased estimators, only perturbation sets with nonzero set effect cbc_{b} contribute to the fixed-design lower bound. Define their index set by

J={b∈{1,…,m}:cb≠0}.J=\{b\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:c_{b}\neq 0\}.

For b∉Jb\notin J, changing the sign on BbB_{b} does not change the estimand, so these sets contribute zero to the lower bound. If qb=0q_{b}=0 for some b∈Jb\in J, the design never detects a perturbation that changes the estimand; no unbiased estimator exists and the claimed lower bound holds. Otherwise, the fixed-design lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2(ii)) gives

Runb​(P)≥∑b∈Jcb2qb−∑b∈Jcb2.R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P)\geq\sum_{b\in J}\frac{c_{b}^{2}}{q_{b}}-\sum_{b\in J}c_{b}^{2}. (67)

Fix nonnegative weights u=(ub)b=1mu=(u_{b})_{b=1}^{m} with νu​(ℋobsa,ℬ)>0\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})>0. Cauchy–Schwarz gives

(∑b∈J|cb|​ub)2=(∑b∈J|cb|qb​ub​qb)2≤(∑b∈Jcb2qb)​(∑b∈Jub​qb).\left(\sum_{b\in J}|c_{b}|\sqrt{u_{b}}\right)^{2}=\left(\sum_{b\in J}\frac{|c_{b}|}{\sqrt{q_{b}}}\sqrt{u_{b}q_{b}}\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sum_{b\in J}\frac{c_{b}^{2}}{q_{b}}\right)\left(\sum_{b\in J}u_{b}q_{b}\right). (68)

For every feasible hyperedge EE, nonnegativity of the weights and the definition of νu\nu_{u} imply

∑b∈J:E∩Bb≠∅ub≤∑1≤b≤m:E∩Bb≠∅ub≤νu(ℋobsa,ℬ).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in J:\ E\cap B_{b}\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}u_{b}\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq b\leq m:\ E\cap B_{b}\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}u_{b}\leq\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B}). (69)

Taking expectations in equation (69), the expected detected weight of the sets indexed by JJ satisfies

∑b∈Jubqb=𝔼Q[∑b∈J:E∩Bb≠∅ub]≤νu(ℋobsa,ℬ).\sum_{b\in J}u_{b}q_{b}=\mathbb{E}_{Q}\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in J:\ E\cap B_{b}\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}u_{b}\right]\leq\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B}). (70)

Combining equation (70) with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in equation (68) and dividing by the positive quantity νu​(ℋobsa,ℬ)\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B}) gives

∑b∈Jcb2qb≥(∑b∈J|cb|​ub)2νu​(ℋobsa,ℬ).\sum_{b\in J}\frac{c_{b}^{2}}{q_{b}}\geq\frac{\bigl(\sum_{b\in J}|c_{b}|\sqrt{u_{b}}\bigr)^{2}}{\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})}. (71)

Substituting equation (71) into the fixed-design unbiased lower bound in equation (67) yields

Runb​(P)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P) ≥(∑b∈J|cb|​ub)2νu​(ℋobsa,ℬ)−∑b∈Jcb2\displaystyle\geq\frac{\bigl(\sum_{b\in J}|c_{b}|\sqrt{u_{b}}\bigr)^{2}}{\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})}-\sum_{b\in J}c_{b}^{2} (72)
=(∑b=1m|cb|​ub)2νu​(ℋobsa,ℬ)−∑b=1mcb2,\displaystyle=\frac{\bigl(\sum_{b=1}^{m}|c_{b}|\sqrt{u_{b}}\bigr)^{2}}{\nu_{u}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a},\mathcal{B})}-\sum_{b=1}^{m}c_{b}^{2},

where the equality uses cb=0c_{b}=0 for b∉Jb\notin J. The right-hand side is the same for every PP. Taking the infimum over all designs proves equation (65). ∎

B.6.2 Lower bounds based on one arm of an estimand

In this subsection, we derive lower bounds for the joint minimax risks using the sampling rank of one equal-weight arm of an estimand. The sampling rank r⁡(V)r(V) is the largest number of potential outcomes in VV that any feasible assignment can observe. For unbiased estimators, we use singleton perturbation sets to get the rank based lower bounds. For lower bounds on all estimators, we group potential outcomes into perturbation sets so that every assignment leaves sufficiently many sets of potential outcomes unobserved. We obtain both lower bounds by applying the general lower bounds from the sampling hypergraph (Theorem B.6.1). We restate the one-arm theorem before giving the two constructions.

For the chosen arm VV, define the observed exposure count nV​(z)=|Of​(z)∩V|n_{V}(z)=|O_{f}(z)\cap V|. nV​(z)n_{V}(z) is the number of units revealing a potential outcome in VV under assignment zz. For a full exposure-dd arm, nV​(z)=nd​(z)n_{V}(z)=n_{d}(z) from Section 3.3. Since r⁡(V)=maxz∈𝒵0⁡nV​(z)r(V)=\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}}n_{V}(z), every design PP on 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0} satisfies

𝔼P​[nV​(Z)]=∑k∈VπP,k≤r⁡(V).\mathbb{E}_{P}[n_{V}(Z)]=\sum_{k\in V}\pi_{P,k}\leq r(V).

Thus no design can make the expected exposure count within VV 𝔼P​[nV​(Z)]\mathbb{E}_{P}[n_{V}(Z)] exceed the rank r⁡(V)r(V). For unbiased estimation, the singleton lower bound and Cauchy–Schwarz give Runb​(P)≥A2​{1/𝔼P​[nV​(Z)]−1/NV}R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P)\geq A^{2}\{1/\mathbb{E}_{P}[n_{V}(Z)]-1/N_{V}\} whenever all indices in VV have positive observation probability. Substituting 𝔼P​[nV​(Z)]≤r⁡(V)\mathbb{E}_{P}[n_{V}(Z)]\leq r(V) gives the reciprocal-rank lower bound below; if a relevant index has zero observation probability, no unbiased estimator exists. The all-estimator argument instead uses the grouped perturbations described above.

Theorem 4.3.1 (Reciprocal sampling-rank lower bound).

Let V⊆KaV\subseteq K_{a} contain NV=|V|N_{V}=|V| relevant potential outcomes from one estimand arm, each with estimand coefficient satisfying |ak|=A/NV|a_{k}|=A/N_{V}. Write ℋobs​(f,𝒵0)=(K,ℰ)\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{obs}}(f;\mathcal{Z}_{0})=(K,\mathcal{E}) and define the sampling rank

r⁡(V)=maxE∈ℰ⁡|E∩V|.r(V)=\max_{E\in\mathcal{E}}|E\cap V|.

If r⁡(V)≥1r(V)\geq 1, then

Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥A2​{1r⁡(V)−1NV}.R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\geq A^{2}\left\{\frac{1}{r(V)}-\frac{1}{N_{V}}\right\}. (18)

For all estimators, if 1≤r⁡(V)≤(1−ϵ)​NV1\leq r(V)\leq(1-\epsilon)N_{V} for some 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, then

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥A2​cϵr⁡(V)R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\geq\frac{A^{2}c_{\epsilon}}{r(V)} (19)

for a constant cϵ>0c_{\epsilon}>0 depending only on ϵ\epsilon.

Here A=∑k∈V|ak|A=\sum_{k\in V}|a_{k}| is the total absolute coefficient weight on VV. Throughout the proof, use the restricted outcome class

𝒴V​(f)={Y∈𝒴⁡(f):Yk=0​ for every ​k∉V}.\mathcal{Y}_{V}(f)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f):Y_{k}=0\text{ for every }k\notin V\}.

Since 𝒴V​(f)⊆𝒴​(f)\mathcal{Y}_{V}(f)\subseteq\mathcal{Y}(f), the worst-case risk of any fixed design and estimator over 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f) is at least its worst-case risk over 𝒴V​(f)\mathcal{Y}_{V}(f). Thus a lower bound on the minimax risk over 𝒴V​(f)\mathcal{Y}_{V}(f) is also a lower bound for the original problem. The same conclusion holds for unbiased estimation: every estimator unbiased on 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f) is also unbiased on 𝒴V​(f)\mathcal{Y}_{V}(f). If r⁡(V)=0r(V)=0, every assignment misses VV. Apply the lower bounds from disjoint perturbations in Theorem 4.1.2 with the one-set packing ℬ={V}\mathcal{B}=\{V\} and signs s1,k=sign⁡(ak)s_{1,k}=\operatorname{sign}(a_{k}) for k∈Vk\in V. Then c1=∑k∈V|ak|=Ac_{1}=\sum_{k\in V}|a_{k}|=A and ρP​(V)=1\rho_{P}(V)=1 for every design PP. Part (i) of Theorem 4.1.2 gives the all-estimator lower bound A2A^{2}, and part (ii) of the same theorem shows that no unbiased estimator exists when A>0A>0. In the remainder assume r⁡(V)≥1r(V)\geq 1. To prove equation (18), use the singleton packing of VV and take ub=1u_{b}=1. Since every assignment reveals at most r⁡(V)r(V) potential outcomes in VV, νu=r⁡(V)\nu_{u}=r(V), while |cb|=A/NV|c_{b}|=A/N_{V}. Theorem  B.6.1 gives

Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥(NV​A/NV)2r⁡(V)−NV​(A/NV)2=A2​{1r⁡(V)−1NV}.R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\geq\frac{(N_{V}A/N_{V})^{2}}{r(V)}-N_{V}(A/N_{V})^{2}=A^{2}\left\{\frac{1}{r(V)}-\frac{1}{N_{V}}\right\}.

In some cases, the lower bounds based on each individual arm are not sufficient. The following two subsections obtains stronger lower bounds by considering both arms together. For example, for the total treatment effect under neighborhood interference, each arm can be observed in full under a separate assignment: z=1nz=1^{n} reveals Yi​(1Ni+)Y_{i}(1_{N_{i}^{+}}) for all units, while z=0nz=0^{n} reveals Yi​(0Ni+)Y_{i}(0_{N_{i}^{+}}) for all units. Thus both arms have rank nn, and the one-arm rank lower bounds in Theorem 4.3.1 are uninformative. We first use singleton perturbations and unbiasedness to obtain bounds based on expected exposure counts (Section B.6.3). We then allow grouped perturbations to obtain bounds valid for all estimators. (Section B.6.4)

B.6.3 Lower bounds for unbiased estimators based on expected exposure counts

In this subsection, we derive lower bounds for the joint minimax risk over all designs and unbiased estimators in terms of the expected exposure counts achievable by a single design. The one-arm rank bounds from the previous section maximize each arm’s observed exposure count nV​(z)n_{V}(z) separately over assignments, giving r⁡(V)=maxz∈𝒵0⁡nV​(z)r(V)=\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}}n_{V}(z). Here we instead consider the expected exposure counts of both arms jointly attainable under a single design. This retains the tradeoff between counts in the two arms. We first consider two arms and then extend the argument to multiple arms.

Consider an equal-weight contrast between two arms. Let V+,V−⊆KaV_{+},V_{-}\subseteq K_{a} be the positive and negative arms, which partition KaK_{a}, and write N+=|V+|N_{+}=|V_{+}| and N−=|V−|N_{-}=|V_{-}|. Since E=Of​(z)∩KaE=O_{f}(z)\cap K_{a}, we have n±​(z)=|E∩V±|n_{\pm}(z)=|E\cap V_{\pm}|. We call r±​(E)r_{\pm}(E) the exposure-count vector. Writing ℋobsa=(Ka,ℰa)\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a}=(K_{a},\mathcal{E}_{a}), define the region of attainable expected exposure counts by

ℭ±​(ℋobsa)=conv⁡{r±​(E):E∈ℰa}.\mathfrak{C}_{\pm}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a})=\operatorname{conv}\{r_{\pm}(E):E\in\mathcal{E}_{a}\}.

The pair (x+​(P),x−​(P))(x_{+}(P),x_{-}(P)) is an average of the feasible exposure-count vectors, with probabilities supplied by PP, and therefore belongs to ℭ±\mathfrak{C}_{\pm}. Conversely, choose a point x=∑j=1Jλj​r±​(Ej)∈ℭ±x=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\lambda_{j}r_{\pm}(E_{j})\in\mathfrak{C}_{\pm}, where Ej∈ℰaE_{j}\in\mathcal{E}_{a}, λj≥0\lambda_{j}\geq 0, and ∑j=1Jλj=1\sum_{j=1}^{J}\lambda_{j}=1. The lower bound involves the reciprocals of the expected exposure counts in both arms, with the finite-arm corrections 1/N+1/N_{+} and 1/N−1/N_{-}. Optimizing over the attainable region allows the design to balance these counts, subject to the constraints imposed by feasible assignments.

B.6.4 Lower bounds for all estimators based on paired perturbation sets

The exposure-count lower bounds of Section B.6.3 need not capture the full difficulty of estimation. Consider again the total treatment effect, now on a complete graph. Each arm has sampling rank nn, so the one-arm rank lower bounds in Theorem 4.3.1 give a trivial lower bound of zero. On the other hand, Corollary B.6.2 gives the lower bound 2/n2/n for unbiased estimators: every assignment reveals either an entire arm or neither arm, so the expected exposure counts satisfy x++x−≤nx_{+}+x_{-}\leq n. The reciprocal-count expression is minimized at x+=x−=n/2x_{+}=x_{-}=n/2, achieved by choosing the all-treated or all-control assignment with equal probability, and its value is 2/n2/n.

However, no assignment reveals outcomes from both TTE arms. Put a prior on potential-outcome tables by setting every treatment-arm outcome equal to one uniform random sign and every control-arm outcome equal to another independent uniform random sign, with all other potential outcomes fixed at zero. Every assignment leaves at least one of these signs unobserved. The resulting posterior variance of the TTE is therefore at least 11, giving a lower bound of 11 over all designs and estimators.

Theorem B.6.4 below generalizes this construction to paired groups from the two arms and yields the stronger lower bound in this example. Specifically, we group potential outcomes within each arm and pair the groups across arms, assigning an independent unknown sign to each group. Unlike the singleton construction used for the exposure-count lower bounds, each group may contain several potential outcomes. An assignment reveals both signs in a pair only if it observes at least one outcome in each group. Otherwise, at least one sign remains unknown and contributes to the posterior variance of the estimand.

Bounding how many pairs a single assignment can observe on both sides gives a lower bound for the joint minimax risk over all designs and estimators. We obtain this bound by applying the general hypergraph lower bound (Theorem B.6.1) to the disjoint sets forming the pairs. Theorem B.6.4 allows unequal weights across pairs; its equal-weight specialization gives Theorem 4.3.2, used in the neighborhood and bipartite examples. The same bounds hold for unbiased estimators because they form a smaller estimator class.

Definition B.2 (Arm-paired packing and maximum jointly observed pair count).

An arm-paired packing is a perturbation packing ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\} in which every set carries a splitting Bb=Bb+∪Bb−B_{b}=B_{b}^{+}\cup B_{b}^{-} into two disjoint nonempty parts, one drawn from each arm of the contrast, together with perturbation signs sb,ks_{b,k} for which the two parts carry equal weight,

wb=|∑k∈Bb+sb,k​ak|=|∑k∈Bb−sb,k​ak|.w_{b}=\Bigl|\sum_{k\in B_{b}^{+}}s_{b,k}a_{k}\Bigr|=\Bigl|\sum_{k\in B_{b}^{-}}s_{b,k}a_{k}\Bigr|. (83)

The two parts carry separate unknown signs under the hypercube prior. A hyperedge E∈ℋobsaE\in\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a} reveals both signs, and hence resolves the pair BbB_{b}, when it meets both parts, E∩Bb+≠∅E\cap B_{b}^{+}\neq\varnothing and E∩Bb−≠∅E\cap B_{b}^{-}\neq\varnothing. The maximum jointly observed pair count of the packing is the largest number of pairs any one feasible hyperedge resolves,

ℳ⁡(ℬ)=maxE∈ℋobsa⁡#⁡{b≤m:E​ resolves ​Bb}.\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{B})=\max_{E\in\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a}}\#\{b\leq m:\ E\text{ resolves }B_{b}\}. (84)
Theorem B.6.4 (Arm-paired set certificate).

Let ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{m}\} be an arm-paired packing with per-arm weights wbw_{b} and maximum jointly observed pair count ℳ=ℳ⁡(ℬ)\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{B}). Then the joint minimax risks satisfy

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥∑b=1mwb2−max⁡∑b∈SS⊆[m],|S|≤ℳ⁡wb2,R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\ \geq\ \sum_{b=1}^{m}w_{b}^{2}\ -\ \max_{S\subseteq[m],\,|S|\leq\mathcal{M}}\ \sum_{b\in S}w_{b}^{2}, (85)

that is, the total squared per-arm weight less its ℳ\mathcal{M} largest terms. The same bound holds for Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr). In particular:

  1. (i)

    if no feasible hyperedge resolves any set, then Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥∑bwb2R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\geq\sum_{b}w_{b}^{2};

    if the per-arm weights are equal, wb=A/mw_{b}=A/m for every bb, then

    Suppose in addition that arm-paired packings with equal per-arm weights exist for every m≤Nm\leq N and that their maximum jointly observed pair counts obey a common bound ℳ⁡(ℬm)≤ℳ\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{B}_{m})\leq\mathcal{M}. Then optimizing mm gives A2/(4​ℳ)A^{2}/(4\mathcal{M}) when 1≤ℳ≤N/21\leq\mathcal{M}\leq N/2, and A2A^{2} when ℳ=0\mathcal{M}=0.

The collection

ℬ~={Bb+,Bb−:b=1,…,m}\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}=\{B_{b}^{+},B_{b}^{-}:b=1,\ldots,m\}

For the next restatement, let Bb+B_{b}^{+} and Bb−B_{b}^{-}, b=1,…,mb=1,\ldots,m, be nonempty, pairwise disjoint sets of potential outcomes from the two respective arms, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the largest number of pairs for which one feasible observed set meets both parts, as in equation (84).

Theorem 4.3.2 (Lower bound from paired perturbation sets).

For the arm-paired packing {Bb+,Bb−:b≤m}\{B_{b}^{+},B_{b}^{-}:b\leq m\}, suppose that each of the 2​m2m parts carries the same estimand weight,

∑k∈Bb+|ak|=∑k∈Bb−|ak|=Am,b=1,…,m.\sum_{k\in B_{b}^{+}}|a_{k}|=\sum_{k\in B_{b}^{-}}|a_{k}|=\frac{A}{m},\qquad b=1,\ldots,m.

The same bound holds for Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr).

The pairs in the theorem form an arm-paired packing. Choose the fixed signs to align with the estimand coefficients on each part. Then

wb=∑k∈Bb+|ak|=∑k∈Bb−|ak|=Am.w_{b}=\sum_{k\in B_{b}^{+}}|a_{k}|=\sum_{k\in B_{b}^{-}}|a_{k}|=\frac{A}{m}.

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))≥A2​m−ℳm2,R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr)\geq A^{2}\frac{m-\mathcal{M}}{m^{2}},

and the same bound for Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0))R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0})\bigr). ∎

Theorem B.6.4 is applied in Appendices F and G. When no assignment resolves any pair, part (i) gives the sum of squared per-arm weights as a lower bound, as in the packed-neighborhood bound for the total effect (Lemma F.4.1). When at most ℳ\mathcal{M} pairs can be resolved, equal-weight packings and part (ii) give a reciprocal-capacity lower bound under the stated packing-size condition. This is used in the block-resolution bound for the total effect (Lemma F.4.2) and in the bipartite dose example.

B.7 Comparison with conflict-graph lower bounds

In this subsection, we compare the lower bounds based on the sampling hypergraph with lower bounds based on the conflict graph of Kandiros et al. (2026a) for the all-design minimax problem. We first show that the independence number of the conflict graph is an upper bound of the sampling rank, so replacing the rank by the independence number can weaken the resulting lower bound. We then show that under the setting of neighborhood interference with the identity exposure mapping and unrestricted treatment assignments, the conflict graph and sampling hypergraph determine one another. We also prove the corresponding statement for the restriction of the hypergraph and the conflict graph to estimand-relevant potential outcomes. As a consequence, in this specific setting, the independence number of the conflict graph is equal to the sampling rank, and the conflict graph contains all the information needed for the all-design minimax problem. Finally, we consider cases when assignment restrictions or coarsened exposure mappings break this equivalence, and the sampling hypergraph strictly contains more information than the conflict graph.

B.7.1 Pairwise observability and sampling rank

Fix an exposure mapping ff and a nonempty set of feasible treatment assignments 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}. Recall that the sampling hypergraph is ℋops=(K,ℰ)\mathcal{H}_{\rm ops}=(K,\mathcal{E}), where KK is the set of potential outcomes and ℰ={Of​(z):z∈𝒵0}\mathcal{E}=\{O_{f}(z):z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}\} is the collection of hyperedges recording the maximal sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly observed. For a given assignment z∈𝒵0z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}, write E=Of​(z)E=O_{f}(z) for the corresponding hyperedge. Fix a nonempty set T⊆KT\subseteq K of potential outcomes, each individually attainable under 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}. In the sampling hypergraph, a collection of nodes is contained in a hyperedge if and only if the corresponding potential outcomes can be jointly observed under a single treatment assignment. The sampling rank of TT is defined as

r⁡(T)=maxE∈ℰ⁡|E∩T|.r(T)=\max_{E\in\mathcal{E}}|E\cap T|. (91)

r⁡(T)r(T) is the largest number of potential outcomes in TT that one feasible assignment reveals.

Definition B.3 (Pairwise conflicts and conflict graph).

For an exposure mapping ff and nonempty feasible assignment set 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}, two distinct potential outcomes Yk,YℓY_{k},Y_{\ell} have a pairwise conflict if Ik​(z)​Iℓ​(z)=0I_{k}(z)I_{\ell}(z)=0 for every z∈𝒵0z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}: at least one outcome in the pair must remain missing under every feasible assignment. The conflict graph HconfH_{\rm conf} has vertex set KK. Distinct vertices k,ℓ∈Kk,\ell\in K are adjacent in the conflict graph if and only if their potential outcomes have a pairwise conflict. For T⊆KT\subseteq K, write Hconf​[T]H_{\rm conf}[T] for the induced subgraph on TT, retaining exactly the conflict edges with both endpoints in TT.

Recall from Section 4.2 that a collection S⊆TS\subseteq T is pairwise observable if each pair of distinct potential outcomes in SS can be observed under some feasible assignment; the assignment may differ across pairs. The collection is jointly observable if one feasible assignment observes every potential outcome in SS. To express this distinction in terms of assignments, recall the revelation sets

𝒵k={z∈𝒵0:Ik​(z)=1}={z∈𝒵0:k∈Of​(z)},k∈K.\mathcal{Z}_{k}=\{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}:I_{k}(z)=1\}=\{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}:k\in O_{f}(z)\},\qquad k\in K. (92)

Thus SS is pairwise observable if and only if 𝒵k∩𝒵ℓ≠∅\mathcal{Z}_{k}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\neq\varnothing for every distinct k,ℓ∈Sk,\ell\in S, equivalently SS is an independent set in Hconf​[T]H_{\rm conf}[T]. In contrast, SS is jointly observable if and only if ⋂k∈S𝒵k≠∅\bigcap_{k\in S}\mathcal{Z}_{k}\neq\varnothing, equivalently SS is contained in a hyperedge of the sampling hypergraph. Pairwise intersections need not imply a common intersection, so pairwise observability of SS need not imply joint observability.

However, every jointly observable collection SS is pairwise observable. In particular, the set of potential outcomes E∩TE\cap T is an independent set in Hconf​[T]H_{\rm conf}[T] for every hyperedge E∈ℰE\in\mathcal{E}, giving

r⁡(T)≤α⁡{Hconf​[T]}.r(T)\leq\alpha\{H_{\rm conf}[T]\}. (93)

Here r⁡(T)r(T) is the largest size of a jointly observable collection in TT, whereas α​{Hconf​[T]}\alpha\{H_{\rm conf}[T]\} is the largest size of a pairwise observable collection in TT. When TT lies in one estimand arm, the rank-based lower bounds of Theorem 4.3.1 have r⁡(T)r(T) in the denominator. Replacing r⁡(T)r(T) by the potentially larger independence number can therefore weaken these lower bounds.

B.7.2 Equivalence of the conflict graph and sampling hypergraph under identity neighborhood exposures

We now show that under identity neighborhood exposures and unrestricted treatment assignments, pairwise observability implies joint observability. Consequently, the rank inequality in (93) is an equality. In particular, the next theorem shows that under neighborhood interference with identity exposure mapping, and unrestricted treatment assignments, the hyperedges of the sampling hypergraph with the maximal independent sets in HconfH_{\rm conf}, showing that the two representations determine one another.

Theorem B.7.1 (Equivalence of the conflict graph and sampling hypergraph).

Suppose 𝒵0={0,1}n\mathcal{Z}_{0}=\{0,1\}^{n} and, for every k=(i,e)∈Kk=(i,e)\in K, observing Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e) requires precisely the neighborhood configuration zNi+=ez_{N_{i}^{+}}=e, with treatment assignments outside Ni+N_{i}^{+} unrestricted. Thus

𝒵(i,e)={z∈{0,1}n:zNi+=e}.\mathcal{Z}_{(i,e)}=\{z\in\{0,1\}^{n}:z_{N_{i}^{+}}=e\}.

Then the hyperedge set ℰ\mathcal{E} is exactly the family of maximal independent sets of the conflict graph HconfH_{\rm conf}:

ℰ={S⊆K:S​ is maximal independent in ​Hconf}.\mathcal{E}=\{S\subseteq K:S\text{ is maximal independent in }H_{\rm conf}\}. (94)

Conversely, two distinct vertices are adjacent in HconfH_{\rm conf} if and only if no hyperedge contains both. Thus the conflict graph and sampling hypergraph determine one another.

First, note that the sampling hypergraph determines the conflict graph: two distinct vertices are adjacent in the conflict graph whenever no hyperedge contains both vertices.

Next, we prove that every independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf} is jointly observable. In terms of the revelation sets, the key implication is that, for every S⊆KS\subseteq K,

[𝒵k∩𝒵ℓ≠∅ for every distinct k,ℓ∈S]⟹⋂k∈S𝒵k≠∅.\bigl[\mathcal{Z}_{k}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\neq\varnothing\text{ for every distinct }k,\ell\in S\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bigcap_{k\in S}\mathcal{Z}_{k}\neq\varnothing.

To prove this implication, suppose 𝒵k∩𝒵ℓ≠∅\mathcal{Z}_{k}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\neq\varnothing for every distinct k,ℓ∈Sk,\ell\in S. For k=(i,e)k=(i,e) and ℓ=(j,e′)\ell=(j,e^{\prime}), an assignment in 𝒵k∩𝒵ℓ\mathcal{Z}_{k}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\ell} satisfies both neighborhood configurations. Therefore,

ev=ev′for every ​v∈Ni+∩Nj+.e_{v}=e^{\prime}_{v}\qquad\text{for every }v\in N_{i}^{+}\cap N_{j}^{+}.

Define the assignment zS=(z1S,…,znS)∈{0,1}nz^{S}=(z^{S}_{1},\ldots,z^{S}_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n} by

zvS={ev,if ​v∈Ni+​ for some ​(i,e)∈S,0,otherwise.z^{S}_{v}=\begin{cases}e_{v},&\text{if }v\in N_{i}^{+}\text{ for some }(i,e)\in S,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The agreement above ensures that this assignment is well-defined. By construction, zNi+S=ez^{S}_{N_{i}^{+}}=e for every (i,e)∈S(i,e)\in S. Since all binary treatment assignments are feasible,

zS∈⋂k∈S𝒵k.z^{S}\in\bigcap_{k\in S}\mathcal{Z}_{k}.

Hence the common intersection is nonempty. Thus every independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf} is jointly observable. Conversely, every jointly observable collection is an independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf}, because an assignment observing the entire collection also observes each pair.

We now show that the hyperedges are exactly the maximal independent sets in HconfH_{\rm conf}. Let SS be a maximal independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf}. By the preceding argument, there exists an assignment zz such that S⊆Of​(z)S\subseteq O_{f}(z). The set Of​(z)O_{f}(z) is an independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf}, because all its potential outcomes are observed together under zz. Maximality of SS therefore gives S=Of​(z)S=O_{f}(z), so SS is a hyperedge.

Conversely, let E=Of​(z)E=O_{f}(z) be a hyperedge. It is an independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf} because its potential outcomes are jointly observable. To show maximality, take any vertex (i,e′)∉E(i,e^{\prime})\notin E. Since EE contains exactly one potential outcome for each unit, it contains (i,e)(i,e) for some e≠e′e\neq e^{\prime}. The two distinct potential outcomes Yi​(e)Y_{i}(e) and Yi​(e′)Y_{i}(e^{\prime}) cannot be observed together, so their vertices are adjacent in HconfH_{\rm conf}. Consequently, no vertex outside EE can be added while preserving the property of being an independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf}. Hence EE is a maximal independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf}, proving (94).

∎

As a consequence of the above theorem, the rank inequality in (93) is an equality. Indeed, for any nonempty T⊆KT\subseteq K, taking SS to be a maximum independent set of Hconf​[T]H_{\rm conf}[T] gives r⁡(T)≥|S|=α⁡{Hconf​[T]}r(T)\geq|S|=\alpha\{H_{\rm conf}[T]\}. Combining this inequality with equation (93) gives r⁡(T)=α⁡{Hconf​[T]}r(T)=\alpha\{H_{\rm conf}[T]\}.

Restriction to estimand-relevant potential outcomes

Theorem B.7.1 establishes equivalence of the conflict graph and the sampling hypergraph defined on KK under neighborhood interference with the identity exposure mapping and unrestricted treatment assignments. We next use this result to show that the induced conflict graph on the estimand-relevant potential outcomes Ka={k∈K:ak≠0}K_{a}=\{k\in K:a_{k}\neq 0\} retains enough information to determine the all-design minimax risks over all estimators and over unbiased estimators. The relevant graph is the induced subgraph Hconf​[Ka]H_{\rm conf}[K_{a}], and the corresponding hypergraph is the estimand trace ℋobsa=(Ka,ℰa)\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a}=(K_{a},\mathcal{E}_{a}), where ℰa={Of​(z)∩Ka:z∈𝒵0}\mathcal{E}_{a}=\{O_{f}(z)\cap K_{a}:z\in\mathcal{Z}_{0}\}. Unlike hyperedges of ℋobs\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}, trace hyperedges can have different sizes and can strictly contain one another.

Under the assumptions of Theorem B.7.1, the maximal trace hyperedges of ℋobsa\mathcal{H}_{\rm obs}^{a} are exactly the maximal independent sets of Hconf​[Ka]H_{\rm conf}[K_{a}]. The next theorem shows, for any exposure mapping, that maximal trace hyperedges suffice for all-design minimax for both all-estimator and unbiased estimator classes. Corollary B.7.3 then combines this result with Theorem B.7.1 to establish the induced-conflict-graph consequence.

Theorem B.7.2 (Maximal estimand trace hyperedges suffice for all-design minimax risk).

Fix an exposure mapping ff, a nonempty feasible assignment set 𝒵0\mathcal{Z}_{0}, estimand coefficients aa, and the bounded-table class 𝒴⁡(f)=[−1,1]K\mathcal{Y}(f)=[-1,1]^{K}. Let ℰamax\mathcal{E}_{a}^{\max} be the inclusion-maximal members of ℰa\mathcal{E}_{a}, and define

𝒞max={P∈𝒫⁡(𝒵0):P⁡(Of​(Z)∩Ka∈ℰamax)=1}.\mathcal{C}_{\max}=\left\{P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}):P\bigl(O_{f}(Z)\cap K_{a}\in\mathcal{E}_{a}^{\max}\bigr)=1\right\}.

Then, for both estimator classes,

Rη∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵0),f,a)=Rη∗​(𝒞max,f,a),η∈{all,unb}.R^{*}_{\eta}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0});f,a\bigr)=R^{*}_{\eta}(\mathcal{C}_{\max};f,a),\qquad\eta\in\{\mathrm{all},\mathrm{unb}\}. (95)

We show that any design–estimator pair (P,τ^)(P,\hat{\tau}) can be replaced by a pair whose design belongs to 𝒞max\mathcal{C}_{\max}, without increasing worst-case risk or losing unbiasedness. Write

rY​(P,τ^)=𝔼P​[(τ^​(Z,YOf​(Z))−τa​(Y))2]r_{Y}(P,\hat{\tau})=\mathbb{E}_{P}\bigl[(\hat{\tau}(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)})-\tau_{a}(Y))^{2}\bigr]

for its squared-error risk at a fixed table YY.

First, we remove the dependence on outcomes outside the estimand revelant potential outcomes KaK_{a}. Given YY, define Y0Y^{0} by Yk0=YkY^{0}_{k}=Y_{k} for k∈Kak\in K_{a} and Yk0=0Y^{0}_{k}=0 otherwise. Then Y0∈[−1,1]KY^{0}\in[-1,1]^{K} and τa​(Y0)=τa​(Y)\tau_{a}(Y^{0})=\tau_{a}(Y). Define

τ^0​(z,yOf​(z))=τ^​(z,yOf​(z)0),\hat{\tau}_{0}(z,y_{O_{f}(z)})=\hat{\tau}(z,y^{0}_{O_{f}(z)}),

where yOf​(z)0y^{0}_{O_{f}(z)} is obtained by replacing the observed coordinates outside KaK_{a} by zero. Consequently,

rY​(P,τ^0)=rY0​(P,τ^),supYrY​(P,τ^0)≤supYrY​(P,τ^).r_{Y}(P,\hat{\tau}_{0})=r_{Y^{0}}(P,\hat{\tau}),\qquad\sup_{Y}r_{Y}(P,\hat{\tau}_{0})\leq\sup_{Y}r_{Y}(P,\hat{\tau}).

Next, for each E∈ℰaE\in\mathcal{E}_{a}, let q(E)=P{Of(Z)∩Ka=E}q(E)=P\{O_{f}(Z)\cap K_{a}=E\} be the probability that the observed estimand-relevant indices are exactly EE. For q⁡(E)>0q(E)>0, define an estimator depending only on (E,YE)(E,Y_{E}) by

τ^1(E,yE)=∑z:Of​(z)∩Ka=EP⁡(z)q⁡(E)τ^0(z,y~Of​(z)z),\hat{\tau}_{1}(E,y_{E})=\sum_{z:O_{f}(z)\cap K_{a}=E}\frac{P(z)}{q(E)}\hat{\tau}_{0}(z,\widetilde{y}^{\,z}_{O_{f}(z)}),

𝔼q​[τ^1​(E,YE)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q}[\hat{\tau}_{1}(E,Y_{E})] =𝔼P​[τ^0​(Z,YOf​(Z))],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{P}[\hat{\tau}_{0}(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)})],

q′(M)=∑E:M⁡(E)=Mq(E),M∈ℰamax.q^{\prime}(M)=\sum_{E:M(E)=M}q(E),\qquad M\in\mathcal{E}_{a}^{\max}.

Estimators on events of probability zero may be defined arbitrarily. Taking infima proves that restricting designs to 𝒞max\mathcal{C}_{\max} cannot increase either minimax risk. The reverse inequality follows from 𝒞max⊆𝒫⁡(𝒵0)\mathcal{C}_{\max}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}), proving (95). ∎

We show that any design–estimator pair (P,τ^)(P,\hat{\tau}) can be replaced by a pair whose design belongs to 𝒞max\mathcal{C}_{\max}, without increasing worst-case risk or losing unbiasedness.

Fix a design PP and an estimator τ^​(Z,YOf​(Z))\hat{\tau}(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}). For a table YY, let Y0Y^{0} agree with YY on KaK_{a} and be zero elsewhere. 𝔼q​[τ^1​(E,YE)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q}[\hat{\tau}_{1}(E,Y_{E})] =𝔼P​[τ^​(Z,YOf​(Z)0)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{P}[\hat{\tau}(Z,Y^{0}_{O_{f}(Z)})],

For each E∈ℰaE\in\mathcal{E}_{a}, choose M⁡(E)∈ℰamaxM(E)\in\mathcal{E}_{a}^{\max} with E⊆M⁡(E)E\subseteq M(E), and set

q′(M)=∑E:M⁡(E)=Mq(E),q^{\prime}(M)=\sum_{E:M(E)=M}q(E),

The reverse inequality follows from 𝒞max⊆𝒫⁡(𝒵0)\mathcal{C}_{\max}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{0}), proving (95). ∎

Corollary B.7.3 (Induced conflict graph determines all-design minimax risks).

Under the assumptions of Theorem B.7.1, the maximal trace hyperedges ℰamax\mathcal{E}_{a}^{\max} are exactly the maximal independent sets in Hconf​[Ka]H_{\rm conf}[K_{a}]. Consequently, with the estimand coefficients aa and bounded-table outcome class 𝒴⁡(f)=[−1,1]K\mathcal{Y}(f)=[-1,1]^{K} fixed, the induced conflict graph determines both all-design minimax risks.

Let S⊆KaS\subseteq K_{a} be an independent set in Hconf​[Ka]H_{\rm conf}[K_{a}]. It is also an independent set in HconfH_{\rm conf}, so Theorem B.7.1 gives an assignment zz with S⊆Of​(z)S\subseteq O_{f}(z). Hence S⊆Of​(z)∩Ka∈ℰaS\subseteq O_{f}(z)\cap K_{a}\in\mathcal{E}_{a}. Conversely, every trace hyperedge is an independent set in Hconf​[Ka]H_{\rm conf}[K_{a}], since its potential outcomes are observed together. Thus the independent sets in Hconf​[Ka]H_{\rm conf}[K_{a}] are exactly the subsets of trace hyperedges. Taking inclusion-maximal members identifies the maximal independent sets with ℰamax\mathcal{E}_{a}^{\max}.

By Theorem B.7.2, designs supported on these maximal trace hyperedges suffice for both all-design minimax problems. Every probability distribution on these hyperedges is attainable by choosing a corresponding assignment for each hyperedge. The sampling-design reduction of Proposition 4.2.1 then shows that, with the estimand and outcome class fixed, the induced conflict graph determines both risks. ∎

The graph of Kandiros et al. (2026a) is defined on the estimand-relevant potential outcomes and corresponds to Hconf​[Ka]H_{\rm conf}[K_{a}]. Their maximal-independent-set realization result (Kandiros et al., 2026a, Proposition A.6) identifies the same maximal observation sets. Theorem B.7.2 shows explicitly why these sets suffice for the all-design minimax problem, both over all estimators and over unbiased estimators. For one equal-weight arm, our sampling-rank lower bound takes the independence-number form corresponding to the uniformly bounded case q=∞q=\infty of their Theorem 3.2.

B.7.3 When pairwise observability does not imply joint observability

Assignment restrictions can make a pairwise-observable collection impossible to observe jointly. For example, with three units, no interference, and a budget of at most two treated units, any pair of Y1​(1),Y2​(1),Y3​(1)Y_{1}(1),Y_{2}(1),Y_{3}(1) can be observed together, but all three cannot. For the treatment arm TT, the induced conflict graph Hconf​[T]H_{\rm conf}[T] is edgeless, so α​{Hconf​[T]}=3\alpha\{H_{\rm conf}[T]\}=3, whereas r⁡(T)=2r(T)=2. The set TT contains only one potential outcome per unit, so the same-unit conflicts of HconfH_{\rm conf} have no edges in this induced subgraph.

Coarsened exposures can impose joint constraints that are not determined by pairwise conflicts, even when every binary treatment assignment is feasible. Consider six units: three focal units 1,2,31,2,3 and three other units a,b,ca,b,c, with focal-unit neighbor sets

N1={a,b},N2={b,c},N3={a,c}.N_{1}=\{a,b\},\qquad N_{2}=\{b,c\},\qquad N_{3}=\{a,c\}.

For each focal unit, let the exposure record its own treatment and the number of treated neighbors: fi​(z)=(zi,∑j∈Nizj)f_{i}(z)=(z_{i},\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j}). For d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\}, let Td={(i,(1,d)):i=1,2,3}T_{d}=\{(i,(1,d)):i=1,2,3\} index the arm in which the focal unit is treated and has exactly dd treated neighbors.

Any two potential outcomes in T1T_{1} can be observed together. Observing all three, however, would require

za+zb=1,zb+zc=1,za+zc=1.z_{a}+z_{b}=1,\qquad z_{b}+z_{c}=1,\qquad z_{a}+z_{c}=1.

Adding these equations gives 2​(za+zb+zc)=32(z_{a}+z_{b}+z_{c})=3, which is impossible for binary assignments. Thus the induced graph Hconf​[T1]H_{\rm conf}[T_{1}] is edgeless and has independence number 33, whereas r⁡(T1)=2r(T_{1})=2. In contrast, treating a,b,ca,b,c and all three focal units reveals every potential outcome in T2T_{2}. Hence the induced graph Hconf​[T2]H_{\rm conf}[T_{2}] is also edgeless, but r⁡(T2)=3r(T_{2})=3. The induced conflict graphs on these two arms have the same pairwise structure, while their sampling ranks differ. The sampling hypergraph records the additional fact that the three outcomes in the first arm cannot be observed jointly.

Our applications exhibit the same distinction. In the complex-contagion example, pairs of treated-low potential outcomes can be jointly observed even though some larger collections cannot; Lemma F.7.9 describes the pairwise projection, and Corollary 8.3.2 gives the resulting lower-bound gap. The bipartite interior-dose example also has pairwise-observable collections that are not jointly observable; Corollary 9.2 gives the corresponding lower-bound gap.

C Supporting results for Section 5

This appendix first derives the exact variance of exposure HT for a fixed potential-outcome table, then obtains two upper bounds for its worst-case variance. Combining these upper bounds with the lower bounds from Appendix B proves the fixed-design minimax comparisons in Theorems 5.1.1 and 5.2.1. We then verify the main-text examples. Finally, we prove Proposition 5.3.1, which uses an example to show that the H-T estimator is not always minimax optimal. Throughout this appendix, the variance calculations fix a design PP, an exposure mapping ff, and estimand coefficients aa, so that the estimand is τa​(Y)=∑(i,e)∈Kaai,e​Yi​(e)\tau_{a}(Y)=\sum_{(i,e)\in K_{a}}a_{i,e}Y_{i}(e), and every potential outcome table Y∈𝒴⁡(f)Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f) satisfies |Yi​(e)|≤1|Y_{i}(e)|\leq 1. Recall from Section 5 the observation indicators Ii,e=𝟏{fi(Z)=e}I_{i,e}=\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=e\} and the inclusion probabilities πP,i​(e)=P⁡(Ii,e=1)\pi_{P,i}(e)=P(I_{i,e}=1). We assume that PP is positive on KaK_{a}, that is, πP,i​(e)>0\pi_{P,i}(e)>0 for every (i,e)∈Ka(i,e)\in K_{a}. The variance calculations also use the pairwise inclusion probabilities

πP,i​j​(e,e′)=P⁡{Ii,e=1,Ij,e′=1}.\pi_{P,ij}(e,e^{\prime})=P\{I_{i,e}=1,I_{j,e^{\prime}}=1\}.

C.1 Exact variance identity

We derive the exact variance of the exposure HT estimator in equation (96) and split it into four terms in equation (97) below. The exposure-wise bound in Proposition C.2.2 and the cross-exposure bound in Proposition C.2.4 control these terms. Recall that the exposure HT estimator is

τ^HT,P=∑(i,e)∈Kaai,e​Ii,e​Yi​(e)πP,i​(e).\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}=\sum_{(i,e)\in K_{a}}a_{i,e}\frac{I_{i,e}Y_{i}(e)}{\pi_{P,i}(e)}.

For a fixed potential outcome table YY, the estimator is a linear combination of the variables Ii,e/πP,i​(e)I_{i,e}/\pi_{P,i}(e) with coefficients ai,e​Yi​(e)a_{i,e}Y_{i}(e). For any two relevant potential outcome indices (i,e),(j,e′)∈Ka(i,e),(j,e^{\prime})\in K_{a}, the covariance of these variables is

CovP⁡{Ii,eπP,i​(e),Ij,e′πP,j​(e′)}=πP,i​j​(e,e′)πP,i​(e)​πP,j​(e′)−1=:ϕP,i​j​(e,e′).\operatorname{Cov}_{P}\left\{\frac{I_{i,e}}{\pi_{P,i}(e)},\frac{I_{j,e^{\prime}}}{\pi_{P,j}(e^{\prime})}\right\}=\frac{\pi_{P,ij}(e,e^{\prime})}{\pi_{P,i}(e)\pi_{P,j}(e^{\prime})}-1=:\phi_{P,ij}(e,e^{\prime}).

This includes the case (i,e)=(j,e′)(i,e)=(j,e^{\prime}), where πP,i​i​(e,e)=πP,i​(e)\pi_{P,ii}(e,e)=\pi_{P,i}(e) and the covariance is the variance πP,i​(e)−1−1\pi_{P,i}(e)^{-1}-1. Therefore

VarP⁡(τ^HT,P∣Y)=∑(i,e)∈Ka(j,e′)∈Kaai,e​aj,e′​Yi​(e)​Yj​(e′)​ϕP,i​j​(e,e′).\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(i,e)\in K_{a}\\ (j,e^{\prime})\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}a_{i,e}a_{j,e^{\prime}}Y_{i}(e)Y_{j}(e^{\prime})\phi_{P,ij}(e,e^{\prime}). (96)

All sums over pairs of indices in this section use ordered pairs. We split the sum in equation (96) according to whether the two potential outcomes belong to the same unit and whether they have the same exposure:

VarP⁡(τ^HT,P∣Y)=Da​(Y,P)+ODa​(Y,P)+CDself,a​(Y,P)+CDpair,a​(Y,P),\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y)=D_{a}(Y;P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}(Y;P)+\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{self},a}(Y;P)+\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{pair},a}(Y;P), (97)

where

Da​(Y,P)\displaystyle D_{a}(Y;P) =∑(i,e)∈Kaai,e2​Yi​(e)2​{1πP,i​(e)−1},\displaystyle=\sum_{(i,e)\in K_{a}}a_{i,e}^{2}Y_{i}(e)^{2}\left\{\frac{1}{\pi_{P,i}(e)}-1\right\},
ODa​(Y,P)\displaystyle\mathrm{OD}_{a}(Y;P) =∑i≠j(i,e),(j,e)∈Kaai,e​aj,e​Yi​(e)​Yj​(e)​ϕP,i​j​(e,e),\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j\\ (i,e),(j,e)\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}a_{i,e}a_{j,e}Y_{i}(e)Y_{j}(e)\phi_{P,ij}(e,e),
CDself,a​(Y,P)\displaystyle\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{self},a}(Y;P) =∑i∑e≠e′(i,e),(i,e′)∈Kaai,e​ai,e′​Yi​(e)​Yi​(e′)​ϕP,i​i​(e,e′),\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\neq e^{\prime}\\ (i,e),(i,e^{\prime})\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}a_{i,e}a_{i,e^{\prime}}Y_{i}(e)Y_{i}(e^{\prime})\phi_{P,ii}(e,e^{\prime}),
CDpair,a​(Y,P)\displaystyle\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{pair},a}(Y;P) =∑i≠j,e≠e′(i,e),(j,e′)∈Kaai,e​aj,e′​Yi​(e)​Yj​(e′)​ϕP,i​j​(e,e′).\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j,\ e\neq e^{\prime}\\ (i,e),(j,e^{\prime})\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}a_{i,e}a_{j,e^{\prime}}Y_{i}(e)Y_{j}(e^{\prime})\phi_{P,ij}(e,e^{\prime}).

The diagonal term DaD_{a} collects the pairs with (i,e)=(j,e′)(i,e)=(j,e^{\prime}); the off-diagonal term ODa\mathrm{OD}_{a} collects pairs of distinct units with the same exposure; and the cross-exposure terms CDself,a\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{self},a} and CDpair,a\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{pair},a} collect pairs with different exposures, for the same unit and for two distinct units, respectively. A unit cannot have two exposures at once, so πP,i​i​(e,e′)=0\pi_{P,ii}(e,e^{\prime})=0 and ϕP,i​i​(e,e′)=−1\phi_{P,ii}(e,e^{\prime})=-1 for e≠e′e\neq e^{\prime}. Since |Yi​(e)|≤1|Y_{i}(e)|\leq 1, the diagonal term satisfies Da​(Y,P)≤Da​(P)D_{a}(Y;P)\leq D_{a}(P) for every Y∈𝒴⁡(f)Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f), where Da​(P)D_{a}(P) is defined in equation (20). The quantities with an argument YY are contributions to the exact variance for that table. The corresponding quantities without YY bound these contributions uniformly over 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f). For the off-diagonal term, taking absolute values gives |ODa​(Y,P)|≤ODa+​(P)+ODa−​(P)|\mathrm{OD}_{a}(Y;P)|\leq\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{-}(P), where ODa−​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{-}(P) is defined in Section C.2. Lemma C.2.1 bounds the contribution from negative observation-indicator covariances by Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)D_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P). Note that the signs in the superscripts refer to covariances between sampling indicators; the signs of the variance contributions also depend on the coefficients and potential outcomes.

Remark C.1 (Independent observation indicators).

Suppose that each unit has at most one relevant potential outcome, and that the observation indicators Ii,eI_{i,e}, (i,e)∈Ka(i,e)\in K_{a}, are pairwise independent. Then ϕP,i​j​(e,e′)=0\phi_{P,ij}(e,e^{\prime})=0 for every pair of distinct potential outcome indices, and equation (96) reduces to

VarP⁡(τ^HT,P∣Y)=∑k∈Kaak2​Yk2​(πP,k−1−1).\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y)=\sum_{k\in K_{a}}a_{k}^{2}Y_{k}^{2}(\pi_{P,k}^{-1}-1).

Its maximum over 𝒴⁡(f)\mathcal{Y}(f), attained when |Yk|=1|Y_{k}|=1 for every k∈Kak\in K_{a}, equals the unbiased singleton lower bound in equation (17). Thus exposure HT is minimax among unbiased estimators. The first assumption is needed because two exposures of the same unit are mutually exclusive, so their indicators are dependent whenever both have positive probability.

Sampling from a finite population of NN units is the special case with one potential outcome per unit, observed when the unit is sampled with inclusion probability πi\pi_{i}. For the population mean of outcomes in [−1,1][-1,1], equation (17) gives the lower bound N−2​∑i(πi−1−1)N^{-2}\sum_{i}(\pi_{i}^{-1}-1). Aronow and Lopatto (2026) prove the corresponding lower bound for the population total, with outcomes in known intervals, for all design-unbiased estimators. Their population-total lower bound is attained exactly when the inclusion indicators are pairwise independent. The calculation above shows that pairwise independence suffices for HT to attain the population-mean lower bound in our setting. Theorem 5.1.1 extends this sufficient condition, at the level of rates, to designs with bounded positive dependence, including negatively dependent indicators, and to causal contrasts under interference, where the exposures of a unit are mutually exclusive and pairwise independence cannot hold.

C.2 Upper bounds for the variance of exposure HT

We use two approaches to bound the worst-case variance of exposure HT. Proposition C.2.2 bounds the variance within each exposure level and combines the exposure-specific errors by Cauchy–Schwarz, introducing a factor equal to the number of exposure levels. This bound is used in the fixed-design minimax comparisons. Proposition C.2.4 instead bounds the cross-exposure covariance terms directly, avoiding the extra factor on number of exposure levels; we use this bound for the bounded-local-interference example.

For the first approach, Lemma C.2.1 controls the negative same-exposure covariance terms. Let 𝒟a={e:(i,e)∈Ka​ for some ​i}\mathcal{D}_{a}=\{e:(i,e)\in K_{a}\text{ for some }i\} and La=|𝒟a|L_{a}=|\mathcal{D}_{a}|. Define

Da,e​(P)\displaystyle D_{a,e}(P) =∑i:(i,e)∈Kaai,e2{1πP,i​(e)−1},\displaystyle=\sum_{i:(i,e)\in K_{a}}a_{i,e}^{2}\left\{\frac{1}{\pi_{P,i}(e)}-1\right\},
ODa,e+​(P)\displaystyle\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P) =∑i≠j(i,e),(j,e)∈Ka|ai,e​aj,e|​{ϕP,i​j​(e,e)}+,\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j\\ (i,e),(j,e)\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}|a_{i,e}a_{j,e}|\{\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)\}^{+},
ODa,e−​(P)\displaystyle\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{-}(P) =∑i≠j(i,e),(j,e)∈Ka|ai,e​aj,e|​{ϕP,i​j​(e,e)}−.\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j\\ (i,e),(j,e)\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}|a_{i,e}a_{j,e}|\{\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)\}^{-}.

Write Da​(P)=∑eDa,e​(P)D_{a}(P)=\sum_{e}D_{a,e}(P) and ODa±​(P)=∑eODa,e±​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{\pm}(P)=\sum_{e}\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{\pm}(P).

Lemma C.2.1 (Sign bound for same-exposure association).

For every e∈𝒟ae\in\mathcal{D}_{a},

ODa,e−​(P)≤Da,e​(P)+ODa,e+​(P).\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{-}(P)\leq D_{a,e}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P).

Consequently, ODa−​(P)≤Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{-}(P)\leq D_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P).

For fixed ee, consider

We=∑i:(i,e)∈Ka|ai,e|Ii,eπP,i​(e).W_{e}=\sum_{i:(i,e)\in K_{a}}|a_{i,e}|\frac{I_{i,e}}{\pi_{P,i}(e)}.

Expanding VarP⁡(We)\operatorname{Var}_{P}(W_{e}), we get

0≤VarP⁡(We)\displaystyle 0\leq\operatorname{Var}_{P}(W_{e}) =Da,e​(P)+∑i≠j(i,e),(j,e)∈Ka|ai,e​aj,e|​ϕP,i​j​(e,e)\displaystyle=D_{a,e}(P)+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j\\ (i,e),(j,e)\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}|a_{i,e}a_{j,e}|\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)
=Da,e​(P)+ODa,e+​(P)−ODa,e−​(P).\displaystyle=D_{a,e}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P)-\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{-}(P).

The second line splits ϕP,i​j​(e,e)={ϕP,i​j​(e,e)}+−{ϕP,i​j​(e,e)}−\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)=\{\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)\}^{+}-\{\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)\}^{-}. Rearranging gives ODa,e−​(P)≤Da,e​(P)+ODa,e+​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{-}(P)\leq D_{a,e}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P). Summing this inequality over e∈𝒟ae\in\mathcal{D}_{a} proves the second claim. ∎

Proposition C.2.2 (Exposure-wise HT upper bound).

For every positive design PP,

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡(τ^HT,P∣Y)≤2​{∑e∈𝒟aDa,e​(P)+ODa,e+​(P)}2.\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y)\leq 2\left\{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{a}}\sqrt{D_{a,e}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P)}\right\}^{2}.

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡(τ^HT,P∣Y)≤2​La​{Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)}.\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y)\leq 2L_{a}\{D_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\}.

Ue=∑i:(i,e)∈Kaai,eYi(e){Ii,eπP,i​(e)−1}.U_{e}=\sum_{i:(i,e)\in K_{a}}a_{i,e}Y_{i}(e)\left\{\frac{I_{i,e}}{\pi_{P,i}(e)}-1\right\}.

VarP⁡(Ue∣Y)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}_{P}(U_{e}\mid Y) ≤Da,e​(P)+∑i≠j(i,e),(j,e)∈Ka|ai,e​aj,e|​|ϕP,i​j​(e,e)|\displaystyle\leq D_{a,e}(P)+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j\\ (i,e),(j,e)\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}|a_{i,e}a_{j,e}|\,|\phi_{P,ij}(e,e)|

≤2​{Da,e​(P)+ODa,e+​(P)},\displaystyle\leq 2\{D_{a,e}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P)\},

where the last inequality follows from Lemma C.2.1.

We now combine the exposure-specific contributions. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for covariances gives

VarP⁡(∑e∈𝒟aUe|Y)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}_{P}\left(\sum_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{a}}U_{e}\middle|Y\right) =∑e,e′∈𝒟aCovP⁡(Ue,Ue′∣Y)\displaystyle=\sum_{e,e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{a}}\operatorname{Cov}_{P}(U_{e},U_{e^{\prime}}\mid Y)
≤∑e,e′∈𝒟aVarP⁡(Ue∣Y)​VarP​(Ue′∣Y)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{e,e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{a}}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{P}(U_{e}\mid Y)\operatorname{Var}_{P}(U_{e^{\prime}}\mid Y)}
={∑e∈𝒟aVarP⁡(Ue∣Y)}2\displaystyle=\left\{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{a}}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{P}(U_{e}\mid Y)}\right\}^{2}
≤2​{∑e∈𝒟aDa,e​(P)+ODa,e+​(P)}2.\displaystyle\leq 2\left\{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{a}}\sqrt{D_{a,e}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P)}\right\}^{2}.

Taking the supremum over Y∈𝒴⁡(f)Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f) proves the first result. Finally, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (∑exe)2≤La​∑exe2(\sum_{e}x_{e})^{2}\leq L_{a}\sum_{e}x_{e}^{2}, applied with xe={Da,e​(P)+ODa,e+​(P)}1/2x_{e}=\{D_{a,e}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P)\}^{1/2}, gives

{∑e∈𝒟aDa,e​(P)+ODa,e+​(P)}2≤La​{Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)},\left\{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{a}}\sqrt{D_{a,e}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a,e}^{+}(P)}\right\}^{2}\leq L_{a}\{D_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\},

which proves the second result. ∎

The factor LaL_{a} in Proposition C.2.2 comes from combining the exposure levels by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. We also use an HT upper bound that keeps the cross-exposure covariance terms and has no factor LaL_{a}. Since |ϕP,i​i​(e,e′)|=1|\phi_{P,ii}(e,e^{\prime})|=1 for e≠e′e\neq e^{\prime}, the same-unit term below carries no covariance factor.

To bound cross-exposure terms directly, define

CDself,a​(P)\displaystyle\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{self},a}(P) =∑i∑e≠e′(i,e),(i,e′)∈Ka|ai,e​ai,e′|,\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\neq e^{\prime}\\ (i,e),(i,e^{\prime})\in K_{a}\end{subarray}}|a_{i,e}a_{i,e^{\prime}}|,

Lemma C.2.3 (Same-unit cross-exposure bound).

CDself,a​(P)≤Da​(P)\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{self},a}(P)\leq D_{a}(P).

∑exe2πP,i​(e)≥(∑exe)2∑eπP,i​(e)≥(∑exe)2.\sum_{e}\frac{x_{e}^{2}}{\pi_{P,i}(e)}\geq\frac{(\sum_{e}x_{e})^{2}}{\sum_{e}\pi_{P,i}(e)}\geq(\sum_{e}x_{e})^{2}.
