∑e≠e′|ai,e​ai,e′|≤∑eai,e2​{πP,i​(e)−1−1}.\sum_{e\neq e^{\prime}}|a_{i,e}a_{i,e^{\prime}}|\leq\sum_{e}a_{i,e}^{2}\{\pi_{P,i}(e)^{-1}-1\}.

Summing over the units proves the bound. ∎

Proposition C.2.4 (HT upper bound with cross-exposure component).

For every positive design PP,

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡(τ^HT,P∣Y)≤3​Da​(P)+2​ODa+​(P)+CDpair,a​(P).\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y)\leq 3D_{a}(P)+2\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)+\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{pair},a}(P). (98)

Consequently, if CDpair,a​(P)≤Ccross​{Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)}\mathrm{CD}_{\mathrm{pair},a}(P)\leq C_{\mathrm{cross}}\{D_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\}, then

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarP⁡(τ^HT,P∣Y)≤(3+Ccross)​{Da​(P)+ODa+​(P)}.\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y)\leq(3+C_{\mathrm{cross}})\{D_{a}(P)+\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\}.

C.3 Proofs of the fixed-design comparisons

Each proof combines the exposure-wise HT upper bound with fixed-design lower bounds from Appendix B. The first comparison uses singleton lower bounds. The second also uses a packing lower bound to account for stronger positive same-exposure dependence.

Theorem 5.1.1 (Bounded positive dependence).

Suppose that PP has bounded positive same-exposure dependence with ODa+​(P)≤C0​Da​(P)\mathrm{OD}_{a}^{+}(P)\leq C_{0}D_{a}(P), and that La≤L0L_{a}\leq L_{0}. Then

Proposition C.4.2 (A fixed design lower bound for the regular-graph DTE).

Let GG be a dd-regular graph on nn units, let PP be Bernoulli assignment with p=1/(d+2)p=1/(d+2), and let aa be the DTE coefficients. If n≥6​(d+2)3n\geq 6(d+2)^{3}, then

The square graph G2G^{2}, which joins units at distance at most two, has maximum degree at most d+d⁡(d−1)=d2d+d(d-1)=d^{2}, so a greedy coloring partitions the units into at most d2+1d^{2}+1 classes. Two units in the same class are at distance at least three, so their closed neighborhoods are disjoint. Split each color class into disjoint groups of exactly kk units, and denote all the resulting groups by A1,…,AmA_{1},\ldots,A_{m}. C.5 Improving exposure HT by conditioning on randomized saturation

In this section we present an example design with a different exposure mapping and estimand where the exposure HT is not minimax optimal. Instead, a conditional HT estimator that conditions on the realized saturation improves estimation.

Recall the design in Section 5.3: the n=ξ​mn=\xi m units form ξ\xi administrative clusters, each containing m/2m/2 two-person households. Interference is confined to households, and the estimand contrasts exposures (1,1)(1,1) and (0,0)(0,0). Each cluster independently draws a saturation level Qg∈{qL,qH}Q_{g}\in\{q_{L},q_{H}\} with P⁡(Qg=qH)=rP(Q_{g}=q_{H})=r, then treats exactly m​QgmQ_{g} units uniformly. Closely related multilevel designs, with households nested in administrative clusters and saturation randomized at the cluster level, are used in field experiments on voter mobilization (Sinclair et al., 2012) and cash transfers (Egger et al., 2022); see also Hudgens and Halloran (2008), Baird et al. (2018), and Vazquez-Bare (2023).

Write Ii(e)=𝟏{fi(Z)=e}I_{i}(e)=\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=e\} and πi​(e∣q)=P⁡{fi​(Z)=e∣Qg⁡(i)=q}\pi_{i}(e\mid q)=P\{f_{i}(Z)=e\mid Q_{g(i)}=q\}. The conditional estimator is

τ^cond=1n​∑i{Ii​(1,1)​Yi​(1,1)πi​(1,1∣Qg⁡(i))−Ii​(0,0)​Yi​(0,0)πi​(0,0∣Qg⁡(i))}.\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cond}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\left\{\frac{I_{i}(1,1)Y_{i}(1,1)}{\pi_{i}(1,1\mid Q_{g(i)})}-\frac{I_{i}(0,0)Y_{i}(0,0)}{\pi_{i}(0,0\mid Q_{g(i)})}\right\}.

Exposure HT uses πi​(e)=(1−r)​πi​(e∣qL)+r​πi​(e∣qH)\pi_{i}(e)=(1-r)\pi_{i}(e\mid q_{L})+r\pi_{i}(e\mid q_{H}) in the denominators. We compute the conditional probabilities in the proof below.

Lemma C.5.1 (Conditional unbiasedness and variance).

Fix a potential outcome table YY, and let QQ be the vector (Q1,…,Qξ)(Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{\xi}) of realized cluster saturations, which is a function of the assignment ZZ and is therefore observed. If TT has finite second moment and 𝔼P​(T∣Q,Y)=τa​(Y)\mathbb{E}_{P}(T\mid Q,Y)=\tau_{a}(Y) almost surely, then TT is design-unbiased and

VarP⁡(T∣Y)=𝔼P​{VarP⁡(T∣Q,Y)∣Y}.\operatorname{Var}_{P}(T\mid Y)=\mathbb{E}_{P}\{\operatorname{Var}_{P}(T\mid Q,Y)\mid Y\}.

For any estimator HH with finite second moment,

VarP⁡(H∣Y)≥VarP⁡{𝔼P​(H∣Q,Y)∣Y}.\operatorname{Var}_{P}(H\mid Y)\geq\operatorname{Var}_{P}\{\mathbb{E}_{P}(H\mid Q,Y)\mid Y\}.

Iterated expectation gives 𝔼P​(T∣Y)=𝔼P​{𝔼P​(T∣Q,Y)∣Y}=τa​(Y)\mathbb{E}_{P}(T\mid Y)=\mathbb{E}_{P}\{\mathbb{E}_{P}(T\mid Q,Y)\mid Y\}=\tau_{a}(Y). The law of total variance gives, for any HH with finite second moment,

VarP⁡(H∣Y)=𝔼P​{VarP⁡(H∣Q,Y)∣Y}+VarP⁡{𝔼P​(H∣Q,Y)∣Y}.\operatorname{Var}_{P}(H\mid Y)=\mathbb{E}_{P}\{\operatorname{Var}_{P}(H\mid Q,Y)\mid Y\}+\operatorname{Var}_{P}\{\mathbb{E}_{P}(H\mid Q,Y)\mid Y\}.

For H=TH=T the second term vanishes because 𝔼P​(T∣Q,Y)\mathbb{E}_{P}(T\mid Q,Y) is the constant τa​(Y)\tau_{a}(Y). For general HH, dropping the nonnegative first term gives the inequality.

∎

Proposition 5.3.1 (Conditioning on randomized saturation).

Under the design above, assume that r,qL,qHr,q_{L},q_{H} are bounded away from zero and one, that qL<qHq_{L}<q_{H} with qH−qLq_{H}-q_{L} bounded away from zero, and that m​qmq is an integer satisfying 2≤m​q≤m−22\leq mq\leq m-2 for each q∈{qL,qH}q\in\{q_{L},q_{H}\}, with all bounds uniform in the population size. Then

Rall​(P,f,a)≍Runb​(P,f,a)≍1n,VHT​(P)≍1ξ.R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\asymp R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a)\asymp\frac{1}{n},\qquad V_{\mathrm{HT}}(P)\asymp\frac{1}{\xi}.

We first show that the conditional estimator is unbiased and has worst-case variance O⁡(1/n)O(1/n). Conditional on Qg=qQ_{g}=q, the target exposure probabilities are

πi​(1,1∣Qg=q)=(m​q)2(m)2,πi​(0,0∣Qg=q)=(m−m​q)2(m)2,\pi_{i}(1,1\mid Q_{g}=q)=\frac{(mq)_{2}}{(m)_{2}},\qquad\pi_{i}(0,0\mid Q_{g}=q)=\frac{(m-mq)_{2}}{(m)_{2}},

where (x)k=x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1)(x)_{k}=x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1) denotes the falling factorial. Under the count conditions in the proposition, m​q≥2mq\geq 2 and m−m​q≥2m-mq\geq 2 for both saturations. Since (t)2≥t2/2(t)_{2}\geq t^{2}/2 for integers t≥2t\geq 2, the conditional exposure probabilities are at least q2/2q^{2}/2 and (1−q)2/2(1-q)^{2}/2, respectively, and hence are uniformly bounded away from zero.

Therefore, for every fixed potential outcome table,

𝔼P​(τ^cond∣Q,Y)=1n​∑i{Yi​(1,1)−Yi​(0,0)}=τ⁡(Y).\mathbb{E}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cond}}\mid Q,Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\{Y_{i}(1,1)-Y_{i}(0,0)\}=\tau(Y).

Iterated expectation therefore gives 𝔼P​(τ^cond∣Y)=τ⁡(Y)\mathbb{E}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cond}}\mid Y)=\tau(Y).

We next bound the conditional variance. Write τ^cond=n−1​∑iXi\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cond}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}X_{i}. The variables XiX_{i} are uniformly bounded because the outcomes and inverse conditional exposure probabilities are bounded. Two units in the same household contribute a bounded covariance, and there are O⁡(n)O(n) such ordered pairs.

Conditional on QQ, the design within cluster gg is a uniform m​qmq-subset of the mm units. Put t=m​qt=mq and u=m−tu=m-t. For two distinct households, the joint probabilities of their target exposure events are

(t)4(m)4,(u)4(m)4,(t)2​(u)2(m)4,\frac{(t)_{4}}{(m)_{4}},\qquad\frac{(u)_{4}}{(m)_{4}},\qquad\frac{(t)_{2}(u)_{2}}{(m)_{4}},

(t)4(m)4−{(t)2(m)2}2\displaystyle\frac{(t)_{4}}{(m)_{4}}-\left\{\frac{(t)_{2}}{(m)_{2}}\right\}^{2} =O⁡(m−1),\displaystyle=O(m^{-1}),
(u)4(m)4−{(u)2(m)2}2\displaystyle\frac{(u)_{4}}{(m)_{4}}-\left\{\frac{(u)_{2}}{(m)_{2}}\right\}^{2} =O⁡(m−1),\displaystyle=O(m^{-1}),

These are the covariances of the two treated-household indicators, the two control-household indicators, and a treated- and control-household indicator. |CovP(Xi,Xj∣Q,Y)|≲m−1\bigl|\operatorname{Cov}_{P}(X_{i},X_{j}\mid Q,Y)\bigr|\lesssim m^{-1}

C.5.1 Conditioning on randomized saturation without interference

τ⁡(Y)=1n​∑i{Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)}.\tau(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\{Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\}.

Write q¯=𝔼⁡(Qg)\bar{q}=\mathbb{E}(Q_{g}). Exposure HT uses the unconditional probabilities q¯\bar{q} and 1−q¯1-\bar{q}. The estimator that conditions on the observed saturations is

τ^cond=1n​∑i{Zi​Yi​(1)Qg⁡(i)−(1−Zi)​Yi​(0)1−Qg⁡(i)}.\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cond}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\left\{\frac{Z_{i}Y_{i}(1)}{Q_{g(i)}}-\frac{(1-Z_{i})Y_{i}(0)}{1-Q_{g(i)}}\right\}.

Conditional on QQ, the treated units of cluster gg form a uniform m​QgmQ_{g}-subset, so for distinct units in the same cluster CovP(Zi,Zj∣Q)=−Qg(1−Qg)/(m−1)\operatorname{Cov}_{P}(Z_{i},Z_{j}\mid Q)=-Q_{g}(1-Q_{g})/(m-1), of order 1/m1/m, while units in different clusters are conditionally independent. without conditioning on QQ. The treatment and control exposures of each unit are mutually exclusive, so the all-estimator singleton lower bound gives Rall​(P,f,a)≥1/nR_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)\geq 1/n, as in the proof of Proposition 5.3.1. Hence both fixed-design minimax risks are of order 1/n1/n.

Exposure HT has worst-case variance of order 1/ξ1/\xi. For the table Yi​(1)=1Y_{i}(1)=1 and Yi​(0)=0Y_{i}(0)=0,

𝔼P​(τ^HT,P∣Q,Y)=1ξ​∑g=1ξQgq¯.\mathbb{E}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Q,Y)=\frac{1}{\xi}\sum_{g=1}^{\xi}\frac{Q_{g}}{\bar{q}}.

VarP⁡(τ^HT,P∣Y)≥Var⁡(Qg)ξ​q¯2=r⁡(1−r)​(qH−qL)2ξ​q¯2≳1ξ,\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT},P}\mid Y)\geq\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Q_{g})}{\xi\bar{q}^{2}}=\frac{r(1-r)(q_{H}-q_{L})^{2}}{\xi\bar{q}^{2}}\gtrsim\frac{1}{\xi},

and the cluster decomposition used in the proof of Proposition 5.3.1 gives the matching upper bound. Thus, when m=n/ξm=n/\xi grows, the worst-case variance of exposure HT exceeds the fixed-design minimax risk by a factor of order mm.

D Supporting results for Section 6

We prove the all-desgin minimax risk for the average treatment effect under no interference, in Theorem 6.1.1 using the weighted sampling hypergraph. We then establish the exact finite-sample optimality of independent Bernoulli assignment with treatment probability 1/21/2 for the all-estimator problem and prove the constrained-design benchmark in Theorem 6.2.1.

D.1 No-interference ATE

The sharp lower bound for all estimators follows from a Bayes-risk calculation for a shifted binomial count. We first give that calculation and then show how the same count arises on every sampling hyperedge.

Lemma D.1.1 (Bayes risk for a shifted binomial count).

Fix M>0M>0 and L>M+1L>M+1. Let Θ\Theta be uniform on [L−M,L+M][L-M,L+M] and put m=⌊n​Θ⌋m=\lfloor\sqrt{n}\,\Theta\rfloor. For sufficiently large nn, suppose we observe Cn=m+BnC_{n}=m+B_{n}, where, conditional on Θ\Theta, Bn∼Binomial⁡(n−m,1/2)B_{n}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n-m,1/2). The conditional law of BnB_{n} depends on Θ\Theta only through mm. For every 0<A<M0<A<M,

lim infn→∞infδ𝔼⁡[(δ⁡(Cn)−m/n)2]≥(1−A/M)​∫−AAz2​ϕ​(z)​𝑑z,\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\delta}\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\delta(C_{n})-m/\sqrt{n})^{2}\bigr]\geq(1-A/M)\int_{-A}^{A}z^{2}\phi(z)\,dz,

where ϕ\phi is the standard normal density.

We first show that adding uniform noise to the rescaled count preserves the minimum Bayes risk for estimating m/nm/\sqrt{n}. Define

Vn=2​Cn−nn+ηn,ηn∼Uniform[−1/n,1/n),ηn⟂(Θ,Cn).V_{n}=\frac{2C_{n}-n}{\sqrt{n}}+\eta_{n},\qquad\eta_{n}\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[-1/\sqrt{n},1/\sqrt{n}),\qquad\eta_{n}\perp(\Theta,C_{n}).

Rounding VnV_{n} to the nearest point of the rescaled lattice recovers the count. In terms of the original count,

Cn=⌊n​Vn+n2+12⌋almost surely.C_{n}=\left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{n}\,V_{n}+n}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right\rfloor\quad\text{almost surely}.

Thus any estimator based on CnC_{n} can be evaluated from VnV_{n}. Conversely, for any estimator δ⁡(Vn)\delta(V_{n}) of finite risk, define δ¯​(Cn)=𝔼⁡[δ⁡(Vn)∣Cn]\bar{\delta}(C_{n})=\mathbb{E}[\delta(V_{n})\mid C_{n}]. Independence of the added noise gives 𝔼[δ(Vn)∣Cn,Θ]=δ¯(Cn)\mathbb{E}[\delta(V_{n})\mid C_{n},\Theta]=\bar{\delta}(C_{n}). Conditional Jensen’s inequality then gives

𝔼⁡[(δ¯​(Cn)−m/n)2]≤𝔼⁡[(δ⁡(Vn)−m/n)2].\mathbb{E}[(\bar{\delta}(C_{n})-m/\sqrt{n})^{2}]\leq\mathbb{E}[(\delta(V_{n})-m/\sqrt{n})^{2}].

Next we show that the conditional law of VnV_{n} given Θ\Theta converges in total variation to N⁡(Θ,1)N(\Theta,1), uniformly over the prior support ℐ=[L−M,L+M]\mathcal{I}=[L-M,L+M]. For c=0,…,nc=0,\ldots,n, define

sn,c=2​c−nn,Jn,c=[sn,c−1/n,sn,c+1/n).s_{n,c}=\frac{2c-n}{\sqrt{n}},\qquad J_{n,c}=[s_{n,c}-1/\sqrt{n},s_{n,c}+1/\sqrt{n}).

D.2 Exact optimality of independent Bernoulli assignment

Theorem 6.1.1 gives the first-order joint minimax risk over all estimators. The following design reduction identifies an optimal design for this problem at each finite nn.

Lemma D.2.1 (Design reduction for the no-interference ATE).

For every design–estimator pair (P,T)(P,T), there is an estimator T∗T^{*} under independent Bernoulli assignment P1/2P_{1/2} with treatment probability 1/21/2 whose worst-case squared-error risk is no larger than that of (P,T)(P,T). In particular, P1/2P_{1/2} minimizes the fixed-design minimax risk over all designs.

We use within-unit swaps to turn any design PP into P1/2P_{1/2}. For a swapped unit, we also reverse both outcome signs so that its contribution to the ATE is preserved.

Assignment law. Use the population index set K=[n]×{0,1}K=[n]\times\{0,1\} and the sampling edges Of​(z)={(i,zi):i∈[n]}O_{f}(z)=\{(i,z_{i}):i\in[n]\}. Yig​(d)=(−1)gi​Yi​(d⊕gi).Y_{i}^{g}(d)=(-1)^{g_{i}}Y_{i}(d\oplus g_{i}).

Draw Z∼PZ\sim P and independently draw GG uniformly on {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}. Set W=Z⊕GW=Z\oplus G. For each w∈{0,1}nw\in\{0,1\}^{n},

=2−n​∑g∈{0,1}nr⁡(P,T,Yg)≤supY′∈𝒴⁡(f)r⁡(P,T,Y′).\displaystyle=2^{-n}\sum_{g\in\{0,1\}^{n}}r(P,T;Y^{g})\leq\sup_{Y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}r(P,T;Y^{\prime}).

infPRall​(P,f,a)=Rall​(P1/2,f,a).\inf_{P}R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a)=R_{\mathrm{all}}(P_{1/2};f,a).

D.3 No-interference ATE under a constraint on the number of treated units

Theorem 6.2.1 (Minimax risk of ATE under constraints on the number of treated units).

For the ATE in equation (27) and every m∈{1,…,n−1}m\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}, the following statements hold.

  1. (i)

    The joint minimax risk over all designs with exactly mm treated units is

    Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵m))≍Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵m))≍1m+1n−m.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{m}))\asymp R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{m}))\asymp\frac{1}{m}+\frac{1}{n-m}.
  2. (ii)

    Let km=min⁡{m,⌊n/2⌋}k_{m}=\min\{m,\lfloor n/2\rfloor\}. The joint minimax risk over all designs with at most mm treated units is

    Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m))≍Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m))≍1km+1n−km≍1m.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}))\asymp R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}))\asymp\frac{1}{k_{m}}+\frac{1}{n-k_{m}}\asymp\frac{1}{m}.

The implied constants are universal and do not depend on mm or nn.

Write Vd={(i,d):i∈[n]}V_{d}=\{(i,d):i\in[n]\} for the arm indexed by d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\}. We first give a fixed-design unbiased lower bound that applies to both assignment spaces.

for a universal constant c>0c>0.

For 𝒫⁡(𝒵m)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{m}), the proof gives

nm⁡(n−m)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵m))≤n2(n−1)​m​(n−m),\frac{n}{m(n-m)}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{m}))\leq\frac{n^{2}}{(n-1)m(n-m)},

E Supporting results for Section 7

This appendix proves Lemma 7.2.2 and Proposition 7.2.1, then establishes the cluster-count probability and HT variance bounds used to prove Theorem 7.2.3.

Remark E.1 explains why the direct effects are indexed by the number of treated peers and not by the number of treated units in the cluster.

Remark E.1 (Number of treated peers versus number of treated units in the cluster).

For an assignment zz, let kg(z)=∑j:g⁡(j)=gzjk_{g}(z)=\sum_{j:g(j)=g}z_{j} be the number of treated units in cluster gg. Under a random assignment ZZ, write Kg=kg​(Z)K_{g}=k_{g}(Z). Since kg​(z)=Ci​(z)+zik_{g}(z)=C_{i}(z)+z_{i}, the pairs (zi,Ci​(z))(z_{i},C_{i}(z)) and (zi,kg​(z))(z_{i},k_{g}(z)) contain the same information. They give two ways to index the potential outcomes. However, holding the second coordinate fixed gives different contrasts under the two indexings.

To see this, write Y~i​(t,k)=Yi​(t,k−t)\widetilde{Y}_{i}(t,k)=Y_{i}(t,k-t) for the table indexed by own treatment and the number of treated units in the cluster. A direct effect with aa treated peers is Yi​(1,a)−Yi​(0,a)Y_{i}(1,a)-Y_{i}(0,a). With a fixed number 1≤k≤m−11\leq k\leq m-1 of treated units in the cluster, the contrast is instead

Y~i​(1,k)−Y~i​(0,k)=Yi​(1,k−1)−Yi​(0,k).\widetilde{Y}_{i}(1,k)-\widetilde{Y}_{i}(0,k)=Y_{i}(1,k-1)-Y_{i}(0,k).

This changes both own treatment and the number of treated peers. It can be nonzero even if every direct effect is zero. For example, if m≥2m\geq 2 and Yi​(t,a)=a/(m−1)Y_{i}(t,a)=a/(m-1), every direct effect is zero, but the contrast at a fixed number of treated units in the cluster is −1/(m−1)-1/(m-1). This contrast includes a spillover effect.

A contrast that averages Yi​(1,a)Y_{i}(1,a) and Yi​(0,a)Y_{i}(0,a) over different distributions of aa can likewise be nonzero when all direct effects vanish. To average direct effects, use the same peer-count weights for both treatment arms.

E.1 Permutation-invariant designs

Throughout, the population is partitioned into ξ\xi clusters of common size mm with n=ξ​mn=\xi m and ξ≥2\xi\geq 2, and 𝒞inv\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}} is the class of Definition 7.1.

Let M=∑i=1nZiM=\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i} be the number of treated units. Any two assignments with the same treated count are related by a permutation of the unit labels, so a permutation-invariant design gives them the same probability. For each kk with P⁡(M=k)>0P(M=k)>0, it follows that

P⁡(Z=z∣M=k)=(nk)−1for every ​z​ with ​∑i=1nzi=k.P(Z=z\mid M=k)=\binom{n}{k}^{-1}\qquad\text{for every }z\text{ with }\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}=k.

Thus we can generate the design by drawing MM from its marginal law and then choosing the treated set uniformly among sets of size MM. Conversely, every permutation preserves the count and maps the uniform law on treated sets of that size to itself. ∎

The design PP must be chosen before the partition is known. The estimator can use the partition once it is revealed. Write R⁡(P,π)=Rall​(P,fπ,aπ)R(P,\pi)=R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f^{\pi},a^{\pi}).

Relabelling the experiment. For a permutation σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, define (σ​z)i=zσ−1​(i)(\sigma z)_{i}=z_{\sigma^{-1}(i)} and let σ​π\sigma\pi be the partition obtained by relabelling each unit ii as σ⁡(i)\sigma(i). Write Pσ​(z)=P⁡(σ​z)P_{\sigma}(z)=P(\sigma z) for the law of σ−1​Z\sigma^{-1}Z when Z∼PZ\sim P. Relabelling gives a bijection between admissible tables for π\pi and σ​π\sigma\pi, preserving the estimand and relabelling the observed data. Transporting estimators in both directions gives

R⁡(P,σ​π)=R⁡(Pσ,π).R(P,\sigma\pi)=R(P_{\sigma},\pi).

Every partition in Π\Pi is a relabelling of π0\pi_{0}. Hence a permutation-invariant PP has supπ∈ΠR⁡(P,π)=R⁡(P,π0)\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}R(P,\pi)=R(P,\pi_{0}). Taking the infimum over such designs gives the upper bound on the left-hand side of equation (32).

Averaging the relabelled designs. For an arbitrary PP, put N=|𝔖n|N=|\mathfrak{S}_{n}| and P¯=N−1​∑σPσ\bar{P}=N^{-1}\sum_{\sigma}P_{\sigma}. This design is permutation invariant because relabelling permutes the mixture components. A uniform σ\sigma maps π0\pi_{0} to a uniform partition in Π\Pi, since each partition has the same number of preimages. Thus

supπ∈ΠR⁡(P,π)≥1|Π|​∑π∈ΠR⁡(P,π)=1N​∑σ∈𝔖nR⁡(Pσ,π0).\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}R(P,\pi)\geq\frac{1}{|\Pi|}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi}R(P,\pi)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}R(P_{\sigma},\pi_{0}).

We show that the last average bounds R⁡(P¯,π0)R(\bar{P},\pi_{0}) from above.

Averaging out the component label. Let UU be uniform on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} and draw Z|U=σZ\mid U=\sigma from PσP_{\sigma}. The joint law of (U,Z)(U,Z) is fixed by PP and does not depend on the outcome table. At the reference partition π0\pi_{0}, write D=(Z,YOfπ0​(Z))D=(Z,Y_{O_{f^{\pi_{0}}}(Z)}) and τ=τaπ0​(Y)\tau=\tau_{a^{\pi_{0}}}(Y). If the average component risk is infinite, the desired bound is immediate. Otherwise, for ϵ>0\epsilon>0, choose TσT_{\sigma} with worst-case risk at most R⁡(Pσ,π0)+ϵR(P_{\sigma},\pi_{0})+\epsilon. Averaging over UU gives

supY∈𝒴⁡(fπ0)𝔼⁡[(TU​(D)−τ)2∣Y]\displaystyle\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f^{\pi_{0}})}\mathbb{E}[(T_{U}(D)-\tau)^{2}\mid Y] =supY∈𝒴⁡(fπ0)1N​∑σ∈𝔖n𝔼Pσ​[(Tσ​(D)−τ)2∣Y]\displaystyle=\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f^{\pi_{0}})}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\mathbb{E}_{P_{\sigma}}[(T_{\sigma}(D)-\tau)^{2}\mid Y]
≤1N​∑σ∈𝔖nR⁡(Pσ,π0)+ϵ.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}R(P_{\sigma},\pi_{0})+\epsilon.

By Lemma 3.4.1, averaging over UU conditional on the observed data gives an estimator under P¯\bar{P} with no greater risk at any table. The conditional weights depend only on ZZ. For zz in the support of P¯\bar{P}, the resulting estimator is

T¯(z,yOfπ0​(z))=∑σ:Pσ​(z)>0Pσ​(z)∑ρ∈𝔖nPρ​(z)Tσ(z,yOfπ0​(z)).\bar{T}(z,y_{O_{f^{\pi_{0}}}(z)})=\sum_{\sigma:\,P_{\sigma}(z)>0}\frac{P_{\sigma}(z)}{\sum_{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}P_{\rho}(z)}T_{\sigma}(z,y_{O_{f^{\pi_{0}}}(z)}).

Letting ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow 0 gives R⁡(P¯,π0)≤N−1​∑σR⁡(Pσ,π0)R(\bar{P},\pi_{0})\leq N^{-1}\sum_{\sigma}R(P_{\sigma},\pi_{0}). Since P¯\bar{P} is invariant, taking the infimum over PP gives the reverse inequality in equation (32).

For the unbiased risk, relabelling preserves unbiasedness, so the same risk identity holds. When the average component risk is finite, choose each TσT_{\sigma} to be unbiased under PσP_{\sigma} and within ϵ\epsilon of its unbiased minimax risk. Then 𝔼[TU(D)∣U,Y]=τ\mathbb{E}[T_{U}(D)\mid U,Y]=\tau, so mixing preserves unbiasedness. Averaging out UU preserves the mean and weakly decreases the squared-error risk at each table. The same inequalities and infima therefore give the unbiased identity. ∎

E.2 Bounds on cluster-count probabilities

Conditional on the number of treated units in the population, permutation invariance gives a hypergeometric cluster count. We need bounds on the probability of an interior count and on the two extreme counts.

Lemma E.2.1 (Bounds on cluster-count probabilities).

Fix a cluster gg and let n≥2​mn\geq 2m.

  1. (i)

    For every δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) there is a constant CδC_{\delta} such that every P∈𝒞invP\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}} satisfies

    Pr⁡(Kg=ℓ)≤Cδm,δ​m≤ℓ≤(1−δ)​m.\Pr(K_{g}=\ell)\leq\frac{C_{\delta}}{\sqrt{m}},\qquad\delta m\leq\ell\leq(1-\delta)m.
  2. (ii)

    For every P∈𝒞invP\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{inv}} and every value of the number MM of treated units in the population,

    min⁡{Pr⁡(Kg=m∣M),Pr⁡(Kg=0∣M)}≤2−m.\min\bigl\{\Pr(K_{g}=m\mid M),\ \Pr(K_{g}=0\mid M)\bigr\}\leq 2^{-m}.

By Lemma 7.2.2 it is enough to treat a design that treats a uniformly chosen set of MM units, and then to average over MM. Under such a design

h⁡(M)=Pr⁡(Kg=ℓ∣M)=(Mℓ)​(n−Mm−ℓ)(nm)=(mℓ)​(n−mM−ℓ)(nM),h(M)=\Pr(K_{g}=\ell\mid M)=\frac{\binom{M}{\ell}\binom{n-M}{m-\ell}}{\binom{n}{m}}=\frac{\binom{m}{\ell}\binom{n-m}{M-\ell}}{\binom{n}{M}}, (102)

which is positive exactly for ℓ≤M≤n−m+ℓ\ell\leq M\leq n-m+\ell.

(i) On that range,

h⁡(M+1)h⁡(M)=(M+1)​(n−M−m+ℓ)(M+1−ℓ)​(n−M),\frac{h(M+1)}{h(M)}=\frac{(M+1)(n-M-m+\ell)}{(M+1-\ell)(n-M)},

E.3 Upper bound under independent cluster assignments

The upper-bound designs assign treatments independently across clusters. The following lemma bounds the variance of exposure HT through the probabilities of the two cluster counts required by the estimand.

Lemma E.3.1 (Independent-cluster upper bound).

Assign clusters independently, drawing their numbers of treated units from a common law qq, where qj=P⁡(Kg=j)q_{j}=P(K_{g}=j) and choosing a uniform subset conditional on each count. supYVar⁡(τ^HT∣Y)≤1ξ​(1qj++1qj−).\sup_{Y}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT}}\mid Y)\leq\frac{1}{\xi}\left(\frac{1}{q_{j_{+}}}+\frac{1}{q_{j_{-}}}\right).

F Supporting results for Section 8

We first prove the ordering-design bounds used for the DTE and TTE constructions. The DTE proofs and core–periphery example follow, then the TTE lower and upper bounds and their comparison with the conflict-graph bounds. We next prove the treatment-budget results for both contrasts. The appendix ends with the threshold-contrast bounds and the clique and complete-bipartite community examples.

F.1 General lemmas for ordering designs

We define a design that selects units whose requested assignments are compatible, then derive its selection probabilities and an estimator variance bound. The DTE and distance-two TTE constructions specialize this design.

Throughout, Si⊆[n]S_{i}\subseteq[n] denotes the block of assignment coordinates that unit ii’s exposure depends on, so that fi​(z)f_{i}(z) depends only on zSiz_{S_{i}}; for the DTE and TTE constructions, Si=Ni+S_{i}=N^{+}_{i}. We write the estimand as a two-arm contrast

τ⁡(Y)=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(+)−Yi​(−)},\tau(Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(+)-Y_{i}(-)\}, (103)

with ++ and −- naming the two exposure levels being compared.

F.1.1 Ordering designs

For each unit ii and arm a∈{+,−}a\in\{+,-\}, choose an assignment on SiS_{i} that puts unit ii at exposure aa. We call this assignment a request. More generally, one may specify a distribution over such assignments for each unit and arm. For the treated DTE arm, the request treats ii and leaves its neighbors untreated; the control request leaves all of Ni+N_{i}^{+} untreated. For the TTE, the two requests treat all of B1​(i)B_{1}(i) or leave all of it untreated.

Two requests can be implemented together if they agree on the intersection of their assignment blocks. We say that units ii and jj conflict if some choice of their arms and supported requests assigns different treatments to a unit in Si∩SjS_{i}\cap S_{j}. Define

𝒩i={j≠i:i​ and ​j​ conflict},𝒩i+=𝒩i∪{i}.\mathcal{N}_{i}=\{j\neq i:i\text{ and }j\text{ conflict}\},\qquad\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}=\mathcal{N}_{i}\cup\{i\}. (104)

The sets 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i} are fixed by the blocks and request distributions. The design selects units with no conflicts between them, then draws their arms.

Definition F.1 (Ordering design).

Fix assignment blocks SiS_{i} and their requests, proposal probabilities pi∈(0,1]p_{i}\in(0,1], and a total order ≺\prec on the units, either fixed in advance or drawn at random independently of everything else. Assign treatment as follows.

  1. 1.

    Propose. Each unit ii proposes with probability pip_{i}, independently across units, to join a set ℐ\mathcal{I}. Let BiB_{i} denote the proposal indicator.

  2. 2.

    Select. A proposing unit is added to ℐ\mathcal{I} when no conflicting unit precedes it in ≺\prec and proposed:

    Ri=𝟏{i∈ℐ}=Bi∏j∈𝒩i:j≺i(1−Bj).R_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}\}=B_{i}\prod_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}:\,j\prec i}(1-B_{j}). (105)
  3. 3.

    Assign. Each unit of ℐ\mathcal{I} draws an arm uniformly from {+,−}\{+,-\}, independently across units and independently of the proposals and order, and the design implements its request on SiS_{i}. If requests are random, draw them from the specified distributions independently of the proposals and order. Units outside the selected blocks are left untreated.

The assignment is well defined on the full cube. If two conflicting units both propose, the later unit is excluded. Thus selected units have requests that agree on every overlapping block, whatever their arms, and each selected unit attains its assigned exposure. Under a restricted assignment space, one must also check that the completed assignment belongs to that space.

Write

qi=Pr⁡(i∈ℐ),Ci​j=Cov⁡(Riqi,Rjqj)=𝔼⁡[Ri​Rj]qi​qj−1,q_{i}=\Pr(i\in\mathcal{I}),\qquad C_{ij}=\operatorname{Cov}\left(\frac{R_{i}}{q_{i}},\frac{R_{j}}{q_{j}}\right)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[R_{i}R_{j}]}{q_{i}q_{j}}-1, (106)

where Ci​jC_{ij} is defined when qi,qj>0q_{i},q_{j}>0. The event that unit ii is selected and assigned a specified arm has probability qi/2q_{i}/2. A unit outside ℐ\mathcal{I} may also attain the exposure, so its full exposure probability can exceed qi/2q_{i}/2.

Lemma F.1.1 (Selection probabilities).

Under Definition F.1, qi=pi𝔼∏j∈𝒩i:j≺i(1−Bj)q_{i}=p_{i}\,\mathbb{E}\prod_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}:\,j\prec i}(1-B_{j}), and in particular:

  1. (i)

    if 𝒩i=∅\mathcal{N}_{i}=\varnothing, then qi=piq_{i}=p_{i};

  2. (ii)

    for a fixed order, qi=pi∏j∈𝒩i:j≺i(1−pj)q_{i}=p_{i}\prod_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}:\,j\prec i}(1-p_{j});

  3. (iii)

    for a uniformly random order,

    qi=pi​∫01∏j∈𝒩i(1−t​pj)​𝑑t,q_{i}=p_{i}\int_{0}^{1}\prod_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}}(1-tp_{j})\,dt, (107)

    which for a common proposal probability pp equals {1−(1−p)|𝒩i+|}/|𝒩i+|\{1-(1-p)^{|\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}|}\}/|\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}|, and at p=1p=1 equals 1/|𝒩i+|1/|\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}| exactly.

Equation (105) gives the first expression, because BiB_{i} is independent of the order and the other proposal indicators. If 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i} is empty, the product equals one, proving part (i). For a fixed order, independence of the proposal indicators gives the product in part (ii). For part (iii), attach independent uniform marks UjU_{j} on [0,1][0,1] and order by them. Conditionally on Ui=tU_{i}=t, each j∈𝒩ij\in\mathcal{N}_{i} blocks ii exactly when Bj=1B_{j}=1 and Uj<tU_{j}<t, which has probability t​pjtp_{j}, independently across jj. Integrating over tt gives equation (107). With pj≡pp_{j}\equiv p the integral is p​∫01(1−t​p)m​𝑑t={1−(1−p)m+1}/(m+1)p\int_{0}^{1}(1-tp)^{m}dt=\{1-(1-p)^{m+1}\}/(m+1) with m=|𝒩i|m=|\mathcal{N}_{i}|; at p=1p=1 the design keeps ii exactly when ii precedes every conflicting unit, and the earliest element of 𝒩i+\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i} is uniform on that set. ∎

A uniformly random order gives qi>0q_{i}>0 for every unit, including when every proposal probability equals one. For a fixed order, qi>0q_{i}>0 precisely when every earlier conflicting unit has proposal probability less than one.

The estimator

Because selection together with either specified arm has probability qi/2q_{i}/2, define the Horvitz–Thompson estimator based on ℐ\mathcal{I},

τ^ℐ=2n∑i∈ℐ1qi{𝟏{fi(Z)=+}−𝟏{fi(Z)=−}}Yiobs,\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{1}{q_{i}}\bigl\{\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=+\}-\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=-\}\bigr\}Y_{i}^{\rm obs}, (108)

which is unbiased whenever qi>0q_{i}>0 for every unit. The estimator uses the selection indicators RiR_{i}, which need not be determined by the observed assignment ZZ. To obtain an estimator in the observed-data class 𝒯⁡(P,f)\mathcal{T}(P,f), define

τ^RB=𝔼[τ^ℐ∣Z,YOf​(Z)].\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}].

Conditional on ZZ, the law of the auxiliary randomization is known and does not depend on the potential outcome table. Lemma 3.4.1 therefore shows that τ^RB\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB} is a valid observed-data estimator, remains unbiased, and has no larger variance. We bound the variance of τ^ℐ\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}} and use the bound for τ^RB\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}.

Proposition F.1.2 (Variance upper bound for ordering designs).

Suppose |Yi​(±)|≤1|Y_{i}(\pm)|\leq 1. Under any ordering design with qi>0q_{i}>0 for every unit, the estimator in equation (108) and τ^RB\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB} are unbiased and both obey

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)Var⁡(τ^RB∣Y)≤supY∈𝒴⁡(f)Var⁡(τ^ℐ∣Y)≤4n2​{2​∑i=1n1qi+∑i≠j|Ci​j|}.\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}\mid Y)\leq\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid Y)\leq\frac{4}{n^{2}}\left\{2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{q_{i}}+\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|\right\}. (109)

Put

di=Yi​(+)−Yi​(−),si=Yi​(+)+Yi​(−).d_{i}=Y_{i}(+)-Y_{i}(-),\qquad s_{i}=Y_{i}(+)+Y_{i}(-).

Fix YY and write R=(R1,…,Rn)R=(R_{1},\ldots,R_{n}). Let AiA_{i} be 11 for the positive arm and −1-1 for the negative arm, extending the arm draws to unselected units by independent signs. Conditional on RR, the AiA_{i} are independent with mean zero and variance one. Then

τ^ℐ=1n​∑iRiqi​(di+Ai​si).\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\frac{R_{i}}{q_{i}}(d_{i}+A_{i}s_{i}).

Since Ri2=RiR_{i}^{2}=R_{i}, this gives

𝔼⁡(τ^ℐ∣R,Y)=1n​∑iRiqi​di,Var⁡(τ^ℐ∣R,Y)=1n2​∑iRiqi2​si2.\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid R,Y)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\frac{R_{i}}{q_{i}}d_{i},\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid R,Y)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i}\frac{R_{i}}{q_{i}^{2}}s_{i}^{2}.

The conditional mean identity and 𝔼​Ri=qi\mathbb{E}R_{i}=q_{i} prove unbiasedness. Taking expectations in the conditional variance identity and using |si|≤2|s_{i}|\leq 2 gives

𝔼⁡{Var⁡(τ^ℐ∣R,Y)}≤4n2​∑i1qi.\mathbb{E}\{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid R,Y)\}\leq\frac{4}{n^{2}}\sum_{i}\frac{1}{q_{i}}.

For the conditional mean, the definition of Ci​jC_{ij} gives

Var⁡{𝔼⁡(τ^ℐ∣R,Y)}\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\{\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid R,Y)\} =1n2​∑i,jdi​dj​Ci​j\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}d_{i}d_{j}C_{ij}
≤4n2​{∑i(1qi−1)+∑i≠j|Ci​j|},\displaystyle\leq\frac{4}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i}\left(\frac{1}{q_{i}}-1\right)+\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|\right\},

because Ci​i=qi−1−1C_{ii}=q_{i}^{-1}-1 and |di|≤2|d_{i}|\leq 2. Combining the conditional variance and conditional mean bounds by the law of total variance gives

Var⁡(τ^ℐ∣Y)≤4n2​{2​∑iqi−1−n+∑i≠j|Ci​j|}.\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid Y)\leq\frac{4}{n^{2}}\left\{2\sum_{i}q_{i}^{-1}-n+\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|\right\}.

Dropping −n-n and taking the supremum over YY yields equation (109). Finally, τ^RB=𝔼⁡(τ^ℐ∣Z,YOf​(Z))\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}=\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathcal{I}}\mid Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}) is unbiased and cannot have larger variance. ∎

The first term in equation (109) depends on the selection probabilities. The second depends on covariances between selection indicators, including pairs with shared conflicting units. The following lemma gives these covariances when all units propose and the order is uniform.

Lemma F.1.3 (Membership covariances under a uniformly random order).

Take pi≡1p_{i}\equiv 1 and a uniformly random order, so that qi=1/|𝒩i+|q_{i}=1/|\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}|. For i≠ji\neq j,

  1. (i)

    if ii and jj conflict, then Ci​j=−1C_{ij}=-1;

  2. (ii)

    if 𝒩i+∩𝒩j+=∅\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{j}=\varnothing, then Ci​j=0C_{ij}=0;

  3. (iii)

    otherwise Ci​j=|𝒩i+∩𝒩j+||𝒩i+∪𝒩j+|≤|𝒩i+∩𝒩j+|/|𝒩j+∖𝒩i+|C_{ij}=\frac{|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}\cap\mathcal{N}_{j}^{+}|}{|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}\cup\mathcal{N}_{j}^{+}|}\leq|\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}\cap\mathcal{N}^{+}_{j}|\,/\,|\mathcal{N}^{+}_{j}\setminus\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}|.

Consequently, if the second-order sets satisfy |⋃j∈𝒩i+𝒩j+|≤κ​|𝒩i+||\bigcup_{j\in\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}}\mathcal{N}^{+}_{j}|\leq\kappa|\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}| for every ii, then

∑i≠j|Ci​j|≤κ​∑i=1n|𝒩i+|.\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|\ \leq\ \kappa\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}|. (110)

Here Ri=𝟏​{i​ is the earliest element of ​𝒩i+}R_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{i\text{ is the earliest element of }\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}\}. If j∈𝒩ij\in\mathcal{N}_{i} then Ri​Rj=0R_{i}R_{j}=0, giving (i). If 𝒩i+\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i} and 𝒩j+\mathcal{N}^{+}_{j} are disjoint, the pair of earliest elements of the two sets is uniform on 𝒩i+×𝒩j+\mathcal{N}^{+}_{i}\times\mathcal{N}^{+}_{j} by symmetry of the uniform order, so the two events are independent and (ii) holds. For units i,ji,j that do not conflict, put a=|𝒩i+|a=|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}|, b=|𝒩j+|b=|\mathcal{N}_{j}^{+}|, and c=|𝒩i+∩𝒩j+|c=|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}\cap\mathcal{N}_{j}^{+}|. Integrating the independent uniform priority marks over Ui=x<Uj=yU_{i}=x<U_{j}=y gives

∫01∫x1(1−x)a−c−1​(1−y)b−1​𝑑y​𝑑x=1b⁡(a+b−c).\int_{0}^{1}\int_{x}^{1}(1-x)^{a-c-1}(1-y)^{b-1}\,dy\,dx=\frac{1}{b(a+b-c)}.

Here the a−c−1a-c-1 marks belonging only to the first set must exceed xx; the b−1b-1 marks other than jj in the second set must exceed yy. The reverse ordering contributes 1/{a⁡(a+b−c)}1/\{a(a+b-c)\}, so

Pr⁡(Ri=Rj=1)=1b⁡(a+b−c)+1a⁡(a+b−c).\Pr(R_{i}=R_{j}=1)=\frac{1}{b(a+b-c)}+\frac{1}{a(a+b-c)}.

Dividing by qi​qj=1/(a​b)q_{i}q_{j}=1/(ab) and subtracting one gives

Ci​j=a+ba+b−c−1=ca+b−c≤c|𝒩j+∖𝒩i+|,C_{ij}=\frac{a+b}{a+b-c}-1=\frac{c}{a+b-c}\leq\frac{c}{|\mathcal{N}_{j}^{+}\setminus\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}|},

proving part (iii). The denominator on the right is positive because it contains jj.

For the sum bound, the exact formula in part (iii) gives Ci​j≤1C_{ij}\leq 1 because the intersection is contained in the union. Such a covariance vanishes unless the two conflict neighborhoods intersect. For fixed ii, at most

|⋃j∈𝒩i+𝒩j+|−|𝒩i+|≤(κ−1)​|𝒩i+|\left|\bigcup_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}}\mathcal{N}_{j}^{+}\right|-|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}|\leq(\kappa-1)|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}|

units outside 𝒩i+\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+} have a nonzero covariance with RiR_{i}. The |𝒩i+|−1|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}|-1 units that conflict with ii each contribute |Ci​j|=1|C_{ij}|=1. Therefore

∑i≠j|Ci​j|≤∑i{(κ−1)​|𝒩i+|+|𝒩i+|−1}≤κ​∑i|𝒩i+|,\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|\leq\sum_{i}\{(\kappa-1)|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}|+|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}|-1\}\leq\kappa\sum_{i}|\mathcal{N}_{i}^{+}|,

which proves equation (110). ∎

F.2 Proofs for the DTE rates and the ordered proposal design

The treated DTE potential outcomes can be jointly observed exactly on independent sets of GG. We use this observation constraint for the lower bound, then apply the ordering-design variance bound to prove Theorem 8.1.1.

Proposition F.2.1 (General DTE lower bound).

For the DTE on any graph GG,

Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≥max⁡{4n,1α⁡(G)−1n}≥12​α​(G),R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE}\bigr)\geq\max\left\{\frac{4}{n},\frac{1}{\alpha(G)}-\frac{1}{n}\right\}\geq\frac{1}{2\alpha(G)}, (111)

and, for a universal constant c>0c>0,

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≥cα⁡(G).R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE}\bigr)\geq\frac{c}{\alpha(G)}. (112)

Write V+={(i,(1,0Ni)):i∈[n]}V_{+}=\{(i,(1,0_{N_{i}})):i\in[n]\} for the treated arm. Its sampling rank is r⁡(V+)=α⁡(G)r(V_{+})=\alpha(G), since the units observed in this arm form an independent set and treating exactly an independent set observes its treated-arm outcomes.

We first prove the unbiased lower bounds in equation (111). If any target exposure has probability zero under PP, then Runb​(P,f,aDTE)=+∞R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P;f,a_{\rm DTE})=+\infty. For the unbiased calculation below, fix a design with positive target-exposure probabilities and a design-unbiased estimator TT. For the term 1/α⁡(G)−1/n1/\alpha(G)-1/n, write πi,+\pi_{i,+} for the probability of observing unit ii’s treated-arm potential outcome under PP. Since every assignment observes at most α⁡(G)\alpha(G) such potential outcomes, ∑iπi,+≤α⁡(G)\sum_{i}\pi_{i,+}\leq\alpha(G). The unbiased singleton lower bound in equation (17) gives the first inequality, and Lemma B.1.4, with wi=1w_{i}=1 and pi=πi,+p_{i}=\pi_{i,+}, gives the second:

supYVar⁡(T∣Y)≥1n2​∑i(1πi,+−1)≥1α⁡(G)−1n\sup_{Y}\operatorname{Var}(T\mid Y)\geq\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i}\left(\frac{1}{\pi_{i,+}}-1\right)\geq\frac{1}{\alpha(G)}-\frac{1}{n}

for every design-unbiased estimator TT.

The term 4/n4/n instead uses the nn pairs {Yi​(1,0Ni),Yi​(0,0Ni)}\{Y_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}}),Y_{i}(0,0_{N_{i}})\}, one pair for each unit. No assignment observes both members of any pair. If their inclusion probabilities are πi,+,πi,−\pi_{i,+},\pi_{i,-}, then πi,++πi,−≤1\pi_{i,+}+\pi_{i,-}\leq 1. The paired lower bound in equation (53), applied to coefficients 1/n1/n and −1/n-1/n, gives

supYVar⁡(T∣Y)≥1n2​∑i(1πi,++1πi,−)≥4n.\sup_{Y}\operatorname{Var}(T\mid Y)\geq\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i}\left(\frac{1}{\pi_{i,+}}+\frac{1}{\pi_{i,-}}\right)\geq\frac{4}{n}.

Taking the infimum over positive designs gives the maximum in equation (111). If α⁡(G)≤n/2\alpha(G)\leq n/2, then 1/α⁡(G)−1/n≥1/{2​α​(G)}1/\alpha(G)-1/n\geq 1/\{2\alpha(G)\}. If α⁡(G)>n/2\alpha(G)>n/2, the bound 4/n4/n is at least 1/{2​α​(G)}1/\{2\alpha(G)\}.

For the all-estimator risk, the sampling-rank lower bound (Theorem 4.3.1) applied to V+V_{+} gives c1/2/α⁡(G)c_{1/2}/\alpha(G) when α⁡(G)≤n/2\alpha(G)\leq n/2. If α⁡(G)>n/2\alpha(G)>n/2, the singleton lower bound in equation (16) gives n−2​∑i(2−πi,+−πi,−)≥1/n≥1/{2​α​(G)}n^{-2}\sum_{i}(2-\pi_{i,+}-\pi_{i,-})\geq 1/n\geq 1/\{2\alpha(G)\}. Taking the infimum over designs proves equation (112). ∎

Proposition F.2.2 (Variance of the ordered proposal design for the DTE).

Suppose |Yi​(e)|≤1|Y_{i}(e)|\leq 1 and consider the DTE on a graph GG. Let RiR_{i} indicate that unit ii is included under the ordered proposal design P≺,pP_{\prec,p}, write qi=P⁡(Ri=1)q_{i}=P(R_{i}=1), and define the normalized selection covariances

Ci​j=Cov⁡(Riqi,Rjqj).C_{ij}=\operatorname{Cov}\left(\frac{R_{i}}{q_{i}},\frac{R_{j}}{q_{j}}\right). (113)

There is a universal constant c>0c>0 such that, whenever qi>0q_{i}>0 for every unit,

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)Var⁡(τ^RB∣Y)≤VDTE​(≺,p):=4n2​{2​∑i=1n1qi+∑i≠j|Ci​j|},\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}\mid Y)\leq V_{\rm DTE}(\prec,p):=\frac{4}{n^{2}}\left\{2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{q_{i}}+\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|\right\}, (114)

and consequently, for every choice of order and proposal probabilities with positive selection probabilities,

cα⁡(G)≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤VDTE​(≺,p).\frac{c}{\alpha(G)}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq V_{\rm DTE}(\prec,p). (115)

The two DTE requests on Ni+N_{i}^{+} treat or control unit ii and leave its neighbors untreated. Requests at nonadjacent units agree on shared neighbors; requests at adjacent units can conflict. Thus the conflict neighborhood in Definition F.1 is 𝒩i=Ni\mathcal{N}_{i}=N_{i}, and the selected set ℐ\mathcal{I} is independent in GG. Each selected unit attains its assigned DTE arm, with selection-and-arm probability qi/2q_{i}/2.

Proposition F.1.2 gives equation (114) for the observed-data estimator τ^RB\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}. Since this estimator is unbiased,

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤supYVar⁡(τ^RB∣Y).R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq\sup_{Y}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}\mid Y).

Combining these inequalities with Proposition F.2.1 proves equation (115). ∎

Rates for representative graph families. The table gives the common minimax rates and the inputs to the ordered proposal design that attains them with τ^RB\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}. Here η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) is fixed and mjm_{j} is the size of star component jj.

Family Order Proposal probabilities Rate
Bounded degree any pi=ηp_{i}=\eta 1/n1/n
Disjoint stars center first center: η/mj\eta/m_{j}; leaves: η\eta 1/n1/n
Cliques of size mm any pi=η/mp_{i}=\eta/m m/nm/n

A large maximum degree alone need not make the DTE difficult. The star construction keeps each component’s contribution to the variance bound of order mjm_{j} before the n−2n^{-2} normalization. Since the component sizes sum to nn, the risk is O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) even for a single large star.

For bounded-degree graphs, take any fixed order and proposal probabilities bounded away from zero and one. Then all qiq_{i}’s are bounded below and each RiR_{i} depends on proposals in Ni+N_{i}^{+}. Selection indicators with disjoint proposal sets are independent, and each Ni+N_{i}^{+} intersects only a bounded number of other such sets. Thus ∑i≠j|Ci​j|=O⁡(n)\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|=O(n) and ∑iqi−1=O⁡(n)\sum_{i}q_{i}^{-1}=O(n). Proposition F.2.2 gives an upper bound of order 1/n1/n, matching Proposition F.2.1 because α⁡(G)≍n\alpha(G)\asymp n.

For a disjoint union of stars, fix η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1). In a component of size mm, put the center hh first, take ph=η/mp_{h}=\eta/m, and set pi=ηp_{i}=\eta on its leaves. Then

qh=η/m,qi=η⁡(1−η/m),Ch​i=−1,Ci​j=η/m1−η/mq_{h}=\eta/m,\qquad q_{i}=\eta(1-\eta/m),\qquad C_{hi}=-1,\qquad C_{ij}=\frac{\eta/m}{1-\eta/m}

for distinct leaves i,ji,j. Consequently ∑iqi−1=O⁡(m)\sum_{i}q_{i}^{-1}=O(m) and ∑i≠j|Ci​j|=O⁡(m)\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|=O(m), with constants depending only on η\eta; the formulas also cover an isolated center, with empty leaf sums. Different components use independent proposal coins, so their covariance terms vanish. Summing over component sizes gives O⁡(n)O(n) for both sums and hence the upper rate 1/n1/n. Choosing all leaves in nontrivial stars and all isolated vertices shows n/2≤α⁡(G)≤nn/2\leq\alpha(G)\leq n, so the lower rate matches uniformly over component sizes.

For disjoint mm-cliques, take any order inside each clique and proposal probabilities pi≍1/mp_{i}\asymp 1/m. Then qi≍1/mq_{i}\asymp 1/m, so ∑iqi−1=O⁡(n​m)\sum_{i}q_{i}^{-1}=O(nm). At most one unit is selected from each clique, giving Ci​j=−1C_{ij}=-1 within a clique; different cliques have independent proposal coins. Hence ∑i≠j|Ci​j|=O⁡(n​m)\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|=O(nm) and equation (114) gives an upper bound of order m/nm/n. Since α⁡(G)=n/m\alpha(G)=n/m, the lower bound matches.

F.2.1 Proof of the regular-graph DTE bounds

Use a uniformly random order and proposal probability one. A unit is selected exactly when it is first in its closed neighborhood, so qi=1/(d+1)q_{i}=1/(d+1). Lemma F.1.3 gives Ci​j=−1C_{ij}=-1 for adjacent units and

Ci​j=|B1​(i)∩B1​(j)||B1​(i)∪B1​(j)|for nonadjacent units.C_{ij}=\frac{|B_{1}(i)\cap B_{1}(j)|}{|B_{1}(i)\cup B_{1}(j)|}\qquad\text{for nonadjacent units}.

The covariance sum counts ordered pairs of distinct units, so the adjacent pairs contribute n​dnd. For nonadjacent units, |B1​(i)∪B1​(j)|≥d+1|B_{1}(i)\cup B_{1}(j)|\geq d+1. Hence their contribution is at most

1d+1​∑i,j|B1​(i)∩B1​(j)|=n⁡(d+1),\frac{1}{d+1}\sum_{i,j}|B_{1}(i)\cap B_{1}(j)|=n(d+1),

because

∑i,j|B1​(i)∩B1​(j)|=∑v|{i:v∈B1​(i)}|2=n​(d+1)2.\sum_{i,j}|B_{1}(i)\cap B_{1}(j)|=\sum_{v}|\{i:v\in B_{1}(i)\}|^{2}=n(d+1)^{2}.

Substituting ∑iqi−1=n⁡(d+1)\sum_{i}q_{i}^{-1}=n(d+1) and ∑i≠j|Ci​j|≤n​d+n⁡(d+1)\sum_{i\neq j}|C_{ij}|\leq nd+n(d+1) into equation (114) gives

Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤4​(4​d+3)n.R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq\frac{4(4d+3)}{n}. (116)
Theorem 8.1.1 (Minimax rates for the neighborhood DTE).

There are universal constants c,C>0c,C>0 such that the following hold.

  1. (i)

    For every graph GG,

    cα⁡(G)≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE).\frac{c}{\alpha(G)}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE}).
  2. (ii)

    If GG is dd-regular, then

    cα⁡(G)≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤C​d+1n.\frac{c}{\alpha(G)}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq C\,\frac{d+1}{n}.
  3. (iii)

    If GG is a uniformly random simple dd-regular graph, there are universal constants d0,c0>0d_{0},c_{0}>0 such that, whenever d0≤d<n−c0​n/log⁡nd_{0}\leq d<n-c_{0}n/\log n and n​dnd is even, with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1) as n→∞n\to\infty,

    dn​log⁡d≲Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≲dn.\frac{d}{n\log d}\lesssim R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\lesssim\frac{d}{n}.

Part (i) is Proposition F.2.1, together with inclusion of the unbiased estimator class in the all-estimator class. For part (ii), use the uniformly random order with proposal probability one. Equation (116) gives

Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aDTE)≤4​(4​d+3)n≤16​(d+1)n.R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm DTE})\leq\frac{4(4d+3)}{n}\leq\frac{16(d+1)}{n}.

The lower bound is again Proposition F.2.1.

Under the random-regular assumptions in part (iii), the independence-number bound gives α⁡(G)≲n​log⁡d/d\alpha(G)\lesssim n\log d/d with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1) (Frieze and Łuczak, 1992; Cooper et al., 2002; Krivelevich et al., 2001). On this event, Proposition F.2.1 gives Rall∗≳d/(n​log⁡d)R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\gtrsim d/(n\log d), and part (ii) gives Runb∗≲d/nR^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\lesssim d/n because d≥d0>0d\geq d_{0}>0. This proves part (iii). ∎

F.3 Proof for the core-periphery DTE

Let CC be the core, with |C|=S|C|=S, and let P=V∖CP=V\setminus C be the periphery. The core is a clique, every core unit is adjacent to every peripheral unit, and Δ⁡(G⁡[P])≤r\Delta(G[P])\leq r.

Write BC={(i,(1,0Ni)):i∈C}B_{C}=\{(i,(1,0_{N_{i}})):i\in C\} and BP={(i,(1,0Ni)):i∈P}B_{P}=\{(i,(1,0_{N_{i}})):i\in P\} for the treated-arm blocks in the core and periphery. We first give the lower bounds, then construct a strategy attaining each rate.

All-estimator lower bound. Proposition F.2.1 gives Rall∗≳1/nR^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\gtrsim 1/n. For S≥2S\geq 2, restrict to tables whose only nonzero coordinates are in BCB_{C}. Since CC is a clique, r⁡(BC)=1r(B_{C})=1. Their contribution is S/nS/n times their mean, so the sampling-rank lower bound (Theorem 4.3.1) gives Rall∗≳S2/n2R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\gtrsim S^{2}/n^{2}. For S=1S=1, this term is absorbed by 1/n1/n. Taking the maximum gives the lower bound of order 1/n+S2/n21/n+S^{2}/n^{2}.

Unbiased lower bound. Fix a design PZP_{Z}. If a target exposure has zero probability, then Runb​(PZ,f,aDTE)=+∞R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{Z};f,a_{\rm DTE})=+\infty. Otherwise write πi,+\pi_{i,+} for the probability of observing unit ii’s treated DTE potential outcome. Since this potential outcome can be observed for at most one core unit, ∑i∈Cπi,+≤1\sum_{i\in C}\pi_{i,+}\leq 1. For S≥2S\geq 2, the singleton lower bound and Cauchy–Schwarz give

Runb​(PZ,f,aDTE)≥1n2​∑i∈C(πi,+−1−1)≥S2−Sn2≥S22​n2.R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{Z};f,a_{\rm DTE})\geq\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i\in C}(\pi_{i,+}^{-1}-1)\geq\frac{S^{2}-S}{n^{2}}\geq\frac{S^{2}}{2n^{2}}.

When BPB_{P} is nonempty, we use BCB_{C} and BPB_{P} as disjoint perturbation blocks. Define

u=PZ{Of(Z)∩BC≠∅},v=PZ{Of(Z)∩BP≠∅}.u=P_{Z}\{O_{f}(Z)\cap B_{C}\neq\varnothing\},\qquad v=P_{Z}\{O_{f}(Z)\cap B_{P}\neq\varnothing\}.

Both are positive under the exposure condition above. The sampled edge cannot meet both blocks because every core unit is adjacent to every peripheral unit, so u+v≤1u+v\leq 1. The lower bound from disjoint perturbations (Theorem 4.1.2(ii)) gives

Runb​(PZ,f,aDTE)≥1n2​{S2​1−uu+(n−S)2​1−vv}≥2​S​(n−S)n2.R_{\mathrm{unb}}(P_{Z};f,a_{\rm DTE})\geq\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left\{S^{2}\frac{1-u}{u}+(n-S)^{2}\frac{1-v}{v}\right\}\geq\frac{2S(n-S)}{n^{2}}.

For fixed uu, the expression decreases as vv increases, so it is minimized at v=1−uv=1-u. The last inequality then follows from the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. Combining the core and core–periphery bounds gives a lower bound of order

S2+S⁡(n−S)n2=Sn.\frac{S^{2}+S(n-S)}{n^{2}}=\frac{S}{n}.

If BPB_{P} is empty, the core bound alone gives the required rate for S≥2S\geq 2. For S=1S=1, Proposition F.2.1 supplies the same order 1/n1/n. These bounds hold for every design, so they also hold after taking the infimum over designs.

All-estimator upper bound. If the periphery is empty, the zero estimator has risk at most 4=4​S2/n24=4S^{2}/n^{2}. Otherwise, we keep the core untreated, run the bounded-degree ordered proposal design on G⁡[P]G[P], and use the HT estimator of Proposition F.2.2 on G⁡[P]G[P] with weights 1/n1/n in place of 1/|P|1/|P|. The bounded-degree calculation gives variance Or​(|P|/n2)≤Or​(1/n)O_{r}(|P|/n^{2})\leq O_{r}(1/n). Omitting the core contribution incurs absolute bias at most 2​S/n2S/n, giving risk of order 1/n+S2/n21/n+S^{2}/n^{2}.

Unbiased upper bound. Use Proposition F.2.2, ordering the core before the periphery. Give each core unit proposal probability η/(n+1)\eta/(n+1) and each peripheral unit proposal probability η/(r+2)\eta/(r+2), where 0<η≤1/40<\eta\leq 1/4 is fixed. For unit ii, let DiD_{i} be its earlier neighbors. Their total proposal probability is at most 2​η≤1/22\eta\leq 1/2, so

qi=pi​∏h∈Di(1−ph)≥pi​(1−∑h∈Diph)≥pi/2.q_{i}=p_{i}\prod_{h\in D_{i}}(1-p_{h})\geq p_{i}\left(1-\sum_{h\in D_{i}}p_{h}\right)\geq p_{i}/2.

∑iqi−1≲rS(n+1)+(n−S)≲rSn.\sum_{i}q_{i}^{-1}\lesssim_{r}S(n+1)+(n-S)\lesssim_{r}Sn.

Ci​j=∏h∈Di∩Dj(1−ph)−1−1≲∑h∈Di∩Djph.C_{ij}=\prod_{h\in D_{i}\cap D_{j}}(1-p_{h})^{-1}-1\lesssim\sum_{h\in D_{i}\cap D_{j}}p_{h}.

∑i≠j:i​j∉E|Ci​j|≲Sηn+1n2+(n−S)ηr+2r2≲rSn.\sum_{i\neq j:\,ij\notin E}|C_{ij}|\lesssim S\frac{\eta}{n+1}n^{2}+(n-S)\frac{\eta}{r+2}r^{2}\lesssim_{r}Sn.

Substituting these bounds in equation (114) gives worst-case variance Or​(S/n)O_{r}(S/n) for the unbiased observed-data estimator τ^RB\widehat{\tau}_{\rm RB}.

S/n1/n+S2/n2=S​nn+S2≍min⁡{S,n/S},\frac{S/n}{1/n+S^{2}/n^{2}}=\frac{Sn}{n+S^{2}}\asymp\min\{S,n/S\},

F.4 Proofs for the TTE bounds

We prove Theorem 8.2.1. The first lower bound uses disjoint closed neighborhoods, within each of which treatment- and control-arm potential outcomes cannot be observed together. The second bounds how many pairs of blocks of potential outcomes an assignment can resolve. The restricted-growth condition then gives a matching graph-cluster upper bound.

Write 11 and 00 for the fully treated and fully untreated neighborhood exposures, respectively. Define

𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1(G)=maxC⊆V:distG⁡(c,c′)≥3∑c∈C|B1(c)|2,\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)=\max_{C\subseteq V:\operatorname{dist}_{G}(c,c^{\prime})\geq 3}\sum_{c\in C}|B_{1}(c)|^{2},

where the distance condition applies to distinct centers c,c′∈Cc,c^{\prime}\in C. For a treated set T⊆VT\subseteq V, put

AT={i:B1​(i)⊆T},BT={i:B1​(i)∩T=∅},M⁡(G)=maxT⊆V⁡min⁡{|AT|,|BT|}.A_{T}=\{i:B_{1}(i)\subseteq T\},\qquad B_{T}=\{i:B_{1}(i)\cap T=\varnothing\},\qquad M(G)=\max_{T\subseteq V}\min\{|A_{T}|,|B_{T}|\}. (117)

The sets ATA_{T} and BTB_{T} index the treatment- and control-arm potential outcomes observed under TT. Thus M⁡(G)M(G) is the largest number of potential outcomes that can be observed from each arm in one assignment. Combine the two lower bounds by setting

LTTE​(G)=max⁡{𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)n2,max1≤K≤n⁡(K−M⁡(G))+​⌊n/K⌋2n2}.L_{\rm TTE}(G)=\max\left\{\frac{\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)}{n^{2}},\ \max_{1\leq K\leq n}(K-M(G))_{+}\frac{\lfloor n/K\rfloor^{2}}{n^{2}}\right\}. (118)

Lemma F.4.2 shows that the second term equals 11 when M⁡(G)=0M(G)=0 and is at least 1/(16​M​(G))1/(16M(G)) when M⁡(G)≥1M(G)\geq 1.

Lemma F.4.1 (Packed-neighborhood TTE lower bound).

For the full-neighborhood TTE on every graph GG,

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≥𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)n2.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\geq\frac{\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)}{n^{2}}. (119)

Consequently the same lower bound holds for Runb∗R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}.

Choose a set CC of units attaining 𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G). These units serve as neighborhood centers. Take the arm-paired packing indexed by CC,

Bc+={(i,1):i∈B1​(c)},Bc−={(i,0):i∈B1​(c)},B_{c}^{+}=\{(i,1):i\in B_{1}(c)\},\qquad B_{c}^{-}=\{(i,0):i\in B_{1}(c)\},

with positive perturbation signs. Each pair has per-arm weight wc=|B1​(c)|/nw_{c}=|B_{1}(c)|/n, so ∑cwc2=𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)/n2\sum_{c}w_{c}^{2}=\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)/n^{2}. The centers are at pairwise distance at least three, so the balls B1​(c)B_{1}(c) are disjoint and the blocks are a packing. No feasible hyperedge meets both Bc+B_{c}^{+} and Bc−B_{c}^{-}. For any i,j∈B1​(c)i,j\in B_{1}(c), both closed neighborhoods contain cc. Observing the treatment-arm potential outcome of ii requires Zc=1Z_{c}=1, while observing the control-arm potential outcome of jj requires Zc=0Z_{c}=0. Thus no assignment observes both parts of the pair, and the resolution capacity is ℳ⁡(ℬ)=0\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{B})=0. Theorem B.6.4(i) gives equation (119). ∎

Lemma F.4.2 (Lower bound from block resolution).

For the full-neighborhood TTE, with M⁡(G)M(G) defined in equation (117), the joint minimax risk satisfies

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≥max1≤K≤n⁡(K−M⁡(G))+​⌊n/K⌋2n2≥{1,M⁡(G)=0,116​M​(G),M⁡(G)≥1.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\ \geq\ \max_{1\leq K\leq n}(K-M(G))_{+}\frac{\lfloor n/K\rfloor^{2}}{n^{2}}\ \geq\ \begin{cases}1,&M(G)=0,\\[4.0pt] \dfrac{1}{16M(G)},&M(G)\geq 1.\end{cases} (120)

Partition VV into KK blocks W1,…,WKW_{1},\dots,W_{K} of size at least ⌊n/K⌋\lfloor n/K\rfloor and take the arm-paired packing Wk+={(i,1):i∈Wk}W_{k}^{+}=\{(i,1):i\in W_{k}\}, Wk−={(i,0):i∈Wk}W_{k}^{-}=\{(i,0):i\in W_{k}\} with positive signs, so the per-arm weight is wk=|Wk|/nw_{k}=|W_{k}|/n. Under the assignment zz with T={i:zi=1}T=\{i:z_{i}=1\}, the sampled edge Of​(z)O_{f}(z) resolves pair kk when it meets both Wk+W_{k}^{+} and Wk−W_{k}^{-}. This happens exactly when WkW_{k} meets both ATA_{T} and BTB_{T} in equation (117). Each resolved pair uses at least one unit of ATA_{T} and one unit of BTB_{T}. Since the WkW_{k} are disjoint, the number of resolved pairs is at most min⁡{|AT|,|BT|}≤M⁡(G)\min\{|A_{T}|,|B_{T}|\}\leq M(G). Theorem B.6.4(ii) therefore gives

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≥(K−M⁡(G))+​⌊n/K⌋2n2.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\geq(K-M(G))_{+}\frac{\lfloor n/K\rfloor^{2}}{n^{2}}.

Maximizing over KK proves the first inequality. If M⁡(G)=0M(G)=0, take K=1K=1. Otherwise 1≤M⁡(G)≤n/21\leq M(G)\leq n/2, so K=2​M​(G)K=2M(G) is admissible and ⌊n/K⌋≥n/(2​K)\lfloor n/K\rfloor\geq n/(2K) gives

(K−M⁡(G))​⌊n/K⌋2n2≥M⁡(G)4​K2=116​M​(G).(K-M(G))\frac{\lfloor n/K\rfloor^{2}}{n^{2}}\geq\frac{M(G)}{4K^{2}}=\frac{1}{16M(G)}.

∎

Combining Lemmas F.4.1 and F.4.2 gives

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≥LTTE​(G).R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\geq L_{\rm TTE}(G). (121)

We next bound the variance of exposure HT under independent cluster assignments.

Proposition F.4.3 (TTE upper bound for graph-cluster randomization).

For the full-neighborhood TTE with |Yi​(1)|,|Yi​(0)|≤1|Y_{i}(1)|,|Y_{i}(0)|\leq 1, fix a partition 𝒞\mathcal{C} and assign clusters independently to treatment with probability ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). Exposure HT is unbiased and satisfies the following bound. Here 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} is the set of clusters meeting B1​(i)B_{1}(i) and πi⋆=min⁡{ρ|𝒞i|,(1−ρ)|𝒞i|}\pi_{i}^{\star}=\min\{\rho^{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|},(1-\rho)^{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}\}:

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)Var(τ^GCR,HT∣Y)≤4n2∑i,j:𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅1πi⋆​πj⋆.\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm GCR,HT}\mid Y)\leq\frac{4}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j:\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\varnothing}\frac{1}{\pi_{i}^{\star}\pi_{j}^{\star}}. (122)

Consequently,

LTTE(G)≤Rall∗(𝒫(𝒵);f,aTTE)≤Runb∗(𝒫(𝒵);f,aTTE)≤4n2∑i,j:𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅1πi⋆​πj⋆.L_{\rm TTE}(G)\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq\frac{4}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j:\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\varnothing}\frac{1}{\pi_{i}^{\star}\pi_{j}^{\star}}. (123)

The exposure HT estimator is

τ^GCR,HT=1n​∑i[Yi(1)𝟏{fi(Z)=1}πi1−Yi(0)𝟏{fi(Z)=0}πi0].\widehat{\tau}_{\rm GCR,HT}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\left[\frac{Y_{i}(1)\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=1\}}{\pi_{i}^{1}}-\frac{Y_{i}(0)\mathbf{1}\{f_{i}(Z)=0\}}{\pi_{i}^{0}}\right].

Write the estimator as n−1​∑iXin^{-1}\sum_{i}X_{i}, where XiX_{i} is the expression in brackets. The exposure probabilities are πi1=ρ|𝒞i|\pi_{i}^{1}=\rho^{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|} and πi0=(1−ρ)|𝒞i|\pi_{i}^{0}=(1-\rho)^{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}, so both are positive and 𝔼⁡(Xi∣Y)=Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)\mathbb{E}(X_{i}\mid Y)=Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0). This proves unbiasedness.

For fixed YY, only the two exposure indicators in XiX_{i} are random, and both depend only on the assignments of clusters in 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}. Since at most one indicator is nonzero, |Xi|≤1/πi⋆|X_{i}|\leq 1/\pi_{i}^{\star}. If 𝒞i∩𝒞j=∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}=\varnothing, the variables XiX_{i} and XjX_{j} are independent. For the remaining pairs, Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|Cov⁡(Xi,Xj∣Y)|≤Var⁡(Xi∣Y)​Var⁡(Xj∣Y)≤4πi⋆​πj⋆.|\operatorname{Cov}(X_{i},X_{j}\mid Y)|\leq\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X_{i}\mid Y)\operatorname{Var}(X_{j}\mid Y)}\leq\frac{4}{\pi_{i}^{\star}\pi_{j}^{\star}}.

Summing over ordered pairs proves equation (122). Equation (121) and the unbiasedness of exposure HT give equation (123). ∎

Lemma F.4.4 (Restricted-growth packing).

If GG has restricted growth coefficient κ\kappa from radius one, then

𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)≥1κ​∑i=1n|B1​(i)|=n⁡(d¯+1)κ.\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)\geq\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|B_{1}(i)|=\frac{n(\bar{d}+1)}{\kappa}. (124)

Let wi=|B1​(i)|w_{i}=|B_{1}(i)|. Greedily choose a remaining unit cc of maximal wiw_{i}, add it to CC, and exclude the units in B2​(c)B_{2}(c). The selected units have pairwise distance at least three. When cc is selected, every newly excluded unit v∈Dc=B2​(c)∩{remaining units}v\in D_{c}=B_{2}(c)\cap\{\text{remaining units}\} has wv≤wcw_{v}\leq w_{c}, so the sum of neighborhood sizes over these excluded units is at most

∑v∈Dcwv≤|B2​(c)|​wc≤κ​|B1​(c)|​wc=κ​wc2.\sum_{v\in D_{c}}w_{v}\leq|B_{2}(c)|w_{c}\leq\kappa|B_{1}(c)|w_{c}=\kappa w_{c}^{2}.

The sets DcD_{c} partition the units, since each unit is excluded once. Summing over the selected centers therefore gives ∑iwi≤κ​∑c∈Cwc2\sum_{i}w_{i}\leq\kappa\sum_{c\in C}w_{c}^{2}, which is equation (124). ∎

Proposition F.4.5 (Restricted-growth TTE bounds).

For the full-neighborhood TTE, if GG has restricted growth coefficient κ\kappa, then

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≥d¯+1κ​n.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\geq\frac{\bar{d}+1}{\kappa n}. (125)

Moreover, choose a maximal set of centers at pairwise distance at least three and assign each unit to a nearest center, breaking ties by a fixed rule. Assign clusters independently to treatment with probability ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). The HT estimator under this design obeys

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)Var⁡(τ^GCR,HT∣Y)≤C⁡(κ,ρ)​d¯+1n.\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm GCR,HT}\mid Y)\leq C(\kappa,\rho)\frac{\bar{d}+1}{n}. (126)

Consequently, for fixed κ\kappa and fixed ρ\rho,

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≍Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≍d¯+1n.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\asymp R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\asymp\frac{\bar{d}+1}{n}.

For dd-regular graphs and fixed κ\kappa, the rate is (d+1)/n(d+1)/n.

Lemmas F.4.1 and F.4.4 give

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≥𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)n2≥d¯+1κ​n.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\geq\frac{\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)}{n^{2}}\geq\frac{\bar{d}+1}{\kappa n}.

For the upper bound, choose a maximal set of units at pairwise distance at least three to serve as cluster centers. Assign each unit to a nearest center, breaking ties by a fixed rule. Maximality ensures that every unit is within distance two of a center, so each cluster is contained in the two-hop ball around its center. Assign clusters independently to treatment with probability ρ\rho.

Let 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} be the set of clusters intersecting B1​(i)B_{1}(i). If a cluster with center cc intersects B1​(i)B_{1}(i), then distG⁡(c,i)≤3\operatorname{dist}_{G}(c,i)\leq 3. The closed neighborhoods of these centers are disjoint. For each contributing center cc, B1​(i)⊆B4​(c)B_{1}(i)\subseteq B_{4}(c) and restricted growth gives |B1​(i)|≤|B4​(c)|≤κ3​|B1​(c)||B_{1}(i)|\leq|B_{4}(c)|\leq\kappa^{3}|B_{1}(c)|. All these center neighborhoods lie in B4​(i)B_{4}(i). Hence

|𝒞i|​κ−3​|B1​(i)|≤|B4​(i)|≤κ3​|B1​(i)|,so|𝒞i|≤κ6.|\mathcal{C}_{i}|\kappa^{-3}|B_{1}(i)|\leq|B_{4}(i)|\leq\kappa^{3}|B_{1}(i)|,\qquad\text{so}\qquad|\mathcal{C}_{i}|\leq\kappa^{6}.

Therefore

πi1=ρ|𝒞i|≥ρκ6,πi0=(1−ρ)|𝒞i|≥(1−ρ)κ6.\pi_{i}^{1}=\rho^{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}\geq\rho^{\kappa^{6}},\qquad\pi_{i}^{0}=(1-\rho)^{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}\geq(1-\rho)^{\kappa^{6}}.

Let π⋆=min⁡{ρκ6,(1−ρ)κ6}\pi_{\star}=\min\{\rho^{\kappa^{6}},(1-\rho)^{\kappa^{6}}\}. If 𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\varnothing, a shared cluster has its center within distance three of both ii and jj, so distG⁡(i,j)≤6\operatorname{dist}_{G}(i,j)\leq 6. Proposition F.4.3 therefore gives

supYVar⁡(τ^GCR,HT∣Y)\displaystyle\sup_{Y}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm GCR,HT}\mid Y) ≤4π⋆2​n2​∑i|B6​(i)|\displaystyle\leq\frac{4}{\pi_{\star}^{2}n^{2}}\sum_{i}|B_{6}(i)|
≤4​κ5π⋆2​n2​∑i|B1​(i)|=4​κ5π⋆2​d¯+1n.\displaystyle\leq\frac{4\kappa^{5}}{\pi_{\star}^{2}n^{2}}\sum_{i}|B_{1}(i)|=\frac{4\kappa^{5}}{\pi_{\star}^{2}}\frac{\bar{d}+1}{n}.

This proves equation (126) and the matching rates. ∎

Theorem 8.2.1 (Minimax rates for the neighborhood TTE).

The following hold.

  1. (i)

    For every graph GG with M⁡(G)≥1M(G)\geq 1,

    max⁡{𝖯𝖺𝖼𝗄1​(G)n2,116​M​(G)}≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE).\max\left\{\frac{\mathsf{Pack}_{1}(G)}{n^{2}},\frac{1}{16M(G)}\right\}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE}).

    If M⁡(G)=0M(G)=0, then Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≥1R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\geq 1.

  2. (ii)

    If GG has restricted-growth coefficient κ\kappa, then

    d¯+1κ​n≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aTTE)≤C⁡(κ)​d¯+1n,\frac{\bar{d}+1}{\kappa n}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\rm TTE})\leq C(\kappa)\frac{\bar{d}+1}{n},

    where C⁡(κ)C(\kappa) depends only on κ\kappa. For fixed κ\kappa, both minimax risks therefore have rate (d¯+1)/n(\bar{d}+1)/n.

Part (i) follows from Lemmas F.4.1 and F.4.2. For part (ii), apply Proposition F.4.5 with ρ=1/2\rho=1/2. The lower bound has constant 1/κ1/\kappa, and the upper-bound constant depends only on κ\kappa. ∎

F.4.1 Comparison with the conflict-graph bounds

Remark F.1 (Neighborhood packing in the conflict graph).

For full-neighborhood TTE, treated copy ii and control copy jj conflict exactly when B1​(i)∩B1​(j)≠∅B_{1}(i)\cap B_{1}(j)\neq\varnothing. There are no conflicts within one arm. If W=B1​(c)W=B_{1}(c), every treated copy from WW conflicts with every control copy from WW, since the corresponding neighborhoods contain cc. The paired-set lower bound therefore assigns squared per-arm mass |W|2/n2|W|^{2}/n^{2} to this complete bipartite subgraph. Disjoint neighborhoods provide disjoint sets of potential outcomes, so the paired-set lower bounds add. Thus the neighborhood-packing lower bound uses the complete bipartite subgraphs associated with disjoint neighborhoods.

All comparisons here use the uniformly bounded endpoint q=∞q=\infty of Kandiros et al. (2026a). For n≥5n\geq 5, let HH denote their conflict graph on 2​n2n target exposures. Their global and local lower theorems give, respectively,

Lglob​(H)=supT⊆V⁡(H),|T|≥5(|T|/n)2α⁡(H⁡[T]),L_{\rm glob}(H)=\sup_{T\subseteq V(H),\,|T|\geq 5}\frac{(|T|/n)^{2}}{\alpha(H[T])},
Lloc​(H)=1n2​supT⊆V⁡(H),|T|≥5min⁡{dmin​(H,T)2,|T|∑v∈TdH​(v)−2,|T|2}.L_{\rm loc}(H)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sup_{T\subseteq V(H),\,|T|\geq 5}\min\left\{d_{\min}(H,T)^{2},\frac{|T|}{\sqrt{\sum_{v\in T}d_{H}(v)^{-2}}},\ |T|^{2}\right\}.

Here dmin​(H,T)d_{\min}(H,T) is the minimum over TT of the degrees in HH. Their unbiased upper theorem specializes to davg​(H)/nd_{\rm avg}(H)/n. Thus, up to universal constants,

max⁡{Lglob​(H),Lloc​(H)}≲Rall∗≤Runb∗≲davg​(H)n.\max\{L_{\rm glob}(H),L_{\rm loc}(H)\}\lesssim R^{*}_{\rm all}\leq R^{*}_{\rm unb}\lesssim\frac{d_{\rm avg}(H)}{n}.

For full-neighborhood TTE, put Φ⁡(G)=n−2​∑i|B2​(i)|\Phi(G)=n^{-2}\sum_{i}|B_{2}(i)|. Then davg​(H)=davg​(G2)+1=n​Φ​(G)d_{\rm avg}(H)=d_{\rm avg}(G^{2})+1=n\Phi(G), including the own-unit opposite-arm conflict. Their q=∞q=\infty upper therefore gives Runb∗≲Φ⁡(G)R^{*}_{\rm unb}\lesssim\Phi(G) on every graph. Proposition F.4.5 gives a direct variance proof for the restricted-growth class.

Suppose now that GG is dd-regular with restricted-growth coefficient κ\kappa. Each vertex of HH has degree |B2​(i)||B_{2}(i)|, and hence d+1≤dH​(i)≤κ⁡(d+1)d+1\leq d_{H}(i)\leq\kappa(d+1). For every T⊆V⁡(H)T\subseteq V(H), bipartiteness gives α⁡(H⁡[T])≥|T|/2\alpha(H[T])\geq|T|/2. Consequently,

Lglob​(H)≤4n.L_{\rm glob}(H)\leq\frac{4}{n}.

Taking T=V⁡(H)T=V(H) gives Lglob​(H)=4/nL_{\rm glob}(H)=4/n: one arm is an independent set of size nn, and the nn own-unit conflicts form a perfect matching, so α⁡(H)=n\alpha(H)=n. The degree upper bound also gives, for every nonempty TT,

|T|∑v∈TdH​(v)−2≤κ⁡(d+1)​|T|≤κ⁡(d+1)​2​n.\frac{|T|}{\sqrt{\sum_{v\in T}d_{H}(v)^{-2}}}\leq\kappa(d+1)\sqrt{|T|}\leq\kappa(d+1)\sqrt{2n}.

The degree lower bound gives

Lloc​(H)≥1n2​min⁡{(d+1)2,(d+1)​2​n,4​n2}.L_{\rm loc}(H)\geq\frac{1}{n^{2}}\min\{(d+1)^{2},(d+1)\sqrt{2n},4n^{2}\}.

When d+1≤nd+1\leq\sqrt{n}, the global bound supplies 1/n1/n; when d+1>nd+1>\sqrt{n}, the local bound supplies order (d+1)/n3/2(d+1)/n^{3/2}. Thus, for n≥5n\geq 5,

max{Lglob(H),Lloc(H)}≍κmax{1n,d+1n3/2},\max\{L_{\rm glob}(H),L_{\rm loc}(H)\}\asymp_{\kappa}\max\left\{\frac{1}{n},\frac{d+1}{n^{3/2}}\right\},

while their unbiased upper bound is of order (d+1)/n(d+1)/n. The resulting lower and upper bounds differ by a factor of order min⁡{d+1,n}\min\{d+1,\sqrt{n}\}. Lemma F.4.1 and the restricted-growth packing bound raise the lower bound to order (d+1)/n(d+1)/n, matching the upper bound.

Lemma F.4.7 (Identification of M⁡(G)M(G)).

Write N⁡[S]=⋃i∈SB1​(i)N[S]=\bigcup_{i\in S}B_{1}(i) and N2​[S]=⋃i∈SB2​(i)N^{2}[S]=\bigcup_{i\in S}B_{2}(i). Define the vertex-neighborhood profile by ψ(s)=min{|N[S]|:S⊆V,|S|=s}\psi(s)=\min\{|N[S]|:S\subseteq V,\ |S|=s\} for s=0,…,ns=0,\ldots,n, so that ψ⁡(0)=0\psi(0)=0. Then

M⁡(G)=maxA⊆V⁡min⁡(|A|,n−|N2​[A]|)≤max⁡{m∈{0,…,⌊n/2⌋}:m+ψ⁡(ψ⁡(m))≤n}.M(G)=\max_{A\subseteq V}\min\bigl(|A|,\,n-|N^{2}[A]|\bigr)\ \leq\ \max\bigl\{m\in\{0,\ldots,\lfloor n/2\rfloor\}:\,m+\psi(\psi(m))\leq n\bigr\}. (127)

Equivalently M⁡(G)M(G) is the largest mm for which G2G^{2} contains two disjoint mm-sets with no edge between them—the bipartite hole number of G2G^{2}.

If ATA_{T} is the set of units whose closed neighborhoods lie in the treated set TT, then every vertex of BTB_{T} has distance greater than two from ATA_{T}. Otherwise the two closed neighborhoods would share a vertex required to be both treated and controlled. Hence BT⊆V∖N2​[AT]B_{T}\subseteq V\setminus N^{2}[A_{T}], giving one direction of the equality. Conversely, for any A⊆VA\subseteq V, treat T=N⁡[A]T=N[A]. Then A⊆ATA\subseteq A_{T} and BT=V∖N2​[A]B_{T}=V\setminus N^{2}[A], proving the reverse direction. Taking subsets of the larger of the two sets gives the bipartite-hole characterization.

The profile ψ\psi is nondecreasing: every larger set contains a smaller one whose closed neighborhood it contains. Thus, for |A|=m|A|=m, |N2​[A]|≥ψ⁡(|N⁡[A]|)≥ψ⁡(ψ⁡(m))|N^{2}[A]|\geq\psi(|N[A]|)\geq\psi(\psi(m)). Two separated mm-sets therefore require m+ψ⁡(ψ⁡(m))≤nm+\psi(\psi(m))\leq n, proving the inequality. ∎

F.5 Proofs for the hard-budget TTE example

The lit-ball design samples a fixed number of units and treats their closed neighborhoods. We account for sampling without replacement when bounding the covariance of the control-arm observation indicators. We first prove the covariance bound in Lemma F.5.1, then apply it to prove Theorem 8.2.2. Proposition F.5.2 gives the subsequent expansion-based refinement.

Recall the lit-ball design in Definition 8.2, and write PℓP_{\ell} for its law. Since |T|≤ℓ⁡(d+1)≤m|T|\leq\ell(d+1)\leq m, it respects the treatment budget.

For each unit ii, define

Ai={j:B1​(j)∩B1​(i)≠∅}=B2​(i),qi=Pr⁡(Clit∩Ai=∅).A_{i}=\{j:B_{1}(j)\cap B_{1}(i)\neq\varnothing\}=B_{2}(i),\qquad q_{i}=\Pr(C_{\rm lit}\cap A_{i}=\varnothing).

Each sampled unit attains the treated arm, while unit ii attains the control arm exactly when Clit∩Ai=∅C_{\rm lit}\cap A_{i}=\varnothing. The corresponding augmented-data estimator is

τ^ball=1n​∑i=1n{𝟏{i∈Clit}ℓ/n​Yiobs−𝟏{Clit∩Ai=∅}qi​Yiobs}.\widehat{\tau}_{\rm ball}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{\mathbf{1}\{i\in C_{\rm lit}\}}{\ell/n}\,Y_{i}^{\rm obs}-\frac{\mathbf{1}\{C_{\rm lit}\cap A_{i}=\varnothing\}}{q_{i}}\,Y_{i}^{\rm obs}\right\}. (128)

It is unbiased whenever every qi>0q_{i}>0. Because ClitC_{\rm lit} cannot generally be reconstructed from ZZ, the observed-data estimator is τ^ball,RB=𝔼[τ^ball∣Z,YOf​(Z)]\widehat{\tau}_{{\rm ball},{\rm RB}}=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\tau}_{\rm ball}\mid Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)}]; Lemma 3.4.1 preserves unbiasedness and the variance bound.

Remark F.2 (The budgeted design and thinning).

The ordering design on G2G^{2} keeps selected neighborhoods disjoint because each selected neighborhood receives an independent arm assignment. If two selected neighborhoods overlapped and received different arms, their assignments would conflict on the shared units.

The lit-ball design uses selected neighborhoods only to observe treated-arm potential outcomes. Overlapping balls therefore make the same treatment request on their shared units. Control-arm potential outcomes are observed separately for units whose neighborhoods avoid the entire treated union. Thus the lit-ball design can use overlapping sampled neighborhoods.

Lemma F.5.1 (Covariance control for lit balls).

Let A1,…,An⊆{1,…,n}A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, let B=maxi⁡|Ai|B=\max_{i}|A_{i}|, and let ClitC_{\rm lit} be a uniform ℓ\ell-subset of {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}, where 1≤ℓ≤n1\leq\ell\leq n. Assume ∑i,j|Ai∩Aj|≤n​B2\sum_{i,j}|A_{i}\cap A_{j}|\leq nB^{2}. Put qi=Pr⁡(Clit∩Ai=∅)q_{i}=\Pr(C_{\rm lit}\cap A_{i}=\varnothing) and Wi=𝟏{Clit∩Ai=∅}/qiW_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{C_{\rm lit}\cap A_{i}=\varnothing\}/q_{i}. If ℓ​B≤c0​n\ell B\leq c_{0}n for a sufficiently small universal constant c0c_{0}, then

∑i,j=1n|Cov⁡(Wi,Wj)|≤C​ℓ​B2,so1n2​∑i,j=1n|Cov⁡(Wi,Wj)|≤Cℓ,\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}|\operatorname{Cov}(W_{i},W_{j})|\leq C\,\ell B^{2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}|\operatorname{Cov}(W_{i},W_{j})|\leq\frac{C}{\ell}, (129)

with CC universal.

For A,B′⊆{1,…,n}A,B^{\prime}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} of size at most BB, write a=|A|a=|A|, b=|B′|b=|B^{\prime}|, and t=|A∩B′|t=|A\cap B^{\prime}|. If q⁡(A)=Pr⁡(Clit∩A=∅)q(A)=\Pr(C_{\rm lit}\cap A=\varnothing), then

q⁡(A)=∏r=0ℓ−1(1−|A|n−r).q(A)=\prod_{r=0}^{\ell-1}\left(1-\frac{|A|}{n-r}\right).

The case B=0B=0 is trivial; assume B,ℓ≥1B,\ell\geq 1. Then ℓ≤c0​n\ell\leq c_{0}n, B≤c0​nB\leq c_{0}n, and the factors in the avoidance probabilities for AA, B′B^{\prime}, and A∪B′A\cup B^{\prime} are bounded away from zero. q⁡(A∪B′)q⁡(A)​q​(B′)−1.\frac{q(A\cup B^{\prime})}{q(A)q(B^{\prime})}-1.

We bound the log of the ratio, separating the effect of overlap from the dependence due to sampling without replacement. For u=n−ru=n-r, first put t=0t=0. The ratio of the three factors is

∑i,j|Cov⁡(Wi,Wj)|≤C⁡{ℓn​∑i,j|Ai∩Aj|+ℓ​B2}.\sum_{i,j}|\operatorname{Cov}(W_{i},W_{j})|\leq C\left\{\frac{\ell}{n}\sum_{i,j}|A_{i}\cap A_{j}|+\ell B^{2}\right\}.

The rate statement follows from ℓ​B≤c0​n\ell B\leq c_{0}n, which implies ℓ2​B2≤c02​n2\ell^{2}B^{2}\leq c_{0}^{2}n^{2}. ∎

Theorem 8.2.2 (Budgeted TTE under restricted growth).

Let GG be dd-regular with restricted-growth coefficient κ\kappa. There is crg​(κ)∈(0,1]c_{\rm rg}(\kappa)\in(0,1] such that, if 1≤m≤n/21\leq m\leq n/2 and (d+1)/m≤crg​(κ)(d+1)/m\leq c_{\rm rg}(\kappa), then

Write w=d+1w=d+1 and J=⌊m/w⌋≥1J=\lfloor m/w\rfloor\geq 1. Choose a maximal set CC of units at pairwise distance at least five, and put L=|C|L=|C|. L≥nκ3​w.L\geq\frac{n}{\kappa^{3}w}. (131)

BH={(i,1):i∈⋃c∈HB1​(c)}B_{H}=\{(i,1):i\in\textstyle\bigcup_{c\in H}B_{1}(c)\}

be its treated-arm perturbation block. These blocks are disjoint and each has total coefficient magnitude at least w​L/(4​J​n)wL/(4Jn). If the sampled edge meets BHB_{H} at a vertex (i,1)(i,1) with i∈B1​(c)i\in B_{1}(c), then the assignment treats all ww units in B1​(i)⊆B2​(c)B_{1}(i)\subseteq B_{2}(c). The balls B2​(c)B_{2}(c) are disjoint across centers, so each block met costs at least ww distinct treated units. Thus the sampled edge meets at most JJ blocks. Rall​(P,f,aTTE)≥J​(w​L4​J​n)2≥w16​κ6​mR_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a_{\rm TTE})\geq J\left(\frac{wL}{4Jn}\right)^{2}\geq\frac{w}{16\kappa^{6}m}

where c0c_{0} is the constant in Lemma F.5.1. The choice of ℓ\ell satisfies ℓ​w≤m\ell w\leq m and ℓ​B2max≤c0​n\ell B_{2}^{\max}\leq c_{0}n, including the case ℓ=1\ell=1. Lit-ball variance calculation. The treatment-arm term in equation (128) is the sample mean of ℓ\ell uniformly sampled treatment-arm potential outcomes. Its variance is at most C/ℓC/\ell. For the control-arm term, Lemma F.5.1 gives

Var⁡(1n​∑iWi​Yi​(0)|Y)≤1n2​∑i,j|Cov⁡(Wi,Wj)|≤Cℓ.\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}W_{i}Y_{i}(0)\,\middle|\,Y\right)\leq\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j}|\operatorname{Cov}(W_{i},W_{j})|\leq\frac{C}{\ell}.

The variance of the difference of the two terms is at most twice the sum of their variances, and is therefore at most C/ℓC/\ell. Since m≤n/2m\leq n/2 and B2max≤κ​wB_{2}^{\max}\leq\kappa w,

1ℓ≤C​max⁡{wm,B2maxn}≤C⁡(κ)​wm.\frac{1}{\ell}\leq C\max\left\{\frac{w}{m},\frac{B_{2}^{\max}}{n}\right\}\leq C(\kappa)\frac{w}{m}.

Lemma 3.4.1 transfers unbiasedness and the variance bound to the observed-data estimator. ∎

Definition F.2 (Budget expansion).

A dd-regular graph is (m,cexp)(m,c_{\rm exp})-budget expanding if

|N⁡[S]|≥cexp​(d+1)​|S|whenever ​|N⁡[S]|≤m,|N[S]|\geq c_{\rm exp}(d+1)|S|\qquad\text{whenever }|N[S]|\leq m, (132)

where N⁡[S]=⋃i∈SB1​(i)N[S]=\bigcup_{i\in S}B_{1}(i).

Proposition F.5.2 (Budgeted TTE on expanding regular graphs).

Let GG be dd-regular, d≥1d\geq 1, and (m,cexp)(m,c_{\rm exp})-budget expanding, with d+1≤m≤n/2d+1\leq m\leq n/2. Put B=maxi⁡|B2​(i)|≤1+d2B=\max_{i}|B_{2}(i)|\leq 1+d^{2}. Then

|AT|≤|T|cexp​(d+1)≤mcexp​(d+1).|A_{T}|\leq\frac{|T|}{c_{\rm exp}(d+1)}\leq\frac{m}{c_{\rm exp}(d+1)}.

J=maxT⊆V:|T|≤m|AT|.J=\max_{T\subseteq V:\,|T|\leq m}|A_{T}|.

Finally, m​B≤C1​n​(d+1)mB\leq C_{1}n(d+1) makes the two upper terms comparable to the budget lower term and proves the claimed rate. ∎

F.6 The direct treatment effect under a treatment budget

Restrict the assignment space to 𝒵≤m={z∈{0,1}n:|T⁡(z)|≤m}\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}=\{z\in\{0,1\}^{n}:|T(z)|\leq m\}, as in Section 8.2.1. The DTE exposure mapping is unchanged, but the budget limits how many treatment-arm potential outcomes can be observed together.

Proposition F.6.1 (Budgeted DTE).

Let 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n be an integer. For the DTE on any graph GG, the sampling rank of the treated arm over 𝒵≤m\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m} is

rm=min⁡{m,α⁡(G)}.r_{m}=\min\{m,\alpha(G)\}.

If GG is dd-regular, with dd allowed to depend on nn, then

max⁡{1m,1α⁡(G)}\displaystyle\max\left\{\frac{1}{m},\frac{1}{\alpha(G)}\right\} ≲Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m),f,aDTE)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵≤m),f,aDTE),\displaystyle\lesssim R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m});f,a_{\rm DTE}\bigr)\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m});f,a_{\rm DTE}\bigr), (134)

Write V+={(i,(1,0Ni)):i∈[n]}V_{+}=\{(i,(1,0_{N_{i}})):i\in[n]\} for the treated arm. An assignment observes the treated DTE potential outcome of unit ii exactly when ii is treated and all its neighbors are controlled. Hence the units whose treated potential outcomes are observed form an independent set and have cardinality at most mm. Conversely, treating any independent set of size at most mm observes all of its treated potential outcomes. The treated-arm sampling rank is therefore r⁡(V+)=rm=min⁡{m,α⁡(G)}r(V_{+})=r_{m}=\min\{m,\alpha(G)\} over 𝒵≤m\mathcal{Z}_{\leq m}.

If rm>n/2r_{m}>n/2, the pairwise conflicts between the treated and control DTE potential outcomes of each unit give an all-estimator lower bound of order 1/n1/n, as in the proof of Proposition F.2.1; since rm>n/2r_{m}>n/2, 1/n≥1/(2​rm)1/n\geq 1/(2r_{m}). The same bound holds for the smaller class of unbiased estimators.

For the upper bound on a dd-regular graph, fix a sufficiently small universal constant c1>0c_{1}>0 and first suppose d+1≤c1​n/2d+1\leq c_{1}n/2. Put

Ψs(k)=(n−t)s(n−k)s.\Psi_{s}^{(k)}=\frac{(n-t)_{s}}{(n-k)_{s}}.

When t≥kt\geq k, this is the probability that ss specified units are controlled, conditional on kk other specified units being treated. For distinct nonadjacent units i,ji,j, put h=|Ni∩Nj|h=|N_{i}\cap N_{j}|. If t≥2t\geq 2, the treatment-arm joint probability and normalized covariance satisfy
