F.7 Details for the complex-contagion example

We prove the rank and packing lemmas used in the lower bound of Theorem F.7.7, then the Bernoulli upper bound in Theorem F.7.8. Together these prove Theorem 8.3.1. We also prove Corollary 8.3.2 and the clique and complete-bipartite community rates.

For an integer s≥0s\geq 0, write disss⁡(G)=max⁡{|S|:Δ⁡(G⁡[S])≤s}\operatorname{diss}_{s}(G)=\max\{|S|:\Delta(G[S])\leq s\}. Thus diss0⁡(G)=α⁡(G)\operatorname{diss}_{0}(G)=\alpha(G). Let L0(z)={i:zi=1,Ci(z)≤θ−1}L_{0}(z)=\{i:z_{i}=1,C_{i}(z)\leq\theta-1\} and ℒθ​(G)={S⊆V:Δ⁡(G⁡[S])≤θ−1}\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(G)=\{S\subseteq V:\Delta(G[S])\leq\theta-1\}. The assignment space is the full binary cube, as in the main-text example.

F.7.1 Arm ranks and the sampling reduction

Lemma F.7.1 (Single-arm rank of the treated-high threshold arm).

Let GG be dd-regular with d≥θd\geq\theta. Then r⁡(bhi)=nr(b_{\rm hi})=n, and the minimax risk of estimating the high-arm mean on its own is zero.

Under z=𝟏Vz=\mathbf{1}_{V} every unit is treated and has Ci​(z)=d≥θC_{i}(z)=d\geq\theta, so every unit attains bhib_{\rm hi}. A single deterministic assignment therefore observes the whole high arm, the high-arm sampling rank is nn, and the degenerate design placing all mass on 𝟏V\mathbf{1}_{V} estimates the high-arm mean without error. ∎

Lemma F.7.2 (Sampling rank of the treated-low threshold arm).

For every graph GG and every θ≥1\theta\geq 1, the sampling rank of the treated-low threshold arm blob_{\rm lo} is

r⁡(blo)=dissθ−1⁡(G).r(b_{\rm lo})=\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G). (135)

Consequently, when both target exposures are attainable at every unit,

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aθ)≥cdissθ−1⁡(G)≥cθ​α​(G)R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\geq\frac{c}{\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G)}\geq\frac{c}{\theta\,\alpha(G)} (136)

for a universal constant c>0c>0.

Let SS be a set of units whose treated-low threshold potential outcomes are observed simultaneously. Every unit in SS must be treated. Treating units outside SS can only increase the numbers of treated neighbors, so the largest feasible observed set is achieved by assignments of the form z=𝟏Sz=\mathbf{1}_{S}. Under this assignment, each i∈Si\in S has exactly |Ni∩S||N_{i}\cap S| treated neighbors. Thus all units in SS attain the low arm if and only if Δ⁡(G⁡[S])≤θ−1\Delta(G[S])\leq\theta-1, proving equation (135).

Every graph with maximum degree at most θ−1\theta-1 contains an independent set of size at least a 1/θ1/\theta fraction of its vertices. Hence dissθ−1⁡(G)≤θ​α​(G)\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G)\leq\theta\alpha(G). Write r=dissθ−1⁡(G)r=\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G). If r≤n/2r\leq n/2, Theorem 4.3.1 gives Rall∗≥c/rR^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\geq c/r. If r>n/2r>n/2, write πilo,πihi\pi_{i}^{\rm lo},\pi_{i}^{\rm hi} for the two exposure probabilities under any design PP. Since the two exposures are mutually exclusive, equation (16) gives

Rall​(P,f,aθ)≥1n2​∑i=1n(2−πilo−πihi)≥1n≥12​r.R_{\mathrm{all}}(P;f,a_{\theta})\geq\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(2-\pi_{i}^{\rm lo}-\pi_{i}^{\rm hi})\geq\frac{1}{n}\geq\frac{1}{2r}.

Taking the infimum over designs and using r≤θ​α​(G)r\leq\theta\alpha(G) proves equation (136). ∎

F.7.1.1 Reduction to low-arm sampling.

The lower bound in Theorem F.7.7 is proved through a sampling problem that keeps only the low arm. For a law QQ on ℒθ​(G)\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(G) and an estimator μ^\widehat{\mu} of the finite population mean from the sampled units and their values, define

𝖲θ​(G)=infQinfμ^supx∈[−1,1]V𝔼S∼Q​[{μ^​(S,xS)−1n​∑i=1nxi}2].\mathsf{S}_{\theta}(G)=\inf_{Q}\ \inf_{\widehat{\mu}}\ \sup_{x\in[-1,1]^{V}}\ \mathbb{E}_{S\sim Q}\left[\left\{\widehat{\mu}(S,x_{S})-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right\}^{2}\right]. (137)
Lemma F.7.3 (The contrast dominates low-arm sampling).

For every graph GG and threshold θ≥1\theta\geq 1 for which both target exposures are attainable at every unit, Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aθ)≥𝖲θ​(G)R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\geq\mathsf{S}_{\theta}(G).

For such tables τθ(Y)=−1n∑ixi\tau_{\theta}(Y)=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}x_{i}, and under an assignment zz the realized outcome vector is determined by zz together with xL0​(z)x_{L_{0}(z)}, the remaining observed entries being known constants. A design PP therefore induces a law QQ on ℒθ​(G)\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(G). Write S=L0​(Z)S=L_{0}(Z) for the sampled unit set. On the restricted tables, the observed data are (Z,YOf​(Z))=(Z,hZ​(xS))(Z,Y_{O_{f}(Z)})=(Z,h_{Z}(x_{S})), where hzh_{z} places the sampled values in their low-arm coordinates and fills every other observed coordinate with zero. For a contrast estimator TT and a sample SS with Q⁡(S)>0Q(S)>0, define

μ^(S,xS)=−∑z:L0​(z)=SP⁡(Z=z)>0P(Z=z∣L0(Z)=S)T(z,hz(xS)).\widehat{\mu}(S,x_{S})=-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}z:L_{0}(z)=S\\ P(Z=z)>0\end{subarray}}P(Z=z\mid L_{0}(Z)=S)\,T(z,h_{z}(x_{S})).

Conditional averaging therefore gives a sampling estimator with no larger squared-error risk. Conversely, any estimator of the sampled mean gives a contrast estimator by applying it to L0​(z)L_{0}(z) and changing its sign. Thus, for fixed PP, the restricted minimax risk equals the sampling risk under its induced QQ. Taking the infimum over all laws QQ gives the claimed lower bound. ∎

F.7.2 Packing lower bound on regular graphs

For the packing lower bound, fix a law QQ on ℒθ​(G)\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(G), write πv=Q⁡(v∈S)\pi_{v}=Q(v\in S), and let 𝖲θ​(G,Q)\mathsf{S}_{\theta}(G;Q) denote the infimum over sampling estimators in equation (137) with QQ fixed. We use Theorem 4.1.2(i) in the following form. If A1,…,Am⊆VA_{1},\ldots,A_{m}\subseteq V are disjoint sets of common size ℓ\ell, take the potential outcome packing whose bbth block is Bb={(i,blo):i∈Ab}B_{b}=\{(i,b_{\rm lo}):i\in A_{b}\}, with coefficient cb=ℓ/nc_{b}=\ell/n. The observed set meets BbB_{b} exactly when Ab∩S≠∅A_{b}\cap S\neq\varnothing, so equation (14) reads

𝖲θ​(G,Q)≥(ℓn)2​∑b=1mQ⁡(Ab∩S=∅).\mathsf{S}_{\theta}(G;Q)\geq\left(\frac{\ell}{n}\right)^{2}\sum_{b=1}^{m}Q(A_{b}\cap S=\varnothing). (138)

We choose the blocks according to the low-arm inclusion probabilities.

Lemma F.7.4 (Blocks in a low-inclusion level set).

Let s∈(0,1/4]s\in(0,1/4], Vs={v:πv≤s}V_{s}=\{v:\pi_{v}\leq s\}, and ℓ′=⌈1/(2​s)⌉\ell^{\prime}=\lceil 1/(2s)\rceil. If |Vs|≥n/2|V_{s}|\geq n/2 and n≥4​ℓ′n\geq 4\ell^{\prime}, then 𝖲θ​(G,Q)≥ℓ′/(16​n)\mathsf{S}_{\theta}(G;Q)\geq\ell^{\prime}/(16n).

For any such block, Q⁡(A∩S≠∅)≤∑i∈Aπi≤ℓ′​s≤12+s≤34Q(A\cap S\neq\varnothing)\leq\sum_{i\in A}\pi_{i}\leq\ell^{\prime}s\leq\frac{1}{2}+s\leq\frac{3}{4}, so Q⁡(A∩S=∅)≥14Q(A\cap S=\varnothing)\geq\frac{1}{4}. Now use equation (138). ∎

Lemma F.7.5 (Blocks inside a neighborhood).

Let GG be any graph, let v∈Vv\in V, let F⊆NvF\subseteq N_{v}, and let 1≤ℓ≤|F|/(2​θ)1\leq\ell\leq|F|/(2\theta). Then some A⊆FA\subseteq F with |A|=ℓ|A|=\ell satisfies Q⁡(A∩S=∅)≥πv/2Q(A\cap S=\varnothing)\geq\pi_{v}/2.

The neighborhood-block construction uses the constraint that vv and any θ\theta of its neighbors cannot all attain the low arm. For θ≥2\theta\geq 2, every pair of potential outcomes within such a set can be jointly observed.

Lemma F.7.6 (Packing neighborhood blocks).

Let GG be dd-regular, W⊆VW\subseteq V, and 1≤ℓ≤d/21\leq\ell\leq d/2. There are units v1,…,vm∈Wv_{1},\ldots,v_{m}\in W and pairwise disjoint sets AvbA_{v_{b}} of size ℓ\ell with Avb⊆Nvb∖⋃b′<bAvb′A_{v_{b}}\subseteq N_{v_{b}}\setminus\bigcup_{b^{\prime}<b}A_{v_{b^{\prime}}}, each drawn from a free part of NvbN_{v_{b}} of size at least d/2d/2, and m≥|W|/(2​ℓ)m\geq|W|/(2\ell). Centers may repeat; the selected blocks do not. At each step any ℓ\ell-subset of the free neighborhood may be chosen.

Choose the blocks greedily. Writing BB for the union of the blocks chosen so far, call vv available if |Nv∩B|≤d/2|N_{v}\cap B|\leq d/2. This is the only step of the argument that uses regularity. Since GG is dd-regular, ∑v∈V|Nv∩B|=d​|B|\sum_{v\in V}|N_{v}\cap B|=d|B|, so at most 2​|B|2|B| units of VV fail to be available. Hence while 2​|B|<|W|2|B|<|W| some v∈Wv\in W is available, and Nv∖BN_{v}\setminus B has at least d/2≥ℓd/2\geq\ell elements, so another block can be added. The process stops only once m​ℓ=|B|≥|W|/2m\ell=|B|\geq|W|/2. ∎

Remark F.3 (The probability-based packing bounds).

Fix a design and write πv\pi_{v} for the probability that unit vv attains the low arm. We use two block packings: one for units with small πv\pi_{v} and one for units with large πv\pi_{v}. Where πv\pi_{v} is small, a block of about 1/πv1/\pi_{v} units is missed with constant probability by the union bound. Where πv\pi_{v} is large, take the block inside the neighborhood NvN_{v} instead: attaining the low arm at vv forces at most θ−1\theta-1 treated neighbors, so a block of ℓ≤d/(4​θ)\ell\leq d/(4\theta) units drawn from NvN_{v} misses the sampled low-arm set with probability at least πv/2\pi_{v}/2. Blocks of this second kind can be packed disjointly because ℓ\ell is a small fraction of dd. The low-inclusion packing gives 1/(π​n)1/(\pi n) and the neighborhood packing gives d​π/nd\pi/n; they cross at π≍d−1/2\pi\asymp d^{-1/2}, giving the d/n\sqrt{d}/n term in equation (139). The separate rank bound gives 1/dissθ−1⁡(G)1/\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G).

Theorem F.7.7 (Lower bound on every regular graph).

Fix θ≥1\theta\geq 1. Let GG be dd-regular on nn units with d≥16​θd\geq 16\theta and n≥4​dn\geq 4\sqrt{d}. Then

Set s=t=d−1/2s=t=d^{-1/2}, and split VV into Vs={v:πv≤s}V_{s}=\{v:\pi_{v}\leq s\} and Wt={v:πv>t}W_{t}=\{v:\pi_{v}>t\}. One of the two has at least n/2n/2 elements. Note s≤1/4s\leq 1/4 because d≥16d\geq 16.

𝖲θ​(G,Q)≥(ℓn)2​|Wt|2​ℓ​t2=ℓ​t​|Wt|4​n2≥(d/8θ)d−1/2(n/2)4​n2=d64​θ​n.\mathsf{S}_{\theta}(G;Q)\geq\left(\frac{\ell}{n}\right)^{2}\frac{|W_{t}|}{2\ell}\frac{t}{2}=\frac{\ell\,t\,|W_{t}|}{4n^{2}}\geq\frac{(d/8\theta)\,d^{-1/2}\,(n/2)}{4n^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{d}}{64\,\theta\,n}.

F.7.3 Bernoulli upper bound

πlo=pPr{Bin(d,p)≤θ−1},πhi=pPr{Bin(d,p)≥θ}.\pi^{\rm lo}=p\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(d,p)\leq\theta-1\},\qquad\pi^{\rm hi}=p\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(d,p)\geq\theta\}.

Theorem 8.3.1 (Threshold-contrast bounds on regular graphs).

Fix θ≥1\theta\geq 1. Let GG be dd-regular on nn units, with d≥16​θd\geq 16\theta and n≥4​dn\geq 4\sqrt{d}. Then

cθ​max⁡{1dissθ−1⁡(G),dn}≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aθ)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aθ)≤Cθ​dn.c_{\theta}\max\left\{\frac{1}{\operatorname{diss}_{\theta-1}(G)},\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n}\right\}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\leq C_{\theta}\frac{d}{n}.

Combine Theorems F.7.7 and F.7.8. ∎

F.7.4 Pairwise conflicts and community examples

Lemma F.7.9 (Pairwise projection for threshold contagion).

For the treated-low threshold arm in equation (41), the induced conflict subgraph on that arm is GG when θ=1\theta=1 and is edgeless when θ≥2\theta\geq 2. Moreover, if θ≥2\theta\geq 2 and every distinct pair i,ji,j has at least θ\theta neighbors of ii outside Nj∪{j}N_{j}\cup\{j\}, then the induced conflict graph on the potential outcomes in the two arms blo,bhib_{\rm lo},b_{\rm hi} has only the same-unit high/low conflicts. A sufficient condition is girth at least five and d≥θ+1d\geq\theta+1 on a dd-regular graph.

For θ=1\theta=1, the low-arm potential outcomes of units ii and jj are jointly observable if and only if ii and jj are nonadjacent: both units must be treated, and adjacency would give each a treated neighbor. Hence the induced conflict graph on the low arm is GG.

For θ≥2\theta\geq 2, any two distinct low-arm potential outcomes are jointly observable by treating exactly those two units; each sees at most one treated neighbor. High-arm potential outcomes are jointly observable by the all-treated assignment. Finally, for a high-arm potential outcome of unit ii and a low-arm potential outcome of a distinct unit jj, treat ii, jj, and θ\theta neighbors of ii outside Nj∪{j}N_{j}\cup\{j\}. Then ii has at least θ\theta treated neighbors, while jj has at most one treated neighbor. The only remaining pairwise conflict is that the same unit cannot occupy both threshold arms. For the sufficient condition, girth at least five implies |Ni∩Nj|≤1|N_{i}\cap N_{j}|\leq 1 for nonadjacent i,ji,j and no shared neighbors for adjacent i,ji,j. At most one neighbor of ii therefore lies in Nj∪{j}N_{j}\cup\{j\}, leaving at least d−1≥θd-1\geq\theta available neighbors. ∎

Remark F.4 (Low-arm pairwise observability at θ=1\theta=1).

At θ=1\theta=1, observing the low arm requires the unit to be treated and all its neighbors to be controlled. A set of low-arm potential outcomes is therefore jointly observable exactly when its units form an independent set of GG. Thus the conflict graph records all low-arm sampling constraints, and r⁡(blo)=α⁡(G)r(b_{\rm lo})=\alpha(G).

Girth at least five and d≥θ+1d\geq\theta+1 give the pairwise-witness condition, so Lemma F.7.9 shows that the induced conflict graph on the two target arms consists of the nn same-unit pairs only. The same-unit conflicts give the 1/n1/n singleton lower bound, as in the proof of Lemma F.7.2. The neighborhood packing uses an additional joint observation constraint: a unit and θ\theta of its neighbors cannot all attain the low arm. Theorem F.7.7 instead gives the hypergraph-based lower bound cθ​d/nc_{\theta}\sqrt{d}/n, which is larger by a factor of order d\sqrt{d}. ∎

Theorem F.7.10 (Threshold-contrast rate for clique communities).

Let GG be the disjoint union of G0G_{0} cliques of size m=d+1m=d+1, so that n=G0​mn=G_{0}m, and let 1≤θ≤m−21\leq\theta\leq m-2. Then

Rall∗(𝒫(𝒵);f,aθ)≍θRunb∗(𝒫(𝒵);f,aθ)≍θdn.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\asymp_{\theta}R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\asymp_{\theta}\frac{d}{n}.

The independent clique design that assigns each clique either θ\theta or θ+1\theta+1 treated units attains the upper bound.

For the lower bound, restrict to the low arm. In a clique, if KK units are treated, every treated unit has K−1K-1 treated peers. Hence at most θ\theta low-arm potential outcomes can be observed in one clique, and this is attained by treating exactly θ\theta units. Across the G0G_{0} cliques,

r⁡(blo)=θ​G0=θ​nd+1.r(b_{\rm lo})=\theta G_{0}=\theta\frac{n}{d+1}.

If r⁡(blo)≤n/2r(b_{\rm lo})\leq n/2, the rank lower bound gives

Rall∗(𝒫(𝒵);f,aθ)≳θ1G0≍dn.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\gtrsim_{\theta}\frac{1}{G_{0}}\asymp\frac{d}{n}.

If r⁡(blo)>n/2r(b_{\rm lo})>n/2, then d+1<2​θd+1<2\theta. The same-unit high- and low-arm potential outcomes are mutually exclusive, so the all-estimator singleton lower bound in equation (16) gives Rall∗≥1/nR^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\geq 1/n. Since dd is then bounded by a constant depending only on θ\theta, this is again a lower bound of order d/nd/n.

For the upper bound, independently choose the number of treated units in each clique as θ\theta or θ+1\theta+1, each with probability 1/21/2, then sample uniformly with that number of treated units. A treated unit has the low exposure under the first choice and the high exposure under the second, so

qilo=θ2​m,qihi=θ+12​m.q_{i}^{\rm lo}=\frac{\theta}{2m},\qquad q_{i}^{\rm hi}=\frac{\theta+1}{2m}.

The exposure HT estimator is unbiased. Its contribution from one clique is either −2m/(nθ)-2m/(n\theta) times a sum of θ\theta bounded low-arm potential outcomes, or 2​m/[n⁡(θ+1)]2m/[n(\theta+1)] times a sum of θ+1\theta+1 bounded high-arm potential outcomes. Its absolute value is at most 2​m/n2m/n. Independence across cliques gives

supYVar⁡(τ^θ∣Y)≤G0​4​m2n2=4G0≍dn.\sup_{Y}\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\tau}_{\theta}\mid Y)\leq G_{0}\frac{4m^{2}}{n^{2}}=\frac{4}{G_{0}}\asymp\frac{d}{n}.

Since Rall∗≤Runb∗R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}, the theorem follows. ∎

Proposition F.7.11 (Complete bipartite communities).

Let GG be the disjoint union of n/(2​d)n/(2d) copies of Kd,dK_{d,d} and fix 1≤θ≤d−11\leq\theta\leq d-1. For the threshold contrast equation (41),

Rall∗(𝒫(𝒵);f,aθ)≍θRunb∗(𝒫(𝒵);f,aθ)≍θdn.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\asymp_{\theta}R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\asymp_{\theta}\frac{d}{n}.

Index the components by gg and write Lg,RgL_{g},R_{g} for the two sides of the ggth copy of Kd,dK_{d,d}, so there are 2​n/(2​d)=n/d2n/(2d)=n/d sides in all, each of size dd.

For the lower bound, fix a side, say LgL_{g}, and pair its two arm blocks

Bglo={(i,blo):i∈Lg},Bghi={(i,bhi):i∈Lg},B_{g}^{\rm lo}=\{(i,b_{\rm lo}):i\in L_{g}\},\qquad B_{g}^{\rm hi}=\{(i,b_{\rm hi}):i\in L_{g}\},

with coefficients −d/n-d/n and d/nd/n. If XR≤θ−1X_{R}\leq\theta-1 they all attain blob_{\rm lo}; if XR≥θX_{R}\geq\theta they all attain bhib_{\rm hi}. No assignment therefore meets both blocks, so qP​(Bglo)+qP​(Bghi)≤1q_{P}(B_{g}^{\rm lo})+q_{P}(B_{g}^{\rm hi})\leq 1.

Repeat this construction for both sides of every component. The resulting m=n/dm=n/d paired perturbation sets are pairwise disjoint, and each has per-arm weight wb=d/nw_{b}=d/n. The common number of treated neighbors on each side shows that no feasible assignment resolves a pair, so their resolution capacity is ℳ=0\mathcal{M}=0. Part (i) of Theorem B.6.4 therefore gives

Rall∗​(𝒫⁡(𝒵),f,aθ)≥∑b=1n/d(dn)2=dn.R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z});f,a_{\theta})\geq\sum_{b=1}^{n/d}\left(\frac{d}{n}\right)^{2}=\frac{d}{n}.

For the upper bound, use a design that observes whole side-arm blocks. In each component independently pick one of the four blocks Bg,Llo,Bg,Lhi,Bg,Rlo,Bg,RhiB_{g,L}^{\rm lo},B_{g,L}^{\rm hi},B_{g,R}^{\rm lo},B_{g,R}^{\rm hi} with probability 1/41/4 and assign treatment so that it is observed: treat all of LgL_{g} together with θ−1\theta-1 units of RgR_{g} to observe Bg,LloB_{g,L}^{\rm lo}, with θ\theta units of RgR_{g} to observe Bg,LhiB_{g,L}^{\rm hi}, and symmetrically for RgR_{g}. Every target potential outcome has exposure probability at least 1/41/4, because selecting its own block reveals that outcome. The outcome may also be revealed when another block is selected. Use each target outcome’s full exposure probability in the exposure HT estimator. The HT contribution from one component is bounded in absolute value by 8​d/n8d/n, and the component contributions are independent. Hence the variance of the HT estimator is at most a constant times

n2​d​(dn)2=O⁡(d/n).\frac{n}{2d}\left(\frac{d}{n}\right)^{2}=O(d/n).

Since Rall∗≤Runb∗R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}, the two bounds match. ∎

G Supporting results for Section 9

We prove the shared-pool bounds in Theorem 9.1, then the conflict-graph comparison in Corollary 9.2.

G.1 Proofs for the shared-pool bipartite example

The lower bound limits the number of target potential outcomes observed under any assignment. For the fixed-count upper bound, we first bound the exposure probabilities, then the covariance operator that controls HT variance.

Fix the setting of Theorem 9.1. Throughout this subsection, 0<k′<k<d0<k^{\prime}<k<d, Δ=k−k′\Delta=k-k^{\prime},

s=min⁡{k,d−k}+1,Δ≤c0​s,s=\sqrt{\min\{k,d-k\}+1},\qquad\Delta\leq c_{0}s,

and tt is a nearest integer to M⁡(k+k′)/(2​d)M(k+k^{\prime})/(2d). Put p=t/Mp=t/M,

b⁡(j,d,p)=(dj)​pj​(1−p)d−j,qk=max0≤x≤1⁡b⁡(k,d,x)=b⁡(k,d,k/d),σ2=d​p​(1−p).b(j;d,p)=\binom{d}{j}p^{j}(1-p)^{d-j},\qquad q_{k}=\max_{0\leq x\leq 1}b(k;d,x)=b(k;d,k/d),\qquad\sigma^{2}=dp(1-p).

Unless stated otherwise, constants depend only on c0c_{0} and on the fixed comparison constants in M≍n/sM\asymp n/s.

G.1.1 Binomial probabilities near the target doses

b(j;d,p)≍{dj⁡(d−j)}1/2exp{−dD(x∥p)},D(x∥p)=xlogxp+(1−x)log1−x1−p,b(j;d,p)\asymp\left\{\frac{d}{j(d-j)}\right\}^{1/2}\exp\{-d\,D(x\|p)\},\qquad D(x\|p)=x\log\frac{x}{p}+(1-x)\log\frac{1-x}{1-p}, (141)

G.1.2 The capacity lower bound

Lemma G.1.2 (Shared-pool lower bound).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 9.1, define

𝒥k=maxT⊆U⁡#⁡{v:|Av∩T|=k}.\mathcal{J}_{k}=\max_{T\subseteq U}\#\{v:|A_{v}\cap T|=k\}.

where (a)r=a(a−1)⋯(a−r+1)(a)_{r}=a(a-1)\cdots(a-r+1) and d2≤Md^{2}\leq M bounds Md/(M)d≤exp⁡(2​d2/M)≤e2M^{d}/(M)_{d}\leq\exp(2d^{2}/M)\leq e^{2}. For u=0u=0 or MM, the mass is zero because 0<k<d0<k<d. Writing XT=#⁡{v:|Av∩T|=k}X_{T}=\#\{v:|A_{v}\cap T|=k\}, independence gives

𝔼​eXT={1+(e−1)​Pr⁡(|Av∩T|=k)}n≤exp⁡(C​n​qk).\mathbb{E}e^{X_{T}}=\{1+(e-1)\Pr(|A_{v}\cap T|=k)\}^{n}\leq\exp(Cnq_{k}).

Markov’s inequality applied to eXTe^{X_{T}} therefore gives

Pr{XT>Cnqk+x}≤e−x.\Pr\{X_{T}>Cnq_{k}+x\}\leq e^{-x}.

Take x=M​log⁡2+2​log⁡nx=M\log 2+2\log n and sum over the 2M2^{M} assignments. With probability at least 1−n−21-n^{-2},

Fix a graph satisfying the bound on 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k}. For j∈{k,k′}j\in\{k,k^{\prime}\}, let Nj​(T)=#⁡{v:|Av∩T|=j}N_{j}(T)=\#\{v:|A_{v}\cap T|=j\} and define

K0=maxT⊆U⁡min⁡{Nk​(T),Nk′​(T)}.K_{0}=\max_{T\subseteq U}\min\{N_{k}(T),N_{k^{\prime}}(T)\}.

Since the doses are distinct, K0≤n/2K_{0}\leq n/2; also K0≤𝒥kK_{0}\leq\mathcal{J}_{k}. If K0≥1K_{0}\geq 1, partition VV into 2​K02K_{0} groups WbW_{b}, each of size at least ⌊n/(2​K0)⌋≥n/(4​K0)\lfloor n/(2K_{0})\rfloor\geq n/(4K_{0}). Pair the perturbation sets

Bb+={(v,k):v∈Wb},Bb−={(v,k′):v∈Wb},B_{b}^{+}=\{(v,k):v\in W_{b}\},\qquad B_{b}^{-}=\{(v,k^{\prime}):v\in W_{b}\},

G.1.3 The fixed-count upper bound

Condition on the realized graph and draw a uniform tt-subset of treatment units. We first bound the two exposure probabilities. The covariance calculation then gives a variance bound uniform over bounded potential outcome tables.

Lemma G.1.3 (Exposure probabilities under the fixed-count design).

Suppose M≥16M\geq 16 and 3≤d≤M3\leq d\leq\sqrt{M}, and let TT be a uniform tt-subset of UU. For every dd-set AA,

πj=Pr{|A∩T|=j}=(tj)​(M−td−j)(Md),j∈{k,k′},\pi_{j}=\Pr\{|A\cap T|=j\}=\frac{\binom{t}{j}\binom{M-t}{d-j}}{\binom{M}{d}},\qquad j\in\{k,k^{\prime}\},

and c​qk≤πj≤C​qkcq_{k}\leq\pi_{j}\leq Cq_{k}.

πjb⁡(j,d,p)=(t)jtj​(M−t)d−j(M−t)d−j​Md(M)d,\frac{\pi_{j}}{b(j;d,p)}=\frac{(t)_{j}}{t^{j}}\,\frac{(M-t)_{d-j}}{(M-t)^{d-j}}\,\frac{M^{d}}{(M)_{d}},

The first two factors are at most one, and the last lies between one and exp⁡(2​d2/M)≤e2\exp(2d^{2}/M)\leq e^{2}. To bound the first two factors below, note that M≥d2M\geq d^{2}, k′≥1k^{\prime}\geq 1, and k≤d−1k\leq d-1 give

t≥M⁡(k+k′)2​d−12≥d⁡(k+1)2−12≥d​k2,t\geq\frac{M(k+k^{\prime})}{2d}-\frac{1}{2}\geq\frac{d(k+1)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\geq\frac{dk}{2},

and

M−t≥M⁡(2​d−k−k′)2​d−12≥d⁡(d−k′+1)2−12≥d⁡(d−k′)2.M-t\geq\frac{M(2d-k-k^{\prime})}{2d}-\frac{1}{2}\geq\frac{d(d-k^{\prime}+1)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\geq\frac{d(d-k^{\prime})}{2}.

Thus, for either (a,r)=(t,j)(a,r)=(t,j) or (M−t,d−j)(M-t,d-j),

ra≤2d≤23,r2a≤2.\frac{r}{a}\leq\frac{2}{d}\leq\frac{2}{3},\qquad\frac{r^{2}}{a}\leq 2.

Both falling products are positive. Using log⁡(1−x)≥−3​x\log(1-x)\geq-3x for 0≤x≤2/30\leq x\leq 2/3 gives

log⁡(a)rar=∑h=0r−1log⁡(1−h/a)≥−3​r​(r−1)2​a≥−3.\log\frac{(a)_{r}}{a^{r}}=\sum_{h=0}^{r-1}\log(1-h/a)\geq-\frac{3r(r-1)}{2a}\geq-3.

Both factors are therefore at least e−3e^{-3}, so the ratio πj/b⁡(j,d,p)\pi_{j}/b(j;d,p) is bounded above and below by positive universal constants. Lemma G.1.1 now gives πj≍qk\pi_{j}\asymp q_{k}. ∎

Covariance operators.

For a fixed dose jj, the HT error for its arm mean is an outcome-weighted sum of centered observation indicators. We regard each centered indicator as a function of the random treatment set TT. The next lemma bounds the covariance operator obtained by averaging over a random neighborhood; Lemma G.1.5 transfers the bound to the nn neighborhoods in the realized graph.

Lemma G.1.4 (Population covariance operator on a slice).

Let M≥16M\geq 16, 2≤d≤M2\leq d\leq\sqrt{M}, and 0<t<M0<t<M. Fix a dose jj with πj=PrT⁡(|A∩T|=j)∈(0,1)\pi_{j}=\Pr_{T}(|A\cap T|=j)\in(0,1) for any fixed dd-set AA. On the space of real functions of uniform tt-subsets, use the inner product ⟨h1,h2⟩=𝔼T​[h1​(T)​h2​(T)]\langle h_{1},h_{2}\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{T}[h_{1}(T)h_{2}(T)] and define

gA​(T)=𝟏{|A∩T|=j}πj−1,Lj=‖gA‖22=πj−1−1,Σj=𝔼A​[gA⊗gA],g_{A}(T)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{|A\cap T|=j\}}{\pi_{j}}-1,\qquad L_{j}=\|g_{A}\|_{2}^{2}=\pi_{j}^{-1}-1,\qquad\Sigma_{j}=\mathbb{E}_{A}[g_{A}\otimes g_{A}],

where AA is a uniform dd-subset and (g⊗g)​h=⟨g,h⟩​g(g\otimes g)h=\langle g,h\rangle g. Then, with p=t/Mp=t/M,

‖Σj‖op≤max⁡{(j−d​p)2d⁡(M−d)​p​(1−p),Lj(M2)−M}.\|\Sigma_{j}\|_{\rm op}\leq\max\left\{\frac{(j-dp)^{2}}{d(M-d)p(1-p)},\ \frac{L_{j}}{\binom{M}{2}-M}\right\}. (143)

Under Lemma G.1.3, for j∈{k,k′}j\in\{k,k^{\prime}\},

‖Σj‖op≤C⁡{Δ2s2​M+sM2}≤CM,Lj≤C​s.\|\Sigma_{j}\|_{\rm op}\leq C\left\{\frac{\Delta^{2}}{s^{2}M}+\frac{s}{M^{2}}\right\}\leq\frac{C}{M},\qquad L_{j}\leq Cs.

Let FF map functions of uniform dd-subsets to functions of uniform tt-subsets by

(F​h)​(T)=𝔼A​[gA​(T)​h​(A)],(F∗​h)​(A)=𝔼T​[gA​(T)​h​(T)].(Fh)(T)=\mathbb{E}_{A}[g_{A}(T)h(A)],\qquad(F^{*}h)(A)=\mathbb{E}_{T}[g_{A}(T)h(T)].

Then F​F∗=ΣjFF^{*}=\Sigma_{j}, while F∗​FF^{*}F has kernel K⁡(A,B)=⟨gA,gB⟩K(A,B)=\langle g_{A},g_{B}\rangle. These two operators have the same nonzero eigenvalues. The kernel depends only on |A∩B||A\cap B|, so it belongs to the Johnson association scheme. Its orthogonal degree spaces have dimensions

Dr=(Mr)−(Mr−1),0≤r≤d,D_{r}=\binom{M}{r}-\binom{M}{r-1},\qquad 0\leq r\leq d,

and the operator is scalar on each such space (Filmus, 2016, Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.3). Since 𝔼A​gA​(T)=0\mathbb{E}_{A}g_{A}(T)=0 for every fixed-size TT, the degree-zero eigenvalue is zero. Writing λr\lambda_{r} for the eigenvalue on degree rr, positivity and the trace identity give

λr≥0,∑r=1dDr​λr=𝔼A​‖gA‖22=Lj.\lambda_{r}\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{r=1}^{d}D_{r}\lambda_{r}=\mathbb{E}_{A}\|g_{A}\|_{2}^{2}=L_{j}.

For 2≤r≤d≤M2\leq r\leq d\leq\sqrt{M}, Dr≥D2=(M2)−MD_{r}\geq D_{2}=\binom{M}{2}-M. Indeed Dr+1/Dr=(M−2​r−1)​(M−r+1)/{(r+1)​(M−2​r+1)}≥1D_{r+1}/D_{r}=(M-2r-1)(M-r+1)/\{(r+1)(M-2r+1)\}\geq 1 through the needed range. Thus every eigenvalue of degree at least two is at most Lj/D2L_{j}/D_{2}.

To compute the degree-one eigenvalue, put xu(A)=𝟏{u∈A}−d/Mx_{u}(A)=\mathbf{1}\{u\in A\}-d/M. For fixed TT, conditional on |A∩T|=j|A\cap T|=j, the inclusion probability of uu in AA is j/tj/t when u∈Tu\in T and (d−j)/(M−t)(d-j)/(M-t) otherwise. Thus

𝔼A[gA(T)xu(A)]=j−d​pM​p​(1−p)(𝟏{u∈T}−p).\mathbb{E}_{A}[g_{A}(T)x_{u}(A)]=\frac{j-dp}{Mp(1-p)}(\mathbf{1}\{u\in T\}-p).

For fixed AA, conditional on dose jj, the treatment probability of uu is j/dj/d when u∈Au\in A and (t−j)/(M−d)(t-j)/(M-d) otherwise. Hence

𝔼T[gA(T)(𝟏{u∈T}−p)]=(j−d​p)​Md⁡(M−d)xu(A).\mathbb{E}_{T}[g_{A}(T)(\mathbf{1}\{u\in T\}-p)]=\frac{(j-dp)M}{d(M-d)}x_{u}(A).

Composing these identities gives

(F∗​F)​xu=λ1​xu,λ1=(j−d​p)2d⁡(M−d)​p​(1−p).(F^{*}F)x_{u}=\lambda_{1}x_{u},\qquad\lambda_{1}=\frac{(j-dp)^{2}}{d(M-d)p(1-p)}.

The functions xux_{u} span the degree-one space. Combining this eigenvalue with the bound λr≤Lj/D2\lambda_{r}\leq L_{j}/D_{2} for r≥2r\geq 2 proves equation (143). For j∈{k,k′}j\in\{k,k^{\prime}\}, Lemma G.1.1 gives |j−d​p|≤Δ|j-dp|\leq\Delta and d​p​(1−p)=σ2≍s2dp(1-p)=\sigma^{2}\asymp s^{2}, so the degree-one eigenvalue is at most C​Δ2/(s2​M)≤C​c02/MC\Delta^{2}/(s^{2}M)\leq Cc_{0}^{2}/M. Lemma G.1.3 gives Lj≤C/qk≤C​sL_{j}\leq C/q_{k}\leq Cs, so the remaining eigenvalues are at most C​s/M2≤C/MCs/M^{2}\leq C/M, since s≤d≤Ms\leq\sqrt{d}\leq M. ∎

Lemma G.1.5 (Sampling the covariance operator).

Let g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} be independent vectors in a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space with ‖gv‖2=L>0\|g_{v}\|^{2}=L>0 and a common second-moment operator Σ=𝔼⁡[gv⊗gv]\Sigma=\mathbb{E}[g_{v}\otimes g_{v}] for every vv, where ‖Σ‖op≤γ\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}\leq\gamma and γ>0\gamma>0. For 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1, with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon,

‖1n​∑vgv⊗gv‖op≤C⁡{γ+Ln​log⁡8​(1+L/γ)ε}.\left\|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v}g_{v}\otimes g_{v}\right\|_{\rm op}\leq C\left\{\gamma+\frac{L}{n}\log\frac{8(1+L/\gamma)}{\varepsilon}\right\}. (144)

Write Xv=gv⊗gvX_{v}=g_{v}\otimes g_{v}. Then λmax​(Xv−Σ)≤L\lambda_{\max}(X_{v}-\Sigma)\leq L and 𝔼​(Xv−Σ)2=L​Σ−Σ2⪯L​Σ\mathbb{E}(X_{v}-\Sigma)^{2}=L\Sigma-\Sigma^{2}\preceq L\Sigma. To apply matrix Bernstein with a variance bound of norm n​L​γnL\gamma, put

Zv=diag⁡(Xv−Σ,0),V=diag⁡(n​L​Σ,n​L​γ).Z_{v}=\operatorname{diag}(X_{v}-\Sigma,0),\qquad V=\operatorname{diag}(nL\Sigma,nL\gamma).

The ZvZ_{v} are independent and centered, λmax​(Zv)≤L\lambda_{\max}(Z_{v})\leq L, and

∑v𝔼​Zv2⪯V,‖V‖op=n​L​γ,tr⁡V‖V‖op=1+Lγ.\sum_{v}\mathbb{E}Z_{v}^{2}\preceq V,\qquad\|V\|_{\rm op}=nL\gamma,\qquad\frac{\operatorname{tr}V}{\|V\|_{\rm op}}=1+\frac{L}{\gamma}.

Set ℓ=log⁡{8​(1+L/γ)/ε}\ell=\log\{8(1+L/\gamma)/\varepsilon\}. The intrinsic-dimension matrix Bernstein inequality (Tropp, 2015, Theorem 7.7.1) gives, with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon,

λmax​(∑v(Xv−Σ))≤C⁡{n​L​γ​ℓ+L​ℓ}.\lambda_{\max}\left(\sum_{v}(X_{v}-\Sigma)\right)\leq C\{\sqrt{nL\gamma\ell}+L\ell\}.

The constant CC can be chosen so the deviation threshold also exceeds n​L​γ+L/3\sqrt{nL\gamma}+L/3, as required by that theorem. Divide by nn, add ‖Σ‖op≤γ\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}\leq\gamma, and use L​γ​ℓ/n≤(γ+L​ℓ/n)/2\sqrt{L\gamma\ell/n}\leq(\gamma+L\ell/n)/2 to obtain equation (144). ∎

Theorem 9.1 (Nearby interior doses on a shared pool).

Assume a uniform dd-out bipartite interference graph, with n≥3n\geq 3, M≥16M\geq 16, and 3≤d≤M3\leq d\leq\sqrt{M}. Let 0<k′<k<d0<k^{\prime}<k<d with k−k′≤c0​sk-k^{\prime}\leq c_{0}s for fixed c0c_{0}, and suppose M≍n/sM\asymp n/s. With probability at least 1−2/n21-2/n^{2} over the graph draw,

c​sn≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡({0,1}U),f,ak,k′)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡({0,1}U),f,ak,k′)≤C​s​log⁡nn.c\frac{s}{n}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\{0,1\}^{U});f,a_{k,k^{\prime}})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\{0,1\}^{U});f,a_{k,k^{\prime}})\leq C\frac{s\log n}{n}.

The constants depend only on c0c_{0} and the comparison constants in M≍n/sM\asymp n/s.

Lemma G.1.2 proves the lower bound with probability at least 1−n−21-n^{-2}. We prove the upper bound using the fixed-count design and exposure HT.

Fix 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1. For each j∈{k,k′}j\in\{k,k^{\prime}\}, apply Lemma G.1.5 to the functions gAvg_{A_{v}} of Lemma G.1.4. The neighborhoods AvA_{v} are independent, and these functions have common squared norm Lj≤C​sL_{j}\leq Cs and second-moment operator Σj\Sigma_{j} with ‖Σj‖op≤C/M\|\Sigma_{j}\|_{\rm op}\leq C/M. Take γ=C/M\gamma=C/M and failure probability ε/2\varepsilon/2 for each arm. Since Lj/γ≤C​s​M≤C​M2L_{j}/\gamma\leq CsM\leq CM^{2}, equation (144) gives, simultaneously for both arms,

‖Hj‖op≤C⁡{1M+s​ℓεn},Hj=1n​∑vgAv⊗gAv,ℓε=log⁡8​Mε,\|H_{j}\|_{\rm op}\leq C\left\{\frac{1}{M}+\frac{s\ell_{\varepsilon}}{n}\right\},\qquad H_{j}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v}g_{A_{v}}\otimes g_{A_{v}},\qquad\ell_{\varepsilon}=\log\frac{8M}{\varepsilon}, (145)

with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon over the graph draw.

Condition on a graph satisfying equation (145). For dose jj, write yv=Yv​(j)y_{v}=Y_{v}(j) and define

Fj​y=1n​∑vyv​gAv.F_{j}y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{v}y_{v}g_{A_{v}}.

Then Fj​Fj∗=HjF_{j}F_{j}^{*}=H_{j}, so ‖Fj‖op2=‖Hj‖op\|F_{j}\|_{\rm op}^{2}=\|H_{j}\|_{\rm op}. The HT error for the dose-jj mean is the function n−1​∑vyv​gAv​(T)n^{-1}\sum_{v}y_{v}g_{A_{v}}(T). Its variance under the fixed-count design is

VarT⁡(1n​∑v𝟏{|Av∩T|=j}yvπj)=1n​‖Fj​y‖22≤‖y‖22n​‖Hj‖op≤‖Hj‖op,\operatorname{Var}_{T}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v}\frac{\mathbf{1}\{|A_{v}\cap T|=j\}y_{v}}{\pi_{j}}\right)=\frac{1}{n}\|F_{j}y\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{\|y\|_{2}^{2}}{n}\|H_{j}\|_{\rm op}\leq\|H_{j}\|_{\rm op}, (146)

since |yv|≤1|y_{v}|\leq 1. The contrast estimator is

τ^fix=1n​∑v{𝟏{|Av∩T|=k}πk−𝟏{|Av∩T|=k′}πk′}​Yvobs.\widehat{\tau}_{\rm fix}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v}\left\{\frac{\mathbf{1}\{|A_{v}\cap T|=k\}}{\pi_{k}}-\frac{\mathbf{1}\{|A_{v}\cap T|=k^{\prime}\}}{\pi_{k^{\prime}}}\right\}Y_{v}^{\rm obs}.

Lemma G.1.3 gives positive exposure probabilities, so the estimator is unbiased. The variance of the difference is at most twice the sum of the arm variances. Combining equations (145) and (146) therefore gives

supY∈𝒴⁡(f)VarT⁡(τ^fix∣Y)≤C⁡{1M+s​ℓεn}.\sup_{Y\in\mathcal{Y}(f)}\operatorname{Var}_{T}(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm fix}\mid Y)\leq C\left\{\frac{1}{M}+\frac{s\ell_{\varepsilon}}{n}\right\}.

The operator event depends on the graph, and the bound holds for every bounded outcome table on that graph.

Take ε=n−2\varepsilon=n^{-2}. Since M≍n/s≲nM\asymp n/s\lesssim n, ℓε=O⁡(log⁡n)\ell_{\varepsilon}=O(\log n) and 1/M≍s/n1/M\asymp s/n, yielding the upper bound C​s​log⁡n/nCs\log n/n. Intersecting the operator-concentration event with the lower-bound event from Lemma G.1.2 gives probability at least 1−2/n21-2/n^{2} and completes the proof. ∎

G.1.4 Comparison with the conflict graph

We first determine the pairwise conflicts, then compare the experiment that permits all independent sets of the conflict graph with the actual shared-pool experiment. Throughout this comparison, the graph is the induced conflict graph on the two target-dose arms, containing Yv​(k)Y_{v}(k) and Yv​(k′)Y_{v}(k^{\prime}) for each outcome unit vv.

Let A,BA,B be two dd-sets with |A∩B|=r|A\cap B|=r. To give AA dose kk and BB dose k′≤kk^{\prime}\leq k, an assignment must treat xx shared units, k−xk-x units of A∖BA\setminus B, and k′−xk^{\prime}-x units of B∖AB\setminus A. Such an assignment exists exactly when an integer xx satisfies

max⁡{0,k−d+r}≤x≤min⁡{k′,r}.\max\{0,k-d+r\}\leq x\leq\min\{k^{\prime},r\}. (147)

Since 0≤k′≤k≤d0\leq k^{\prime}\leq k\leq d, equation (147) is equivalent to k−k′≤d−rk-k^{\prime}\leq d-r. Thus any same-dose pair of potential outcomes is jointly observable. For adjacent doses, a cross-dose pair can be jointly observed exactly when r<dr<d, that is, when the neighborhoods are distinct. The two target potential outcomes of the same unit have a pairwise conflict because they require different doses in the same neighborhood.

Two independently drawn neighborhoods are identical with probability 1/(Md)1/\binom{M}{d}. A union bound therefore gives

Pr{Av≠Aw for all v≠w}≥1−n⁡(n−1)2​(Md).\Pr\{A_{v}\neq A_{w}\text{ for all }v\neq w\}\geq 1-\frac{n(n-1)}{2\binom{M}{d}}. (148)

On this event, this induced conflict graph is the matching formed by the nn same-unit pairs of target potential outcomes.

Consider the sampling experiment that permits every independent set of this matching. Independently for each unit, choose one of its two target potential outcomes with probability 1/21/2. The corresponding HT estimator is

τ^pair=2n∑v{𝟏{Jv=k}Yv(k)−𝟏{Jv=k′}Yv(k′)},\widehat{\tau}_{\rm pair}=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{v}\{\mathbf{1}\{J_{v}=k\}Y_{v}(k)-\mathbf{1}\{J_{v}=k^{\prime}\}Y_{v}(k^{\prime})\},

where JvJ_{v} is the sampled dose label. The estimator is unbiased and has variance at most 4/n4/n, since the unit contributions are independent and bounded in absolute value by 2/n2/n. For the lower bound, put independent Rademacher signs on all target potential outcomes. Every independent set leaves at least one sign unobserved per unit. Each missing sign contributes 1/n21/n^{2} to the posterior variance of the contrast, so the Bayes risk is at least 1/n1/n. Hence both minimax risks in this sampling experiment are of order 1/n1/n.

For the shared-pool experiment, apply Theorem 9.1 with Δ=1\Delta=1 and c0=1c_{0}=1. With probability at least

1−2n2−n⁡(n−1)2​(Md),1-\frac{2}{n^{2}}-\frac{n(n-1)}{2\binom{M}{d}},

the induced conflict graph on the two target-dose arms is a matching and the minimax risks satisfy

c​sn≤Rall∗​(𝒫⁡({0,1}U),f,ak,k′)≤Runb∗​(𝒫⁡({0,1}U),f,ak,k′)≤C​s​log⁡nn.c\frac{s}{n}\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{all}}(\mathcal{P}(\{0,1\}^{U});f,a_{k,k^{\prime}})\leq R^{*}_{\mathrm{unb}}(\mathcal{P}(\{0,1\}^{U});f,a_{k,k^{\prime}})\leq C\frac{s\log n}{n}.

The condition (Md)/n2→∞\binom{M}{d}/n^{2}\to\infty makes this probability tend to one. ∎
